Oxygen with three bonds and a plus still has lone pairs and a full octet; the carbon is the atom that is short, and the minor contributor placing the positive charge on it says so. Hunt for the deficient atom, not the symbol.

A resonance structure of an enone shows the C=C pi electrons shifting all the way to the very electronegative oxygen, leaving a positive charge on the beta carbon; this explains why nucleophiles can add either directly to the carbonyl carbon or to this more remote beta carbon (conjugate addition).

The two electronegative oxygens withdraw significant electron density from the central carbon, making it quite electrophilic; Grignard reagents readily attack this carbon to eventually form a carboxylic acid after workup.

A protonated carbonyl has two contributors: one with the plus on oxygen and every octet full, and one with the plus on carbon and only six electrons there. The second is minor but real, and its share of the hybrid is what deepens the carbon's positive character. That is why so many carbonyl reactions are run under acid.
The acidic C–H proton is the electrophilic site being attacked by the base's lone pair; the carbon framework itself is not what is directly attacked in this proton-transfer step.

Like halides, the oxygen in a sulfonate ester polarizes the attached carbon (making it electrophilic), and the resulting sulfonate anion is exceptionally stable (weak base) due to extensive resonance and charge delocalization, making it depart easily as a leaving group.

Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (by induction/hyperconjugation) and also physically block approach, so more substitution at a potentially electrophilic carbon generally reduces how strongly and how accessibly electrophilic it is (this is part of why more substituted carbonyls are less reactive toward nucleophiles).

Alkyl groups donate electron density to an adjacent positive charge, so a tertiary cation sits lower in energy than a primary one and the ionization that produces it is easier. Every carbocation remains a strong electrophile once formed; this comparison is about how readily they appear, not how hungry they are.

Even though the C–I bond is only modestly polarized, the weak, long C–I bond breaks easily and iodide is a very stable, weakly basic leaving group, so the overall reaction is fast even if carbon itself is not the most electron-poor among the halomethanes.
leaving-groups: Good leaving groups are stable as the departed anion/molecule — i.e., weak bases, since weak bases are comfortable holding the extra electron density.
Iodide is a large, very weak base — very stable once it leaves — making it an excellent leaving group, unlike OH⁻, NH₂⁻, or CH₃⁻ which are strong bases.

Nothing was wrong with the nucleophile: bromide is the same species in both flasks. The blocked step was the departure, because hydroxide (pKaH 15.7) will not leave a carbon. Protonation changes the departing species to neutral water (pKaH −1.7), and the reaction goes.
Good leaving groups are stable, weak bases, which are exactly the conjugate bases of strong acids (like HI, HBr, or TsOH); weak bases hold their extra electron pair loosely and leave readily.

TsCl with pyridine converts the alcohol to a tosylate under mild, neutral conditions. Sulfuric acid also activates the OH, by protonation, but every acid-sensitive group in the molecule then has to survive it; the other two reagents do nothing useful here at all.

Leaving group ability tracks with anion stability (weak basicity); I- is the weakest base of the three halides and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group, followed by Br- then Cl-.

F- is a much stronger base than the other halide ions because its small size concentrates negative charge, making the C–F bond strong and fluoride reluctant to depart with the electron pair, unlike the larger, more stable, weaker-base halide ions.

The negative charge on a sulfonate leaving group is delocalized over multiple oxygens by resonance (and stabilized further by the electron-withdrawing sulfonyl group), making it a very weak base and thus an excellent, stable leaving group.
NH2- is the conjugate base of ammonia, an extremely weak acid, making amide ion an extremely strong base that holds on tightly to its electrons and essentially never leaves under normal conditions.

Once protonated, the group that leaves is neutral water rather than negatively charged hydroxide; water is a much weaker base (conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+) and leaves far more easily, which is why acid catalysis activates alcohols for substitution/elimination.

A carbanion like CH3- is an extraordinarily strong base (conjugate base of methane, an exceedingly weak acid) and essentially never acts as a leaving group under normal conditions, unlike halides or neutral water.

Delocalizing the negative charge over several atoms lowers the energy of the anion, making it more stable (a weaker base) and thus more willing to depart, which is exactly why sulfonate esters are popular synthetic leaving groups.

As a nucleophile attacks a ring carbon, the strained C–O bond breaks and the oxygen (now bearing the electron pair) becomes an alkoxide leaving group still attached elsewhere in the molecule, relieving ring strain.

Base strength measures how strongly a species wants to grab and hold a proton (or, analogously, electron density); weak bases are inherently stable on their own and 'happy' to leave with the bonding electron pair, which is the core reason leaving group ability and base strength are inversely related.
Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), meaning acetate is a much weaker base than ethoxide and therefore a considerably better leaving group.

Because the leaving group departs with the bonding electrons, its ability to stabilize that extra electron density (i.e., be a weak, stable base) directly controls how readily ionization occurs and therefore the rate of SN1/E1 reactions.

Sulfonate esters are prepared under mild, non-acidic conditions and then provide a highly stabilized, weak-base leaving group, giving chemists a practical alternative to strongly acidic activation of alcohols.

Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKaH 15.7, so it is a strong base and does not depart from carbon on its own. The missing piece is an activation step — protonate the OH, tosylate it, or convert it to a halide — and only then can something leave.

Tosylate's negative charge is spread over three oxygens and stabilized further by the adjacent aromatic sulfonyl group, making it one of the best common leaving groups, generally outperforming simple halides.

The amide anion ⁻NH₂ is far too strong a base to leave a carbon. Put a positive charge on the nitrogen first, by protonation or by alkylation to a quaternary ammonium, and the departing species is a neutral amine rather than an anion, which is a much cheaper thing to become.

Since leaving groups are conjugate bases, the pKa of their conjugate acid directly reflects base strength: a low pKa (strong acid) means a weak, stable conjugate base, and therefore a good leaving group.

A conjugate acid pKa of -7 corresponds to an extremely strong acid (such as HI), meaning its conjugate base is extremely weak and stable — exactly the profile of an excellent leaving group, far better than one with a conjugate acid pKa of 9.

HCN is only a moderately weak acid (pKa around 9), making cyanide a fairly strong base relative to halides or sulfonates, so it does not readily depart as a leaving group under typical substitution conditions.

Because strong bases/nucleophiles and good leaving groups are generally opposite ends of the same stability spectrum, a reactive carbanion (strong base) is a very poor leaving group — it simply does not want to depart and take the electron pair in an already-stable low-energy form elsewhere.

Protonation shifts the leaving species from hydroxide (conjugate base of water, pKa ≈ 15.7, a fairly strong base) to water itself (conjugate base of H3O+, pKa ≈ -1.7, a very weak base), dramatically improving its willingness to leave.

Bromide on its own cannot displace hydroxide, and deprotonating the alcohol makes the leaving group worse rather than better. PBr₃ converts the OH into a good leaving group and delivers bromide in the same operation, which is why it is the standard one-step route.

Like sulfonates and carboxylates, phosphate leaving groups spread their negative charge over several oxygen atoms via resonance, lowering their basicity and making them effective leaving groups despite the formal negative charge, which is central to many biochemical substitution reactions.

Hydroxide is a strong base and a poor leaving group, so it is clearly last. Tosylate and iodide are both conjugate bases of very strong acids and belong to the same top tier; measured substitution rates put tosylate marginally ahead of iodide, which is the order keyed here. Getting the tiers right matters more than the order inside one.

The three highly electronegative fluorine atoms further withdraw electron density and help delocalize/stabilize the negative charge on the departing sulfonate oxygen, making triflate an exceptionally weak base and outstanding leaving group, even better than a simple tosylate.

Since SN1 rate depends on how readily the substrate ionizes, a poor leaving group (strong base, high-energy anion) makes that ionization step slow or unfavorable, often requiring the substrate to be activated first (e.g., protonation or conversion to a sulfonate) before substitution can proceed.
energy-diagrams: The vertical axis is free energy: higher on the page means less stable. Time and concentration do not appear on this diagram at all, which is why it can describe a reaction without saying how long anything takes.

A barrier is a climb. It starts at whatever the step begins from and ends at that step's maximum. For the first step of a mechanism that starting point is the reactants; for a later step it is the intermediate in front of it.

Exergonic means a negative overall free-energy change, so the products sit lower than the reactants. It is a statement about the two flat stretches and says nothing about the height of the hill between them.
Maxima are transition states and minima are ordinary species. This is the fastest way to tell the two apart, and it needs no chemical knowledge about what the species actually is.
A minimum is a real species with all its bonds made, which is what an intermediate is. Transition states sit at maxima, and an activation energy is a height rather than a point on the curve.
Each hump is one step, so three humps means three steps. The wells between consecutive humps are the intermediates, and three humps have two wells between them, giving two intermediates.

Rate depends on the barrier that has to be crossed, so the activation energy of the slow step is the number that governs it. The overall energy change and the equilibrium constant describe where the reaction ends up, not how quickly it gets there.

Anything at a maximum rolls off it immediately, so there is no well to hold it and no lifetime to speak of. An intermediate, by contrast, sits in a minimum and can sometimes be trapped or observed even when it is wildly reactive.

A catalyst offers a route over a lower hill and is regenerated afterwards, so the compounds at either end are unchanged and so are their energies. Every crossing still passes through some transition state; it is simply a cheaper one.

The reaction coordinate tracks the extent of bond making and bond breaking, which is why a molecule does not move along it at any particular speed. Reading it as a time axis is what produces the mistaken idea that a wider hill means a slower reaction.

Only the barrier enters a rate. B's 14 kcal/mol hill is crossed enormously more often than A's 35 kcal/mol hill, so B is faster by many orders of magnitude. A's large negative overall change means only that A ends up essentially complete, whenever it finally gets there.

Compare climbs, not altitudes. Step 1 climbs 20 from the reactants; step 2 starts at the intermediate already 12 up, so it climbs only 24 − 12 = 12. The taller peak belongs to the easier step, which is exactly the trap this arrangement is built to set.

The catalyst changes the height of the hill and leaves the two plateaus untouched, so the overall free-energy change and therefore the equilibrium constant are the same. Forward and reverse barriers both drop by the same amount, so the ratio holds and only the waiting time falls.

Temperature moves nothing on the diagram. Energy is distributed over a population, and heating fattens the high-energy tail of that distribution, so more collisions arrive with enough to cross an unchanged barrier. Treat the doubling as a rule of thumb, since the real factor depends on how large the barrier is.

About 1.4 kcal/mol corresponds to a factor of ten in K at 25 °C, so a gap of 2.8 kcal/mol between the two is two factors of ten. The relationship is logarithmic, which is why a difference that looks small in kcal/mol is large in K.

A transition state resembles whatever it is closest to in energy. For a downhill step the peak sits just above the starting materials and far above nothing else, so the structure there still looks like the reactants.

An endothermic step has a late, product-like transition state, so whatever stabilizes the product stabilizes the transition state by nearly as much and the barrier falls almost the full amount. In an exothermic step the peak resembles the reactants, which are identical for both routes, so the stability difference barely reaches the barrier. Temperature is not the lever here: with both steps irreversible the ratio is fixed by the two barriers, and raising the temperature shrinks the rate ratio rather than enlarging it. Heat favors the more stable product only when the steps are reversible and the mixture can equilibrate.

Molecules queue at the 22 kcal/mol hill and fall over the small one the moment they arrive, so nothing was waiting at the second step for the improvement to help. A chain is as slow as its slowest link, and this change speeds up a link that was never the bottleneck.

About 1.4 kcal/mol buys a factor of ten, so 2.8 kcal/mol buys two such factors. This is why differences of two or three kcal/mol between competing transition states routinely show up as one product and no detectable trace of the other.

The reverse reaction starts at the product plateau, 8 kcal/mol below the reactants, and climbs to the same peak. So it must climb 20 + 8 = 28. The general rule is that the reverse barrier equals the forward barrier minus the overall change.

Brackets and a double dagger label a transition state, and what identifies one on paper is partial bonding: dotted lines and partial charges. The other three are ordinary species with every bond fully made, so they belong in wells and are drawn without the brackets.

The two numbers are measured from different places on the same picture and are independent. Diamond converting to graphite is downhill and has never been observed, because nothing gets over the hill. A large release of energy predicts a favorable equilibrium and predicts nothing about the waiting time.

'Early' and 'late' describe position along the reaction coordinate, not clock time or altitude. An uphill step reaches its maximum close to its finish, which is why that structure resembles the product being formed.

The radical stability gap is about 5 kcal/mol for both halogens. Bromine's step is uphill, so its peak comes late and the radical is nearly formed there, putting almost all of that 5 kcal/mol into the barrier. Chlorine's step is downhill, its peak comes early, and at that point the radical barely exists.

Both directions cross the same peak, so lowering that peak subtracts the same amount from each climb. That symmetry is precisely why the equilibrium constant cannot move, and it is why a good catalyst for a hydrogenation is also a good catalyst for the corresponding dehydrogenation.

Step 1 climbs from 0 to 14, a barrier of 14. Step 2 climbs from the shallow well at +2 up to 18, a barrier of 16. The second climb is the larger one, so step 2 is rate-determining. Note that reading TS2's altitude of 18 as the barrier would give the right step for the wrong reason and the wrong number.

An uphill step has a late transition state, so at the peak the cation is largely formed and carries most of its eventual charge. Anything that stabilizes that cation therefore lowers the barrier by nearly as much, which is why a tertiary substrate ionizes so much faster than a primary one.

The products sit 6 kcal/mol above the reactants and share the same peak, so the reverse climb is 15 − 6 = 9. A smaller barrier means a faster crossing, and the reverse being faster is exactly what an unfavorable equilibrium looks like from the kinetic side.

With no way back, whatever forms first is trapped, so the product ratio simply mirrors the relative rates and the lower barrier wins. P2's greater stability would decide the outcome only if the system were free to revisit the intermediate and re-sort itself, which heat and reversibility allow.

The plateaus do not move, so the products remain 10 kcal/mol below the reactants and the reverse climb is the forward barrier plus 10. Uncatalyzed that is 25 + 10 = 35; catalyzed it is 18 + 10 = 28. Both directions gained the same 7 kcal/mol, which is why the equilibrium constant is untouched.
carbocations: Three bonds and no lone pair means three electron domains, which spread to 120° and make the carbon sp². That uses three of its four valence orbitals; the leftover unhybridized p orbital is empty and stands perpendicular to the plane of the bonds. A lone pair anywhere on that carbon would make it a carbanion instead.

The carbon has three bonds and nothing else, and three bonds hold six electrons between them. That is two short of an octet, and the shortfall is exactly why a carbocation is so reactive: it is looking for an electron pair.

Formal charge is valence electrons minus what the atom owns. Neutral carbon has four; here it owns no lone-pair electrons and one electron from each of three bonds, so 4 − (0 + 3) = +1. Running the same arithmetic on three bonds plus a lone pair gives 4 − 5 = −1, which is a carbanion.

Each alkyl group attached to the charged carbon brings C–H bonds that can align with the empty p orbital and donate into it. The tertiary cation has nine such bonds, the secondary six, the primary three and the methyl cation none, so the ordering is 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

Hyperconjugation is the partial sharing of a sigma bonding pair with a neighboring empty (or partly empty) orbital. It is distinct from resonance, which moves charge fully onto another atom through a π system, and from induction, which is electron density sliding along a sigma bond without any orbital overlap being the point.

Heterolytic loss of a leaving group is the standard route: the C–X bond breaks unevenly, the leaving group keeps both electrons, and the carbon is left with three bonds and the positive charge. The other common route is protonation of a π bond, which also leaves one carbon short of a bonding pair.

A benzylic cation spreads its charge over four carbons by resonance, which is worth roughly as much as the nine hyperconjugating bonds of a tertiary alkyl cation. That is the standard pairing to remember, and it is why a formally primary benzylic substrate behaves like a tertiary one.

The whole C–H bond moves: the hydrogen travels with both of its bonding electrons, which is why the arrow is drawn starting on the bond. Because the electrons go with it, the carbon it left behind is the one that ends up positive.

The unhybridized p orbital has one lobe above the plane and one below, and nothing occupies either. That symmetry is why a nucleophile arriving later has no reason to prefer a side, and it is the structural origin of racemization in mechanisms that pass through a free cation.

A carbon chain has a larger, looser electron cloud than a hydrogen atom, so it shifts electron density toward an adjacent positive charge more readily. It is a smaller effect than hyperconjugation and needs no particular alignment, and it never relocates the charge — it only smears it.

Solvolysis rate is the rate of forming the cation, so it tracks cation stability, not steric access. The tertiary substrate gives a cation with nine hyperconjugating C–H bonds; the primary one would give a cation with three and in practice does not ionize at all. Crowding matters for concerted backside attack, which is the opposite preference.

An oxygen lone pair on the charged carbon closes the gap completely, giving a second resonance structure with a C=O π bond and a complete octet on every atom. Positive oxygen is expensive, but a full octet everywhere beats six electrons on carbon. The tertiary cation is next, the primary one far behind, and the phenyl cation cannot form at all.

The ring holds that carbon at sp² and will not let it relax, so its vacancy is an in-plane sp² hybrid pointing outward while the six π electrons sit in p orbitals standing perpendicular to the plane. Orbitals at right angles cannot overlap. Contrast a benzylic cation, whose empty orbital is on a carbon outside the ring and lies parallel to the π system.

Counting what the carbon owns: two lone-pair electrons plus one from each of three bonds is five, against four valence electrons for neutral carbon, giving 4 − 5 = −1. A carbocation carbon owns nothing beyond its share of three bonds. The orbital that would hold a lone pair is precisely the one that must stay empty.

A 1,2-shift is not restricted to hydrogen. The neighboring quaternary carbon carries three methyls, and moving one across with its bonding pair leaves the charge on that carbon, which still holds two methyls and the new ethyl group — a tertiary cation from a primary one. A hydrogen two carbons out is unreachable, because only the immediate neighbor can migrate.

Curved arrows always start where the electrons currently are, and here the electrons in question are the pair inside the C–CH₃ bond that is about to move. Starting the arrow on the cation would mean electrons flowing out of an empty orbital, and a cationic carbon has no lone pair to start from.

The proton bonds to one alkene carbon using the π pair; the other carbon gets no share of that pair and becomes the cation. Since the barrier is lower for the route to the more stable cation, the proton adds so as to leave the charge on the more substituted carbon. The carbon that takes the proton is therefore the one that stays neutral.

Two problems stack. The cationic carbon relaxes to linear sp hybridization, and an sp orbital has fifty percent s character, which is the worst place to put a positive charge. And the empty p orbital ends up at right angles to the π bond beside it, so no overlap and no delocalization is possible. Vinyl halides are consequently inert to any mechanism that needs a cation.

The rule is comparative: a 1,2-shift happens when it would give a more stable cation. A shift to an equally stable cation has nothing driving it, so there is no reason to write it into a mechanism, and there is no basis for inventing a second shift to somewhere the substrate cannot reach.

A rearranged skeleton requires a species with a lifetime long enough for a 1,2-shift, which is exactly what an intermediate is. Clean inversion and a rate that depends on the nucleophile both point to a concerted step with no intermediate at all, and so does the polar aprotic preference.

This is the Hammond postulate applied to ionization. Breaking a bond into two charged fragments is strongly uphill, so the transition state lies late along the coordinate and looks like the cation it is becoming. Anything that lowers the cation's energy therefore lowers the barrier by nearly as much. Nothing about the second step is involved, because the first one is rate-determining.

The first is a vinyl cation, with the charge on a doubly bonded carbon whose empty orbital cannot reach the π bond beside it — it does not form at all. The allylic cation is the most stable of the group, the secondary cation next, and even the primary alkyl cation is far better than a vinyl one.

Oxygen does withdraw inductively, and on its own that would destabilize a neighboring positive charge. Resonance more than pays it back: a lone pair on the oxygen swings into the empty p orbital and gives a second structure, CH₃–O⁺=CH₂, an oxocarbenium ion in which the carbon has a full octet and so does the oxygen. Six electrons on carbon has become eight on every atom, and a complete octet everywhere is worth more than an electronegative atom minds carrying a formal charge. That is also why the effect needs a lone pair — a merely electronegative neighbor with nothing to donate, such as a CF₃ group, destabilizes the cation instead.

Bromobenzene would have to give an aryl cation, whose empty sp² orbital lies in the ring plane and cannot overlap the perpendicular π cloud — so it does not form. Benzyl bromide gives a benzylic cation, the tertiary bromide gives a tertiary cation, and the allylic bromide gives an allylic cation; all three ionize readily.

The screening question is always what the shift makes, not what it starts from. A hydride on a carbon that would be left tertiary migrates; one on a carbon that would be left primary does not, no matter how many hydrogens are available there. Distance only sets what is reachable, and only the immediate neighbor ever is.

The carbon next to the would-be primary cation is a ring carbon, and one of its ring C–C bonds can migrate. When the far end of that bond lands on the exocyclic carbon, that carbon joins the ring, the ring grows from four members to five, and the charge is left behind on a ring carbon as a secondary cation. Two things improve at once: 1° becomes 2°, and a badly strained ring becomes an almost strain-free one. The competing hydride shift gives only a strained secondary cyclobutyl cation.

After protonation, water leaves from C2 to give a secondary cation. The neighboring C3 is quaternary, so it offers no hydrogen — but it carries three methyls, and moving one across leaves the charge on C3 as a tertiary cation. Bromide then captures C3. Looking only for hydride shifts finds none and gives the unrearranged bromide, which is the trap this substrate is built around.

A free primary cation is too high in energy to have a meaningful lifetime, so drawing it as a discrete intermediate is bookkeeping rather than physics. The neighboring bond starts migrating while the C–X bond is still breaking, which is precisely why such a substrate reacts at all instead of not reacting. Drawing it in two steps is acceptable for predicting the product as long as you know the caveat.

The charge in an allylic cation is genuinely in two places at once, so both carbons at the ends of the delocalized system are electrophilic. Attack at the carbon that held the chlorine gives one alcohol; attack at the far end gives the other, with the double bond apparently moved. Nothing migrated here — the structure was delocalized from the start, which is what separates this from a 1,2-shift.

A lone pair adjacent to the charge produces a structure with a full π bond and an octet on every atom, which is worth far more than the nine hyperconjugating bonds of a tertiary cation. So when a molecule offers both options, the bond that breaks is the one giving the oxocarbenium, not the one giving the more substituted alkyl cation. This is why acetals hydrolyze where they do rather than at whatever carbon looks most substituted.
electron-rich-poor: Electron-rich atoms have extra electron density to donate, making them nucleophilic.
The electronegativity difference polarizes the pi bond, making O δ− (electron-rich) and C δ+ (electron-poor).
Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making it electron-rich (and strongly nucleophilic/basic).
Electron-poor atoms lack sufficient electron density and therefore seek it out from an electron-rich partner, which is exactly the defining behavior of an electrophile.

Electronegative substituents pull electron density away from the attached carbon through the polar sigma bond (an inductive effect), leaving that carbon partially positive (δ+) relative to one surrounded only by similarly electronegative C and H.

Oxygen (3.44) is more electronegative than chlorine (3.16), so the carbons flanking the ether oxygen are polarized at least as strongly as the Cl-bearing one. What decides it is the second condition: only the chlorine-bearing carbon holds a group that will actually depart. Electron-poor makes a carbon a candidate; a leaving group makes it the answer.

The resonance structure placing the negative charge on oxygen is the larger contributor to the hybrid, since oxygen is far better suited to stabilize a negative charge than carbon is — making the oxygen the more electron-rich site overall.

Electron-donating substituents push additional electron density into the aromatic ring (by resonance and/or induction), increasing the ring's overall nucleophilicity and accelerating electrophilic aromatic substitution.

The halogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling bonding electron density toward itself and leaving hydrogen partially positive (δ+), which is why H–X compounds act as proton (acid) sources.

The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing (both by induction and resonance, since nitrogen is positively charged with electronegative oxygens), making an attached ring more electron-poor, not electron-rich.

Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (through hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H/C–C bonds and simple induction), so each additional alkyl substituent on a double bond increases the electron density of the pi bond, making the alkene a better nucleophile.

Fluorine's very high electronegativity creates a strongly polarized C–F bond, pulling substantial electron density away from carbon, more so than the much less electronegative iodine does in a C–I bond, even though the C–I bond is actually weaker and breaks more easily.

A carbanion carries a full negative charge and a lone pair (electron-rich, nucleophilic), while a carbocation has an empty orbital and a full positive charge (electron-poor, electrophilic) — they sit at opposite ends of the electron-density spectrum.

A resonance structure of the enol places a lone pair from oxygen into the pi system, shifting electron density to the terminal (alpha) carbon and giving it significant nucleophilic, electron-rich character, which is why enols react with electrophiles at that carbon.

Conjugation of the nitrogen lone pair with the carbonyl pi system pulls electron density away from nitrogen toward the electronegative oxygen, leaving the amide nitrogen considerably less electron-rich than an isolated amine nitrogen.

The nitrogen of a nitrile carries a lone pair in an sp orbital and, despite nitrogen's electronegativity pulling some density toward it within the triple bond, this lone pair is the most electron-rich, available site for interacting with electrophiles or protons.

The two effects point opposite ways in this molecule. Induction pulls density out of the ring, because nitrogen is the more electronegative atom, while resonance pushes a whole lone pair in. A relocated pair beats a tilted one, so resonance wins and the ring ends up electron-rich.

Boron's electronegativity is lower than carbon's, so the shared electrons in a C–B bond sit closer to carbon, making that carbon somewhat electron-rich, similar to the polarization seen in Grignard C–Mg bonds though less pronounced.

Inductive effects act through sigma bonds and fall off quickly with distance, so a halogen's electron-withdrawing influence is strongest on the carbon it's directly attached to and becomes much weaker two or three carbons away.

Adding a full positive charge directly onto the already electronegative oxygen dramatically increases its pull on the shared electrons, making the attached carbon even more electron-deficient and far more reactive to nucleophilic attack.

The negatively charged oxygen of an enolate strongly donates its extra electron density through resonance into the adjacent carbon, making the enolate's nucleophilic carbon considerably more electron-rich (and thus more reactive) than a simple, unactivated alkene carbon.

Although oxygen holds its own electrons more tightly (higher electronegativity, stronger base), sulfur's larger, more polarizable, more loosely held electron cloud makes it more willing to donate electron density in bond-forming reactions, so it behaves as more nucleophilic/electron-rich in a reactivity sense.

The carbon directly bonded to the electronegative chlorine experiences the strongest inductive pull of electron density, making it the most electron-poor carbon in the molecule; the effect diminishes sharply at the next carbon over.

One of the hydroxyl oxygen's lone pairs conjugates with the carbonyl pi system, pulling electron density toward the carbonyl oxygen; this depletion of electron density on the OH oxygen is part of why the O–H bond is more acidic (and the oxygen less basic) than in a simple alcohol.

Nitrogen's higher electronegativity polarizes the triple bond, leaving the nitrile carbon partially positive and electrophilic, which is why Grignard and organolithium reagents can add to nitriles to eventually form ketones after hydrolysis.
Inductive (sigma-bond) electron withdrawal falls off rapidly with each bond, so while the alpha carbon feels the halogen's pull strongly, the beta carbon experiences only a faint residual effect.

Just as an enolate's oxygen lone pair activates the alpha carbon through resonance, an enamine's nitrogen lone pair conjugates through the C=C pi system to make the beta carbon unusually electron-rich and nucleophilic, a key feature exploited in many carbon-carbon bond-forming reactions.

A classic example is a halogen substituent on an aromatic ring: it withdraws electron density inductively (making the ring somewhat electron-poor overall) while donating electron density by resonance at the ortho/para positions (making those specific positions more electron-rich), so the two effects can genuinely pull in opposite directions.

Push the C=C electrons into the central C–C bond and the carbonyl pi electrons onto oxygen, and the result carries a minus on oxygen and a plus on the far, beta carbon. That contributor is a genuine part of the hybrid, which is why nucleophiles add at the beta position — conjugate addition.

Although bromine formally bears the positive charge in the strained three-membered bromonium ring, the nucleophile actually attacks one of the electrophilic ring carbons from the backside, displacing bromine and opening the ring; formal charge location does not always mark the exact site of nucleophilic attack.
naming-parent-chain: Count the row: six carbons, and the methyl is a one-carbon branch that cannot extend any path, so the parent is hexane. From the left the methyl is on C3, from the right on C4; 3 beats 4. 3-methylhexane.

Trace from the far end of the ethyl through the branch carbon and along the row: two ethyl carbons, the branch carbon, then two more is five. The row was only four. So the parent is pentane, and the carbon left over (the near end of the row) is a methyl on C3. An ethyl on C2 can never be right, because the route through it always beats the row by one.

An ethyl on the second carbon of a chain always extends it: two ethyl carbons plus C2 plus the rest of the chain is one longer than the chain itself. 2-ethylbutane is really 3-methylpentane. The other three describe a molecule where the row is genuinely the longest path.

Three arms leave the branch carbon: three carbons to the left, three in the propyl, two to the right. A chain joins the two longest arms through that carbon: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7. The two-carbon arm is an ethyl on C4: 4-ethylheptane. Counting every carbon in the molecule (nine) as one chain would need the path to pass through the branch carbon twice.
The longest unbroken path of carbons, turning as many corners as it needs to. It is very often not the row lying across the page, which is why every end has to be checked.

A tie on length is broken by the number of substituents, and the chain with more wins. It reads backwards, but a name should put as much of the molecule as possible into numbered prefixes instead of hiding it inside a big branch name.

Two five-carbon chains tie. The one along the row carries a methyl and an ethyl (two substituents); the one through the ethyl carries a single isopropyl. More substituents wins, so the parent is the row with methyl at C2 and ethyl at C3. Then the alphabet orders the words: ethyl before methyl.
Compare term by term and stop at the first difference. Both open with 2; then 2 beats 5. That settles it without looking at the third term.

Seven carbons in the row and nothing longer through a methyl. From the left the methyls are at {2, 5}; from the right at {3, 6}. 2 beats 3 at the first term. Two methyls take di- and two locants: 2,5-dimethylheptane.
Always one fewer bond than carbons. Counting the line segments and calling a hexane a pentane is the standard off-by-one, and it is the same miscount as forgetting the ends of a skeletal structure.
A methyl on the end carbon is one more carbon in a straight line, so the chain is six long, not five. A name with a 1-alkyl locant on an unbranched chain is a sign the parent was chosen wrongly.

Pentane is five in a row; put methyls on the second and third. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2,4-dimethylpentane, CH₃C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2,2-dimethylpentane, and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ has six carbons in the row (2,3-dimethylhexane).

The longest path runs through one of the two end methyls: six carbons, hexane. The other methyl is the branch, on C2 counting from that end (C5 from the other). Isopropylbutane buries two chain carbons in the branch name.

Seven in a row with a two-carbon branch on the fourth. CH₃CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is a hexane (3-ethylhexane), CH₃CH₂CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ has two methyls on one carbon, and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 4-methylheptane.

Four two-carbon arms leave the central carbon, so every route through it is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. All the candidate chains tie at five with the same two substituents, and the name is 3,3-diethylpentane. The longest-chain rule only changes an answer when an arm is longer than the ones it competes with.
Eight in the row. From the left the methyls are at {3, 5}, from the right at {4, 6}; 3 beats 4. The ethyl name has the wrong parent, since an ethyl on C2 would extend the chain.

Three ends: the two row ends and the ethyl end. Row end to row end is five. Ethyl end to either row end is two, plus the middle carbon, plus two: also five. Nothing is longer than the row, so it stays the parent.
Pentane parent, two-carbon branch on C3 from either end. The ethyl survives as an ethyl because every route through it ties the row instead of beating it.

A chain is a path and cannot pass through the same carbon twice, so only two arms can be joined: the two three-carbon arms plus the center is seven. The two-carbon arm is an ethyl on C4: 4-ethylheptane.
Pick the wrong parent and the numbering, the locants and the substituent names that follow are all wrong too. It is the step where a name goes wrong earliest and most completely.
Current IUPAC puts a locant immediately before the part of the name it refers to. Older texts write 2-butene, so read both; write the first.
When chains tie on length, the one carrying more substituents is the parent. If that ties too, the numbering rule decides: the chain whose substituents get the lower locants.
First point of difference: 2 against 3, decided at once. The totals (17 against 16) point the other way, which is exactly why adding locants up is not the rule.
From the branch carbon: one carbon to the left, three in the branch, three to the right. Join the two longest arms through it: 3 + 1 + 3 = 7. The leftover carbon is a methyl: 4-methylheptane.
Four in a row with two methyls on the second carbon, which gives a carbon bearing three methyls at one end. The first is 2-methylpentane, the third 2,2-dimethylpentane, the last 2,3-dimethylbutane.
Six in the row, methyls on the middle two carbons. From either end the set is {3, 4}: the molecule is symmetric, so there is no direction to choose and the name is simply 3,4-dimethylhexane.
Number the same chain from the other end and the methyl lands on C4. Same structure, wrong direction. The other three are genuinely different molecules.
Comma between the two numbers, hyphen between the numbers and the word, and no space anywhere inside the name of a single compound.
After length and substituent count, the numbering rule is the next tie-break: take the chain whose substituents get the lower set of locants at the first point of difference.

Hexane row, methyl on C2, ethyl on C3. Check the parent: from C3 the arms are 2 (left), 2 (ethyl) and 3 (right), so the six-carbon row is the longest and the ethyl is a real branch. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane, and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2,3-dimethylhexane.
naming-substituents: Attached through a CH₂, then a CH carrying two methyls: a three-carbon chain attached at its end with a methyl on its second carbon. That is isobutyl. sec-Butyl attaches through the branch point itself.
Isopropyl, systematically propan-2-yl, attaches at C2 of a three-carbon fragment. Propyl and butyl attach at an end; isobutyl attaches at the end of a branched three-chain.

The attached carbon carries three methyls: a propane chain attached through its middle carbon with a methyl on that same carbon, so propan-2-yl with a 2-methyl. Almost nobody says it aloud, but you should be able to decode it.
Four carbons, attached through the second one: butan-2-yl, called sec-butyl. Isobutyl attaches through a CH₂; tert-butyl through a carbon bearing three methyls.

fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo. A halogen is a prefix wherever it sits and is not a suffix, but it ranks equally with alkyl groups for numbering, so a chloro can claim the low locant over a methyl on first-point-of-difference terms.
An ether has no suffix; it is an alkoxy prefix on the longer chain. Propane is the parent, and the –OCH₃ is methoxy on C1, numbered from the end nearer it.
Two methyls on C2 of a pentane. Each substituent keeps its own locant even when they share a carbon: di- promises two numbers, and the repeated 2 is the only thing saying where the second methyl is.

Six in the longest row; from either end the branch carbon is C3 or C4, and 3 wins. Both substituents sit on C3, and the alphabet orders the words: ethyl before methyl. The numbers being equal does not change the word order.

From the left: chloro 2, methyl 4, so {2, 4}. From the right: methyl 3, chloro 5, so {3, 5}. 2 beats 3, and the halogen and the alkyl are equals in that comparison. Then chloro before methyl alphabetically.

Ignore di- when alphabetizing: you are comparing ethyl with methyl, and e comes before m, so ethyl is cited first despite its higher locant. di- needs two locants, which rules out “4-ethyl-2-dimethylhexane”, and a name cannot run two prefixes together without locants, which rules out “2,2,4-dimethylethylhexane”.
The italic, hyphenated tert- is ignored, so the name files under b. The typography is the tell: hyphenated italic prefixes are skipped, prefixes joined to the word are counted.
File each name: tert-butyl under b (tert- ignored), isopropyl under i (iso counts), dimethyl under m (di- ignored). b, i, m.
sec- is an italic hyphenated prefix and is ignored, so sec-butyl files under b, ahead of ethyl under e. Locants play no part in the order of the words.
Collect the two methyls as 2,4-dimethyl, then alphabetize with di- ignored: ethyl before methyl. Identical substituents are always gathered under one multiplying prefix.
Common halide names are alkyl group plus halide: the chlorine sits on a carbon bearing three methyls. Systematically, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. The others are isobutyl, sec-butyl and butyl chloride.

Both directions give {3, 6}: a genuine tie, and the one situation where the alphabet touches the numbering. The substituent cited first (ethyl) takes the lower locant. 6-ethyl-3-methyloctane numbers the wrong way.
First number for lowest locants; then, only on an exact tie, give the alphabetically first substituent the lower number; last, write the substituents in alphabetical order whatever their numbers.
Alphabetical order sets the order of the words: bromo, methyl, propyl. The numbers travel with their substituents, so they end up out of numerical order, which is normal.
Parentheses tell the reader that the number inside counts along the branch, from its attaching carbon, and not along the parent chain.
The attaching carbon is C1 of the substituent, always. So –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂ is (2-methylpropyl), with the methyl on the branch’s own C2.
Numbered from the attachment point, the CH₂ is C1 and the CH bearing the methyl is C2; the branch is three carbons long. This group is also called isobutyl.

A complex substituent files under the first letter of its complete name, m. The common name files under i, because iso is joined to the word. Which name you use can change where the group sits in a longer name.
Alkyl group plus halide: the bromine is on the end carbon of a three-chain, so propyl bromide (1-bromopropane). Isopropyl bromide would put it on the middle carbon.

Heptane row, with a three-carbon group attached through its middle carbon on C4. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 4-propylheptane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH(CH₃)₂)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ puts the branch on C3, and (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is 2-methyloctane.
sec-Butyl is butan-2-yl. C1 of a four-chain is butyl; C2 of a three-chain is isopropyl; a carbon bearing three methyls is tert-butyl.

Five in the longest row, methyls on C2, C3 and C4 from either end. Three identical substituents take tri- and three locants; they are never split between two prefixes. A methyl on C1 would extend the chain.

From either end the locant set is {1, 3}: a tie, so the alphabetically first substituent takes the lower number. Bromo before chloro, so the bromine gets 1. The words are then written in that same order.

Seven in the longest chain (the route through the ethyl also gives seven, with the same two substituents). From the left: methyl 3, ethyl 5. From the right: ethyl 3, methyl 5. Both {3, 5}, so ethyl, cited first, takes the 3.
Ignore di-, tri-, tetra- and the italic sec-, tert-. Do not ignore iso, neo or cyclo, which are joined to the word and count as part of it.

Propane parent with a methyl on C2 and a chlorine on C1, cited alphabetically: chloro before methyl. The group carrying the chlorine is –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂, isobutyl, so the common name is isobutyl chloride.
naming-functional-groups: Ketone outranks alcohol, so the suffix is -one and the OH is demoted to hydroxy-. The ketone claims the lower locant: C2 from its end, which puts the OH on C4.
acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene/alkyne. The acid and its derivatives are the top block.
The acid carbon is C1 by necessity and needs no locant; count from it and the chlorine sits on C3. Halogens are prefixes in every name.
A demoted alcohol becomes hydroxy-. Nothing about the oxygen changed; its rank did. oxo- is a demoted ketone, carboxy- a demoted acid.
The IUPAC prefix is oxo-, not keto-. A compound chemists call a keto acid has no mention of a ketone in its systematic name.
Aldehyde outranks alcohol: suffix -al, C1 is the CHO and no locant is written for it. The OH is hydroxy- on C3.
The acid wins the suffix and is C1. Counting from it, the OH is on C3. The acid needs no locant; writing -1-oic is redundant.

Nitrile outranks alcohol, so -nitrile is the suffix and the nitrile carbon is C1 (four carbons in the parent, including it). The OH is hydroxy- on C4. Nitrile begins with a consonant, so the e of butane stays.
Alcohol outranks amine: suffix -ol, OH on C1. The NH₂ is demoted to amino- on C3.

An aldehyde carbon and a ketone carbon are at the same oxidation level, two bonds to oxygen each; the aldehyde’s extra C–H is why it can be oxidized further, but it does not make it a higher level. The order within that pair, like the order within the acid-derivative block, is convention.

Each has three bonds from carbon to oxygen or nitrogen (the nitrile’s are all to one nitrogen), so all four sit at the same level. The order within the block is a convention that happens to run with their reactivity.

The principal group claims the low number before multiple bonds or substituents are considered at all. The old lowest-locants-to-substituents rule was only ever for molecules with nothing to outrank them.

The alcohol takes the lower locant first: number from its end, OH at C3. The methyl is then C6, whatever it would have been the other way. Giving the methyl the 2 out of habit is the commonest error here.
Priority beats length. The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, so you take the longest chain that does, even when a longer one exists.
The functional carbon is necessarily at the end of a chain, so it is C1 by construction. Butan-1-al is redundant for the same reason.
When the suffix begins with a vowel the parent’s final e is dropped. Before a consonant it stays: propanenitrile.
Two alcohols take -diol with two locants, and because di- begins with a consonant the e of butane is kept. Both OH groups are principal, so neither is demoted to hydroxy-.
Aldehyde outranks ketone: suffix -al, the CHO is C1. The ketone is demoted to oxo- on C3. keto- is not an IUPAC prefix.
Three carbons with the C=O on the middle one. Acetone is a retained name and cannot be read back into a structure; propan-2-one can.
Two carbons, including the acid carbon, so eth-. Methanoic acid is formic acid.
Find the C=O and count its chain: three carbons, so the acid part is propanoate. The carbon on the single-bonded oxygen is the alcohol part: methyl. Two words, alcohol part first.

The first word of an ester name is the alcohol’s carbon chain, attached through the single-bonded oxygen. The second word is the acid’s chain, counted from the C=O. Here both happen to be two carbons, which is why the example is worth checking.
The ketone takes the suffix and C1; the ring is the parent. Going round the direction that reaches the methyl sooner gives 3 rather than 5.

The acid carbon cannot be part of the ring, so it is not counted in the parent: the ring is cyclohexane and the group is the suffix -carboxylic acid. The e is kept because the suffix begins with a consonant.
It is chosen by the fixed priority order, not by size, position or interest, and it is the one group named as the suffix.
Alkenes and alkynes rank below every group in the list, so a functional group always claims the lower locant over a multiple bond.
An ether can never be a suffix, so the amine wins by default: -amine on C1 of a two-carbon parent, and methoxy- on C2.
The alcohol outranks the double bond and takes C1. The double bond then starts at C2. Both suffixes appear, the multiple bond first and with its e dropped before -ol.

Like the acid, the aldehyde carbon hangs off the ring and cannot be part of it, so the ring is the parent and the group becomes -carbaldehyde. Formyl- is the prefix for a demoted aldehyde, and nothing outranks it here.

The top of the list is close to the reactivity ladder of the Carboxylic Acids chapter: an acid or acyl chloride converts to an ester, an ester to an amide. Going back up is not a direct step; an ester or amide is hydrolyzed to the acid first.
naming-rings-unsaturation: Five carbons, double bond between C2 and C3 counting from the nearer end. Only the lower of the two carbons is cited; the reader infers the bond runs to the next one.
The ring has six carbons to the chain’s two, so the ring is the parent. With only one substituent there is nowhere else it could be, and no locant is written.
You choose both the starting carbon and the direction, subject to the same priority rules as a chain: principal group at C1, then lowest locants.
Six ring carbons beat three chain carbons, so the ring is the parent and the chain is a propyl substituent. One substituent needs no locant.
With no higher-priority group present, the parent is whichever has more carbons. Eight beats six, so the ring becomes a cyclohexyl substituent: 1-cyclohexyloctane.
Five against five is a tie, and on a tie the ring is the parent: pentylcyclopentane. Current IUPAC recommendations go further and prefer the ring whatever the chain length, but exams count carbons.
Phenyl is C₆H₅–, the ring itself. Benzyl is the ring plus a CH₂, attached through the CH₂; confusing the two changes the molecule by a carbon.
A benzene ring attached through an extra CH₂ is benzyl. Phenyl is the bare ring, and benzoyl is C₆H₅CO–.
A triple bond takes -yne and one locant, the lower of the two carbons: from the nearer end the bond runs from C2. Nothing else about the procedure changes.

From the left the double bond is at 1 and the triple at 4; from the right it is the other way round. The locant sets tie, so the double bond takes the lower number. The suffix order is fixed, en before yne, and the e of ene is dropped before the y.
Five carbons, double bond starting at C1 from the nearer end. The locant is needed because pent-2-ene is a different compound, and only the first of the two carbons is cited.
By convention the locant is the lower-numbered of the two carbons the bond joins; the reader infers that the bond runs to the next carbon along.
Two double bonds take -diene with two locants, one per bond, from the end that gives the lower set: {1, 3} beats {2, 4}. The a in penta- is kept before the consonant d.
The alcohol outranks the double bond and claims the lower locant, even though that gives the double bond a 5 rather than a 1. The e of ene is dropped before the vowel of -ol.

From the left: ene at 2, yne at 4, so {2, 4}. From the right: yne at 1, ene at 3, so {1, 3}. The lower set wins regardless of which bond it favors, so the triple bond gets the 1 here; the double bond only gets preference on an exact tie.
Both appear, the multiple bond first and the principal group last: hex-5-en-1-ol. The order of suffixes is fixed whatever the locants.
Xylene is the retained name for dimethylbenzene, and adjacent methyls are ortho: o-xylene. Toluene is methylbenzene.
One ring carbon between the two substituents is the 1,3 relationship, meta. The numbers and the word say the same thing, and both are in constant use.
Straight across a six-membered ring is three bonds away, the 1,4 relationship: para. Adjacent is ortho (1,2) and one apart is meta (1,3).

The six-carbon chain misses the double bond, so it is not the parent; the longest chain through the C=C is five, starting at the CH₂. The double bond takes C1 and the two carbons left over are an ethyl on C2. The 2013 IUPAC rules relaxed this, but textbooks and exams still apply it.
The two alkene carbons cannot rotate, so the methyls are fixed either on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans). The name needs a prefix to say which.

The longest chain through the double bond is four carbons, with a methyl on one of the alkene carbons. The double bond is at 2 from either end, a tie; the methyl then takes the lower number, 2 rather than 3.
The double bond takes the lowest possible pair of locants before substituents are considered; only the direction round the ring is left for them to decide.
The alcohol is the principal group and takes C1. Numbering then goes round the way that reaches the double bond soonest, so it starts at C2. The e of ene is dropped before -ol.
Four carbons in the parent, double bond starting at C1, methyl on C3. CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂ is 2-methylbut-2-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbut-1-ene, and CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃ is pent-2-ene.
The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, and that overrides the more-carbons rule exactly as it overrides the longest-chain rule.
Either direction gives {1, 2}: a tie, so the alphabetically first substituent takes C1. Ethyl before methyl. Locants are needed because the two groups could also be 1,3 or 1,4.
First point of difference: both start at 1, then 2 beats 3. On a ring you try every starting carbon and both directions, and {1, 2, 4} is the lowest set this arrangement can give.
The alcohol takes the suffix and C1. Going round the direction that reaches the methyl sooner gives 3 rather than 5.

The locants already say the methyls are adjacent. cis and trans on a ring say whether the two groups are on the same face or opposite faces, which are different compounds; the full treatment is in Stereochemistry.
bronsted: Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors; bases are proton acceptors.
After losing H⁺, the acid becomes its conjugate base (one less proton, one more negative/less positive charge).

Follow the proton. It leaves R–OH₂⁺, so that species is the donor, which is the definition of the Brønsted acid. It lands on chloride, so chloride is the acceptor, the Brønsted base. The fact that the acid is a cation rather than a bottled reagent is what makes this look unfamiliar, and it is also why it works so readily: losing the proton neutralizes the positive charge instead of creating a negative one, which is worth about seventeen pKa units. R–OH₂⁺ sits near pKa −2 while the alcohol it came from sits near 16. Chloride is a very weak base (HCl, pKa −7), so this particular transfer is not especially favorable, but it happens constantly in mechanisms because both species are present and proton transfers are fast.
NH3 accepts a proton from water to form NH4+, making it the Bronsted base while water acts as the acid.

False, and this is the single most common arrow mistake in the chapter. A curved arrow always starts on the electrons that move, and a proton has none — it is a bare nucleus. The electrons that make the new bond are supplied entirely by the base, so the arrow starts on the base’s lone pair and ends on the hydrogen. The second arrow starts on the old X–H bond and ends on the atom that keeps the pair, which is what leaves the conjugate base with its negative charge. Draw the arrow from the hydrogen and you have said the hydrogen donated electrons it does not have.
Accepting H+ turns a base into its conjugate acid, which now carries one more proton.

HCl hands its proton to a water lone pair, giving H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻. That makes HCl the Brønsted acid and water the base — the same water that acts as an acid toward ammonia, which is what amphoteric means. The transfer is essentially complete because HCl (pKa −7) is a far stronger acid than H₃O⁺ (pKa −1.7): the equilibrium constant is about 10⁵. It is also the reason water cannot tell HCl, HBr and HI apart. All three are leveled to hydronium, and their quoted pKa values come from measurements in other solvents.

False. Strength and concentration are different properties and the exam rewards keeping them apart. Acid strength is pKa: a fixed property of the molecule, set by how stable its conjugate base is. Acetic acid has pKa 4.76 whether the bottle is neat or millimolar. Concentration is how much of the substance is present per litre. Diluting lowers the concentration, which lowers the pH of the resulting solution — fewer protons overall — but changes nothing about the molecule. Hence the two combinations students find surprising: glacial acetic acid is concentrated and weak, while dilute hydrochloric acid is dilute and strong.
Acetic acid donates a proton to ammonia, so it is the proton donor (acid) in this transfer.

Water gives a proton to ammonia, so here it is the acid and hydroxide is its conjugate base. Put water with HCl instead and the proton moves the other way: water accepts it to become H₃O⁺, so there it is the base. A species that can do both is amphoteric, and water is the standard example. The point is that "acid" and "base" are roles in a particular reaction, not permanent labels on a bottle. Which role a species plays is decided by the partner: water is more acidic than ammonia (15.7 against 38) so it donates, and far less acidic than HCl (15.7 against −7) so it accepts.
HSO4- can donate its remaining proton to become SO4^2- (acid) or accept a proton to become H2SO4 (base), making it amphoteric.
The conjugate base of HCl is Cl-, formed by loss of H+; OH- is not related to HCl by a single proton loss.
Bicarbonate accepts the proton from the carboxylic acid, forming carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO2 and water), acting as a Bronsted base.

Scan the sites and give each one a pKa. The O–H is an ordinary primary alcohol at about 16. The C–H bonds on either side of the carbonyl — the acetyl methyl and the CH₂ — are alpha hydrogens at about 20, acidic for carbon because the anion is an enolate delocalized onto oxygen. The C–H bonds on the carbon carrying the OH have no such help and sit near 50. Sodium hydride is comfortably strong enough for any of this: its conjugate acid is H₂ at pKa 36. Lowest pKa wins, so the O–H comes off, and it beats the alpha positions by roughly four units — ten thousand to one. This is the comparison students most often get backwards, because a hydrogen next to a carbonyl feels activated and is: by thirty orders of magnitude relative to an alkane, and still not enough to beat an alcohol.

False, and the opposite is close to a rule. Proton transfers between electronegative atoms — O to O, O to N, N to O — are among the fastest reactions known, often limited only by how quickly the two molecules diffuse together. That has a practical consequence you will use constantly: in a multi-step mechanism you may shuffle protons between heteroatoms freely, and a mechanism is not wrong for including such a step. What is genuinely slow is removing a proton from carbon, because the carbanion left behind is high in energy and the geometry has to reorganize. That is why enolate chemistry needs its own treatment and why proton transfers to and from carbon are the ones worth drawing carefully.

Name the acid on each side. On the left the acid is phenol, pKa 10. On the right it would be acetic acid, pKa 4.76. The equilibrium always favors the side holding the weaker acid, that is the higher pKa, so it favors the left, where phenol keeps its proton. Quantitatively, K ≈ 10^(4.76 − 10) = 10^−5.2, which is about one part in 160,000. Acetate is simply too weak a base to take a proton from phenol. To deprotonate phenol you need a base whose conjugate acid has a pKa comfortably above 10 — hydroxide, at 15.7, does it easily, which is why phenols dissolve in sodium hydroxide but not in sodium bicarbonate.
The sp-hybridized C-H of a terminal alkyne is weakly acidic (pKa about 25) and can be deprotonated by a sufficiently strong base like amide ion.

False. A base needs an available electron pair, and a lone pair on a neutral atom is an electron pair. Ammonia, water, alcohols, ethers, amines and the oxygen of a carbonyl are all neutral Brønsted bases, and most of the proton transfers you will draw in mechanisms involve one of them. Charge helps — hydroxide is a far stronger base than water, and alkoxide than an alcohol — because a negative charge makes the pair more available. But helping is not the same as being required. The reliable test is to ask whether the species has a pair it can put on a proton, not whether it has a minus sign.
Any X-H bond can formally act as a Bronsted acid, but methane's conjugate base (CH3-) is extremely unstable, giving methane an extremely high pKa (about 50) and negligible real-world acidity.

Basicity is about how willingly a lone pair is handed to a proton. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it grips its electrons less firmly and gives the pair up more readily — ammonia is the stronger base. The cleanest way to confirm it is to compare conjugate acids: NH₄⁺ has pKa 9.2 and H₃O⁺ has pKa −1.7, so ammonia’s conjugate acid is about eleven orders of magnitude weaker, which means ammonia is about eleven orders of magnitude the stronger base. The other options fail on the facts: nitrogen has one lone pair to oxygen’s two, N–H is less polar than O–H, and size and hindrance are not what separates these two.

Track the proton across the arrow. Sulfuric acid starts with two and ends with one, so it is the donor — the acid — and bisulfate is its conjugate base. The alcohol starts with one hydrogen on oxygen and ends with two, so it accepted a proton: it is the base, and R–OH₂⁺ is its conjugate acid. The instinct to reject this is that an alcohol does not feel basic, and on the pKa scale it is a feeble one — its conjugate acid sits near pKa −2. But basicity is relative, and against sulfuric acid an alcohol is quite basic enough. This exact step is how alcohols are activated for substitution and elimination: protonating the oxygen turns a terrible leaving group, hydroxide, into a good one, water.

A proton transfer moves one hydrogen nucleus, and nothing else, from one species to another. In the first reaction the O–H hydrogen of acetic acid moves onto hydroxide: acetate and water come out, and no heavy atom has changed partners. The bromination is an addition across a pi bond. The third is a Lewis acid–base reaction — water donates a lone pair to the empty p orbital of a carbocation and a new C–O bond forms, with no proton moving. The last is a nucleophilic substitution at carbon. All four are acid–base reactions in the broad Lewis sense; only the first is Brønsted.
One water molecule donates a proton (acid) to the other, which accepts it (base), producing hydronium and hydroxide.
The presence of an aromatic ring does not block the O-H proton from being donated; phenol is a well-known weak Bronsted acid.

Count the charge on R–OH₂⁺. Oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, which is +1, and the whole species is a cation. The only way to reach a neutral alcohol is to lose a proton, and that is a Brønsted step: another water molecule, acting as the base, takes the proton and leaves as H₃O⁺. Notice how strong an acid R–OH₂⁺ is — pKa about −2 against the alcohol’s 16 — so that step is fast and complete. The sequence is worth remembering as a pattern: a Lewis acid–base step makes the bond and creates a charge, and a Brønsted step removes it.

False, and the order is worth committing to memory because polyfunctional molecules are exam favorites. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it is more comfortable carrying the negative charge left behind, which makes the O–H the stronger acid. The numbers are not close: an alcohol O–H sits near pKa 16 and an amine N–H near 38, twenty-two orders of magnitude apart. Add one equivalent of a base strong enough for the alcohol and the nitrogen is untouched. The reverse question has the opposite answer: ask which site a proton goes to and nitrogen wins, because it holds its lone pair more loosely. Most acidic and most basic are different questions with different answers.
Trimethylamine has no N-H bond at all (every substituent is a methyl group), so unlike ammonia or primary and secondary amines, it cannot donate an N-H proton and behaves purely as a Bronsted base.

True, and the gap is enormous rather than marginal. An alkane C–H sits near pKa 50, an amine N–H near 38 and an alcohol O–H near 16, so a typical C–H is about thirty orders of magnitude less acidic than a typical O–H. The reason is where the charge ends up: carbon is the least electronegative of the three and is the least willing to hold the pair left behind. That is why the practical rule for finding an acidic proton is to look on oxygen and nitrogen first. The exceptions are the ones worth learning individually — a C–H next to a carbonyl at about 20, a terminal alkyne C–H at 25, a 1,3-dicarbonyl at 9 — and every one of them is explained by something stabilizing the carbanion.

Two arrows, and each has a job. The first makes the new bond, so it starts on the electrons that will become that bond — a lone pair on methoxide — and ends on the acidic hydrogen. The second breaks the old bond, so it starts on the O–H bonding pair and ends on the oxygen that keeps it, which is what leaves acetate negatively charged. The answer that runs the acidic H at methoxide and acetic acid’s oxygen at the O–H bond reverses both arrows, and has the hydrogen donating electrons it does not possess. The answer that pushes the C=O bond up onto the carbonyl oxygen breaks the wrong bond: the pi bond has nothing to do with deprotonation. And the answer that sends methoxide at the carbonyl carbon is a real reaction later in the course, but it is nucleophilic addition, not proton transfer.
H2CO3 loses one proton to become HCO3-; they differ by exactly one H+ and are therefore a conjugate acid-base pair.
lewis-acids: Lewis acids are electron pair acceptors — a broader definition than Brønsted acids, which must involve a proton.
BF₃ has an empty p orbital on boron and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a Lewis acid despite having no acidic protons.
Metal cations have empty orbitals and coordinate to electron-rich atoms like carbonyl oxygen, pulling electron density away and making the carbon more electrophilic.

The carbocation has six valence electrons at its central carbon and an empty p orbital, so it accepts a pair: it is the Lewis acid. Water supplies the pair from one of its lone pairs, so it is the Lewis base. Now do the formal charges, because this is where the item is really aimed. Before: carbon +1, oxygen 0. After: carbon has four bonds and is neutral, while oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, which is +1. The charge did not disappear — it moved onto the atom that supplied the electrons and got no share of them back. Drawing the product neutral on both atoms is the classic error here. A separate Brønsted step removes that proton to give the neutral alcohol.
Accepting a proton requires donating an electron pair to form the new bond, so every Bronsted base (proton acceptor) is necessarily also a Lewis base.
AlCl3 has an incomplete octet on aluminum and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a powerful Lewis acid catalyst in Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.

Boron brings three valence electrons and uses all three in bonds to fluorine, so it ends with six electrons rather than eight and an empty 2p orbital perpendicular to the trigonal planar molecule. That orbital is a genuine hole, and anything with a spare pair can fill it. The fluorines do help by pulling electron density away inductively, which makes boron hungrier, but that is a secondary effect — the empty orbital is what makes BF₃ an acid at all. The claim that fluorine donates density into boron by resonance is true in part and works against the answer: fluorine lone pairs do donate a little into that p orbital, which is exactly why BF₃ is a weaker Lewis acid than BCl₃.

A Lewis base donates an electron pair, and a pi bond is an electron pair. In ethene the two pi electrons sit above and below the plane of the molecule, held loosely and reaching out into space, which makes them available to anything electron-poor. That is why an alkene reacts with Br₂ or with H⁺: the pi pair attacks, exactly as ammonia’s lone pair attacks boron. Chloride, ether and ammonia are all Lewis bases too, but each has lone pairs, so none answers the question as asked. Recognizing the pi bond as the electron source is the single idea that makes the whole of alkene chemistry make sense.
Ethylene has no lone pairs; it donates electron density from its pi bond to electrophiles such as Br2 or H+, a hallmark of alkene reactivity in organic chemistry.
The carbonyl oxygen's lone pair coordinates to the electron-deficient boron of BF3, activating the carbonyl toward nucleophilic attack, a common strategy in Lewis acid catalysis.

False, and the exceptions are the reason the Lewis definition exists. BF₃ plus ammonia forms a B–N bond with no hydrogen involved anywhere; a carbocation capturing water, AlCl₃ pulling chloride off an acyl chloride, and every nucleophilic attack you will draw are all Lewis acid–base events with no proton transfer. The relationship runs the other way: Brønsted chemistry is the subset of Lewis chemistry in which the electron pair happens to be donated to H⁺. So every Brønsted base is a Lewis base, but a Lewis acid needs only somewhere for a pair to land.
A carbocation's central carbon has only six valence electrons, leaving an empty p orbital that strongly attracts electron pairs from Lewis bases (nucleophiles).

Ask of each one: does it have somewhere for an incoming pair to go? The carbonyl carbon does. Oxygen pulls density out of the C=O pi bond, leaving the carbon with a substantial partial positive charge and a low-lying pi antibonding orbital, so a nucleophile attacks it and the pi pair moves onto oxygen. That is an electron-pair acceptor, which is what Lewis acid means, and it is the single most important example in the second half of the course. The other three are all electron-rich: an ether has lone pairs, an alkene has a pi pair, a chloride has both a charge and lone pairs. All three are Lewis bases.

Boron in BF₃ brings three valence electrons and uses all three, so it ends with six and a genuinely empty 2p orbital — a hole waiting to be filled. Tin in SnCl₄ has no such hole; what it has is room. A metal center with four ligands is usually perfectly comfortable with five or six, so a Lewis base simply adds on and the coordination number goes up. FeBr₃, ZnCl₂ and TiCl₄ all work the same way. The definition covers both because it is about where the pair can go, not about how the space is made available — and a carbonyl carbon is a third route again, with a full octet that accommodates the incoming pair by pushing its pi electrons onto oxygen.
Forming the new B-N bond gives boron four bonding pairs instead of three, changing its hybridization from sp2 (trigonal planar) to sp3 (tetrahedral).
BF3 cannot donate a proton since it has none, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid, yet it is a textbook strong Lewis acid, showing the two acid categories are not equivalent.

Aluminum in AlCl₃ has six valence electrons and an empty orbital, so it is the Lewis acid, and the best pair on offer is a lone pair on the acyl chloride’s chlorine. Coordinating there drains density out of the C–Cl bond until it breaks heterolytically, leaving AlCl₄⁻ and an acylium ion, RC≡O⁺. The acylium ion is a far stronger electrophile than the acyl chloride was — a full positive charge on carbon, stabilized by the oxygen lone pair — and it is powerful enough to attack benzene, which the acyl chloride alone is not. The catalyst did not supply the electrophile; it manufactured one, which is the general job description of a Lewis acid catalyst.

Lewis acid or base character depends on the reaction partner, so the same species can play different roles with different partners depending on which one is electron-rich or electron-poor in that specific interaction.

Nitrogen carries a lone pair and boron has an empty orbital, so the pair goes from nitrogen to boron: ammonia is the Lewis base, BF₃ the Lewis acid. One curved arrow, from the nitrogen lone pair to boron, and nothing breaks. The bookkeeping afterwards is the part worth practising. Nitrogen now has four bonds where it normally has three, so it is +1; boron has four bonds and three valence electrons, 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. The adduct is neutral overall but carries an internal charge separation, and boron has gone from trigonal planar to tetrahedral. A bond made from a pair supplied entirely by one atom is called dative, though once formed it is an ordinary covalent bond.
The oxygen of a carbonyl group has lone pairs that readily coordinate to Lewis acids such as BF3 or AlCl3, a common activation strategy in synthesis.

False, and the exception is a whole class of reagents. BF₃, AlCl₃ and carbocations do work that way: six valence electrons and a genuine empty p orbital. But FeBr₃, ZnCl₂, TiCl₄ and SnCl₄ are metal centers that accept a pair by expanding their coordination number instead — titanium with four bonds is perfectly comfortable with five or six, so a carbonyl oxygen can simply add on as an extra ligand. A carbonyl carbon is a third case again: it has a full octet, and the incoming pair is accommodated by pushing the pi electrons up onto oxygen. Three different mechanisms, one definition: somewhere for a pair to go.
Chloride ion has a full octet and a lone pair to donate, making it a Lewis base, not a Lewis acid; the other three are classic electron-pair acceptors.

Titanium accepts a lone pair from the carbonyl oxygen, expanding its coordination sphere. Once oxygen is donating into the metal it pulls harder on the C=O pi electrons, which drains density off the carbonyl carbon and leaves it more strongly delta positive — a better electrophile. The effect is the same one protonation achieves, and that is the point: a Lewis acid activates a carbonyl under neutral conditions, so a substrate that would not survive strong protic acid can still be activated. Look for the pattern rather than the reagent name: ZnCl₂, BF₃, AlCl₃ and TiCl₄ all do this job.
A bare proton has no electrons at all, so when it bonds to a base, that bond forms entirely from the base's donated electron pair, the defining behavior of a Lewis acid.
By accepting a lone pair from the epoxide oxygen, the Lewis acid withdraws electron density from the ring, weakening the C-O bonds and activating the epoxide carbons for nucleophilic ring-opening.

A bare proton is a nucleus with nothing around it, so its 1s orbital is empty and every bond it ever makes is built entirely from a partner’s donated pair. That is the definition of an electron-pair acceptor, and it is why a proton cannot exist free in solution: it binds the first available lone pair instantly. Seeing it this way also settles how the two definitions fit together. A Brønsted base is always a Lewis base, because accepting a proton means donating a pair to it; and a Brønsted acid works by supplying the Lewis acid H⁺ rather than by being one itself.
In a Lewis acid-base adduct, the base supplies both electrons of the new bond while the acid simply provides the empty orbital to receive them.
Bulky substituents can physically block a Lewis base from approaching the empty orbital, so steric hindrance, not just electronics, influences a Lewis acid's real-world reactivity.

Oxygen donates one of its two lone pairs into boron’s empty p orbital. Count afterwards: oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair, which is 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, and boron has four bonds and three valence electrons, 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. The complex is neutral overall while carrying a charge on each atom, which is exactly what happens with BF₃ and ammonia. Nothing was ionized and no bond broke — that is why “both atoms stay neutral” is tempting — but formal charge counts the electrons each atom can claim, and the donor always loses a claim. Ether–BF₃ complexes are real, isolable substances; BF₃ is sold as its diethyl etherate for this reason.

Protonating a carbonyl oxygen activates the carbon beautifully, but it requires a medium acidic enough to do it, and plenty of substrates — acetals, many protecting groups, acid-sensitive stereocenters — will not survive that.
