A Lewis acid gives the same activation by a different route: the metal accepts a lone pair from the carbonyl oxygen, density is pulled off the carbon, and the carbon becomes more electrophilic, all under neutral conditions. That equivalence is the practical payoff of the Lewis definition. The base option is wrong in a useful way — deprotonating a carbonyl oxygen is not a thing, since there is no hydrogen there to remove.
pka: pKa and acid strength are inversely related — lower pKa means the acid dissociates more, so it’s stronger.
Proton transfer equilibria favor forming the weaker acid (higher pKa) — the reaction runs toward the more stable, less acidic species.

Use K ≈ 10^(pKa of the acid formed − pKa of the acid consumed). The acid consumed is the alkyne, 25. The acid formed is water, 15.7, because that is what hydroxide becomes once it has the proton. So K ≈ 10^(15.7 − 25) = 10^−9.3, about one part in two billion against the product. Hydroxide is simply too weak a base for an alkyne. Swap in sodium amide and the acid formed is ammonia at pKa 38, giving K ≈ 10^(38 − 25) = 10¹³, which is complete — and that is exactly why NaNH₂, not NaOH, is the reagent every textbook specifies for making acetylides.

pKa = −log₁₀(Ka), so a Ka of 10⁻³ gives pKa 3 and a Ka of 10⁻⁷ gives pKa 7. The larger Ka means the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ sits further to the right, so acid A dissociates more and is the stronger acid — and it has the lower pKa. That is the whole content of the minus sign, and it is the source of most of the confusion on this topic: a bigger Ka and a smaller pKa say the same thing. The four-unit gap means A is about ten thousand times the stronger of the two.

Hydride’s conjugate acid is H₂, pKa about 36. Ethanol is 16. K ≈ 10^(36 − 16) = 10²⁰, which is complete by any standard. There is a second reason NaH is the standard reagent for making an alkoxide: the by-product is hydrogen gas, which bubbles out of the flask, so the reaction cannot run backwards even in principle. Compare the alternatives. NaOH has a conjugate acid at 15.7, slightly below ethanol, so K ≈ 10^−0.3 and you get a mixture. Sodium ethoxide is the same molecule’s own conjugate base, so K = 1 and nothing is achieved at all.

A base removes a proton completely when its conjugate acid has a pKa comfortably above the proton’s — three or four units is a working minimum, and ten is decisive. LDA’s conjugate acid is diisopropylamine at about pKa 36, sixteen units above 20, so deprotonation is quantitative. Hydroxide (conjugate acid water, 15.7) and ethoxide (ethanol, 16) both sit about four units below the alpha hydrogen, so they give only a trace of enolate at equilibrium — which is useful when a trace is what you want, as in an aldol, and useless when you need all of it. Acetate (acetic acid, 4.76) is fifteen units short and does nothing. LDA is also bulky enough not to attack the carbonyl itself, which is the second reason it is chosen.
When pH equals pKa, the concentrations of the acid and its conjugate base are equal, meaning the acid is 50 percent dissociated.

Both are O–H bonds on a small, unhindered oxygen with no resonance and nothing withdrawing nearby, so the four ARIO factors give the same answer for each and the pKa values come out within half a unit: water 15.7, ethanol 16. The textbook explanation for the small difference is that an alkyl group is weakly electron-donating compared with a hydrogen, which slightly destabilizes the alkoxide. That is usually how it is taught, and it is worth knowing it is not the whole story: in DMSO the order reverses, with ethanol at 29.8 the stronger acid against water at 31.4. The real driver in water is solvation — hydroxide is smaller and easier for water molecules to surround than ethoxide. Either way, treat water and a simple alcohol as effectively equal in acidity.

Since pKa is a log scale, a difference of about 12 pKa units corresponds to roughly 10^12 difference in Ka, reflecting the large stabilizing effect of resonance in the carboxylate compared to the alkoxide.

For deprotonation to run to completion, the acid produced has to be weaker than the acid consumed — higher pKa, not lower. Write it as K ≈ 10^(pKa of the acid formed − pKa of the acid consumed): with the carboxylic acid at 5, a base whose conjugate acid sits at 10 gives K ≈ 10⁵ and a base whose conjugate acid sits at 2 gives K ≈ 10^−3. The first goes, the second does not. In practice a carboxylic acid is easy: even bicarbonate, pKaH 6.4, is enough, which is why a bicarbonate wash pulls carboxylic acids out of an organic layer.
Since pKa = -log(Ka), an extremely large Ka for a very strong acid produces a negative pKa value.
Higher s-character (sp versus sp3) stabilizes the lone pair left behind in the conjugate base, making sp C-H bonds considerably more acidic than sp3 C-H bonds.

pKa values are measured in a specific solvent, commonly water, because the degree to which that solvent stabilizes the separated charges through solvation strongly affects the measured equilibrium constant.
A pKa difference of 27 units corresponds to an enormous difference in Ka, showing the oxygen-protonated form is vastly more acidic than the alpha C-H, which needs a much stronger base to deprotonate.

Use the rule that an acid is mostly protonated below its pKa and mostly deprotonated above it, one proton at a time. pH 7 is four units above pKa1 = 3, so the first, more acidic proton is long gone — better than 99.99 percent of it. pH 7 is three units below pKa2 = 10, so the second proton is still firmly attached, about a thousand to one. The species that dominates is therefore the one that has lost exactly one proton. Sketching a number line with the two pKa values marked and the pH between them makes this a five-second question rather than a calculation.
pKa values depend on the solvent because solvation stabilizes ions differently in different media; the same acid can show noticeably different pKa values in water versus a solvent like DMSO.

Pick a base whose conjugate acid has a pKa between the two compounds. Bicarbonate’s conjugate acid is carbonic acid, pKa 6.4: above the carboxylic acid at 4.76 and below the phenol at 10. So the carboxylic acid is deprotonated, becomes an ion, and moves into the aqueous layer as its sodium salt, while the phenol stays neutral and stays in the ether. Hydroxide would not work: its conjugate acid is water at 15.7, above both, so it deprotonates both and sends both into the water. HCl protonates neither. Brine changes nothing about either. Acidify the aqueous layer afterwards and the carboxylic acid comes back out clean.

Ethoxide removes a proton well when the substrate’s pKa is below 16, and the further below, the more complete the reaction. Acetic acid at 4.76, a 1,3-diketone at 9 and phenol at 10 are all comfortably below, by eleven, seven and six units, so ethoxide takes all three essentially completely. The terminal alkyne at 25 is nine units above: K ≈ 10^(16 − 25) = 10^−9, about a billion to one against. The diketone is the one worth noticing — its acidic hydrogen is on carbon, and it is still more acidic than phenol, because the anion delocalizes onto two carbonyl oxygens.
The conjugate acids of typical alkyl amines have pKa values in the range of about 9 to 11, reflecting amines' moderate basicity.
pKa = -log(Ka), so a Ka of 10^-5 gives pKa = 5 and a Ka of 10^-3 gives pKa = 3; acid A, with the smaller Ka, has the higher pKa, a difference of 2 units.

In solution, polar solvents like water stabilize charged conjugate bases through solvation, which can significantly change or even reverse relative acidity trends compared to the gas phase, where no such stabilization exists.
Comparing the pKa values of two acids against a common base's conjugate acid lets you predict which acid-base pair favors products versus reactants at equilibrium.
Because H3O+ is the strongest acid species that persists in water, stronger acids added to dilute water are converted essentially completely to H3O+, a phenomenon known as the leveling effect.

Compare each substrate with the base’s pKaH. Acetic acid at 4.76 sits 1.6 units below 6.4, so K ≈ 10^1.6, about forty to one in favor of deprotonation — it goes, and you can see it go, because the carbonic acid produced falls apart into CO₂ and water and the mixture fizzes. Ethanol at 16 sits nearly ten units above, so K ≈ 10^−9.6 and nothing happens. This selectivity is the basis of the standard bicarbonate wash: it removes carboxylic acids from a mixture and leaves alcohols and phenols alone.

A base can remove a proton whose pKa is lower than the pKa of its own conjugate acid. Hydroxide’s conjugate acid is water, pKa 15.7, so that is the number to compare against. Below 15.7 and the reaction is favorable; a few units below and it is essentially complete; above 15.7 and it is not happening. The neutral point of water, pH 7, is a property of a solution rather than of a molecule and has nothing to do with this comparison. Having an O–H bond is not enough either: ethanol has one and sits at 16, just above hydroxide’s reach.

pKa is a base-ten logarithm, so each unit is a factor of ten in Ka and three units is 10³, a thousandfold. This is worth converting every time, because pKa differences look deceptively small on the page. Acetic acid at 4.76 and ethanol at 16 look eleven small steps apart and are a hundred billion to one. The practical calibration: one or two units is a real but incomplete reaction, three or four is enough to call a proton transfer complete for synthetic purposes, and anything past six is absolute.

Name the acid on each side. On the left it is acetic acid, pKa 4.76. On the right it is ammonium, pKa 9.2, formed when ammonia takes the proton. The equilibrium favors the side holding the weaker acid, that is the higher pKa, so it favors the right. K ≈ 10^(9.2 − 4.76) = 10^4.4, roughly 10⁴ — complete for practical purposes. Notice what the calculation does not require: you never had to decide whether acetate or ammonia is the stronger base. Converting everything to acids and comparing two pKa values answers the same question with the numbers pointing the right way.

Two properties decide whether a base is usable, and they are independent. First, strength: the conjugate acid needs a pKa well above 25, which rules out hydroxide at 15.7 and ethoxide at 16 and points to amide bases at 36 to 38. Second, nucleophilicity, which is largely a matter of steric bulk: a small strong base such as amide ion will also add to a carbonyl, whereas a bulky one such as LDA is too hindered to reach the carbonyl carbon and can only reach a proton. This separation of basicity from nucleophilicity is exactly why LDA exists as a reagent.

The question contains its own contradiction, which is the point of it. Ethanol at 16 is the weaker acid of the two, so any base able to remove ethanol’s proton will remove trifluoroethanol’s more easily still. Selectivity runs the other way: you can find a base that takes the more acidic proton and leaves the less acidic one alone, but never the reverse. A base whose pKaH is about 14, for instance, would deprotonate trifluoroethanol and not ethanol. Getting this backwards is a common slip, and the fix is to always rank the substrates by pKa first and then ask which end of the range your base can reach.

Water levels every acid stronger than H₃O⁺. Add HCl, HBr, HI or H₂SO₄ to water and each is converted essentially completely to hydronium, so all four look identical and the solution cannot tell them apart: the strongest acid that can exist in water is H₃O⁺, pKa −1.7. To rank them you have to move to a solvent that is a much weaker base, such as acetic acid or DMSO, measure there, and extrapolate back. The same levelling happens at the basic end — hydroxide is the strongest base water permits — which is why NaNH₂ and LDA have to be used in aprotic solvents like THF.
conjugate: Losing H⁺ from an acid gives its conjugate base — exactly one fewer proton.
Strong acids give up protons easily because their conjugate base is very stable (weak) once formed.
Adding a proton (H⁺) to NH₃ gives NH₄⁺, its conjugate acid.

A conjugate acid is what a species becomes when it gains one proton, so add H⁺ to one of oxygen’s lone pairs. Oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair, which is a formal charge of +1, giving the oxonium ion CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺. Nothing else about the molecule changes. The ion is a strong acid, pKa about −2, eighteen units below the alcohol it came from — which is exactly why protonating an alcohol is the standard way to turn hydroxide, a terrible leaving group, into water, a good one. CH₃CH₂O⁻ is the conjugate base rather than the acid, and the other two options are different compounds altogether.

Remove the terminal C–H proton and leave the bonding pair behind: the result is an acetylide anion, with the negative charge in an sp orbital on carbon. The alkyne is far more acidic than an ordinary hydrocarbon — pKa 25 against about 50 — because an sp orbital is 50 percent s character, so it holds the pair close to the nucleus and low in energy. The other options change the carbon skeleton rather than just removing a proton, which conjugate relationships never do. Acetylides matter because they are carbon nucleophiles: they attack alkyl halides and carbonyls and make carbon–carbon bonds.

False, and the trap catches almost everyone once. "One proton and one unit of charge" means the charge goes down by one, not that it lands on −1. Start from a cation and the conjugate base is neutral: H₃O⁺ gives water, NH₄⁺ gives ammonia, a protonated alcohol gives the alcohol back. Start from a neutral molecule and you do get an anion: water gives hydroxide, ethanol gives ethoxide. The same applies in reverse for conjugate acids, which are not always neutral: the conjugate acid of a neutral amine is an ammonium cation. Write the charge you started with, then add or subtract one.
Removing the single proton from HF gives fluoride ion, F-, its conjugate base.
Because HCN is a much weaker acid than HF (higher pKa), its conjugate base, cyanide, holds onto protons more strongly and is therefore the stronger base of the two.
Water is a much weaker acid than HCl or acetic acid, so its conjugate base, hydroxide, is a correspondingly much stronger base than chloride or acetate.
NH4+ loses a proton to become NH3, making them a properly matched conjugate acid and conjugate base pair, differing by exactly one H+.
Because a strong acid dissociates almost completely, its conjugate base has very little affinity for protons and is correspondingly a weak base, such as Cl- from HCl.

A conjugate pair differs by exactly one proton and by nothing else. Acetic acid loses its O–H proton to give acetate: same carbon skeleton, same atoms apart from that one hydrogen, charge down by one. That is a pair. Acetic acid and ethanol are different compounds with different skeletons. Acetic acid and methyl acetate differ by a methyl group, not a proton — an ester is not a conjugate anything. Acetate and hydroxide are simply the two bases that might appear on opposite sides of some reaction; being on opposite sides of an arrow is the classic reason people pair species that are not conjugates.

Run the definition in both directions on the same molecule. Add a proton to a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen and you get the protonated carbonyl, C=OH⁺ — the conjugate acid, and a strong one at pKa about −7, which is how acid catalysis activates a carbonyl toward nucleophiles. Remove an alpha proton, the one on the carbon next to C=O, and you get the enolate — the conjugate base, from a C–H at pKa about 20, unusually acidic for carbon because the anion delocalizes onto oxygen. Both halves of carbonyl chemistry are on that one line: acid catalysis on the left, enolate chemistry on the right.

Base strength is read off the conjugate acid, inverted: the weaker the acid, the stronger the base it leaves behind. Methane at pKa 50 is the feeblest acid on the list by a wide margin, so methyl anion is the strongest base — strong enough to deprotonate essentially anything organic, which is why organolithiums and Grignards cannot be used in the presence of water or alcohols. Chloride comes from the strongest acid, pKa −7, so it is a spectator: you can eat sodium chloride. Hydroxide and acetate sit in between and in that order. Note that there is no separate base scale to memorize; one pKa column answers both questions.

Both anions came from an O–H, so the atom holding the charge is oxygen in each case and factor A is a tie. What differs is what happens next. Acetate spreads its negative charge equally over two equivalent oxygens by resonance, so each carries about half a unit; ethoxide has nowhere to put it and keeps the whole charge on one oxygen. Half a charge is far easier to hold than a whole one, so acetate is the more stable and therefore the weaker, less reactive base — which is the same statement as acetic acid (pKa 4.76) being eleven orders of magnitude stronger an acid than ethanol (pKa 16).

Bicarbonate forms when carbonic acid (H2CO3) loses a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate base, and also when carbonate (CO3^2-) gains a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate acid; this dual role is why it is amphoteric.
Adding one proton to a carboxylate ion regenerates the neutral carboxylic acid, its conjugate acid.

HCN is the weaker acid of the two — higher pKa — so its conjugate base, cyanide, holds a proton more strongly and is the stronger base. Fluoride, left behind by the stronger acid, is the weaker and more stable of the two anions. A good leaving group is a weak, stable base, so fluoride is the better leaving group of the pair. That chain of reasoning is worth rehearsing because it is one property under four names: conjugate base of a strong acid, weak base, stable anion, good leaving group. Read the pKa column left to right for acid strength and right to left for everything else.
The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the conjugate base; since methane is the weakest acid of the four (highest pKa), methyl anion is the strongest base.
Because a weak acid holds onto its proton fairly well, its conjugate base, once formed, has a correspondingly stronger pull on protons, meaning it is a relatively strong base.

Convert every base to its conjugate acid and rank those by pKa: ammonia 38, water 15.7, acetic acid 4.76, HCl −7. The weakest acid leaves the strongest base, so the base order is the reverse of the acid order: amide, then hydroxide, then acetate, then chloride. The spread is enormous — 45 pKa units from top to bottom — and it maps directly onto what each one does in a flask. Amide deprotonates almost anything organic. Hydroxide handles alcohols and carboxylic acids. Acetate manages only strong acids. Chloride does essentially nothing as a base, which is precisely why it is a good leaving group.

Because N-H, with pKa around 35 to 38, is far less acidic than O-H, with pKa around 16 to 18, the nitrogen-based conjugate base holds its electron pair much more tightly and is therefore a much stronger base than an alkoxide.

Choosing a base is a conjugate-acid comparison. A proton transfer runs downhill when the acid you form is weaker — higher pKa — than the acid you consume, and K ≈ 10^(pKa formed − pKa consumed). Sodium amide forms ammonia at 38 from an alkyne at 25, so K ≈ 10¹³ and the deprotonation is complete. Hydroxide would form water at 15.7, which is 9.3 units below the alkyne — uphill by 10⁻⁹·³, so almost no acetylide. Triethylamine at 10.7 and bicarbonate at 6.4 are further uphill still. The working rule is to pick a base whose conjugate acid sits several pKa units above the proton you want, which is why acetylide chemistry is written with NaNH₂ and never with NaOH.

Removing a proton from nitrogen gives the amide anion RNH⁻. The reagent question is what makes this worth asking: the N–H of an amine sits at pKa about 38, so a base whose conjugate acid is well above 38 is needed — butyllithium, whose conjugate acid is butane at about 50, does it. Hydroxide at 15.7 is twenty-two units short and does nothing at all. The contrast with the conjugate acid is the useful part: RNH₃⁺ forms whenever an amine meets any ordinary acid, because its pKa is only about 10.7. Same molecule, one proton either side, wildly different difficulty.

Every base inherits its strength from its own conjugate acid, and these two have different partners. Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKa 15.7 — a weak acid, so hydroxide is a strong base. Water is the conjugate base of hydronium, pKa −1.7 — a strong acid, so water is a weak base. The seventeen-unit gap between the two conjugate acids is exactly the gap between the two basicities. This is also why "is this a conjugate base?" is not a well-formed question: the answer always requires naming the other party, the way "is this a sibling?" does.

Pair each species with the one it turns into, which means reading vertically down the equation rather than diagonally across the arrow. Acetic acid loses a proton to become acetate: one pair. Methylamine gains that proton to become the methylammonium ion: the other pair. The diagonal readings — pairing acetic acid with methylammonium, or methylamine with acetate — are the classic error, and so is pairing the two species that merely sit on the same side of the arrow. Acetate and methylamine are not conjugates; they are simply the two species that end up on opposite sides. Every proton transfer has all four roles filled at once, and the test for a pair is always the same: do these two differ by exactly one H and one unit of charge, and by nothing else?

Adding a proton to a base gives its conjugate acid, so the carboxylate picks up H⁺ on one of its oxygens and becomes the neutral carboxylic acid. The charge goes from −1 to 0, which is the "one unit of charge" half of the definition. This is not a theoretical step: it is the second half of every acid–base extraction. Wash an organic layer with bicarbonate and the carboxylic acid is converted to its salt and pulled into the water; acidify that aqueous layer and the conjugate acid reforms, comes out of solution and can be collected. Nothing was reduced and no chlorine was installed — dilute HCl here is only a proton source.

The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base; since HI is the strongest acid (most negative pKa) and NH3 is the weakest (highest pKa) of the three, their conjugate bases rank I- as weakest, then OH-, then NH2- as strongest.

The relationship is a strict inverse, and it is not a separate fact to memorize — it follows from what the words mean. An acid is strong precisely because it lets go of its proton readily, which requires that whatever is left behind is comfortable holding the electron pair and has little appetite for the proton back. Comfortable holding it is the definition of a weak base. Run it the other way and the same logic applies: ammonia is a vanishingly weak acid at pKa 38, so amide ion is one of the strongest bases in the course. Every species has a conjugate base, however feeble an acid it is; methane’s is the methyl anion.

Every proton transfer contains exactly two conjugate pairs, and you find them by pairing each species with what it turns into. HCN loses its proton to become CN⁻: one pair. Hydroxide gains that proton to become water: the other pair. Read the equation vertically, not diagonally — HCN and water are simply the two species that happen to sit on opposite sides, and pairing them is the standard mistake. Which way does it run? Left acid HCN, pKa 9.2; right acid water, pKa 15.7. The higher pKa is on the right, so the equilibrium favors the products by about 10⁶.5.
acidity-factors: Run ARIO and watch two factors disagree. A favors ethanol: its anion puts the charge on oxygen, while the diketone’s puts it on carbon, and oxygen is far more electronegative. R favors the diketone by a mile: the anion sits between two carbonyls and delocalizes onto both oxygens, so the charge spends most of its time on oxygen anyway and on two of them, while ethoxide has nowhere to put it. R wins, and not narrowly — seven pKa units, ten million to one. This is the case that shows the ARIO order is a search order, not a ranking of strengths: A is checked first because it settles most comparisons quickly, not because it always wins.
More electronegative atoms stabilize the extra negative charge of the conjugate base better, increasing acidity (e.g., HF > CH₄ in acidity trend logic, comparing across a period).

Both anions are carboxylates, so resonance is identical on both sides and the atom holding the charge is oxygen in each case. What the three fluorines do is pull electron density toward themselves through the sigma framework, which helps spread the carboxylate’s negative charge and stabilizes it. That is induction, and here it is worth 4.3 pKa units — about twenty thousand fold. Two properties of induction are worth carrying away from this: it is cumulative, so three fluorines do far more than one, and it dies quickly with distance, so moving the fluorines three carbons away would leave almost nothing of the effect.

Rank the conjugate acids and invert, because a stable anion is the one left behind by a strong acid. Acetic acid 4.76, ethanol 16, an amine N–H about 38, an alkane about 50. So acetate is by far the most stable of the four and the propyl carbanion the least, spanning 45 pKa units. The reasons stack in the expected order: acetate gets both the electronegative atom and resonance over two equivalent oxygens; ethoxide gets the atom but no resonance; the amide anion is on a less electronegative atom; the carbanion has nothing at all going for it. A stable anion, a weak base and a good leaving group are three names for the same property.

Acidity increases down the column: HF 3.2, HCl −7, HBr −9, HI −10, so HI is about thirteen orders of magnitude stronger than HF. The explanation this course uses is size and polarizability — iodide spreads one unit of charge over a vastly bigger, floppier electron cloud than fluoride can, and that dilution stabilizes the anion far more than the loss of electronegativity costs. A second effect points the same way and some textbooks lead with it: the H–X bond also gets longer and weaker down the group, from about 570 kJ/mol for H–F to 300 for H–I. Both are real; size is the one to quote, with bond strength reinforcing it.

True, and this corrects an over-simple version of the rule. It is true that delocalizing onto an electronegative atom is worth more per atom — acetate, on two oxygens, beats phenoxide, on three carbons. But "onto carbon does not count" is wrong, and the counterexamples are all standard: allyl anion at pKa 43 against propane at 50, triphenylmethane at 31, phenol at 10 against an alcohol at 16, and cyclopentadiene at 16 against a normal alkane at 50 — thirty-four units from delocalization onto carbon alone. Cyclopentadienyl is the extreme case because its anion is also aromatic, six pi electrons in a planar ring, and aromatic stabilization is resonance in its strongest available form.

Only factor A differs here, and it is the down-a-group case rather than the across-a-period one. No resonance in either anion, nothing withdrawing in either molecule, both atoms sp³. Oxygen is more electronegative, which would favor ethanol — but sulfur is much larger, so the thiolate spreads one unit of charge over a far bigger, more polarizable electron cloud, and that dilution beats the loss of electronegativity. Measured: ethanethiol 10.6, ethanol 16, so the thiol is about 250,000 times the stronger acid. The same logic runs down the halogens, where HI beats HF by thirteen orders of magnitude.

Give every site a pKa and take the lowest. The O–H is an ordinary primary alcohol at about 16. The terminal alkyne C–H is 25 — remarkably acidic for carbon, because the pair left behind sits in an sp orbital with 50 percent s character, but still nine units above the alcohol. The CH₂ groups have nothing stabilizing their anions and sit near 50. So sodium hydride, pKaH about 36, takes the O–H: it is comfortably able to, and the nine-unit gap means the alkyne is untouched. To deprotonate the alkyne instead you would need a base above 25, such as NaNH₂ at 38 — and it would take the O–H first, so you would need two equivalents.

Removing that specific proton produces a fully conjugated, aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion, whose resonance and aromatic stabilization dramatically lowers the pKa compared to a typical alkane C-H, around 50.

Orbitals with more s-character are lower in energy and hold electron density closer to the nucleus; since sp has the most s-character of the three, its conjugate base is the most stabilized, making the alkynyl C-H the most acidic.

False — it is the other way round, and this is the single most common inversion on the topic. A base inherits its strength from its conjugate acid by inversion: the weaker that acid is, the higher its pKa, and the stronger the base. Amide ion is a ferocious base because ammonia is a feeble acid at pKa 38. Chloride does essentially nothing as a base because HCl is a very strong acid at −7. The working rule for any "which is the stronger base" question is to convert both bases to their conjugate acids, look up the two pKa values, and pick the higher one. There is no separate base scale to memorize.

Chlorine's high electronegativity withdraws electron density through the sigma bond framework, helping stabilize the adjacent carboxylate anion and thus increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted acetic acid.

Take the differences rather than just the direction. The first chlorine is worth 1.90 pKa units, the second 1.57 and the third only 0.64. So the effects do add — three chlorines take the acid from 4.76 to 0.65, about four orders of magnitude — but each one buys less than the one before, because each finds less charge density left on the carboxylate to pull on. Resonance is not the explanation: both anions are ordinary carboxylates with the same delocalization over two oxygens, and the chlorines are not conjugated to anything. Only the sigma-framework pull differs.

Both acids give up an O–H, so the atom carrying the charge is oxygen in each case and A is a tie. The difference is what the anion can do next. Phenoxide pushes its charge into the aromatic ring, reaching the two ortho positions and the para position — three extra carbons to share it with, and the C–O bond picks up double-bond character in the process. tert-Butoxide has nowhere to send it. That is worth eight pKa units here, phenol 10 against tert-butanol 18. It is real stabilization and still less than acetate gets, because acetate’s charge lands on a second oxygen rather than on carbon.

A basicity question is an acidity question read backwards, and the translation is one line: the stronger base is the one whose conjugate acid has the higher pKa. Ethanol at 16 is the weaker acid, so ethoxide is the stronger base, by the full 11.2-unit gap. Structurally it is the same resonance argument seen from the other side — acetate’s charge is spread over two equivalent oxygens and is therefore comfortable and unreactive, while ethoxide’s sits entirely on one oxygen and is looking for somewhere to go. This is why you can keep sodium acetate in a bottle and buy it by the kilogram, and why sodium ethoxide has to be kept dry.

Compare what each deprotonation creates. Water starts neutral and ends as hydroxide, so a full negative charge has to be invented and found a home. Hydronium starts at +1 and ends neutral, so the charge is simply canceled — nothing new has to be stabilized. That is worth about seventeen pKa units here, and the same pattern holds for every pair you meet: NH₄⁺ at 9.2 against NH₃ at 38, a protonated alcohol at about −2 against an alcohol at 16. Charge is the largest single lever in the whole table, and it is why acid catalysis works: protonating a substrate manufactures a strong acid out of a weak one.

Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating by induction compared to a hydrogen atom, which slightly destabilizes the negative charge on acetate's conjugate base relative to formate, making formic acid marginally more acidic.

False. Bond strength is the argument for going down a group, not across a period, and here it points the wrong way: H–F is the strongest bond of the four and HF is by far the most acidic. What changes across a row is electronegativity, and with the atoms all about the same size that is what decides how comfortably the leftover charge is held. Fluorine holds it best, carbon worst, and the pKa values run 50, 38, 15.7, 3.2. Keep the two trends separate: electronegativity across, size and polarizability down, with the weakening H–X bond helping in the second case only.

These four hydrides are all second period, so the atoms are of similar size and the size argument has nothing to work with. What changes across the row is electronegativity, and it changes a lot: carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine. The more electronegative the atom, the more willingly it holds the negative charge left behind, so the anion is more stable and the acid is stronger. The pKa values are about 50, 38, 15.7 and 3.2 — nearly fifty orders of magnitude from one end to the other. Size only takes over when you go down a column instead, where HF at 3.2 is beaten by HI at −10 despite fluorine being the more electronegative.

Electronegativity is the right tool across a period, where the atoms are all about the same size: C–H, N–H, O–H, H–F run 50, 38, 15.7, 3.2 and the most electronegative atom does hold the charge best. Down a group the atoms change size dramatically and that becomes the dominant term. Iodide spreads one negative charge over a far bigger, more polarizable cloud than fluoride can, and the weaker H–I bond helps, so HI (pKa −10) beats HF (3.2) by thirteen orders of magnitude. Two different trends, two different reasons, and applying the period rule to a group comparison gets the answer exactly backwards.

The O-H formed by protonating a carbonyl oxygen has a pKa around -7, vastly lower than a typical alpha C-H, which has a pKa around 20, because oxygen stabilizes the resulting species far better than an unstabilized carbanion at carbon.

The second carbonyl-containing group, while not a halogen, is still electron-withdrawing by induction since carbonyl carbons are electron-poor, and its proximity to the first carboxylic acid group stabilizes the conjugate base, lowering pKa1 relative to acetic acid.

This is a genuine conflict between the first two factors. A favors the thiol: its charge lands on sulfur, which is large and polarizable and spreads one negative charge over a much bigger cloud than oxygen can — that is exactly why ethanethiol at 10.6 beats ethanol at 16. R favors the acid: acetate delocalizes over two equivalent oxygens while the thiolate has nowhere to send its charge. R wins by six units, ten to the sixth. So checking A first and stopping would give the wrong answer here. The order in ARIO is a search order, and when two factors disagree you have to draw both anions and weigh them.

None of the four structural factors separates these two: the charge is on oxygen in both, neither anion has resonance, neither has an electron-withdrawing group and both oxygens are sp³. What differs is bulk, and bulk matters because every pKa in the table was measured in a solvent. Water molecules can crowd round a small, compact methoxide and stabilize it; three methyl groups keep them away from tert-butoxide, so it is stabilized less and its parent acid is weaker. The proof is what happens when the solvent is removed: in the gas phase the order reverses and tert-butoxide is the more stable anion. Treat solvation as a reminder rather than a fifth factor — structure explains the anion, the solvent has the last word on the number.

Every option is a hydrogen on carbon, so A is fixed and the differences are all about what stabilizes the resulting carbanion. The 1,3-diketone wins at pKa 9: its anion delocalizes onto two carbonyl oxygens, so the charge spends most of its time on the most electronegative atoms available. A simple ketone’s alpha C–H manages 20 with only one oxygen to delocalize onto. A terminal alkyne is 25 — no resonance at all, but the pair sits in an sp orbital with 50 percent s character and is held close to the nucleus. An alkene C–H is sp² and about 44. A hydrogen on carbon as acidic as phenol is worth noticing: it is why 1,3-dicarbonyls are the workhorse nucleophiles of enolate chemistry.

Acidity is ultimately about conjugate base stability, and multiple factors often operate simultaneously, so a careful comparison must weigh all of them together rather than applying a single rule in isolation.

Take the four conjugate bases and ask which is most comfortable. Acetate, 4.76, is best off: full resonance over two equivalent oxygens. Phenoxide, 10, delocalizes into the ring but only onto carbons, so it gets real help and less of it. Trifluoroethoxide, 12.4, has no resonance at all but three fluorines pulling density away through the sigma bonds — pure induction, and worth 3.6 units against ethanol. Ethoxide, 16, has nothing: one charge, one oxygen, no help. So the order is resonance onto oxygen, then resonance onto carbon, then induction, then nothing, and it spans eleven pKa units.

True, and the distance dependence is the fingerprint that distinguishes induction from resonance. Induction is transmitted through the sigma framework and fades sharply with each additional bond: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is pKa 2.86, 3-chlorobutanoic 4.06 and 4-chlorobutanoic 4.52, against butanoic acid itself at 4.82. By the third carbon almost nothing is left. Resonance behaves quite differently: it runs the length of a conjugated system losing very little, so a nitro group four bonds away across a benzene ring still moves phenol’s pKa by nearly three units. When an exam asks which effect is operating, ask what happens when you move the group further away.

Resonance usually wins, because it delocalizes the actual charge onto extra atoms rather than merely shifting density along sigma bonds. But "usually" is doing real work in that sentence and an exam will test it. Phenol against an alcohol is six units from resonance; trifluoroacetic against acetic acid is 4.3 units from induction, and trichloroacetic is four units — comparable. Three fluorines beat the aromatic ring in phenoxide. The reliable approach is the one the ARIO order encodes: work down the list, stop at the first factor that differs, and when two factors point opposite ways draw both anions and weigh them rather than applying a slogan.

Convert both bases to their conjugate acids and compare pKa: ethylammonium 10.7, ammonium 9.2. The higher pKa belongs to the weaker acid, and the weaker acid leaves the stronger base, so ethylamine is the stronger base — by 1.5 units, about thirty fold. Two traps sit beside it. Saying “ammonia, because its conjugate acid is the weaker one” uses the right logic on a backwards fact: ammonium at 9.2 is the stronger acid, not the weaker. And size is not what separates these two — the ethyl group is weakly electron-donating and pushes density onto nitrogen, which is the structural reason ethylamine wins, not a steric one. Converting the base to its conjugate acid first is the habit that stops these going backwards.
newman: The front atom is represented as a point with three lines radiating out; the back atom is the circle behind it.

Sixty degrees between the reference groups is gauche, and gauche is staggered — every front bond sits in a gap, so there is no torsional strain at all. The 0.9 kcal/mol is purely the two methyls bumping into each other at that angle: steric strain with nothing else mixed in.

Sight down C1–C2: the front carbon carries three hydrogens and the back carbon carries two hydrogens and a methyl. Eclipsing lines up three pairs, and only one of them involves the methyl — 1.4 + 1.0 + 1.0 = 3.4 kcal/mol, which is the measured barrier. The point of the per-interaction values is exactly this: you can price a conformer you have never seen.
The front atom sits at the center (its three bonds radiate from the center dot), while the back atom is represented by the circle itself, so its bonds are drawn from the circle's edge.
The dihedral angle describes the angular relationship, looking straight down the C-C bond, between a substituent on the front carbon and one on the back carbon.
Staggered conformations space the front and back substituents as far apart as possible, giving dihedral angles of 60 degrees, 180 degrees, and 300 degrees around the full rotation.
Anti means the two largest groups point in exactly opposite directions when viewed down the bond, which is a 180 degree dihedral angle.
Gauche conformers are staggered but have the two reference groups only 60 degrees apart, rather than fully opposite as in the anti conformer.

Staggering lets each C-H bond on one carbon donate into the antibonding orbital of a C-H bond on the other, and eclipsing switches that hyperconjugative stabilization off. That torsional cost applies to every eclipsed arrangement of ethane, so no eclipsed form is lower in energy than any staggered one.

Torsional strain. The modern account of it is hyperconjugation: in a staggered arrangement each filled C–H sigma orbital lines up with an empty C–H antibonding (sigma*) orbital on the neighboring carbon, which is worth real stabilization, and eclipsing destroys that alignment. Ethane's hydrogens are far too small to be bumping into each other, so nothing steric is involved.
Rotation barriers around single C-C bonds are typically only a few kcal/mol, so at room temperature molecules rotate through all conformations far too quickly to separate them.
Each of the three hydrogens on the front carbon lines up directly with one hydrogen on the back carbon, giving three separate eclipsing interactions.

Anti and gauche are not words about methyl groups — they describe the dihedral angle between whichever pair you have nominated as the reference, conventionally the two largest. Here that is the two bromines, so the anti conformer at 180° puts them as far apart as rotation allows and is the minimum.

Anti means the two reference groups are 180° apart and gauche means 60°. Which pair counts as the reference is a choice you announce, and the convention is to pick the two largest groups because those are the ones whose clash sets the energy. Say which pair you are tracking and the vocabulary works on any molecule.
Even though gauche butane is staggered and free of torsional strain, the two methyl groups are close enough at 60 degrees apart to experience unfavorable steric crowding.
Butane's methyl groups are much bulkier than ethane's hydrogens, so in addition to any torsional effects, gauche butane suffers extra steric strain that small hydrogens in ethane never experience.
C2 of propane is bonded to C1 (the front atom in this view), C3 (a methyl group), and two hydrogens, so in the Newman projection the back atom shows a methyl group and two hydrogens.

Anti butane is the global energy minimum because the methyls are farthest apart, while the two gauche conformers are mirror-image-like and therefore equal in energy to each other, both higher than anti.
The two gauche conformers are related by reflection (one has the methyl rotated +60 degrees, the other -60 degrees from anti) and are otherwise structurally equivalent, so they have identical energy.

The front carbon (C2) carries two methyls and a hydrogen; the back carbon (C3) carries one methyl and two hydrogens. Rotating the back carbon gives three staggered arrangements. Putting the back methyl between the two front methyls gives two gauche CH₃/CH₃ pairs; the other two arrangements give one each. So the best conformers cost about 0.9 kcal/mol, and — unlike butane — there is no conformer with no gauche strain at all.

Eclipsing costs torsional strain whatever the groups are. Two methyl groups brought to 0° are also pushed into each other through space, so they pay van der Waals repulsion as well. Eclipsed conformers carry steric strain on top of torsional strain, which is why the syn conformer is the highest point on butane's curve rather than merely another eclipse.

Rotating 360 degrees passes through three eclipsed arrangements; the one eclipsing both methyl groups is distinctly higher than the other two, which eclipse a methyl with a hydrogen and are equal to each other.
There are three minima (anti plus two gauche) and three maxima (one methyl-methyl eclipsed plus two methyl-hydrogen eclipsed), but anti is lower than the two equal-energy gauche minima.

Ethane's substituents are hydrogen atoms, which are small enough that at 0° they are still not pressing into one another — so there is no steric component to subtract. What remains is the loss of the hyperconjugative overlap that staggering allows, worth about 1 kcal/mol per eclipsing pair and 2.9 kcal/mol for all three. Butane's barrier is larger precisely because its methyl groups add a steric term that ethane has not got.

Each central carbon bears two methyl groups; fixing one pair anti to each other still leaves the remaining methyl groups positioned gauche to groups on the neighboring carbon, contributing extra strain beyond simple butane.

Populations follow ΔG = −RT ln K, and at room temperature RT is about 0.59 kcal/mol — so 0.9 kcal/mol is already more than one factor of e. Note the second ingredient: there are two gauche conformers and one anti, so the count works in gauche's favor, and anti still wins. Small energy differences buy large population differences.
Bulkier substituents add steric strain on top of the intrinsic torsional strain present even in ethane, so rotational barriers tend to rise as the groups attached to the rotating bond get larger.

Read it back out as a chain. The front carbon is bonded to a methyl, two hydrogens and the back carbon; the back carbon is bonded to an ethyl, two hydrogens and the front carbon. Strung together that is CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ — pentane — and the bond joining the dot to the circle is C2–C3.

Anti and gauche butane are both staggered conformations, so there is no eclipsing (torsional) strain difference between them; the energy gap is due to steric strain from the methyl groups being closer together in the gauche form.

With three methyl groups on each central carbon, there is no way to rotate the molecule into a conformation free of substantial steric clash, so all conformers, even the most staggered one, carry extra strain compared to butane.
cyclohexanes: The chair avoids angle strain (near-tetrahedral angles) and torsional strain (fully staggered), unlike boat or planar forms.
The boat has eclipsing interactions along its sides and a steric clash between the two "flagpole" hydrogens.
The twist-boat is a slightly lower-energy variant of the boat that partially relieves the flagpole steric clash, but it’s still well above the chair in energy.

About 111 degrees — within two degrees of the ideal tetrahedral 109.5, so the angle strain is essentially nil. The chair is not quite perfect on angles; what makes it remarkable is that it gets that close while also staggering every ring bond, which a flat hexagon at 120 degrees cannot do.

Burn a cycloalkane completely and it releases a measurable amount of energy. A strain-free CH₂ group releases 157.4 kcal/mol, so multiply that by the ring size to get what the ring ought to give. Anything it releases above that figure was energy stored in its strained bonds, and that excess is the ring strain quoted in the table.

The boat has several eclipsed C-H bonds along its sides, which is torsional strain, plus two flagpole hydrogens on the raised ends that point toward each other, which is steric strain. Bond angles stay near tetrahedral, so angle strain is not the problem here.
The half-chair is actually a high-energy transition state along the ring-flip pathway, not a resting conformation; molecules pass through it only briefly while interconverting between other forms.

Chair is the global minimum; twist-boat is next lowest because twisting relieves some strain present in the regular boat; boat is higher still; and the half-chair, a transition state, is highest in energy.
The twist partially un-eclipses the ring C-C bonds that were aligned in the regular boat and pulls the flagpole hydrogens slightly apart, so twist-boat sits lower in energy than boat.
The chair is a non-planar, puckered arrangement with alternating carbons above and below an average plane; this puckering is exactly what allows ideal tetrahedral angles and staggered bonds.

The chair holds its C–C–C angles at about 111 degrees, within two degrees of tetrahedral, and sighting down any ring bond gives a perfectly staggered Newman projection. Near-ideal angles and no eclipsing at the same time is what no smaller ring can manage.

A planar cyclobutane would have 90° angles; the puckered one has about 88°, which is worse. It accepts that in exchange for partly staggering its C–H bonds. A molecule that trades angle strain away to buy torsional relief is telling you torsional strain is not a small effect — which is the lesson cyclohexane then applies at a ring size where it can escape both.
Experimentally, the boat conformation sits roughly 6 to 7 kcal/mol above the chair, reflecting the substantial torsional and flagpole steric strain present in the boat.

Both isomers burn to the same products, so they finish at the same energy. The strained isomer starts higher up, and the heat released is the drop between start and finish — so it gives out more. This is exactly why 'which isomer has the higher heat of combustion' is answerable at all, and why a conformational difference of a kcal or two is a measurable quantity rather than a bookkeeping device.

27.5, 26.3, 6.2 and essentially 0 kcal/mol. The interesting feature is the cliff between four carbons and five: cyclopropane and cyclobutane are locked into badly wrong angles, while cyclopentane already has near-ideal 108° angles and only has eclipsing left to deal with. By six carbons a ring can pucker its way out of both problems at once.
The half-chair is a saddle point on the conformational energy surface, the highest-energy structure molecules pass through while ring-flipping from one chair-related form to another.
The boat conformation has two carbons that point upward out of the main ring plane; the hydrogens on these two 'tip' carbons point toward each other and are called flagpole hydrogens.

Transannular means 'across the ring'. A seven- or eight-membered ring is loose enough for its two sides to fold toward each other and too tight for the hydrogens on those sides to get out of each other's way. Small rings are too taut to suffer it and rings of a dozen carbons and up are floppy enough to avoid it, which makes the medium rings the most strained sizes after the small ones.

A transition state is a peak: passed over in a single vibration and never occupied. The half-chair is one, and so is the symmetric boat, which sits between two twist-boats. The twist-boat itself is a dip — shallow, short-lived, but a real conformation. Knowing which of the four is a dip and which are peaks is the distinction the energy ladder is drawn to make.
The chair remains the global energy minimum; twist-boat is only the lowest-energy member of the boat family, still several kcal/mol above the chair.

The twist partially un-eclipses ring bonds and separates the flagpole hydrogens, producing a net stabilization relative to the symmetric boat, even though a slight new strain is introduced by the twist itself.

Angle strain is not cyclopentane's problem — 108° is within a degree and a half of tetrahedral. Planarity is: every adjacent C–H pair would be eclipsed. Puckering bends the angles down to around 104°, which is cheap, and buys a large amount of torsional relief, which is not. The residual 6.2 kcal/mol is what is left over after that compromise.
The ring flip proceeds chair to half-chair to twist-boat to half-chair to chair, so two distinct half-chair transition states are crossed in a single flip.
The boat and half-chair are distinct geometries with different numbers and arrangements of eclipsed bonds and ring puckering; they are not interchangeable descriptions of the same structure.

The chair's puckering is a geometric solution unique to a six-membered ring that allows perfect bond angles with no eclipsing, whereas smaller rings like cyclopropane are forced into angle strain and cyclopentane into some torsional strain regardless of puckering.

A planar cyclohexane would have 120° angles and twelve eclipsed C–H pairs — a great deal of strain. What is special about six carbons is that a pucker exists which fixes both at once: 111° angles and a perfectly staggered Newman projection down every ring bond. The strain is absent because of a shape the molecule adopts, not because of an exemption it enjoys.

The actual lowest-energy pathway passes predominantly through twist-boat intermediates, since twist-boat is more stable than the symmetric boat; the plain boat is a higher-energy, less-traveled point on the overall surface.

Because the chair is several kcal/mol more stable than any boat-family conformation, the equilibrium population strongly favors the chair, leaving only a tiny fraction in higher-energy forms at any given moment.
Both chair and boat keep bond angles reasonably close to tetrahedral; the boat's extra energy comes mainly from torsional strain (eclipsed bonds) and flagpole steric strain, not from angle strain.

The chair's near-total absence of both angle and torsional strain is a special geometric outcome of the six-membered ring; larger and smaller rings typically cannot fully escape some strain in any conformation they adopt.
axial-equatorial: Equatorial positions point outward around the ring’s perimeter, avoiding the 1,3-diaxial interactions that axial groups face.
Equatorial placement avoids steric clashes (1,3-diaxial interactions) with other axial substituents, so bulky groups prefer equatorial.

Cis means the same face, so the second group must also point up. Axial directions alternate, so C2's axial points down — which means C2's equatorial bond is the one angled up. Putting the group there makes it up (hence cis) and equatorial at the same time. This is the whole of the 'up is not axial' trap: the face and the label are two separate questions.
Axial positions alternate, pointing up on one carbon and down on the next as you go around the ring, all roughly parallel to the ring's main symmetry axis.

K = e^(ΔG/RT) = e^(1.7/0.59) ≈ 18, which is about 95:5. The relationship is exponential, which is why it is worth running once: tripling the energy gap to tert-butyl's 4.9 multiplies the ratio by more than two hundred rather than by three.

A tert-butyl group does not lock the ring in principle — the flip barrier is barely changed. What it does is make the other chair so sparsely populated that the molecule is, for practical purposes, one conformer. Much of what is known about axial versus equatorial reactivity was measured on rings anchored this way.
Because the ring carbons alternate slightly above and below the average plane, their axial bonds alternate direction, up on one carbon, down on the next, all the way around.
Since cyclohexane is CH2 repeated six times, each carbon's two hydrogens occupy the one axial and one equatorial position available on that carbon.
An axial group points toward axial hydrogens (or groups) on the carbons three atoms away around the ring (1 and 3 relationship), creating steric clashes called 1,3-diaxial interactions.
Counting around the ring, an axial group at C1 points toward the axial substituents at C3 and C5, which are close enough in space to clash with it.
With only hydrogens attached, flipping the ring just swaps which hydrogens are labeled axial versus equatorial on an otherwise identical molecule, so there is no energy difference.
Equatorial bonds radiate outward around the 'equator' of the ring, lying much closer to the average ring plane than the axial bonds do.
The methyl group's modest A-value (about 1.7 kcal/mol) corresponds to roughly a 95:5 equatorial-to-axial ratio at room temperature, strongly favoring equatorial but not completely excluding axial.
When axial, the methyl group clashes sterically with the axial hydrogens at the 3 and 5 positions; moving it equatorial removes most of that strain, making the equatorial conformer more stable.

A halogen is a smooth sphere sitting at the end of a long C–X bond, so it reaches into the 1,3-diaxial space very little. A methyl group is lighter but sticks three hydrogens out sideways at a shorter distance. A-value tracks how much room a group demands near the ring, which is why the ordering follows shape rather than atomic weight.
The A-value is defined as the free energy preference for equatorial over axial, so by definition a larger A-value means a stronger equatorial preference.
Isopropyl is bulkier than methyl, so its 1,3-diaxial clashes when axial are more severe, giving it a larger A-value and a stronger preference for the equatorial position.

Geometrically, an axial substituent and an axial hydrogen three carbons away around the ring are positioned much like the two methyl groups in gauche butane, so the strain is often compared to a gauche interaction.

An axial isopropyl can turn its lone hydrogen toward the 1,3-diaxial space and keep both its methyls pointing away. A tert-butyl group has no hydrogen on that carbon: whichever way it rotates, a whole methyl is aimed into the ring. The cliff between them is about what a group can do to get out of the way, not about how big it is on paper.

An axial group on C1 and an axial group on C3 are on the same face and about the same distance apart as the two methyls of gauche butane. The repulsion is identical in kind. The difference is that butane can rotate out of it and a ring cannot: the geometry is held, which is why the cost shows up as a fixed conformational preference rather than a passing arrangement.

Only C3 and C5 carry axial positions on the same face as C1, so there are two clashes, one with each. A methyl's A-value of 1.7 is close to two gauche-butane interactions at about 0.9 each, which is the arithmetic behind the number rather than a coincidence.
Fluorine is a small atom with a short C-F bond, so its 1,3-diaxial clash is mild; its A-value (roughly 0.2 to 0.3 kcal/mol) is considerably smaller than methyl's (about 1.7 kcal/mol).

A-value scales roughly with steric bulk: small fluorine has the weakest equatorial preference, methyl is intermediate, and the very bulky tert-butyl group has by far the strongest equatorial preference.

Because tert-butyl is essentially three methyl groups bundled on one carbon, placing it axial would force multiple severe steric clashes simultaneously, vastly exceeding the strain from a single axial methyl.

Equatorial substituents still have some gauche-type interactions with neighboring ring bonds; they simply avoid the much larger 1,3-diaxial clashes that axial substituents face, so their strain is reduced, not zero.

Geometrically, the equatorial orientation directs a substituent away from other ring atoms, while the axial orientation aims it straight at the axial groups on the 1,3-related carbons, which is the structural root of the steric difference.
An A-value of zero means there is no free energy preference between the two positions, which corresponds to an equal, 50:50 population at equilibrium.

Because an axial substituent experiences 1,3-diaxial clashes with both the C3 and C5 positions simultaneously, its total strain is often approximated as about twice that of a single gauche interaction.

The ordering follows the room a group demands beside the ring. Cyanide is a thin rod pointing straight out and scores about 0.2; bromide is a smooth sphere on a long bond, about 0.5; hydroxyl is 0.9. tert-Butyl at 4.9 is in a different class, because it cannot avoid pushing a methyl group into the 1,3-diaxial space whichever way it turns.

Even though chlorine is a larger atom, its longer carbon-halogen bond moves it farther from the ring, and its roughly spherical shape clashes less than the three hydrogens of a methyl group, giving it a smaller A-value than expected from atomic size alone.
ring-flips: A ring flip interconverts the two chair forms — every axial position becomes equatorial and vice versa.
Ring flips are conformational changes, not bond-breaking — cis/trans relationships (configuration) are preserved; only which substituents are axial vs. equatorial changes.

For a single non-hydrogen substituent, axial and equatorial chairs differ in energy (the equatorial is lower); only when the "substituent" is H (unsubstituted cyclohexane) are both chair forms identical in energy.

A flip swaps axial for equatorial on every carbon and leaves every group on the face it was already on. Both groups started up, so both finish up; both labels reverse. Note why the methyl sits on C2 for this to be drawable: axial directions alternate round the ring, so C1 axial-up forces C2 axial-down and therefore C2 equatorial-up. On C3, which shares C1's axial direction, the equatorial bond points down instead.
Ring flipping only involves rotation about existing sigma bonds to reshape the ring; it never breaks or forms any covalent bonds, unlike a configurational change such as a reaction.

Every bond in the ring is a sigma bond, and sigma bonds rotate. Turning them in a coordinated way carries the ring through the half-chair and twist-boat shapes and into the other chair, with the same atoms bonded to the same atoms throughout. That is what makes a flip a conformational change rather than a reaction.

A substituent's up/down face assignment is a fixed structural (configurational) feature of the molecule; the ring flip changes only whether that same substituent happens to be axial or equatorial in the new chair.

With a barrier of only about 10–11 kcal/mol, a cyclohexane ring flips roughly 100,000 times a second at room temperature — about a million times slower than an ethane bond rotation, and still far too fast for the two chairs to be seen separately until the sample is cooled to around −90 °C.
As the ring flips, it must pass over an energy barrier corresponding to the half-chair geometry before relaxing into the twist-boat and eventually the other chair.
Because all six ring carbons bear only hydrogens, flipping just relabels which hydrogens are axial and which are equatorial on an otherwise indistinguishable structure, so there is no energy change.

Rate falls off exponentially with barrier height, so the extra 8 kcal/mol costs nearly six orders of magnitude: ethane spins at 10¹⁰–10¹¹ per second and a ring flips at about 10⁵. A million times slower, and still far too fast to catch — which is why cyclohexane has to be cooled to about −90 °C before NMR sees the two kinds of hydrogen separately.
In the trans-1,4 pattern both methyl groups flip together from equatorial to axial (or vice versa), so the ring flip swaps a diequatorial conformer for a diaxial one.
In the cis-1,4 pattern, one methyl is always axial while the other is equatorial; flipping swaps which carbon has which, but the overall strain, and therefore the energy, stays the same.

A flip always reverses both labels, but only some patterns put both groups in the same column to start with. On 1,2 and 1,4 carbons the axial directions are opposite, so a trans (opposite-face) pair lands both equatorial or both axial. On 1,3 carbons the axial directions match, so it is cis that does. Work out the faces first and the pattern falls out of the drawing.
Placing both methyl groups equatorial avoids all the 1,3-diaxial strain that the diaxial alternative would create, making the diequatorial conformer strongly favored.
Cis/trans relationships are configurational, fixed by which face of the ring each substituent is attached to; a ring flip only changes axial/equatorial positions, never the underlying configuration.

Cis-1,4-disubstitution always places one substituent axial and one equatorial; flipping just swaps which carbon carries which role, leaving the overall energy unchanged when the two groups are identical. Each of the others is lopsided: trans-1,2, trans-1,4 and cis-1,3 all offer a diequatorial chair and a diaxial one, and the diequatorial chair wins.
The full lowest-energy pathway goes from chair up over a half-chair transition state, down into the twist-boat, back up over a second half-chair, and finally down into the other chair.
With any substituent bulkier than hydrogen, the axial conformer suffers 1,3-diaxial strain that the equatorial conformer avoids, so the two ring-flip conformers are no longer equal in energy.

Cis on adjacent carbons means one group is up and the other is up too — and since the axial directions alternate, one of them has to be axial whichever chair you pick. Flipping just swaps which one pays, so the two chairs tie. Trans can put both equatorial in one chair and both axial in the other, which is a real difference of about 2.5 kcal/mol.

Since both substituents are identical methyl groups on the same carbon, one is always axial and the other equatorial; flipping swaps which one is which but keeps the total strain, and thus the energy, the same.

Because both tert-butyl groups must move together on a ring flip, the only alternative to the diequatorial conformer is a diaxial one with two extremely bulky groups clashing severely, making that conformer vanishingly rare.
Cis-1,2-disubstitution always gives one axial and one equatorial methyl; flipping swaps which ring carbon carries which role, producing a conformer of identical energy to the first.

Trans on 1,4 carbons allows both groups equatorial in one chair, and the flip would make both axial. Two axial tert-butyl groups is about 4.9 + 4.9, far more than thermal energy will pay for. The ring still flips — the barrier is unchanged — but the other chair is never meaningfully populated, which is the conformational-anchor trick in its strongest form.

A genuine flip pushes the raised end of the chair down and the lowered end up, so every axial/equatorial label reverses while every face stays put. If nothing reversed, the ring is in the same conformation and you have only turned the picture. The test is worth doing every time: exactly one of the two properties should have changed.
The flip passes chair to half-chair to twist-boat to a second half-chair to the other chair, crossing two distinct half-chair energy barriers along the way.

Twist-boat relieves some of the torsional and flagpole strain present in the symmetric boat, so the ring flip pathway favors passing through twist-boat rather than lingering in the higher-energy plain boat.

Cis-1,3-disubstitution allows both substituents to be equatorial together in one chair; ring flipping moves them both to axial together in the other chair, just as with trans-1,4 and trans-1,2 patterns.
Because axial substituents suffer 1,3-diaxial strain that scales with their size, the equilibrium strongly favors whichever chair places a bulky group equatorial, minimizing that strain.

A large A-value says how much the two chairs differ in energy, not how high the hill between them is. tert-Butylcyclohexane flips at much the same rate as cyclohexane itself; it simply spends almost all its time on one side. Confusing a population effect with a rate effect is the standard trap here.
conformational-analysis: Placing bulky groups equatorial minimizes 1,3-diaxial strain, giving the lowest-energy conformation.

The diaxial chair carries 1.7 + 1.7 = 3.4. The diequatorial chair carries no axial penalty, but its two methyls sit on adjacent carbons and are gauche to each other, worth 0.9. The difference is 3.4 − 0.9 = 2.5, against a measured 2.7. Adding A-values alone would have said 3.4; the gauche correction is what brings it into line.
For 1,2-disubstitution, cis substituents are one axial/one equatorial (and trans are both axial or both equatorial) — the reverse of the 1,3 relationship.

On 1,3 carbons the axial directions match, so a cis pair goes both-equatorial in one chair and both-axial in the other. The diaxial chair pays two CH₃/H diaxial contacts plus the direct CH₃/CH₃ clash between the two axial methyls, which is worth about 3.7 on its own — roughly 5.4 in total. Simple A-value addition would have predicted only 3.4, so this is the case where the direct-interaction correction matters most.
Trans-1,4 substitution geometrically allows both substituents to be equatorial simultaneously, which is almost always the lower-energy, preferred arrangement.

A wedge comes up out of the page and a hash goes down behind it, so this pair is on opposite faces: trans. Faces are what survives the ring flip and what decides whether both groups can be equatorial at all, so they are recorded first. Only once the groups are placed on their faces in a numbered chair do the A-values have anything to act on.

Cis on 1,4 carbons forces one group axial whichever chair you pick, so the only question is which one pays. Axial tert-butyl costs 4.9; axial methyl costs 1.7; the difference is 3.2 in favor of axialising the methyl. The bulkier group takes equatorial and the smaller absorbs the cost — and the answer comes out of the arithmetic rather than out of a preference for tert-butyl.

Up, down, up, down round the ring. Adjacent carbons therefore have opposite axial directions, so a pair on opposite faces (trans) lands in matching columns. Carbons two apart have the same axial direction, so it is the same-face pair (cis) that matches. Draw the chair and number it and you never have to remember which is which.
As with trans-1,4, the trans-1,2 relationship allows both substituents to be equatorial together, which is normally the more stable choice.

Trans on 1,4 carbons allows both groups equatorial in one chair, so it does. The flip would put both axial at a cost of 0.9 + 4.9 = 5.8, and 1,4 groups are too far apart for a direct correction. When a diequatorial chair is available the arithmetic barely needs doing — the work is in deciding whether the pattern allows it.

Because a bulkier group (higher A-value) suffers a larger energy penalty when forced axial, the lowest-energy conformer is the one that places the substituent with the greater A-value in the equatorial position.

The cis-1,4 pattern forces one group axial; since tert-butyl's A-value vastly exceeds methyl's, the lower-energy conformer puts the much bulkier tert-butyl group equatorial and accepts methyl axial instead.
Because the trans-1,4 relationship allows both groups to be equatorial simultaneously, and both substituents prefer equatorial, this diequatorial conformer is overwhelmingly the most stable.

The chair fixes the angles: adjacent equatorial groups are about 60° apart and an axial/equatorial pair about 60° as well. Only the two axial positions on adjacent carbons — one pointing up, one pointing down, because axial directions alternate — reach the 180° that anti-periplanar means. That single geometric fact is what makes conformational analysis predictive about elimination.
Since A-values approximate the strain penalty of having a given group axial, the conformation with less total axial strain corresponds to the more stable structure.
The cis-1,3 relationship is the pattern that geometrically permits both substituents to sit equatorial simultaneously, and that diequatorial form is indeed the most stable.

Because trans-1,3 substitution cannot achieve a diequatorial arrangement, both chair conformers have one methyl axial and one equatorial, and the molecule is forced to accept some axial strain either way.
This systematic approach, summing A-value-based penalties for axial groups in each chair, is the standard method for predicting which conformer of a multiply-substituted cyclohexane will dominate.
When neither conformer has a net strain advantage over the other, there is no free energy difference driving the equilibrium toward one side, giving an approximately equal population.

Since ethyl has a somewhat larger A-value than methyl, putting the bulkier ethyl group equatorial (and accepting methyl axial instead) minimizes the total axial strain, making that conformer more stable.

The trans isomer enjoys a genuinely diequatorial lowest-energy conformer, avoiding all 1,3-diaxial strain, whereas the cis isomer is stuck with at least one substituent axial no matter which chair it adopts.

The diaxial chair carries two axial methyls: 1.7 + 1.7 = 3.4. The diequatorial chair carries no axial penalty, but its two methyls are on adjacent carbons and therefore gauche to each other, worth 0.9. So the preference is 3.4 − 0.9 = 2.5, against a measured 2.7. Adding A-values alone overstates it, and the gauche correction is what closes the gap.

For cis-1,2, both interconverting chairs are ax,eq combinations of roughly comparable strain, so the energy gap between them is small; for trans-1,2, one chair is diequatorial (very favorable) and the other diaxial (very unfavorable), producing a much larger gap.

Whether both groups can be equatorial at once is fixed before any energy is considered: it depends on the two faces and the two positions, and a ring flip cannot change either. cis-1,2, cis-1,4 and trans-1,3 rings have one group axial in both chairs, so the question becomes which group pays rather than whether anything has to.

The geometric rule is that trans works for the 1,2 and 1,4 relationships while cis works for the 1,3 relationship; the opposite stereochemistry in each case is always forced into a mixed axial/equatorial arrangement.

Because trans-1,4 substitution permits both substituents to be equatorial at once, and both OH and tert-butyl individually prefer equatorial, the diequatorial conformer is strongly favored with no conflict between them.

Since cis-1,4 substitution forces one group axial, the molecule 'sacrifices' the position of the substituent with the smaller A-value (OH) to keep the much bulkier, higher-A-value tert-butyl group equatorial.

While the bulkiest substituent's A-value often dominates the decision, every substituent contributes some strain energy when axial, so a rigorous analysis sums the contributions of all substituents rather than ignoring the smaller ones.

Because tert-butyl presents three methyl groups on one carbon, forcing it axial creates multiple simultaneous 1,3-diaxial clashes rather than just one, which is why its A-value is so much larger than a simple alkyl group's.

A-values are empirically averaged steric parameters; real molecules can have additional effects (electronic, hydrogen bonding, or unusual geometries) not captured by a simple sum of standard A-values, so predictions are approximate.
radical-halogenation: Br2 and an alkane in a dark flask do nothing at all. The light or heat is what initiates the chain, which is why bromine water distinguishes an alkene from an alkane.
Homolysis sends one electron to each atom, giving two neutral radicals rather than a cation and an anion.
Two fishhooks are needed to break one bond, one for each electron. Mixing arrow types is the commonest drawing error here.
Up from zero is initiation, unchanged is propagation, down to zero is termination. The product is not what distinguishes them.
The count is unchanged, so the chain can go round again. This is propagation even when the product appears in this very step.

Multiply count by rate. Primary: 6 × 1 = 6. Secondary: 2 × 4 = 8. Total 14, so 8/14 ≈ 57% secondary and 6/14 ≈ 43% primary. The four-to-one selectivity nearly cancels against three times as many primary hydrogens, which is why chlorination of propane is a mixture you would have to separate.
Two radicals have to collide, and there are very few in the flask at any moment. A single initiation can turn over thousands of molecules first.
Radicals follow the same order as carbocations, and for the same reason: hyperconjugation from neighboring C-H bonds into the half-filled orbital.
Bromine is highly selective. Chlorine's corresponding figure is only about 5, which is why chlorination gives mixtures.

Primary: 9 × 1 = 9. Tertiary: 1 × 5 = 5. Total 14, so the primary chloride is 9/14 ≈ 64% — the major product comes from the less stable radical. Run the same substrate with bromine (1600 to 1) and the tertiary bromide is about 99%. One molecule, two halogens, opposite answers: that is the whole selectivity story in one calculation.

Abstraction by bromine is endothermic — a C–H at about 98 kcal/mol is traded for an H–Br at 87.5 — so by the Hammond postulate the transition state resembles the products. The radical is essentially fully formed at the top of the barrier, so every kcal/mol of its stability is already showing up in the rate.

ΔH is the bond broken minus the bond made. For chlorine, 98 − 103 = −5, downhill. For bromine, 98 − 87.5 = +10.5, uphill. By the Hammond postulate the downhill step has an early, reactant-like transition state where the radical has barely formed, and the uphill one has a late, radical-like transition state where the radical's stability is already priced in — which is exactly the selectivity difference.
The carbon radical is essentially planar with its electron in a p orbital, so the halogen arrives on either face equally. No conditions make this enantioselective.
Six primary hydrogens at rate 1 against two secondary at about 4 gives 6 to 8 — close to even, because the counts nearly offset the modest selectivity.

Count sets of equivalent hydrogens, not carbons. The two end methyls are equivalent to each other and the two middle CH₂ groups are equivalent to each other, so there are two sets and therefore two products: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane. Finding the sets first is half the marks in any 'how many products' question.
N-bromosuccinimide releases bromine slowly and keeps its concentration permanently low.
Adding Br2 to an alkene is faster than the radical chain, but addition needs a reasonable Br2 concentration and the chain does not. Starve it and substitution wins.
The unpaired electron is delocalized across the pi system, which makes the abstraction much easier than the substitution pattern alone would suggest.
Bromine can end up at either end of the delocalized system. Drawing both resonance forms of the radical is how you predict the second product.
The peroxide starts a radical chain, so a bromine radical adds first rather than a proton.
The first species to add is no longer a proton seeking the better carbocation, but a bromine radical seeking the more stable carbon radical — which puts Br on the other carbon.

Count radicals across each step. The three terminations go from two radicals to none. The odd one out starts with one radical and ends with one — it consumes a carbon radical and hands back a bromine radical, so the chain carries on. It makes the product, which is exactly why it gets mislabeled; the stage is read off the radical count and never off the product.

Radical halogenation of an alkane has to be started, and in a dark flask at room temperature nothing initiates it. A double bond reacts with bromine directly, with no initiation step, which is why the test works. The reaction behind that is taught in the Alkenes & Alkynes chapter — here it matters only as the reason the light in these conditions is not decoration.
Radical steps move single electrons and give neutral species. A charge means a pair of electrons moved, which is a different mechanism.
