It is the same ΔH arithmetic. H–F is 136 kcal/mol, so abstraction by F• is downhill by nearly 40 — unselective to the point of uselessness and often explosive. H–I is only 71, so abstraction by I• is uphill by about 27, a barrier too high to cross at any workable temperature. Chlorine and bromine sit in the narrow window between the two.

Bromine is the selective halogen: 1600 to 1 for tertiary over primary per hydrogen, which beats the nine-to-one head start the primary hydrogens have. Light is not optional — without it there is no initiation and no chain. NBS is for allylic positions, where the point is keeping the bromine concentration low, not reaching a tertiary carbon.
Initiation is the slow, expensive step and only has to happen once per chain. That is the whole trick.
The molecular ion fragments to leave the most stable radical it can, which is the same stability order you learned here.
That planarity is exactly why a new stereocenter formed this way comes out racemic.

The carbon radical is essentially planar, with its unpaired electron in a p orbital sticking out of both faces equally. Bromine arrives on one face or the other with equal ease, so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts. That is a structural fact about the intermediate — no change of solvent or temperature makes a plain radical halogenation enantioselective.
chirality: The vertical plane through Cl, C and H exchanges the two substituents on either side of it. Those are both methyl groups, so the reflection gives back the same molecule and the plane is genuine — 2-chloropropane is achiral. Swap one methyl for an ethyl, making 2-chlorobutane, and the same reflection sends methyl onto ethyl, which is a different molecule; that compound is chiral.

A plane is only a plane of symmetry if reflecting in it returns the same molecule, so every pair of groups it exchanges has to be identical — compared as whole groups, not just first atoms. A plane that swaps a methyl for an ethyl is a feature of the drawing, not of the molecule. Note that the reverse mistake is also common: failing to find a plane in one drawn conformation settles nothing, because a plane present in any accessible conformation makes the compound achiral.
A shoe is a classic macroscopic chiral object — its mirror image (the other foot’s shoe) is not superimposable on the original.
The defining test for chirality is whether a molecule's mirror image can be rotated and translated to exactly overlap the original. If not, the molecule is chiral.

Chirality is a property of the whole molecule's symmetry, not just of individual carbons. Substituted allenes and certain biphenyls are chiral through axial or restricted-rotation chirality without a classic stereocenter.
Dichloromethane's central carbon carries two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, giving it an internal mirror plane, so it is achiral.
If a molecule has two or more such stereocenters arranged symmetrically, their effects can cancel, producing an achiral meso compound even though individual centers have four different substituents.
Chiral compounds (in non-racemic form) rotate the plane of polarized light passing through them; this optical activity is measured with a polarimeter.
Glycine's alpha carbon bears two identical hydrogen atoms in addition to the amino and carboxyl groups, so it fails the four-different-groups test and is achiral.

A stereocenter is a single atom whose substituents can be arranged two ways; chirality is a property of the entire molecule's overall symmetry, which can differ from what any one center suggests (as in meso compounds).

Biological receptors are themselves chiral, so they often bind the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule differently, which is why mirror-image compounds can have different biological or sensory effects despite having identical formulas.
Thalidomide's two enantiomers have very different biological activities, showing why distinguishing and controlling chirality matters in drug development, not just in academic classification.

The two chairs are mirror images of each other and interconvert about a hundred thousand times a second, so the molecule spends half its life as each and cannot be resolved. Flattened out it does have an internal mirror plane between C1 and C2: the compound is meso, and achiral. A plane found in any accessible conformation settles the question; the absence of one in a single drawn conformation does not.

Stereocenter counting is a useful shortcut, but meso compounds show that a molecule with multiple stereocenters can still be achiral overall, so the mirror-image superimposability test is the truly reliable method.

Count outward from C3 in both directions: one way is C2-C1, an ethyl group; the other is C4-C5-C6, a propyl group. With a methyl and a hydrogen as well, that is four different groups, so C3 is a stereocenter and the molecule is chiral. The chains only look symmetric until you count them.
Enantiomers differ only in how they interact with other chiral influences, such as polarized light or chiral reagents; their standard bulk physical properties in an achiral environment are identical.

When bulky ortho substituents prevent free rotation about the biaryl bond, the molecule is locked into a twisted, non-planar shape whose mirror image cannot be superimposed, producing chirality without a traditional stereocenter.

Chirality is a geometric property of overall molecular shape; it can also arise at nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur centers, or from axial chirality in carbon-free frameworks, so carbon is not strictly required.
CHFClBr has a single carbon bonded to four completely different atoms (H, F, Cl, Br) and no internal symmetry to cancel the effect, making it chiral.
Simple rotation of a molecule (or its drawing) in space never changes its configuration or identity; only reflecting it (or swapping substituents) converts it into its mirror image.
In a racemic (50:50) mixture, the rotation caused by one enantiomer is exactly canceled by the equal and opposite rotation from the other, so the net optical rotation observed is zero.

Meso-tartaric acid's two stereocenters have opposite configurations that create an internal mirror plane, so the molecule as a whole coincides with its mirror image even though each center individually has four different substituents.

A center of symmetry is an improper symmetry element; any molecule possessing one is automatically superimposable on its mirror image and therefore achiral, so a truly chiral molecule cannot have one.
C3 carries four distinct groups (H, Br, CH3, and -CH=CH2), satisfying the stereocenter criterion, and there is no internal symmetry to cancel it, so the molecule is chiral.
Stereocenters are a strong clue toward chirality, but because of possible internal symmetry (as in meso compounds), the only fully reliable check is comparing the whole molecule to its mirror image.

Left and right hands look alike but cannot be perfectly overlaid on one another no matter how they are rotated, which is exactly the geometric relationship that defines chiral molecules and their enantiomers.

The alpha carbon of a standard amino acid is attached to a hydrogen, an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a unique side chain, four different substituents that make it a stereocenter and the molecule chiral.

The central carbon of an allene is sp hybridized and its two π systems are at right angles, so the methyl and hydrogen on one end lie in a plane perpendicular to the methyl and hydrogen on the other. That arrangement is handed: no rotation superimposes it on its reflection. Restricted rotation is a distractor here — no alkene rotates about its double bond, and most alkenes are perfectly achiral.

Chirality is a property of the shape of the whole molecule, and a twist can supply it without any tetrahedral carbon. BINOL is the cleanest counterexample: every carbon in it is aromatic and sp², yet bulky groups beside the bond joining its two rings lock them at an angle, and the twisted shape is not superimposable on its mirror image. Substituted allenes make the same point.
The single carbon in CHFClBr carries four different atoms with no internal symmetry, so the molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable enantiomers, confirming the molecule is chiral.
stereocenters: A stereocenter (typically a carbon) must have four different groups attached for swapping two to create a distinct stereoisomer.
Each stereocenter independently can be R or S, giving up to 2ⁿ possible stereoisomers.
Nitrogen can be a stereocenter in specific cases (e.g., locked in a ring, or quaternary ammonium with 4 different substituents) where pyramidal inversion is prevented or irrelevant.

C2 is bonded to Br, H, a methyl group, and an ethyl group, four different substituents, making it the stereocenter; the other carbons each have at least two identical substituents (such as extra hydrogens).

A ring carbon puts two of its four bonds into the ring, and those two bonds are different groups only if the ring differs in the two directions. Walk from C1 one way and the methyl-bearing carbon arrives after two carbons (C2, C3); walk the other way and it arrives after four (C6, C5, C4, C3). Different, so C1 is a stereocenter. Run the same walk on 4-methylcyclohexan-1-ol and both directions give three, so that C1 is not one.
Both C2 and C3 are each bonded to Br, H, a methyl group, and a chain leading to the other substituted carbon, all different, so each qualifies independently as a stereocenter.
A classic tetrahedral stereocenter has four single bonds arranged tetrahedrally around an sp3 carbon; sp2 and sp carbons do not have the tetrahedral geometry needed for this type of stereocenter.
The carbon in CH2Cl2 bears two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, so it fails the four-different-groups test, unlike the other examples listed.

Tracing outward from C3 in both directions gives an ethyl group on each side, so two of C3's four substituents are identical; this classic trick shows that branching alone does not guarantee a stereocenter.

What matters is whether the four substituents are different from each other, not whether they are carbon groups or include hydrogen; a quaternary carbon bonded to four different carbon chains is a valid stereocenter.

Amines undergo fast umbrella-like pyramidal inversion at room temperature, rapidly racemizing any configuration at nitrogen, so the two mirror-image forms interconvert too quickly to be isolated or to show net optical activity.

Because nitrogen in a quaternary ammonium ion has no lone pair and cannot undergo pyramidal inversion, its four-different-group configuration is locked in place, unlike in a neutral trisubstituted amine.

2ⁿ is a ceiling, not a count: each center can take either configuration, giving 2³ = 8 arrangements at most. Internal symmetry can make two of those arrangements the same substance — that is what a meso compound is — so the real number can be smaller. Tartaric acid is the standard case: two stereocenters, 2² = 4 predicted, three actual.

Two stereocenters predict 2² = 4, but the two halves of 2,3-dibromobutane are identical, so the (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) arrangements are one and the same achiral substance — the meso form, which gets a section of its own shortly. What is left is an enantiomeric pair plus that one meso compound: three.
The alpha carbon carries four distinct groups: a hydrogen, an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, and a methyl group, satisfying the requirement for a stereocenter.
Ring carbons can absolutely be stereocenters; for example, in 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, C1 and C2 are each bonded to four different groups once the two distinct ring paths are taken into account.
C1 and C2 each bear a methyl group, a hydrogen, and two different paths around the ring (one shorter, one longer, to reach the other substituted carbon), making each of them a stereocenter.

In a sulfoxide, sulfur's lone pair behaves like a fourth substituent, and unlike nitrogen in amines, the pyramidal inversion at sulfur in a sulfoxide is slow enough at room temperature that the two configurations can be isolated as separate stereoisomers.
Axial chirality, found in certain allenes and restricted biphenyls, shows that a molecule can be chiral without containing any classic tetrahedral stereocenter.

Terminal or symmetric carbons are rarely stereocenters; the reliable method is to identify a tetrahedral (four single-bonded) carbon and compare its four attached groups by tracing outward until a difference (or confirmed sameness) is found.
C4 is flanked by a propyl group on each side of the main chain, making two of its four substituents identical, so despite the methyl branch it is not a stereocenter.

A CH₃ carries three identical hydrogens and a chain CH₂ carries two, so each already has a repeat and is out; a doubly bonded carbon has three groups rather than four and is not tetrahedral. One pass usually clears most of the molecule and leaves a handful of carbons worth a branch-by-branch comparison. Ring carbons survive the pass — they need the walk-both-ways test.

With only a single stereocenter there is no possibility of internal symmetry canceling its effect (that requires at least two stereocenters arranged symmetrically), so one isolated stereocenter always makes the molecule chiral.

The formula 2^n for n stereocenters gives the maximum possible number of stereoisomers; internal molecular symmetry, as seen in meso compounds, can reduce the actual distinct count below that maximum.
Both C2 (bonded to OH, H, CH3, and the rest of the chain) and C3 (bonded to Br, H, CH3, and the rest of the chain) have four different substituents, giving two independent stereocenters.
All four substituents, hydrogen, chlorine, bromine, and the vinyl group, are distinct from one another, so this carbon meets the requirement of four different groups and is a stereocenter.

In an unsymmetrical secondary alcohol, the carbon bearing OH is also bonded to a hydrogen and two alkyl chains of different length or branching, giving four distinct substituents and thus a stereocenter; this is not automatic for every alcohol, such as symmetric ones like 3-pentanol's C3.

The same four-different-groups rule applies inside rings; a ring carbon with two distinguishable ring paths, a substituent, and a hydrogen can absolutely be a stereocenter, as shown in disubstituted cyclohexanes.

One tetrahedral stereocenter has two possible arrangements, and those two are non-superimposable mirror images, so a single stereocenter is enough. The stem rules out the other routes on purpose: a molecule with no stereocenter at all can still be chiral through a twist, as an allene or a hindered biaryl is, so the answer would be zero if those were on the table.

Constitutional isomers are not identical groups; as long as no two of the four substituents are exactly the same, the carbon satisfies the four-different-groups requirement and is a valid stereocenter.
enantiomers: ee = ([α]observed / [α]pure) × 100 = 21/30 = 70%. Read that as 70% of the sample being pure (+) and the remaining 30% being racemic, which works out to 85% (+) and 15% (−). The arithmetic works because rotation is additive: every molecule contributes the same amount regardless of what it is mixed with.
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions and behave differently only in chiral environments (e.g., with enzymes).
A racemic mixture is an equal (50:50) mixture of both enantiomers, which shows no net optical rotation.

Enantiomeric excess is the excess of the major enantiomer over the minor: 92 − 8 = 84%. The 8% of (R) that pairs off against the 8% of (S) is racemic and contributes nothing to the rotation, leaving 84% of the sample behaving as a single pure enantiomer. A sample quoted at 84% ee therefore rotates light to 84% of the pure value.

Enantiomers have identical physical properties, such as boiling point, melting point, and density, in an achiral environment; they differ only in chiral interactions, such as with polarized light or other chiral molecules.

Biological receptors and enzymes are chiral structures, so they can bind the two mirror-image forms of a drug with very different affinities or effects, even though the enantiomers are chemically identical outside a chiral environment.
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by equal magnitudes but in opposite directions, so the mirror-image enantiomer under the same conditions rotates light by -25 degrees.
Zero net rotation occurs either when opposite rotations from equal amounts of both enantiomers cancel out (a racemic mixture) or when the compound itself is achiral and has no rotation to begin with.

Optical rotation drops to zero upon racemization, and in some compounds the racemic mixture also crystallizes differently than the pure enantiomer (sometimes called a racemic compound), giving it a different melting point from the pure enantiomer.

Nothing in the flask can tell the two faces or the two mirror images apart, and no bond at the stereocenter is touched, so the configuration there is carried through untouched and the product is a single enantiomer. The stem has to say ‘away from the stereocenter’ for that to hold: an achiral reagent acting AT the stereocenter can invert it, as SN2 does, or destroy it and hand back a racemate, as SN1 does.

Since enantiomers share identical achiral physical properties like boiling point, melting point, and density, only a chiral-sensitive measurement such as optical rotation can tell the two pure enantiomer samples apart.
A racemic mixture, containing equal parts of both enantiomers, is conventionally labeled with the prefix rac- or the symbol (±), reflecting that it shows no net optical rotation.

In a standard achiral NMR or IR solvent, enantiomers give identical spectra because these techniques do not distinguish mirror-image forms; a chiral shift reagent or chiral environment is needed to tell enantiomers apart by NMR.

The enantiomer of a molecule with a single stereocenter is obtained by inverting the configuration at that stereocenter, converting R to S while keeping the same constitution, giving (S)-2-chlorobutane.

A single stereocenter has exactly two possible spatial arrangements, R and S; these two forms are mirror images of one another, so there is exactly one enantiomer for any given single-stereocenter compound.

Because enzyme active sites are chiral three-dimensional pockets built largely from chiral L-amino acids, they typically bind one enantiomer of a substrate much more effectively than its mirror image.

A chiral catalyst can favor formation of one transition state over its mirror image, leading to an enantioselective synthesis that produces one enantiomer in excess, something an achiral catalyst cannot do from achiral starting materials.

The (+) and (-) signs describe the experimentally measured direction of rotation of polarized light, which must be determined by measurement and is not something that can be predicted directly from the R or S configurational label alone.

While this is often approximately true, some racemic mixtures form a distinct crystal packing (a racemic compound) with a melting point that differs, sometimes substantially, from that of the pure enantiomer.

An achiral reagent reacting with two enantiomers experiences mirror-image transition states that are equal in energy, so the reaction rates with each enantiomer are identical unless a chiral influence is introduced.

Because enantiomers share identical boiling points, melting points, and solubilities in ordinary achiral solvents, standard separation techniques fail; a chiral resolving agent or chromatography using a chiral stationary phase is needed to separate them.

[α] = α / (l × c) = 5.2 / (1.0 × 0.20) = +26°. Both divisions matter: doubling the tube length or doubling the concentration doubles the observed rotation, because the beam meets twice as many molecules on its way through. Dividing them out is what turns a reading off an instrument into a constant of the substance.

Inverting the configuration at every stereocenter converts a molecule into its full mirror image; since both stereocenters are flipped here (R to S at both), these two structures are enantiomers of each other.

Enantiomeric excess quantifies how far a sample is from racemic by reporting the percentage by which the major enantiomer exceeds the minor one; 100 percent ee means a single pure enantiomer, while 0 percent ee means fully racemic.

Combining each of the two original enantiomers with the same chiral resolving agent produces two diastereomeric adducts, which (unlike the original enantiomers) have different melting points and solubilities and so can be separated by standard techniques; this is the classic method of resolving a racemic mixture.

An ordinary achiral stationary phase cannot distinguish the two mirror-image shapes, so both enantiomers travel through at the same rate; a chiral stationary phase forms diastereomeric-like interactions of different strengths with each enantiomer, giving them different retention times.

Refractive index and solubility in an achiral solvent are both achiral physical properties, so like melting point and boiling point they are identical for a pair of pure enantiomers, differing only in chiral interactions.

Standard NMR in an achiral solvent cannot distinguish between enantiomers, so a racemic mixture and a pure single enantiomer of the same compound give indistinguishable spectra unless a chiral shift reagent or chiral solvent is added.

Biology strongly favors a single enantiomeric series; nearly all amino acids incorporated into natural proteins are of the L configuration, reflecting the chiral machinery (itself built from L-amino acids) that synthesizes and uses them.

Enantiomeric excess is calculated as the percent major enantiomer minus the percent minor enantiomer; since the two percentages must sum to 100, an ee of 60 percent corresponds to 80 percent major and 20 percent minor (80 minus 20 equals 60).
diastereomers: Diastereomers differ in configuration at some, but not all, stereocenters, so they are not mirror images.
Diastereomers are genuinely different compounds with different shapes, so their physical properties differ, unlike enantiomers.
Cis/trans ring isomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other — classic diastereomers.

Count the stereocenters in either 2-butene and you get zero, yet the two compounds are distinct stereoisomers and neither is the mirror image of the other — so they are diastereomers. That is why the definition is written as ‘stereoisomers that are not mirror images’ rather than as a stereocenter count: a C=C is a stereogenic unit in its own right. The alcohols differ in connectivity, and two chairs are conformations of one compound.

Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers are genuinely different compounds in terms of shape and polarity in an achiral sense, so they typically have distinct physical properties such as melting point, boiling point, and solubility.
Only one of the two stereocenters (C3) has its configuration flipped while the other (C2) stays the same, so these are stereoisomers but not full mirror images, making them diastereomers.
Cis and trans forms of a disubstituted ring differ in the spatial arrangement at the ring stereocenters but are not mirror images of each other, so they fit the definition of diastereomers.

With three stereocenters there are up to eight stereoisomers total; one of them is the full mirror image (the enantiomer), and the remaining six are diastereomers that differ in configuration at only one or two of the three centers.

Because diastereomers differ in shape and interactions in ways that change melting point, boiling point, and solubility, standard separations can exploit those differences, unlike with enantiomers, which share those properties.

That equal-and-opposite relationship is specific to enantiomers; diastereomers are different compounds, so their specific rotations are generally unrelated in magnitude or sign and must be measured independently.
Epimers are a subset of diastereomers that differ in configuration at exactly one of several stereocenters while all other stereocenters remain the same, making them easy to compare directly.
Since glucose and galactose differ at only one stereocenter (C4) out of several, while sharing the same configuration everywhere else, they are epimers, a specific case of diastereomers.

meso-Tartaric acid, (2R,3S), and (2R,3R)-tartaric acid are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other, so they are diastereomers — and the meso one is achiral while the other is optically active. Being a mirror-image pair is what enantiomers require, and that does force both members to be chiral; diastereomers are defined by what they are not, so nothing constrains them to match in chirality, melting point or any other property.
(2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-tartaric acid have every stereocenter inverted relative to each other, making them full mirror images, or enantiomers, rather than diastereomers.

When two stereocenters are symmetric with respect to each other (as in 2,3-dibromobutane), the R,S and S,R combinations become the same meso compound, reducing four possible stereoisomers down to three distinct ones: two enantiomers plus one meso diastereomer.

Because diastereomers have genuinely different three-dimensional shapes and steric environments (unlike enantiomers in an achiral setting), they can and often do react at different rates with the same achiral reagent.

Both share a molecular formula, and that is where the resemblance stops. Constitutional isomers are built differently — the atoms are joined up in a different order, as in butan-1-ol against butan-2-ol. Diastereomers have exactly the same connectivity and differ only in how that skeleton is arranged in space, and they are not mirror images of each other.

Take (2R,3R). Inverting every center gives (2S,3S), its one enantiomer. The other two, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R), each have one center inverted and one not, so neither is a mirror image — they are its two diastereomers. Every stereoisomer of a two-center compound sits in that same pattern, which is what makes the six pairings break down into two enantiomeric and four diastereomeric relationships.

Cis and trans alkene isomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement around the double bond, and they are not mirror images of one another, so they fall under the broader category of diastereomers.

Because diastereomers are chemically distinct compounds with different local environments around their atoms, they generally give different NMR chemical shifts and coupling patterns even in a standard achiral solvent, unlike enantiomers which appear identical.
Flipping no stereocenters at all leaves the configuration completely unchanged, so you simply reproduce the original compound rather than generating any new stereoisomer.

Since diastereomers are genuinely different compounds with potentially very different properties and activities, chemists often need diastereoselective reactions to favor the desired diastereomer rather than forming an unwanted (though separable) mixture.

With 2 pairs of enantiomers (2 relationships) among the 4 stereoisomers, the remaining pairings across the two pairs are diastereomeric — there are 4 such cross-pairs out of the 6 total pairs possible among 4 stereoisomers.
Same connectivity plus not mirror images plus not identical is exactly the definition of diastereomers — stereoisomers that are not enantiomers.
They share the same connectivity but differ in configuration at one of two stereocenters (not all of them), making them diastereomers rather than enantiomers.
Because diastereomers have genuinely different 3D shapes, their bond vectors add up differently, so their dipole moments (and other physical properties) can differ.
When a reaction favors formation of one diastereomer over another, that preference is called diastereoselectivity.

The mechanism is the same and the stereochemistry of the addition is the same — anti, through a bromonium ion — but the alkene geometry decides which face each methyl ends up on, so switching cis for trans switches the answer. Anti addition to the cis alkene gives the chiral pair as a racemate; anti addition to the trans alkene gives meso. Both flasks read zero on a polarimeter, for completely different reasons.
Differing at only one of the two stereocenters (not both) means they are not mirror images of each other — that relationship is diastereomeric.

Since diastereomers are different compounds with different shapes, even simple achiral reagents can react with them at different rates, unlike enantiomers which need a chiral environment to be distinguished.
meso: A meso compound has stereocenters, but an internal mirror plane makes the whole molecule superimposable on its mirror image — achiral, optically inactive.
A classic meso case is a molecule with two stereocenters bearing the same substituents arranged symmetrically (e.g., meso-tartaric acid).
Because a meso compound is achiral (despite having stereocenters), it does not rotate plane-polarized light.

Opposite descriptors are evidence of meso only after the two halves have been checked for being identical. In 2,3-dibromobutane both halves are CH₃–CHBr–, so the reflection maps one onto the other. In 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane one half ends in bromine and the other in chlorine, and no reflection can send Br onto Cl. That compound is a perfectly ordinary chiral molecule with four stereoisomers and no meso form.

A meso compound is a single, defined achiral substance that shows zero rotation on its own because of internal symmetry, whereas a racemic mixture is a 50:50 blend of two different chiral enantiomers that together also show zero net rotation; they are conceptually different even though both give zero rotation.

Meso-tartaric acid, one of the three possible stereoisomers of tartaric acid, has two stereocenters of opposite configuration related by an internal mirror plane, making it the textbook example of a meso compound.
Tartaric acid's two stereocenters give (R,R) and (S,S) as a pair of enantiomers, while the (R,S) (equivalent to S,R by the molecule's internal symmetry) combination is the single meso diastereomer.

Bromine adds anti, through a bromonium ion opened from the far face, and the geometry of the alkene then decides the relative configuration of the two new stereocenters. The trans alkene delivers the (R,S) arrangement, which is the meso compound. The cis alkene, run the same way, gives the chiral (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair as a racemate. The other two alkenes give only one new stereocenter, or none.

Both readings are zero and both stay zero however carefully you measure, so the polarimeter cannot settle it. A meso compound is one pure achiral substance with one melting point and no enantiomer to be separated from. A racemate is two chiral compounds in a 50:50 mixture, which a chiral resolving agent or a chiral column could in principle pull apart. One compound or two is the whole question.

The two symmetric stereocenters in 2,3-dibromobutane give a chiral (R,R)/(S,S) enantiomeric pair and a separate achiral meso (R,S) form, totaling three stereoisomers instead of the four that unrelated stereocenters would give.

The meso form and the chiral enantiomeric pair of the same constitution are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of one another, so by definition the meso compound is a diastereomer relative to each of the chiral forms.

Due to the molecule's internal symmetry, simply rotating the (2R,3S) structure in space reproduces the (2S,3R) labeling of the same physical molecule, confirming that they are not two different compounds but one single meso compound.

A meso compound requires an internal mirror relationship between parts of the molecule, which is only possible when the relevant stereocenters sit in a symmetric arrangement; if the two stereocenters have completely different substituent sets, no such internal symmetry can form.

The cis isomer of 1,2-dibromocyclohexane has a plane of symmetry passing through the molecule that relates its two stereocenters, making it achiral overall even though each ring carbon individually qualifies as a stereocenter, so it is meso.

Unlike the cis isomer, the trans arrangement of substituents breaks the internal mirror symmetry, so trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane exists as a genuinely chiral pair of enantiomers rather than a single meso compound.

Because the meso form is a diastereomer, not an enantiomer, of the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair, it is a genuinely different compound and commonly shows a distinct melting point and other physical properties from that chiral pair.

Regardless of whether the achirality comes from having no stereocenters at all or from an internal mirror symmetry relating multiple stereocenters (as in a meso compound), the underlying reason for zero optical rotation is the same: the molecule is superimposable on its own mirror image.

The definitive test is to look for an internal symmetry element, most commonly a mirror plane, that maps one half of the molecule (including its stereocenters) onto the other; simply having two stereocenters is not enough, since asymmetric stereocenters give no meso form.

Tartaric acid's two stereocenters would normally allow up to four stereoisomers, but the symmetric substitution pattern collapses the R,S and S,R combinations into one meso form, leaving three total stereoisomers: two enantiomers and one meso diastereomer.

Since the meso form and the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair are diastereomers of each other with different physical properties, they can be separated by standard, non-chiral separation techniques, unlike a true pair of enantiomers.

Draw the chain vertically and look for a horizontal mirror. With Br on a wedge to the left at both centers and H hashed to the right at both, reflecting the top half through a line between the two carbons lands Br on Br, H on H and methyl on methyl — the molecule contains its own mirror image and is achiral. Turn the lower center over so that its bromine points to the right, and the descriptors match instead of opposing — that drawing is the chiral (R,R) or (S,S) form.

The count is about symmetry, not parity. Three stereocenters can give a meso form when the middle one lies on the symmetry element and the outer two carry opposite configurations — ribitol and xylitol are the standard sugar-alcohol examples. What a meso compound needs is an internal improper symmetry element, and nothing about that requires the number of stereocenters to be even.
Being achiral, a meso compound does not rotate plane-polarized light at all — its specific rotation is 0.
Meso forms can occur in molecules with more than two stereocenters as long as the overall structure has an internal mirror plane or similar symmetry relating the configurations.

A meso compound is one molecule that is internally achiral; a racemic mixture is a blend of two different, still-chiral molecules (the two enantiomers) that happens to show zero net rotation because they cancel each other out.

A meso form requires an internal symmetry element (commonly a mirror plane) relating parts of the molecule to each other; this is possible with three stereocenters arranged symmetrically, not just with two.

Opposite descriptors are evidence of meso only once the two halves of the molecule are known to be constitutionally identical. (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane is meso; (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane is an ordinary chiral compound, because no reflection sends Br onto Cl. Draw the structure, or a Fischer projection, and look for the plane.

Although the two halves of a meso compound are related by an internal mirror plane, a chiral reagent experiences them as distinguishable environments (similar to how enantiomers are distinguished by chiral reagents), so reactivity at each half can differ.
Meso-tartaric acid is a diastereomer of the chiral tartaric acid enantiomers (which share one melting point as a pair), so as a genuinely different compound it has its own distinct melting point.

A meso form requires the kind of internal symmetry that only arises when the two (or more) stereocenters are related by equivalent substituent patterns; an unsymmetric arrangement has no such mirror relationship available.
rs-configuration: CIP priority ranks by atomic number at the first point of difference, moving outward if there’s a tie.

The enantiomer is the structure with every stereocenter inverted, so 2R becomes 2S and 3S becomes 3R. Invert only one of them and you get a diastereomer instead: both (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) are diastereomers of the compound named. And the descriptors are the only thing allowed to change — swap the bromine for a chlorine and you have a different compound, not a mirror image of this one.
Priority is based on atomic number at the point of attachment — bromine (35) outranks chlorine (17).

Priorities are OH (1), ethyl (2), methyl (3), H (4): oxygen beats both carbons, and ethyl beats methyl because its first carbon carries (C,H,H) against methyl's (H,H,H). The hydrogen is on a hash, so it already points away from you and the trace can be read as it stands. Counterclockwise is S. Had that hydrogen been on a wedge, the same counterclockwise trace would have meant R.
By CIP convention, a clockwise path from the highest to the second to the third priority group, viewed with the lowest priority pointing away, defines the R (rectus, right-handed) configuration.

CHO outranks CH₂OH on the duplication rule: the aldehyde carbon counts as (O,O,H) against the alcohol carbon's (O,H,H), and they part company at the second term. So the trace OH → CHO → CH₂OH is 1 → 2 → 3, and it runs counterclockwise, which reads as S. But the hydrogen is on a wedge, pointing at you, so you are viewing the center from the wrong side: flip it, and the answer is R.
When the directly attached atoms tie, CIP rules direct you to compare the sets of atoms attached one bond farther out, continuing outward until a difference in atomic number is found.

CIP rules treat a double bond as if each atom were singly bonded to a duplicate 'phantom' copy of the atom on the other end, so a carbon double-bonded to oxygen is treated as bonded to oxygen twice for priority purposes.

The R/S rule strictly requires viewing with the lowest-priority group pointing away; if it points toward the viewer instead, the observed clockwise or counterclockwise sense must be reversed to get the true configuration, so an apparent clockwise trace actually corresponds to S.
Priority follows the atomic number of the directly attached atom: oxygen (8) outranks nitrogen (7), which outranks carbon (6), which outranks hydrogen (1), giving the order OH ≻ NH2 ≻ CH3 ≻ H.
Ranking is by atomic number of the attached atom: bromine (35) outranks chlorine (17), which outranks oxygen (8), which outranks hydrogen (1), giving Br ≻ Cl ≻ OH ≻ H.

R and S describe the three-dimensional spatial configuration based on CIP priority rules, while (+) and (-) describe the experimentally measured direction of optical rotation; there is no simple, universal rule linking R/S directly to the sign of rotation, it must be measured.
Numbering each stereocenter and assigning its own R or S label lets a single name fully specify the configuration at every stereocenter in a molecule with more than one, as in (2R,3S)-.

R/S labels depend entirely on the relative CIP priority ranking of substituents; if a substituent is replaced with a group that reorders the priorities (for example replacing an H with a D, which outranks H), the same physical spatial arrangement can receive a different descriptor.

All three carbon groups tie at carbon, so compare their substituent sets. The double bond to oxygen counts twice, making -CHO (O, O, H), which beats -CH2OH at (O, H, H) at the first point of difference. Duplicating the atoms of a multiple bond is the step people skip.

Apply the duplication rule to both attachment carbons. The phenyl ipso carbon is bonded to two ring carbons plus a duplicate for its share of the aromatic π system, so it reads (C,C,C). The vinyl carbon is bonded to the far CH₂, a duplicate of it, and a hydrogen: (C,C,H). They tie at the first two terms and phenyl wins at the third. Phenyl outranks vinyl, which in turn outranks an ordinary alkyl group.

When a lone pair functions as the fourth 'substituent' at a stereocenter (for example, in some nitrogen or sulfur stereocenters), it is assigned the lowest possible priority, effectively ranked as if it had an atomic number of zero, below even hydrogen.

CIP priority for atoms directly attached increases with atomic number, and among the halogens iodine (53) has the highest atomic number, followed by bromine (35), chlorine (17), and fluorine (9) last.

R/S configuration is an intrinsic property of the actual three-dimensional arrangement of atoms; simply rotating or redrawing the same molecule without breaking any bonds cannot change its true configuration, even if it looks different on paper.

Both groups attach through a carbon, so the first point of comparison is a tie and you look at what that carbon itself carries. Isopropyl's attached carbon holds two carbons and a hydrogen, (C,C,H); n-propyl's holds one carbon and two hydrogens, (C,H,H). C beats H at the first point of difference, so isopropyl wins — chain length never enters into it.

A single swap of any two groups at a stereocenter converts it into its mirror image, so one swap plus one reversal of the answer cancel out exactly. Swap the lowest-priority group with whichever group is on the hash, read 1 → 2 → 3 off the swapped drawing, then reverse. Rotating the page never helps, because a rotation cannot move a bond from the plane of the page to behind it.

The R descriptor is a configurational label assigned purely from applying CIP priority rules to the four groups at a specific stereocenter; it says nothing directly about observed optical rotation or alkene geometry.
Comparing the directly attached atoms Cl (17), O (8), C (6), and H (1), hydrogen has by far the lowest atomic number, so -H is the lowest-priority substituent among these four.

CIP rules rank substituents by atomic number at the point of attachment, not atomic mass — this is why isotopes (same atomic number, different mass) are ranked by mass only as a tiebreaker after atomic number ties.
When atomic number is tied (both are hydrogen, Z=1), CIP rules break the tie using atomic mass — deuterium, being heavier, ranks slightly higher than protium.

The four attached groups must be different from each other, but they don't need to differ at the very first atom — e.g., -CH2CH3 and -CH2CH2CH3 are both carbon-attached but are still different groups that can be ranked by CIP rules going further out.

All three carbon groups tie at the first atom (C), so you compare what's attached to each of those carbons: Br (Z=35) outranks Cl (Z=17), which outranks the three H's on plain -CH3, giving -CH2Br > -CH2Cl > -CH3, with -H lowest overall.

If the lowest-priority group already points away from the viewer in the drawing, you can read the R/S assignment directly from the remaining three groups' clockwise/counterclockwise order without any further manipulation.

Both -NH2 and -NHCH3 attach through nitrogen, so they tie at the first atom; you must then compare what's attached to that nitrogen (H,H vs. H,C) to break the tie, with -NHCH3 ranking higher since carbon outranks hydrogen.

The priority ranking alone only tells you which group is 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th — you still need the actual 3D geometry (which way the groups point) to determine whether 1→2→3 traces clockwise or counterclockwise.
fischer: By convention, horizontal bonds in a Fischer projection come toward the viewer; vertical bonds go back into the page.
One swap inverts configuration at that center, generating the enantiomer (for a single stereocenter) or flipping that one center’s configuration in a larger molecule.
Fischer projections of sugars are drawn with the carbon backbone vertical and the most oxidized carbon (e.g., the aldehyde in an aldose) at the top.

The backbone runs vertically by convention, which uses up both vertical bonds at every internal stereocenter and pushes the hydrogen onto a horizontal one. Horizontal bonds point at the viewer, so the lowest-priority group is on the wrong side for reading the rotation directly: trace the path as drawn, then flip. Check where the H actually is rather than assuming, but in a normally drawn sugar it is horizontal at every center.

D and L are set by one stereocenter only: the one furthest from the carbonyl, C5 in a hexose, whose OH is drawn on the right for D. It is a relational label — it says which glyceraldehyde the configuration traces back to — and nothing more. It does not give the sign of rotation, and it does not fix the other centers: D-glucose is (2R,3S,4R,5R), a mixture of descriptors, and plenty of D sugars are levorotatory.

Only the first entry has changed, and the first entry is C2, so the sugar differs from glucose at exactly one stereocenter — an epimer, and the C2 epimer of glucose is mannose. Galactose is the C4 epimer and reads right, left, left, right. L-glucose would have every entry reversed, since the mirror image inverts all four. Reading sugars as a pattern rather than assigning each center is the reason the notation survived.

Each single swap inverts the configuration once; performing two swaps inverts it twice, returning the drawing to represent the same original configuration, even though the groups' positions on paper have changed.

With both OH groups on the same side, a horizontal line through the middle reflects the top half onto the bottom exactly: OH lands on OH, H on H, COOH on COOH. The molecule contains its own mirror image, so it is meso and reads zero on a polarimeter. Move one OH across and the same reflection sends OH onto H, so no plane exists; that drawing is (2R,3R), one of the chiral pair.

A full 180-degree in-plane rotation of a Fischer projection preserves the relationship of toward-viewer and away-from-viewer bonds, so it represents the same molecule with the same configuration, unlike a 90-degree rotation, which is not allowed.

Priorities: Br (1) > COOH (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4). The lowest priority sits on a horizontal bond, which by the convention points at you, so read the drawing and then reverse what you get. Tracing Br (right) → COOH (top) → CH₃ (bottom) runs counterclockwise, which reads as S as drawn; flip it because H is toward you, and the compound is (R)-2-bromopropanoic acid.

Cyclically rotating any three of the four groups around the stereocenter while keeping the fourth fixed is a valid manipulation that preserves the actual configuration, producing an equivalent representation of the same molecule.
By the historical convention that defines the D and L sugar series, D-glyceraldehyde is drawn with its -OH group on the right side of the Fischer projection at the stereocenter.

By convention, a sugar is classified as D or L based on whether the hydroxyl group at the stereocenter nearest the bottom of the Fischer projection (the reference carbon) points to the right (D) or left (L).

At a single stereocenter the conversion is exact and unambiguous — that is the entire content of the convention, and the first figure in this section performs it. Along a chain it is still a faithful structure, but the one it produces has every C–C bond eclipsed and the backbone curving away from the viewer, which is not how anyone draws a sugar. Getting to the familiar zig-zag means rotating about each bond afterward, and that is where configurations get lost.

Inverting the configuration at only one of two stereocenters while leaving the other unchanged produces a stereoisomer that is not the full mirror image, making the two structures diastereomers rather than enantiomers.
Inverting the configuration at every stereocenter in the molecule produces its full mirror image, so swapping groups at both stereocenters converts the Fischer projection into that of the enantiomer.
L-glyceraldehyde is the enantiomer of D-glyceraldehyde, differing only by a single swap at the one stereocenter, placing its -OH group on the left side of the Fischer projection instead of the right.

Fischer projections are actually especially useful for molecules with several stereocenters in a chain, such as sugars, because stacking the centers vertically makes it easy to compare configurations at each position at a glance.

Because horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away, you must check which type of bond holds the lowest-priority group; if it's on a horizontal bond (toward the viewer), the observed clockwise/counterclockwise sense of the other three groups must be reversed to get the true configuration.

Because a meso compound has an internal mirror plane relating parts of the molecule, its Fischer projection often visibly shows the top half mirroring the bottom half (or similar symmetric patterns), which is part of why Fischer projections are convenient for spotting meso compounds.

A 90-degree (or any odd multiple of 90-degree) in-plane rotation swaps which bonds point toward versus away from the viewer, which inverts the configuration and therefore is not a valid identity-preserving manipulation, unlike a full 180-degree rotation or a three-group rotation.
A standard aldohexose has its aldehyde at C1 and a terminal CH2OH at C6, leaving C2, C3, C4, and C5 as the four carbons that typically bear a hydroxyl group and qualify as stereocenters.

Swap parity has to be counted at each stereocenter separately, not pooled. One swap at the upper center inverts it; two swaps at the lower center cancel and leave it as it was. One center inverted and one not is the definition of a diastereomer. Three swaps all at the same center would have inverted that center alone — also a diastereomer here, and the enantiomer only when every center ends up inverted.
By convention, D/L sugar nomenclature is based on the configuration at the stereocenter farthest from the carbonyl group (for glucose, C5), with -OH on the right defining D.

Both have two stereocenters. Changing the configuration at one of them and leaving the other alone cannot give a mirror image, which would need both inverted, so the two are diastereomers; a diastereomeric pair differing at exactly one center is an epimer pair, and here the difference is at C2. It is also why they are separable substances with their own melting points rather than a pair needing a chiral method to tell apart.

NH₂ on the left in the standard orientation is the definition of L, and the proteinogenic amino acids are all L. Their R/S labels usually come out S, but the descriptor follows CIP priorities rather than the D/L label: in cysteine the CH₂SH side chain outranks COOH, the priority order changes, and L-cysteine is (R) where its relatives are (S). Same geometry, different descriptor — which is the general warning about mapping D/L onto R/S.
By long-standing convention (especially for sugars), the carbon chain is numbered from the top, with the most oxidized carbon placed at the top of the projection.
A three-group rotation (holding one group fixed and cycling the other three) is a valid symmetry operation for Fischer projections that preserves the molecule's identity, just like a full 180° flip.

L and D name a pair of enantiomers, and an enantiomer has every stereocenter inverted — which in a Fischer projection means every horizontal pair swapped left for right. D-threose reads left then right, so L-threose reads right then left. Changing only one of the two would give a diastereomer, which for a four-carbon aldose is erythrose rather than the mirror image of threose.
A meso compound's defining feature is an internal mirror plane; in the Fischer projection of meso-tartaric acid, this shows up as the top half being a direct mirror reflection of the bottom half.
cis-trans-ez: Rotating about a double bond swings one carbon's p orbital out of alignment with the other, so the price of the rotation is the whole pi bond, about 65 kcal/mol. Nothing at room temperature supplies that, which is why alkene geometry is a permanent structural identity rather than a shape the molecule flits between. Both isomers are C4H8, and neither dipoles nor hydrogen bonding is involved.

A wedge puts a group above the plane of the ring and a hash puts it below, so a wedge paired with a hash means the two groups sit on opposite faces, which is the definition of trans on a ring. The reading holds whatever the locants are. Axial and equatorial describe positions within a chair, which is a separate question from which face a group is bonded to.

Cis and trans need one hydrogen and one other group on each alkene carbon, so that the phrase 'the substituent' picks out exactly one group per carbon. But-2-ene meets that with a methyl and an H at each end. Each of the others has an alkene carbon carrying two non-hydrogen groups or two identical groups, so the words have either no referent or nothing to distinguish.

A ring flip exchanges axial for equatorial at every carbon, which changes the energy of the conformer. It carries no group across the plane of the ring, so each methyl stays on the face it is bonded to and the compound is still cis. Turning cis into trans would take breaking a C-C bond and remaking it on the other face.

Their atoms are connected identically and differ only in spatial arrangement, so they are stereoisomers. They are not mirror images of each other, which rules out enantiomers, and stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers. That is also why they have different boiling points and different dipole moments.

A double bond is stereogenic only when each of its carbons carries two different groups. The terminal carbon of but-1-ene is a =CH2 holding two hydrogens, so swapping them returns the identical molecule and there is nothing for a descriptor to distinguish. Every other choice has two different groups at both ends of the bond.

Sigma overlap is cylindrically symmetric about the bond axis, so turning one end leaves it untouched and rotation is essentially free. Pi overlap is side-by-side and is destroyed by the same turn, so rotating a C=C costs the pi bond itself. That gap is what makes alkene geometry configurational rather than conformational.

Geometric isomers are diastereomers, and diastereomers are different substances with different physical properties. The cis isomer has a net dipole because its two C-Cl bond dipoles have components that add; in the trans isomer they point oppositely and cancel. Formula, molar mass and bond counts are identical in both.

Rank each carbon by itself. On C2 the contest is Br, atomic number 35, against a methyl carbon at 6, so bromine wins; on C3 it is a methyl against H, so the methyl wins. Bromine and that far methyl sit on the same side, which makes the compound Z although the carbon skeleton is drawn in a trans arrangement. The word trans was reporting the methyls; E/Z reports the priorities.

Both branches begin with carbon, so the first sphere ties and you list what each of those carbons holds, highest first: (Cl, H, H) against (C, C, H). Read the sets position by position and the very first term settles it, since chlorine is atomic number 17 and carbon is 6. The branch with three carbons loses to the branch with one, because CIP compares sets term by term instead of counting atoms.

Duplicating the double bond gives the vinyl carbon (C, C, H): its real CH2, a phantom duplicate of that CH2, and a hydrogen. The isopropyl carbon genuinely holds (C, C, H), so the first sphere is an exact tie. Go one sphere further and the vinyl's real CH2 counts as (C, H, H) while each isopropyl methyl is (H, H, H), so vinyl takes it.

Stereocenters and stereogenic double bonds both feed the exponent, so the bound is 2^(n+m) = 2^3 = 8. The phrase 'at most' is doing real work: the formula is an upper limit, and internal symmetry can collapse two arrangements into one molecule, which is what happens in meso compounds. Eight is a ceiling rather than a guarantee.

Both isomers have the same bonds and the same degrees of unsaturation, so the difference has to be steric. Putting both methyls on one side of the double bond pushes them into each other, and that strain raises the energy of the cis isomer. The pi bonds are equivalent and neither compound is aromatic.

E/Z asks two separate questions and then compares their answers: rank the two groups attached to one alkene carbon, rank the two attached to the other, then look at where the winners sit. A group on C2 is never weighed against a group on C3, because that comparison is not part of the system and has no meaning.

Two hashes put both groups below the plane of the ring, which is the same face, and same face is cis. The test never consults the distance between the substituents, so a 1,3-ring reads exactly like a 1,2- or a 1,4-ring: the locants say how far apart the groups are and the bonds say which face each one is on.

A ring restricts geometry the way a pi bond does: it has two distinguishable faces, and a substituent cannot cross from one to the other without a bond breaking. With two methyls on the ring, the same-face and opposite-face arrangements are different compounds. Cyclohexane carries no substituents to compare, and the two acyclic compounds rotate freely.

Each set is ordered from highest to lowest and read position by position, and the first place where they differ decides. Oxygen heads one set and carbon heads the other, so the comparison is over at the first term. Adding atomic numbers would give 10 against 18 and the opposite answer, which is exactly why summing is the wrong operation.

The first atoms tie at carbon, so compare what each of them holds: the tert-butyl carbon carries three methyls, giving (C, C, C), while the first carbon of -CH2CH2Br carries one carbon and two hydrogens, giving (C, H, H). The second term already differs, carbon against hydrogen, so tert-butyl wins. The bromine sits two spheres out and is reached after the decision has been made.

A cis double bond puts a permanent kink in a hydrocarbon chain, which keeps neighboring chains from stacking closely and lowers the melting point. A trans double bond leaves the chain nearly straight, so the molecules pack efficiently and the crystal survives to a higher temperature. Chain length and bond strength are untouched by the geometry.

Each alkene carbon here carries one hydrogen and one carbon chain, so the bond is stereogenic and the name is incomplete without a geometric label. The two chains lie on the same side, which is cis, and since a chain outranks hydrogen at both ends the CIP answer agrees: (Z)-pent-2-ene. The descriptor takes the lower locant of the bond, and there is no stereocenter to label.

Both double bonds are stereogenic, so the upper bound is 2^2 = 4. But the molecule carries a methyl at each end and is symmetric about its middle, so labelling the first bond E and the second Z describes the identical substance as labelling the first Z and the second E: rotate the drawing and the two superimpose. That leaves 2E,4E, 2Z,4Z and one mixed isomer, which is three, and it is precisely the overcount the words 'at most' warn about.

Both branches begin with carbon, so list what each of those carbons holds. The aldehyde carbon is doubly bonded to oxygen, and CIP writes a doubly bonded partner in twice, so its set is (O, O, H): one real oxygen and one phantom. The CH2OH carbon really holds (O, H, H). The sets tie at the first term and the aldehyde wins at the second, which is the same comparison that fixes glyceraldehyde's configuration.

For a 1,4-relationship, trans puts the two groups in positions of the same type: diequatorial in one chair and diaxial in the other, with the flip converting one into the other. The diequatorial conformer dominates because it avoids the 1,3-diaxial interactions. It is the cis-1,4 isomer that is stuck with one axial and one equatorial methyl in either chair.

The exponent adds stereocenters and stereogenic double bonds, so the ceiling here is 2^(1+1) = 4. Symmetry and other coincidences can reduce a count below that bound; nothing can push it above. Five distinct stereoisomers therefore cannot come from these two units alone, and a double bond contributes two arrangements, E and Z, not three.

On C2 the contest is the C1 methyl against a hydrogen, so the methyl wins. On C3 it is a methyl against an ethyl: both attach through carbon, so move one sphere out, where the ethyl's CH2 holds (C, H, H) and the methyl holds (H, H, H). The ethyl wins, and it was drawn on the same side as the C1 methyl, so the bond is Z. Cis and trans cannot be used at all, because C3 has no hydrogen and so 'the substituent' on that carbon picks out nothing.

Duplication puts the vinyl carbon at (C, C, H): one real CH₂, one phantom duplicate of it, and one hydrogen. The tert-butyl carbon genuinely holds three carbons, (C, C, C). Compare the sets term by term — C against C, C against C, then C against H — and tert-butyl wins at the third term. Duplication makes a multiple bond comparable with a branch; it does not win comparisons on its own, and the phantom is a dead end with nothing attached to it.

Rank each carbon on its own. On the halogenated carbon the contest is Br (35) against Cl (17), so bromine wins; on the other carbon it is CH₃ against H, so the methyl wins. Bromine and chlorine are on opposite sides of the double bond, so if the chlorine is with the methyl then the bromine is across from it — the two winners are opposite, which is E. Reading the halogen you happen to see beside the methyl is the trap; only the higher-priority group on each carbon is ever compared.

The upper bound 2ⁿ⁺ᵐ gives four, and the word in it is 'at most'. The molecule is symmetric about the central CH₂: the two halves are identical, so labeling one double bond E and the other Z gives the same substance whichever way round you do it. That leaves 2E,5E; 2Z,5Z; and the single mixed isomer — three. It is the same internal symmetry that cuts hexa-2,4-diene from four to three, and the same reason meso compounds cut the count for stereocenters.

Axial directions alternate around the ring, so on carbons an even number apart — 1 and 3 — the two axial positions point the same way. Groups on opposite faces therefore cannot both be axial or both equatorial: one has to be axial and the other equatorial, and a flip only exchanges which is which. The cis isomer is the one that can go diequatorial on a 1,3-ring, which reverses the pattern most students carry over from the 1,2-case.

Both branches begin with carbon, so list what each of those first carbons holds. The isopropyl carbon holds (C, C, H); the first carbon of –CH₂CH₂OH holds (C, H, H). Compare term by term: carbon ties carbon, then carbon beats hydrogen, and the comparison ends there. The oxygen is one sphere further out and is never reached — CIP explores outward only until the first point of difference, so an atom can be the heaviest thing in a branch and still never be weighed.
prochirality: The substitution test reads straight off the relationship between the products. Identical products mean homotopic, mirror-image products mean enantiotopic, diastereomeric products mean diastereotopic. Enantiomers came out, so the hydrogens are enantiotopic — indistinguishable to anything achiral, but distinguishable to a chiral environment such as an enzyme active site.

Rotation about the C–C bond is a genuine symmetry operation that carries each methyl hydrogen onto the position of the next, so replacing any one of them gives the identical product. Homotopic hydrogens share one chemical environment and therefore one signal. Rotation is exactly the argument, not a side issue: freeze a single conformation of a methyl attached to a stereocenter and its three hydrogens sit in three different environments, which is why the word “freely rotating” is in the statement.

A prochiral center is achiral as it stands but becomes a stereocenter when one of two identical groups is exchanged for something new. C1 of ethanol is the standard case. The molecule has not arrived at chirality, it is standing next to it — which is exactly what its two hydrogens being enantiotopic means.

Replace either hydrogen with deuterium and you get CHDCl₂. That carbon carries two chlorines, one H and one D — two identical groups among the four, so no stereocenter forms and only one such compound exists. Both routes reach it, so the hydrogens are homotopic.

Diastereotopic hydrogens sit in genuinely different environments, because no symmetry operation exchanges them, so nothing forces their shifts to coincide. Homotopic and enantiotopic hydrogens are equivalent to any achiral surroundings and share one signal. Hydrogens on different carbons can still be equivalent by symmetry — the six hydrogens of the two methyl groups of propane are one signal, not two.

The test is a thought experiment. Nobody deuterates anything; the label exists so that two groups which currently look alike become distinguishable long enough to ask what relationship the resulting structures have. Any test group works, and the answer does not depend on which one you pick.

Enantiotopic groups do not require a stereocenter anywhere in the molecule; substitution is what creates one. Ethanol is the textbook example — replacing either C1 hydrogen makes that carbon a stereocenter, and the two products are mirror images. A pre-existing stereogenic feature is needed for the diastereotopic case, not this one.

Face descriptors use the same CIP trace as R and S. Clockwise from your side is the Re face, counterclockwise is Si. The far side automatically takes the other name, so labeling one labels both. The rule applies to any trigonal carbon — a carbonyl, an alkene carbon, a carbocation.

C2 is already a stereocenter and neither substitution touches it, so its descriptor is the same in both products. C3 becomes a new stereocenter with opposite configurations in the two. One center matching and one inverted is a diastereomer pair, so the C3 hydrogens are diastereotopic — which is why that CH₂ makes a mess of an otherwise simple spectrum.

The two hydrogens are enantiotopic, which means they are identical toward anything achiral — same bond strength, same shift, same rate with an ordinary oxidant. An enzyme is assembled from single enantiomers of amino acids, so its binding site is chiral and presents the two hydrogens with two different fits. Same logic as a right hand distinguishing two otherwise identical gloves.

Replace one CH₂COOH arm with a test group and the central carbon holds four different groups, so it becomes a stereocenter; replace the other arm instead and you get the mirror image. The molecule itself is achiral, so an ordinary reagent cannot tell the arms apart — which is why an enzyme that does tell them apart was such a famous surprise.

Label one C2 hydrogen and it ends up cis to the methyl group; label the other and it ends up trans. Cis and trans ring isomers are diastereomers, so the hydrogens are diastereotopic. A stereocenter is the commonest source of that distinction but not the required one — a ring or a C=C creates the same top-and-bottom asymmetry.

Acetaldehyde is achiral, so its two carbonyl faces are enantiotopic — attack on one gives one enantiomer of the alcohol, attack on the other gives the mirror image. The two transition states are themselves enantiomeric and equal in energy, so with an achiral reagent in an achiral solvent the rates match and the product is 50:50.

A carbocation is sp² and planar, so the nucleophile can arrive from either side. When the rest of the ion is achiral those faces are enantiotopic and there is nothing to bias the approach, so the two enantiomeric products form at the same rate. The flatness is not incidental to racemization — it is the whole cause of it.

Replace one of the two methyls and C3 becomes a stereocenter while C2 stays one, so the two products are diastereomers and the methyls are diastereotopic. Diastereotopic groups are inequivalent in every environment, achiral or not, so they are entitled to different shifts — and an isopropyl group next to a stereocenter usually takes that entitlement. Rotation rates are irrelevant: both methyls spin freely, and that is what makes each one internally equivalent while leaving the two of them different from each other.

Enantiotopic groups behave identically toward everything achiral — same shift, same bond strength, same rate — so an ordinary spectrum or a bond-energy measurement sees one environment. Introduce chirality into the surroundings, whether an enzyme, a chiral catalyst or a chiral solvating agent, and the two become distinguishable because the interactions are now diastereomeric.

In CH₃CH₂CH₂Br the middle carbon holds H, H, CH₃ and CH₂Br, so substitution makes it a stereocenter in a molecule that had no stereogenic feature at all — the products are mirror images, so those hydrogens are enantiotopic. The C3 hydrogens of 2-chlorobutane and the CH₂ of 2-butanol each sit in a molecule that already has a stereocenter, which is retained, so substitution there gives diastereomers. On methylcyclohexane the ring does the same job without any stereocenter: replacing one C4 hydrogen puts the label cis to the methyl and replacing the other puts it trans.

A prochiral center becomes a stereocenter on one substitution. At ethanol's C1 the result is OH, CH₃, H and D — four different groups. At propane's C2 the result is CH₃, CH₃, H and D, and two of those match, so nothing stereogenic appears. Being a hydrocarbon has nothing to do with it; the count of distinct groups does.

The pre-existing stereocenter makes the two carbonyl faces diastereotopic, so the two transition states are diastereomeric and differ in energy. Different energies mean different rates, so the two diastereomeric products form in unequal amounts. An achiral reagent can give unequal diastereomers; what it cannot do is give unequal enantiomers.

Substitution on an sp² CH₂ does not create a stereocenter, but it does create a geometry: one product has the label cis to the methyl group, the other trans, and those are diastereomers. So the two alkene hydrogens are diastereotopic. A preview of Spectroscopy: this is why a terminal alkene gives two distinct =CH₂ signals rather than one — but the topicity call above is made entirely from the substitution test.

The test compares products, not instantaneous environments. Both substitutions give one and the same compound — the two ring branches leaving C1 are identical, so the labeled carbon never becomes a stereocenter, and axial and equatorial are two conformations of a single substance rather than two substances. Put a substituent elsewhere on the ring and the answer changes, because then the products are cis and trans isomers.

Diastereotopic hydrogens are inequivalent in every environment, so they have their own shifts and, being inequivalent neighbors, they also split each other — a coupling that is invisible whenever a CH₂ is equivalent. The two effects together turn an expected simple pattern into a crowded one. A frozen conformation is not the cause: the hydrogens are diastereotopic whatever the rotation does, and exchange with water broadens and simplifies a spectrum rather than multiplying lines.

The test creates structures whose relationship you then have to classify, and classifying requires descriptors. With D ranked above H by mass number, each product's new center can be assigned and the two compared — mirror images or not. Whether the center is prochiral was already settled by counting distinct groups, and face descriptors never involve the test label at all.

Enantiotopic groups react at exactly equal rates with an achiral reagent, because the two transition states are enantiomeric and therefore equal in energy — a 60:40 result is not a small deviation from that, it is incompatible with it. Something in the molecule must already have been stereogenic, making the pair diastereotopic. Unequal amounts of two products is the diagnostic signature of diastereotopicity.

The labels describe positions within a structure, and they are assigned by a bookkeeping promotion rather than by anything the molecule does. Ethanol is achiral and optically inactive and still has a pro-R and a pro-S hydrogen on C1. A molecule that is already chiral can carry them too. Reading pro-R as evidence of chirality is the commonest confusion in this topic.

Run the test on groups rather than on hydrogens. Replace one methyl with a test group and C2 is left holding H, CH₃, the test group and CH₂CH₃ — four different things, so it is now a stereocenter in a molecule that had none. Replace the other methyl instead and you get the mirror image. Enantiomers out means enantiotopic in, and a carbon that becomes a stereocenter on one such swap is by definition a prochiral center. Contrast an isopropyl group attached to an existing stereocenter, where the same swap gives diastereomers.

Rank the three groups on the trigonal carbon: the oxygen first, then the ethyl carbon (C, H, H), then the methyl (H, H, H). Traced from the side described, 1 → 2 → 3 runs counterclockwise, and counterclockwise is the Si face by definition; the opposite side is automatically Re. Adding hydride to one face converts the flat carbon into a tetrahedral one and fixes its configuration, so the two faces lead to the two enantiomers of butan-2-ol. An achiral reagent picks neither face and gives the racemate, but that is the sum of the two outcomes, not what a single face delivers. There is no 'point the lowest priority away' step here — that belongs to R/S at a tetrahedral center; a face label is read straight from the side you are on.

Substituting either hydrogen creates a new stereogenic feature while the original stereocenter is kept unchanged, so the two products differ at one center and agree at the other — the definition of diastereomers. Distance changes how large the difference is, never what it is; a CH₂ far down a chain is still diastereotopic, just with shifts too close to resolve. This is also why a chiral molecule has no enantiotopic groups anywhere: producing enantiomers would require the molecule itself to be achiral.

In both compounds substitution at C2 makes C2 stereogenic. The difference is what C1 does. In methylcyclohexane C1 carries a methyl, a hydrogen and two ring paths that stop being identical once C2 is labeled, so C1 becomes a stereocenter too — two centers, and the two products are the cis and trans diastereomers. In cyclohexanone C1 is a trigonal carbonyl carbon and can never be a stereocenter, so only C2 changes and the two products are mirror images. A ring is enough to make hydrogens diastereotopic, but only if the ring carries something that can tell its two faces apart.

The test asks what relationship the two products have to each other, not whether one label survived. C2 keeps its arrangement and its descriptor in both products, but C3 is now a stereocenter and comes out R in one product and S in the other, so the pair is (2R,3R) and (2R,3S) — diastereomers, and the hydrogens are diastereotopic. Deuterium does outrank hydrogen, but only where they are actually being compared with each other; against the ordinary hydrogen on the same carbon it ranks above it, and it never displaces carbon or bromine.
sn2: SN2 ("substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular") happens in one step: the nucleophile attacks from the backside as the leaving group departs.
Backside attack requires open space behind the leaving group — methyl/primary carbons have the least steric hindrance.

Two separate things happen and they cancel. Geometrically the carbon inverts, as it does in every SN2. But the priorities are re-ranked in the product: the nitrile carbon is (N,N,N) while the CH₂OCH₃ carbon is (O,H,H), and O beats N at the first point of difference — so the incoming cyanide is priority 2, not the priority 1 that bromine held. Reversing the geometry and swapping the top two priorities are two reversals, and two reversals leave the letter where it was. Assign R/S from the product itself, never by assuming that "inversion" means the letter flips.
SN2 is second order overall and first order in each reactant, so rate is directly proportional to nucleophile concentration.
SN2 needs a nucleophile that is both reactive (strong) and able to physically reach the backside of the carbon, so small size matters as much as strength.
The single concerted step involves both the substrate and the incoming nucleophile, so both concentrations appear in the rate law.
Polar aprotic solvents dissolve ions without hydrogen-bonding to the nucleophile, so the nucleophile stays highly reactive and free to attack.
Backside attack lets the nucleophile's electron pair align with the antibonding orbital of the C-leaving group bond, which is what drives inversion.

Working backwards: pentanenitrile is butyl–C≡N, so a carbon nucleophile has to displace the bromide, and the carbon nucleophile that does it is cyanide. Sodium cyanide supplies it as the free anion, and DMSO is polar aprotic, so the anion is not hydrogen-bonded and attacks at full strength. Hydroxide would give butan-1-ol, tert-butoxide would give elimination, and neutral HCN is far too weak a nucleophile to displace anything.
In the transition state the carbon is partially bonded to both the incoming nucleophile and the departing leaving group, giving five groups arranged around it.

Every curved arrow starts at electrons and ends where they are going. Arrow one starts on a lone pair of the hydroxide oxygen — that is the electron source — and lands on the carbon, which is the new bond. Arrow two starts on the C–Br bonding pair and lands on bromine, which is why bromine leaves as Br⁻ rather than as a bromine atom. The two fire together, which is what makes the reaction one step.

Hydrosulfide is a large, polarizable, weakly basic anion — close to an ideal SN2 nucleophile — and DMSO leaves it unsolvated. It attacks C2 from the face opposite bromine, so the carbon inverts, and there is no intermediate for the stereochemistry to leak away through: the product is a single enantiomer. Here the descriptor flips too, because sulfur takes exactly the rank bromine held (S > ethyl > methyl > H), so the priority order is unchanged and only the geometry has moved.
SN2 rate decreases as alkyl substitution increases because more groups crowd the backside approach path; methyl is fastest and tertiary essentially does not react.
Iodide is the weakest base of the four and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group and giving the fastest reaction.
Steric hindrance isn't limited to the reacting carbon itself; a bulky neighboring group can crowd the backside approach just as effectively.
Removing a proton from the nucleophile to generate its anion greatly increases its electron-donating ability, so the charged species attacks much faster.
SN2 rate depends directly on nucleophile concentration and strength, while SN1 rate depends only on substrate ionization, which doesn't involve the nucleophile at all.
Backside attack forces the three remaining groups to flip through the carbon like an umbrella turning inside out, inverting the spatial arrangement.
