The trigonal planar geometry and the pi electron density around an sp2 carbon prevent the clean backside trajectory that SN2 requires.

Read the two observations separately. A rate that responds to the nucleophile's concentration means the nucleophile is present in the rate-determining step, which rules out both unimolecular pathways at once. Clean inversion with no trace of the other enantiomer means no flat intermediate ever existed — an SN1 cation would have been attacked from both faces. Elimination is out because the product is a substitution product. One step, two species, inversion: SN2.
Backside attack means the nucleophile approaches directly opposite the leaving group, so the two are roughly in a straight line through the central carbon at the transition state.
A polarizable nucleophile, like iodide, can more easily distort its electron cloud toward the electrophilic carbon during the approach, even if it is a comparatively weak base.

SN2 rate is set by how open the backside of the carbon is, and it falls steeply with substitution: methyl is roughly thirty times faster than the primary halide, which is in turn about thirty times faster than the secondary one. The tertiary substrate is not merely slow — its backside is enclosed and SN2 does not happen there at all. So bromomethane wins, and since azide simply replaces bromide, the product is azidomethane.
Even though no cation forms in SN2, the nearby double bond can partially delocalize electron density in the transition state, lowering its energy.
Steric bulk mainly interferes with the tight backside approach needed for substitution, while the base can still reach outward hydrogens for elimination.

The familiar I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ order is a statement about protic solvents, not about the ions. In water or an alcohol, hydrogen bonds wrap the small hard fluoride most tightly of all, and that shell has to be stripped before it can attack — which costs more than its greater basicity gains. A polar aprotic solvent has no O–H to donate, so nothing is caged, the anions are effectively naked, and basicity shows through: the order reverses to F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻. Check the solvent before ranking any halide.
SN2's single transition state has an absolute geometric requirement (backside approach); no amount of favorable electronics can compensate if that pathway is physically blocked.
Every one of these factors independently speeds up SN2: an open backside path, a reactive unshielded nucleophile, and a stable departing group.
Protic solvents solvate small anionic nucleophiles tightly through hydrogen bonding, tying up the electron density that would otherwise attack the substrate.
Azide attacks from the backside in a single concerted step, flipping the spatial arrangement at the carbon that held the leaving group.
sn1: SN1 ("unimolecular") has two steps: ionization to form a carbocation, then nucleophilic attack on that cation.

Acid protonates the OH so it can leave as water, giving a secondary cation at C2. Before bromide arrives, look next door: C3 carries a hydrogen, and moving that hydride across with its bonding pair leaves the charge on a carbon bearing two methyls and the chain — a tertiary cation. That shift is fast and downhill, so it happens first, and bromide then attacks the rearranged cation. The product's skeleton is not the one you get by swapping OH for Br, which is exactly the trap.
Once the carbocation forms, it is planar (sp²) and symmetric, so the nucleophile can attack from either face with roughly equal probability, giving racemization.
SN1 is unimolecular in its rate-determining step, so only the substrate's concentration appears in the rate law.
The leaving group departs first to form a planar carbocation, and only then does the nucleophile attack in a separate second step.
Breaking the C-leaving group bond without any assistance is the slow, high-energy step; capturing the cation afterward is fast.
Since ionization is rate-determining, anything that stabilizes the departing group once it leaves speeds up the whole reaction.

The substrate is tertiary, so SN2 is impossible and the ether has to come from a carbocation trapped by the alcohol — that is, SN1. For that you want a weak nucleophile and an ionizing protic solvent, and warm ethanol alone is both. Adding ethoxide does the opposite of what you want: a strong base on a tertiary substrate forces E2 and gives 2-methylpropene instead. Bulky tert-butoxide is worse still. This is the standard case where the way to get substitution is to add nothing.
Polar protic solvents can hydrogen-bond to and stabilize both the developing carbocation and the departing anion, speeding up the ionization step.
Methyl and primary carbocations are far too unstable to form at any appreciable rate, so ionization never gets going.
Because the nucleophile only participates in the fast second step, changing its concentration does not change the overall observed rate.
Since the rate-determining step involves only the substrate breaking apart, the overall rate law is first order in substrate.
More alkyl substituents donate electron density and provide hyperconjugation to the empty p-orbital, stabilizing the positive charge; tertiary cations are stabilized the most.
Because SN1 generates a real, freestanding carbocation intermediate, that intermediate has time to rearrange to a more stable cation before being trapped.

Ionization gives an allylic cation, and the positive charge is not on one carbon: resonance spreads it over C1 and C3, with the double bond in between shifting accordingly. Water can attack at either end of that delocalized system, so one cation gives two constitutionally different alcohols — but-3-en-2-ol from attack where the chloride left, and but-2-en-1-ol from attack at the far end. Racemization at the original carbon is real too, but it would give two enantiomers, not two different compounds.
The adjacent pi system spreads the positive charge over multiple atoms through resonance, which lowers the cation's energy similarly to extra alkyl substitution.
A weaker carbon-halogen bond combined with a more stable leaving anion makes ionization easier and faster for the iodide.
Since the slow step only involves the substrate ionizing, even a weak nucleophile can still efficiently capture the carbocation once it forms.
The planar carbocation can in principle be attacked equally from both faces, giving near-racemization, though ion pairing can sometimes partially shield one face and skew the ratio slightly.

Three observations, one explanation. A rate that a strong added nucleophile cannot raise means the nucleophile is absent from the rate-determining step. Loss of optical activity means the stereocenter went flat at some point. A rearranged skeleton means an intermediate lived long enough for a group to migrate. Only a carbocation does all three: SN2 would show a nucleophile-dependent rate, clean inversion and no rearrangement, and elimination does not give a substitution product at all.

The two cases fail for related but distinct reasons, and it is worth keeping them apart. A vinyl cation is sp-hybridized: its empty orbital is a p orbital, but the carbon is only two-coordinate and the cation is very high in energy, so ionization is prohibitive. An aryl cation is sp²-hybridized and its empty orbital is an sp² orbital lying in the plane of the ring, perpendicular to the pi cloud — so the ring's electrons, which look as though they should help, cannot overlap with it at all. Neither cation is accessible, so neither substrate does SN1.

Substrate, solvent and reagent are all identical here, so the leaving group is the only variable — and in SN1 it is the whole of the rate-determining step, because nothing is pushing it out. The cost of the step is the cost of making the anion, and tosylate spreads its charge over three oxygens where chloride has to hold it on one atom. A leaving group that is merely adequate when a strong nucleophile is shoving it out can be hopeless when it has to leave unassisted.
Since the rate-determining step is ionization, anything that lowers the solvent's overall polarity and ability to stabilize charge slows the reaction, even if both solvents are polar protic.
A carbocation intermediate has a finite lifetime in which nearby groups can migrate with their bonding electrons if doing so reaches a more stable, lower-energy structure.
Ionization is an equilibrium; adding more of the product anion pushes that equilibrium back toward the un-ionized substrate, slowing the forward (productive) rate.
Before it fully diffuses away, the leaving group can linger near one face of the cation as a tight ion pair, partially blocking nucleophilic attack from that side.
A benzylic cation can spread its positive charge into the ring through resonance in addition to any alkyl hyperconjugation, adding extra stabilization beyond a purely alkyl-substituted cation.
SN1 rate tracks carbocation stability, and stability increases from primary to secondary to tertiary, so the tertiary chloride ionizes fastest and the primary essentially does not react.
Once the carbocation forms, nothing commits it to one specific fate; it is simply captured by whichever available species reacts with it first.
Because the nucleophile isn't involved in the rate-determining step, a solvent's ionizing power (not its nucleophilicity) is what controls SN1 rate.
e1: E1 and SN1 both begin by ionizing the leaving group to form a carbocation; E1 then loses a proton instead of being attacked by a nucleophile.
E1 goes through a carbocation and loses a proton to give the most stable (most substituted) alkene — the Zaitsev product.
E1 and SN1 share the same first step (ionization to a carbocation); from there the cation either loses a proton (E1, elimination) or is attacked by a nucleophile (SN1, substitution).
Just like SN1, the slow step is ionization to form the carbocation; deprotonation afterward is fast.

Dehydration is E1 run in reverse of alkene hydration, and each step of it genuinely goes both ways: the alkene can be reprotonated by the acid to regenerate the cation, and the cation can capture water to give the alcohol back. Left alone, the mixture settles at an equilibrium that is not especially favorable. Alkenes boil far below their parent alcohols, so distilling the alkene out as it appears removes a product from the equilibrium and pulls the whole sequence forward — Le Châtelier, doing the work that the thermodynamics will not.
A base plucks off a hydrogen from a neighboring (beta) carbon, and the electrons from that C-H bond form the new pi bond.
Because deprotonation in E1 happens fast and isn't rate-limiting, even a weak base can remove the proton once the cation has formed; strict base strength or geometry is not required.
Since the first step is identical to SN1, E1 needs a substrate capable of forming a reasonably stable carbocation.
Heat favors elimination pathways generally, and since the rate-determining step doesn't need a strong base, a weak one is often sufficient to pull off the final proton.
E1 is first order overall because its rate-determining step, ionization, only involves the substrate.
Because E1 shares the same carbocation intermediate as SN1, that cation can rearrange to a more stable structure before a proton is ever removed.
Losing the leaving group leaves behind an empty p-orbital on a planar, trigonal carbon, exactly as in SN1's carbocation intermediate.
More alkyl groups attached to the double bond carbons donate electron density into the pi system, lowering its overall energy and making that alkene more stable and, usually, more abundant.
Elimination pathways generally have a more favorable entropy of activation, so heating a reaction mixture tends to push the product distribution toward more alkene.

Bromide leaves to give a secondary cation. Check the neighbor before doing anything else: it is quaternary, so there is no hydride to move — but a whole methyl can migrate with its bonding pair, and doing so leaves the charge on a carbon bearing two methyls and an isopropyl group, a tertiary cation. Now apply Zaitsev to that rearranged skeleton: removing the lone hydrogen on the isopropyl carbon gives the tetrasubstituted 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene. Applying Zaitsev to the original skeleton, before the shift, gives the wrong answer confidently.

The chloride leaves from C3, which carries a methyl and two ethyls. Losing a hydrogen from either ethyl gives the trisubstituted 3-methylpent-2-ene; losing one from the methyl gives the disubstituted 2-ethyl-1-butene. Zaitsev takes the more substituted alkene.

Both E1 and SN1 start from the same cation, so anything that changes the shared first step changes neither ratio. What tips the balance is the second step, and heat tips it toward elimination: elimination makes two molecules from one, so it gains entropy, and the TΔS term in ΔG grows with temperature. A worse leaving group would slow everything down without choosing between them, and adding a strong nucleophile stops being an E1 question at all — it forces the bimolecular pathways instead.
Since the leaving group and the beta-hydrogen depart in two separate steps through a freely rotating carbocation, there's no need for them to have been aligned in any particular way beforehand.
E1's rate-determining step is identical to SN1's, so any solvent effect that helps stabilize a developing carbocation speeds up E1 specifically.
Because the second (deprotonation) step is fast and not rate-limiting, the concentration of the base influences product selectivity far more than it influences overall reaction rate.

Ionization gives the tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃, and two kinds of beta hydrogen are available. Taking one from the ethyl CH₂ puts the double bond between the two inner carbons: 2-methylbut-2-ene, with three carbon groups on it. Taking one from a methyl gives 2-methylbut-1-ene, with two. Zaitsev picks the more substituted one as major even though there are six methyl hydrogens against only two on the CH₂ — it is alkene stability that decides, not a head count.
Elimination proceeds from whichever cation is actually present at that moment, so if rearrangement occurs first, the final alkene reflects the new, rearranged carbon skeleton.

A hydride or methyl shift is fast but not instantaneous, so some of the original cation is captured before it can rearrange. That leaves two different cations in solution, and each of them faces the same fork every carbocation faces: the solvent can attack the positive carbon, giving a substitution product, or take a beta hydrogen, giving an alkene. Two cations times two fates is four products, which is exactly why unimolecular conditions are a poor way to make any one thing on purpose.

Since the cation can rotate freely before deprotonation, there is no anti-periplanar-style constraint linking starting material stereochemistry to product alkene geometry; stability considerations dominate instead.
Since E1's rate-determining step is the same ionization step as SN1's, a better leaving group accelerates E1 in exactly the same way it accelerates SN1.
E1's rate-determining ionization step is highly sensitive to how well the solvent can stabilize developing charge, so diluting the more polar water with less polar ethanol slows that step.

E1 is not under thermodynamic control: deprotonation of the cation is fast and is not reversed under solvolysis conditions, so the alkenes never equilibrate with each other. What is different is the branch point. Both alkenes come off the SAME flat cation, and the only thing that changes between the two paths is which double bond is forming — so relative alkene stability is the only variable left. An E2 transition state has a second bill to pay: the base has to reach in and hold the beta hydrogen while the bond breaks, so a crowded hydrogen can be skipped for steric reasons even when it would give the better alkene. That is exactly why a bulky base pushes E2 toward the Hofmann product, while the same substrate left to solvolyze leans Zaitsev.
Ionization is an equilibrium step; adding more of the anion product (common ion effect) shifts that equilibrium backward and slows the overall forward reaction.
Unlike E2, where the base must be strong and well-positioned to drive a single slow concerted step, E1's second step is inherently fast and forgiving of a less capable base.

Count the beta hydrogens first and the answer looks like "none": the only carbon adjacent to the C–OH is quaternary. That is what kills E2 here, but not this. Acid protonates the OH, and as water leaves, a methyl migrates from the quaternary carbon with its bonding pair — the primary cation is far too poor to form on its own, so the shift happens on the way out. What is left is the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation, which now has beta hydrogens on both sides, and losing one by Zaitsev gives the trisubstituted 2-methylbut-2-ene. The skeleton in the product is not the skeleton you started with, which is the whole point of watching the cation.
e2: E2 ("bimolecular elimination") is concerted: base removes a proton as the leaving group departs, all in one step.
Anti-periplanar alignment lets the breaking C–H bond’s electrons align with the empty orbital forming as the leaving group departs — the best orbital overlap.
A bulky base struggles to approach the crowded carbon for SN2 backside attack, but has no trouble reaching an exposed, less hindered proton for E2.
Since the base participates directly in the single concerted step, both the substrate and the base concentrations appear in the rate law.
Proton removal, pi bond formation, and loss of the leaving group all happen at the same time in a single transition state.
All of this bond reorganization occurs in one coordinated transition state, which is what makes E2 concerted rather than stepwise.
A strong base is needed to remove the relatively unreactive beta-hydrogen in a single concerted step, and bases that are poor nucleophiles help elimination compete successfully against substitution.
Removing a beta-hydrogen, rather than the leaving group's carbon itself, is what allows the new double bond to form between those two adjacent carbons.
Since base concentration appears directly in the E2 rate law, doubling it doubles the reaction rate (all else equal).

Unlike SN2 (blocked at tertiary carbons) or SN1/E1 (essentially unavailable at primary carbons), E2 doesn't require carbocation formation or backside attack at the leaving-group carbon, so it tolerates all substitution levels.
E2 doesn't need to approach the crowded leaving-group carbon directly; the base simply needs access to a hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, which is much less hindered.

The order is 3° > 2° > 1°, which looks like SN1's order and has nothing to do with cations — E2 never makes one. In the E2 transition state the alpha and beta carbons already share partial double-bond character, so whatever stabilizes the alkene being formed also stabilizes the transition state leading to it. Alkyl groups stabilize alkenes, so more of them means a lower barrier. Note this is about rate; which alkene forms is a separate question decided by the base's bulk and by geometry.
Small bases can reach any available beta-hydrogen, so the more stable transition state leading to the more substituted alkene is generally favored.
A bulky base has trouble reaching the more crowded, more substituted hydrogens, so it preferentially grabs a more exposed, less hindered hydrogen, giving the less substituted alkene.

Rotate each diastereomer until the bromine and the beta hydrogen are anti-periplanar — that is the only conformation that can react — and then flatten the picture. The groups that were on one side of the Newman projection stay on that side of the new double bond, so the arrangement of phenyl and methyl across the C=C is fixed by which diastereomer went in. That is what stereospecific means, and it is the best evidence for the concerted mechanism: if anything broke first, the intermediate could rotate and both diastereomers would give the same mixture.
The chair conformation's geometry means only two adjacent axial groups are oriented 180 degrees apart from each other, which is the alignment E2 needs.

Ethoxide is strong but small, so it can reach the crowded beta hydrogen on the internal CH₂, and it does, because the alkene that results is disubstituted rather than monosubstituted — the Zaitsev product. Between the two geometries of but-2-ene, the E isomer dominates: its transition state keeps the two methyl groups on opposite sides of the forming double bond, where they do not crowd each other. But-1-ene is the minor elimination product and some butan-2-yl ethyl ether comes along from SN2, but the major product is (E)-but-2-ene.
The transition state leading to the E alkene generally has larger groups positioned farther apart, lowering steric strain and making it the lower-energy, more commonly favored pathway.
Because E2 is concerted and doesn't generate a free ionic intermediate, it doesn't depend as strongly on a solvent's ability to stabilize charge the way the ionization step of SN1/E1 does.
Hydroxide is simultaneously a good nucleophile and a good base, so on a substrate that is accessible enough for backside attack, both substitution and elimination pathways remain viable and compete.
Since the leaving group departs in the same single step as proton removal, a more stable, easier-to-lose leaving group lowers the activation energy for E2 just as it does for SN2.
Without a hydrogen positioned anti-periplanar to the leaving group on that side, the required transition-state geometry simply cannot be reached, so that elimination pathway is blocked.
E2's strict geometric requirement can override simple product-stability preferences; if the only anti-periplanar hydrogen happens to give the less stable alkene, that's still the product that forms.

Because only certain conformations place a given hydrogen anti-periplanar to the leaving group, the starting material's three-dimensional arrangement directly dictates which hydrogen is removed and therefore the resulting double bond geometry.

A kinetic isotope effect appears specifically when the bond to the isotope is broken in the rate-determining step; since E2's only step breaks the beta C-H bond, while SN2's step does not touch that bond at all, only E2 shows this effect.

The target is the less substituted alkene, which is the Hofmann product, and the way to get it is a base too bulky to reach the crowded internal hydrogen. tert-Butoxide fits: with this substrate it gives about 73% of the terminal alkene, where small ethoxide gives about 70% of the internal one. Iodide is a good nucleophile and a weak base, so it substitutes rather than eliminating; warm water gives unimolecular chemistry and, through the cation, the Zaitsev alkene again.
Since no cationic intermediate ever forms in E2, the usual instability of a primary carbocation is simply irrelevant to whether E2 can proceed.

On a chair, the only pairs of neighboring substituents that are genuinely anti-periplanar are trans-diaxial ones. An equatorial leaving group is roughly 60° from every hydrogen on both neighboring carbons, so no continuous orbital overlap is available and the concerted step cannot run. The ring has to flip first, which puts the bromine axial and every other substituent on the ring into its opposite position — and if those substituents are large, the cost of that flip shows up directly as a slower reaction. Menthyl chloride is the classic case.

Because the leaving group departs in the same concerted step as proton removal, a more stable, weaker-base leaving group like tosylate lowers the activation energy for elimination just as it does for substitution.

As basicity increases sharply, a reagent's tendency to grab a proton (driving elimination) increasingly outcompetes its tendency to attack the carbon directly (driving substitution), even without added steric bulk.
substrate-effects: Bulky strong bases have trouble doing backside attack (poor SN2) but easily deprotonate, favoring E2.
Polar protic solvents solvate (stabilize) carbocations and leaving groups well, favoring the ionization step in SN1/E1.
Primary carbons have minimal steric hindrance for backside attack and cannot stabilize a carbocation well, so SN2 dominates with a decent nucleophile.
With essentially no steric hindrance at the carbon and no ability to form a stable carbocation, backside attack (SN2) dominates.

Tertiary carbons can form stable carbocations, polar protic solvent stabilizes that ionization, and a weak base/nucleophile can't force a bimolecular pathway, so unimolecular substitution and elimination dominate.

Only the solvent moved, and for a secondary substrate that is enough to change the answer. In acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, azide is unsolvated and attacks fast: clean SN2, giving 2-azidobutane with inversion at C2. In water, azide is hydrogen-bonded and blunted while the solvent itself is strongly ionizing, so the substrate's own slow ionization starts to compete — the product becomes a mixture of inverted and racemized azide plus some butan-2-ol and a little alkene. Azide is a weak base either way, so elimination is never the main event.
With minimal alkyl substitution to stabilize the positive charge, a primary cation's energy is too high to form at a useful rate under normal conditions.
SN2's requirement for a clear backside approach is a geometric barrier that no change in reagent or solvent can overcome at a tertiary carbon.
Secondary carbons are sterically open enough for some backside attack yet can also form a moderately stable carbocation, so the outcome hinges heavily on the specific reagents and solvent chosen.
Polar aprotic solvents dissolve ionic reagents without caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, keeping it highly reactive for a bimolecular attack.

tert-Butoxide is a strong base carrying three methyl groups around the reacting oxygen. It is too fat to sit on the backside of C1 and push bromide out, but the beta hydrogens stick out on the outside of the chain where it can still reach one, so the E2 path is the cheap one and but-1-ene is the major product. Swap in ethoxide, which is just as basic but small, and the same substrate gives mostly butyl ethyl ether instead. Sterics on the BASE decide this one, not sterics on the carbon.

Substrate substitution pattern determines both whether backside attack is geometrically possible and whether a stable carbocation can form, which are the two gateway requirements for these mechanisms.
A primary substrate with an open backside path, a strong unhindered nucleophile, and a polar aprotic solvent that doesn't shield the nucleophile is the textbook setup for SN2.
A tertiary substrate in an ionizing polar protic solvent with only a weak nucleophile present is set up to ionize on its own, giving substitution and elimination from the resulting carbocation.
A strong base on a secondary substrate tends to favor elimination, especially with a base that is reasonably hindered, though some competing substitution is still possible.
A strong, minimally basic nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent favors attacking the carbon directly rather than removing a proton, pushing the reaction toward substitution.
Because azide is a much better nucleophile than base, and the solvent keeps it highly reactive, the reaction favors attacking the carbon over removing a proton.
Forming two separate, more freely moving product pieces (the alkene and, e.g., water) from one substrate is entropically favorable, and that advantage becomes more significant as temperature rises.
SN2 is blocked by the tertiary carbon's sterics, so a strong base reaching an available beta-hydrogen drives E2, and its bulk biases the outcome toward the less hindered, less substituted alkene.
Elimination requires a beta-hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, and methyl carbons have no adjacent carbon whatsoever, so substitution is the only mechanistic option available regardless of base bulk.
Steric crowding doesn't have to come from the reacting carbon alone; a hindered neighboring group plus a bulky base together can tip the balance toward elimination even at a formally primary carbon.

Count the beta hydrogens before proposing any elimination. Neopentyl has exactly one beta carbon and it is quaternary — three methyls and no hydrogen — so E2 is not slow here, it is impossible. The carbon bearing bromine is primary, so it will not ionize either, which rules out SN1, E1 and any rearrangement. That leaves SN2, which is allowed but throttled by the same quaternary neighbor blocking the backside: about 10⁵ times slower than ethyl bromide. Neopentyl is famous for being unreactive precisely because its one available pathway is crippled and its obvious alternative does not exist.

Ionizing power and nucleophile/base reactivity are somewhat independent levers; a solvent that strongly favors ionization can tip the balance toward unimolecular pathways even when a competent bimolecular reagent is technically present, partly because that same solvent also dampens the nucleophile's effective reactivity.

Since the bimolecular rate laws depend directly on reagent concentration while the unimolecular ones do not, pushing up reagent concentration makes the bimolecular pathway increasingly competitive, even on a substrate that might otherwise favor ionization.
Both families of mechanism have a hard requirement that this solvent and reagent combination fails to meet: no ionizing power for SN1/E1, and no reactive species at all for SN2/E2.

The substrate is secondary, so all four mechanisms are on the table and the reagent decides. Ethoxide is a strong base as well as a strong nucleophile, so adding it — in any solvent, and especially with heat — buys you mostly but-2-ene. What you want is a weak nucleophile that is an even weaker base, which is what neutral ethanol is: it cannot force a bimolecular step, the substrate ionizes slowly instead, and ethanol traps the cation to give the ether. The price is some racemization and a little E1 alkene, but it is the cleanest route to this ether from this substrate.

Some barriers are about rate (how fast something happens) while others are about feasibility (whether it can happen at all); the tertiary SN2 backside-attack problem is of the second, more absolute kind.

Elimination requires the reagent to act as a base, and a species can be an excellent nucleophile while still being a poor base, which is exactly the combination that shuts down the elimination pathway here.

Protic solvents work against bimolecular pathways by caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, and simultaneously work in favor of unimolecular pathways by stabilizing developing charge, so both effects push the balance the same direction.

SN2 is blocked at tertiary carbons and SN1/E1 are essentially blocked at primary carbons, but E2 needs neither backside access at the reacting carbon nor carbocation stability, so it tolerates the widest range of substrate types.
alkene-structure: Same side means cis. Each alkene carbon here carries one methyl and one hydrogen, so the higher-priority group on each is the methyl, and the two winners are on the same side — Z. The two labels agree in this case, which is exactly why cis/trans survives for simple alkenes. They are separate compounds, not conformers, because the pi bond cannot rotate.

Rank each carbon separately. On C2 the choice is Br against CH3, and bromine (Z=35) wins. On C3 it is CH3 against H, and the methyl wins. Those two winners — the Br and the C4 methyl — sit on the same side, so the alkene is Z. The skeleton looks trans because the methyls are opposed, which is the point: cis/trans reports the carbon chain and E/Z reports the priorities.
Rotating one carbon relative to the other would misalign the parallel p orbitals forming the pi bond, breaking that overlap — this restricted rotation is what gives rise to cis/trans alkene isomers.
Each alkene carbon forms three sigma bonds (to two substituents and the other alkene carbon) plus one pi bond from an unhybridized p orbital, which requires sp2 hybridization with 120° bond angles.
Each pi bond or ring removes two hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane formula CnH2n+2, so one double bond gives CnH2n.
CnH2n+2 is the alkane (fully saturated) formula. Alkenes have one fewer degree of saturation, so they follow CnH2n.
A double bond always consists of one sigma bond (head-on overlap) and one pi bond (side-by-side overlap of p orbitals); you cannot have two sigma bonds between the same two atoms.
The additional pi bond in a double bond pulls the two carbons closer together, shortening the bond compared to a single (sigma-only) bond.
Ethylene has one C-C sigma bond and four C-H sigma bonds (5 total), plus one pi bond that is not counted as a sigma bond.

A halogen caps a chain the way a hydrogen does, so it is counted with the hydrogens: DoU = (2x4 + 2 - 7 - 1)/2 = (10 - 8)/2 = 1. One ring or one pi bond fits — bromocyclobutane and 4-bromobut-1-ene are both C4H7Br.
Degree of unsaturation = (2(5)+2-10)/2 = (12-10)/2 = 1, consistent with one double bond and no ring.
The suffix -ene specifically designates a double bond in the parent chain, as in propene or 2-butene.
More substituted alkenes are stabilized by additional alkyl groups donating electron density (hyperconjugation) into the pi system, so tetrasubstituted alkenes are typically the most stable.

Cis/trans works while each alkene carbon carries one hydrogen and one other group: 'same side' then has an obvious referent. C2 here carries a bromine AND a methyl, so 'the methyls are opposite' and 'the bromine and the C4 methyl are on the same side' describe the same molecule and disagree. CIP priority settles it: Br beats CH3 on C2, CH3 beats H on C3, and the two winners are on the same side, so it is Z.

Nitrogen is added to the numerator, not subtracted: DoU = (2x5 + 2 + 1 - 11)/2 = (13 - 11)/2 = 1. The check is to write the saturated amine first, C5H13N, and notice the compound is two hydrogens short — two missing hydrogens is one ring or one pi bond. Piperidine is the familiar example.
A triple bond itself counts as two degrees of unsaturation (two pi bonds), so DoU=2 is consistent with one triple bond, two double bonds, two rings, or one ring plus one double bond.
CIP priority is assigned first by atomic number at the point of attachment; chlorine (Z=17) outranks a carbon-based methyl group (Z=6) regardless of what else is in the molecule.
If either alkene carbon has two identical substituents, there is no distinct 'other side' to compare, so no cis/trans isomerism exists; each carbon needs two different groups.
Each sp2 carbon retains one unhybridized p orbital oriented perpendicular to the plane of the three sp2 orbitals; side-by-side overlap of these two p orbitals creates the pi bond.

Pi electrons sit above and below the molecular plane, farther from the nuclei and more accessible to electrophiles, making the C=C pi bond a reactive site compared to the strong, low-energy C-C and C-H sigma bonds in alkanes.

In a cycloalkene the ring itself is one substituent on each alkene carbon, and it has to reach from one to the other. On the same side that is a short span; on the opposite side the chain must loop around and twist the pi system. Below roughly eight carbons there is not enough chain, so trans-cyclohexene has never been isolated and trans-cyclooctene is the smallest one that can be bottled.
In the cis isomer, the two methyl groups point to the same side of the double bond and crowd each other, raising the molecule's energy; in trans they point to opposite sides, minimizing steric clash.
DoU = (2×10+2-16)/2 = 3, consistent with, for example, one ring and two double bonds, a common pattern in monoterpenes.

Both attach through carbon, and both present the set (C, C, H) at that first atom — the vinyl only because a doubly bonded carbon is counted twice as a duplicate. The tie breaks one sphere further out: the vinyl's real CH2 carries (C, H, H) while each isopropyl methyl carries (H, H, H), and carbon beats hydrogen at the first point of difference. Duplicate atoms are phantoms with no substituents of their own, so they never win a tie-break.

An sp2 alkene carbon needs its three attached groups and itself to lie in one plane; in small fused or bridged ring systems the bridgehead geometry can't twist into that planar arrangement without severe strain (this limitation is summarized by Bredt's rule).

Placing the ring's two connecting chains on opposite faces of the double bond (trans) in a small ring requires bond angles far from ideal, introducing enormous strain; only larger rings (roughly 8+ membered) can accommodate a stable trans-cycloalkene.

An alkene carbon needs its three neighbors coplanar with it, and a bridgehead is held by three separate chains pulling in different directions. Below eight carbons the geometry is impossible — bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-1-ene cannot be made — while bicyclo[3.3.1]non-1-ene, with a longer bridge to give the room, is a real if reactive compound. The rule bites in elimination: a Zaitsev product that would be a bridgehead alkene simply does not form.
Because each alkene carbon is sp2 hybridized, its three sigma-bonded groups (including the other alkene carbon) are arranged trigonally in one plane, making the whole six-atom C=C unit planar.
Hydrogenation converts all alkene isomers to the same alkane product, so the isomer that starts out lower in energy (more stable) releases less heat upon hydrogenation.

All three end at the same alkane, so the heat released measures how far above that shared floor each one started. Releasing less heat means starting lower, i.e. more stable. The two effects visible here are the ones the chapter names: the disubstituted pentenes beat the monosubstituted one by alkyl donation into the pi system, and trans beats cis because the two substituents are not crowded on one side.
addition-reactions: Addition reactions break the reactive pi bond and add two new groups, one to each former alkene carbon.
Alkenes are electron-rich at the pi bond and act as nucleophiles toward an incoming electrophile, forming a carbocation (or similar) intermediate.
Br₂ is polarized by the approaching alkene and forms a bromonium ion intermediate, a classic electrophilic addition across the double bond.
Addition reactions convert the pi bond into two new sigma bonds to the added atoms, removing one degree of unsaturation from the starting alkene.
Addition reactions consume the pi bond, converting an alkene (or alkyne) into a more saturated product, which decreases the degree of unsaturation, not increases it.

The proton goes to the carbon that already carries more hydrogens — here the CH of the double bond — because that leaves the positive charge on the other carbon, which already bears two methyl groups. That tertiary cation is the more stable of the two on offer, and bromide captures it there, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
Br2 adds across the double bond, putting one bromine on each former alkene carbon, giving the vicinal dihalide 1,2-dibromoethane.
Hydration is the addition of water (formally H and OH) across the pi bond, converting the alkene into an alcohol.
The electron-rich pi bond of the alkene attacks the electrophilic halogen, and both halogen atoms end up added to the former double-bond carbons, making this an electrophilic addition.
Colored Br2 is consumed as it adds across a reactive pi bond, turning colorless; alkanes lack this reactive pi bond and don't decolorize Br2 without light or heat.

Bromine bridges the two carbons first. Water, in vast excess, then opens that bridge at the carbon carrying more positive character — the one with the two methyls — so the OH lands there and the bromine is left on the CH2 end. The product is 1-bromo-2-methylpropan-2-ol, with the two new groups anti to each other.
HX adds H to one carbon and the halogen X to the other, converting the alkene directly into an alkyl halide.

The alkene's pi electrons attack one bromine of Br2, displacing bromide and forming a three-membered ring bromonium ion in which bromine bridges both former alkene carbons, before bromide attacks from the opposite face.

Bromine bridges one face, so bromide has to open the ring from the other — anti addition. Work the two new centers out for the cis alkene and they come out matched, (2R,3R); attacking the other carbon of the same bridged ion gives (2S,3S) at exactly the same rate. The product is therefore a racemate of two chiral molecules, not a meso compound.

Mercury bridges both alkene carbons in a cyclic mercurinium ion; the positive character is delocalized rather than concentrated on one carbon, so water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without a true carbocation able to rearrange.
Since the first bromine already blocks one face as part of the bromonium ion, the incoming bromide ion must attack from the backside, giving net anti addition of the two bromines.
Both the alkene and H2 adsorb onto the same flat metal surface, so both hydrogen atoms are transferred to the same face of the double bond, giving syn addition.

The mechanism does not change — anti addition through the bromonium ion — but the starting geometry does, and that flips the answer. From the trans alkene the two new centers end up opposite, (2R,3S), and that molecule has an internal mirror plane, so it is meso and achiral. Same reagent, different alkene, different stereochemical outcome: that is what stereospecific means.

Two separate decisions. Charge decides which carbon: the bridged ion leans toward the more substituted carbon, so water attacks there and the OH lands on the carbon with the methyl. The blocked face decides which side: the ring still has to open from the far side, so the OH and the remaining Br finish anti. The product is 2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Acid catalysis protonates the alkene to form a carbocation, which water then attacks, adding H and OH across the former double bond in a process called acid-catalyzed hydration.
Without peroxides, HBr adds through a polar (ionic) mechanism: the alkene is protonated to form the more stable carbocation, which is then captured by bromide, giving the Markovnikov product.

A free carbocation is flat, and the nucleophile can reach either face of it, so a single clean diastereomer is the one thing that mechanism cannot deliver. Clean anti points to a bridged ion that seals one face; clean syn points to a concerted step that delivers both groups together. When a question tells you the stereochemical outcome, it has told you what the intermediate was.

Markovnikov puts the OH on C2, but the cation at C2 sits next to a quaternary carbon and would shift a methyl to become tertiary, so aqueous acid gives a rearranged alcohol. Oxymercuration reaches the same Markovnikov position through a bridged mercurinium ion, which never releases an open cation and so cannot rearrange. Hydroboration would give the anti-Markovnikov alcohol instead.

It is the other way round. The bridged halonium ion is unsymmetrical: the bond to the more substituted carbon is longer and weaker, so that carbon carries more positive character and is the one water attacks. The halogen is simply left holding the other carbon. Sterics would have sent water to the less hindered end, and charge overrules them.

In the standard two-step mechanism, the pi bond acts as a nucleophile toward the acidic H of HX, forming the more stable carbocation in the rate-determining first step, after which halide ion rapidly captures that carbocation.

Generating the carbocation requires breaking the pi bond and is the higher-activation-energy step; the subsequent capture of that carbocation by halide ion is fast, so the first step controls the overall rate.

Because a genuine carbocation forms during acid-catalyzed hydration, it is free to rearrange to a more stable carbocation (via a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift) before water attacks, sometimes giving a product with the OH in an unexpected position.

The bridge is not the symmetrical triangle it is usually drawn as. The carbon better able to hold positive charge pulls the ion toward itself: its C-Br bond stretches and weakens, and it takes on real cationic character. Attacking a carbon that is already part way to being a cation is the lower barrier, so charge beats sterics here.

Additional alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi system (making it a better nucleophile toward electrophiles) and stabilize the developing positive charge in the transition state, so more substituted alkenes typically react faster in electrophilic additions.

Protonation at C1 leaves a secondary cation at C2 with a tertiary C-H next door. A hydride migrates with its bonding pair, moving the charge to C3, and chloride captures it there — giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Rearrangement is only possible if a genuine free cation existed, which is why it never shows up in concerted additions such as hydroboration.
markovnikov: Protonating the less substituted carbon is what leaves the positive charge on the more substituted one, and that is the more stable cation. So the hydrogen goes to the carbon with more hydrogens already, and the bromide that arrives afterwards goes to the other one. Naming which species you mean matters: the H and the nucleophile end up on opposite carbons.

Without an initiator the reaction is ionic: the proton adds first, the secondary cation forms at C2, and bromide lands there — 2-bromobutane. With peroxides a bromine radical adds first, and it adds to C1 so as to leave the more stable secondary radical at C2; that radical then picks up a hydrogen. Br therefore finishes at C1 — 1-bromobutane. Same reagents, different first-arriving species.
In ionic (non-radical) addition, the proton adds to give whichever carbon leads to the more stable carbocation — i.e., the more substituted one — and the nucleophile then attacks that cation.
Markovnikov's original empirical rule: the H of HX ends up on the carbon that already bears more hydrogens, while X ends up on the more substituted carbon.

Boron goes to the less substituted, less hindered carbon — C2 — and the OH replaces it there on oxidation, so the product is 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, not the 1-methyl isomer. The Markovnikov alcohol with OH on the methyl-bearing carbon is what aqueous acid or oxymercuration would give instead.
Protonation occurs at the terminal CH2 carbon to generate the more stable secondary carbocation, which chloride then captures, giving 2-chloropropane as the Markovnikov product.

Peroxides generate bromine radicals that initiate a radical chain addition mechanism, which adds Br first and gives the opposite (anti-Markovnikov) regiochemistry compared to the normal ionic pathway.

Under radical (peroxide) conditions, bromine adds first to the terminal carbon to generate the more stable secondary radical, placing Br at the end of the chain — the anti-Markovnikov product, 1-bromopropane.
Protonation generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the central carbon, which water then attacks, giving tert-butanol as the Markovnikov product.

Carbocation stability increases with substitution (methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary) due to hyperconjugation and inductive donation from neighboring alkyl groups, so the reaction favors forming the more substituted, more stable carbocation.

Boron and hydrogen are joined to the two alkene carbons in one four-membered arrangement at the moment of reaction, so neither can arrive from the far side. That closed ring is where syn addition comes from — it is a geometric consequence of the transition state rather than a preference. Oxidation then swaps boron for OH without disturbing it.

The target has the OH on the more substituted carbon, so you want the Markovnikov route: aqueous acid protonates C2, the tertiary cation forms at C1, and water attacks there. Hydroboration would give the anti-Markovnikov alcohol at C2 instead, peroxide HBr would install a bromide, and Br2 in water would give a bromohydrin.

Protonation of the ring double bond occurs at C2 to place the positive charge on C1 (already bearing a methyl group), forming the more stable tertiary carbocation; bromide then attacks C1, so Br and the methyl end up on the same carbon.

Protonating the less substituted alkene carbon generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the other carbon; iodide then attacks that tertiary center, giving 2-iodo-2-methylbutane as the Markovnikov product.

Two things have to be right at once. The OH must end up on C2, which rules out both Markovnikov hydrations, and hydroboration puts boron there because it is the less hindered carbon. And the relative stereochemistry must be defined, which the syn addition supplies: the new H on C1 and the new OH on C2 arrive on the same face, which pushes the existing methyl to the other face.
Protonation at the terminal CH2 carbon generates the more stable carbocation at the internal, more substituted carbon, which halide then attacks, placing X on that more substituted carbon.

Hydroboration adds B and H across the alkene in one four-center transition state, so no free cation forms. The transition state is still polarized: the partial positive charge develops on the more substituted carbon, which is where it is best supported, and that puts boron on the less substituted one. Sterics push the bulky boron the same way, so both arguments point at the same carbon. Oxidation then replaces C-B with C-OH in place, leaving OH on the less substituted carbon.

Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bridged mercurinium ion, where positive character is greater, giving the same overall Markovnikov regiochemistry as acid-catalyzed hydration, but without carbocation rearrangement.

The radical chain begins when a bromine radical adds to the less hindered terminal carbon, generating the more stable internal (secondary or tertiary) carbon radical, which then abstracts H from HBr — this order is why Br ends up terminal.

Radical addition proceeds by bromine radical adding to generate the most stable carbon radical (paralleling how ionic mechanisms favor the most stable carbocation), which dictates where Br ultimately attaches.

Chlorine adds to the alkene very readily — a C-Cl bond at about 84 kcal/mol comfortably repays the 65 kcal/mol pi bond, roughly -19. The failure is the second step: pulling a hydrogen off H-Cl costs about 103 kcal/mol and returns a C-H worth about 98, so it is about +5 and uphill, and the chain stalls. HI fails at the opposite end, on the addition step.

Protonation gives a secondary carbocation adjacent to a carbon bearing three methyl groups; a methyl group can shift over (1,2-shift) to generate a more stable tertiary carbocation, leading to a rearranged chloride product alongside the 'simple' Markovnikov product.

The OH has to land on the terminal carbon, which is the anti-Markovnikov position, so hydroboration is the only route on the list that reaches it. There is a second reason it is the right answer here: a cation at C2 would sit beside a quaternary carbon and shift a methyl to become tertiary, and hydroboration never makes a cation at all, so nothing can rearrange.

Rearrangement needs a discrete carbocation to migrate into, and hydroboration never produces one: boron and hydrogen add in a single concerted step. That is what makes the reaction valuable twice over — it reaches the anti-Markovnikov alcohol, and it reaches any alcohol from a substrate whose cation would have shifted.

Peroxides undergo weak O-O bond homolysis to generate alkoxy radicals, which abstract a hydrogen atom from HBr to generate a bromine radical; this bromine radical is what adds to the alkene to begin the chain.

The simple 'more H's' heuristic can fail to clearly distinguish outcomes for more complex or highly substituted alkenes; the mechanistic version — protonate to form the more stable carbocation — is the general and reliable explanation underlying the empirical rule.

A chain needs both propagation steps to be roughly downhill, and for HBr they are: Br adding to the pi bond is about -5 kcal/mol and taking H from H-Br about -11. The two failures sit at opposite ends of the cycle. HCl stalls at the hydrogen abstraction, since H-Cl is worth 103 kcal/mol against the roughly 98 of the C-H being made, about +5 uphill. HI stalls at the addition, since a C-I bond returns only about 56 kcal/mol against the 65 of the pi bond broken, about +9 uphill.

Hydration and halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) proceed through cationic or bridged-ion intermediates that follow normal Markovnikov-type (most stable intermediate) selectivity; the radical chain pathway that flips the regiochemistry is essentially unique to peroxide-mediated HBr addition.

The ionic pathway is governed by carbocation stability, favoring Br at the more substituted carbon (C2); the radical pathway is governed by radical stability formed by Br adding first to the terminal carbon (C1), flipping the regiochemistry.

Syn is a statement about the two new groups only. The hydrogen lands on C1 and the OH on C2, both from the same face, so those two are cis to each other. The methyl on C1 was already there, and since the new hydrogen took the front face of C1 the methyl is pushed to the back — which leaves it trans to the OH. Oxidation keeps both position and configuration.
alkynes: sp hybrid orbitals have 50% s-character (vs. 25% for sp³), holding the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the conjugate base — more s-character, more acidic.
A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds.
The first HX addition (following Markovnikov) gives a vinyl halide; a second addition of HX to that alkene gives a geminal dihalide, both halogens on the same, more substituted carbon.
Each alkyne carbon forms two sigma bonds (linear, 180°) using sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals to form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.

Amide removes the terminal C-H (pKa 25) to give the acetylide CH3-C=C(-). That carbanion is an excellent SN2 nucleophile, and bromoethane is primary, so it displaces bromide and forms a new carbon-carbon bond. Three carbons plus two carbons, joined at the old terminal position, gives pent-2-yne.

Alkyne pi electrons are held closer to the carbon nuclei due to the higher s-character (more electronegative character) of sp carbons, making the alkyne pi bond somewhat less available to electrophiles compared to the more loosely held pi electrons of an alkene.
A triple bond counts as two degrees of unsaturation, removing four hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane (CnH2n+2), giving CnH2n-2.
In a terminal alkyne, such as HC≡C-CH3 (propyne), one sp carbon of the triple bond is bonded to a hydrogen atom rather than to another carbon, placing the triple bond at the very end of the chain.
An internal alkyne, like 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), has the triple bond flanked on both sides by carbon substituents, distinguishing it from a terminal alkyne, which has a triple-bond C-H.

Just as with alkenes, Br2 adds across one of the two pi bonds of the triple bond first, converting the alkyne into a dihalogenated alkene; a second equivalent of Br2 would be needed to fully saturate it into a tetrahalide.
The suffix -yne is used specifically to denote a triple bond in the parent chain, as in ethyne (acetylene) or 2-butyne.

Two eliminations remove two molecules of HBr, one to reach the vinyl halide and one to reach the alkyne, which accounts for two equivalents. The third is consumed immediately by the product itself: a terminal alkyne C-H at pKa 25 is deprotonated by any amide still in the flask, so the acetylide is what you actually have until water is added at the end.

Build the skeleton first, then set the geometry. Two rounds of deprotonate-and-alkylate with a primary halide put an ethyl group on each end of the triple bond, giving hex-3-yne. Lindlar delivers both hydrogens from one catalyst surface, so the alkene comes out cis; sodium in ammonia would have given the trans isomer, and a tertiary halide would have given E2 instead of alkylation.

A lower pKa means a stronger acid; water at pKa ~15.7 is far more acidic than even a terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25), even though the alkyne C-H is unusually acidic compared to other hydrocarbon C-H bonds.

Since the conjugate acid of amide ion, ammonia (pKa ~38), is a much weaker acid than a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25), sodium amide is a strong enough base to completely deprotonate terminal alkynes to form acetylide ions; hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ~15.7) is not strong enough.

Acetylide ions are strong, relatively unhindered carbanion-like nucleophiles that readily displace halide from primary (unhindered) alkyl halides via SN2, a classic method for extending carbon chains and building larger alkynes.
Markovnikov addition of water places OH on the more substituted alkyne carbon, generating an enol, which rapidly tautomerizes (favoring the more stable keto form) into a ketone.
Boron adds to the less substituted terminal carbon; oxidation replaces boron with OH there, giving an enol with OH on the terminal carbon, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde rather than a ketone.
With an unrestricted (non-poisoned) metal catalyst and excess H2, both pi bonds of the triple bond are hydrogenated in sequence, first to the alkene and then fully to the alkane.

The first addition is Markovnikov and puts the bromine on the internal carbon, giving 2-bromobut-1-ene. The second addition is Markovnikov on that alkene, and the bromine already present stabilizes the cation beside it by donating a lone pair, so the second bromine lands on the same carbon. The product is the geminal dihalide, 2,2-dibromobutane.

An acetylide is a strong base as well as a strong nucleophile, and a secondary substrate is hindered enough at the back side that elimination wins. The alkyne is protonated back to its neutral form and the halide becomes an alkene, so the intended carbon-carbon bond is never made. Acetylide alkylation is reliable on methyl and primary halides only.

Lead and quinoline additives reduce the catalytic activity of Pd just enough that it can still deliver H2 syn across a triple bond but is much less effective at further adsorbing and reducing the resulting alkene, letting the reaction be stopped cleanly at the cis-alkene stage.

The sequence is electron, proton, electron, proton. The first electron and proton give a vinyl RADICAL, which inverts rapidly at the carbon bearing the odd electron and therefore equilibrates to the less crowded trans-like geometry. The second electron makes that a vinyl ANION, which is configurationally stable on the timescale of the reaction, so the geometry it inherits survives the final protonation. Catalytic hydrogenation has no such step: both hydrogens arrive on one face from the metal surface, which is why Lindlar gives cis.

Unless the internal alkyne is symmetrical, Markovnikov addition of water is not perfectly selective for one carbon over the other when both are similarly substituted, so both possible enol/ketone regiochemistries can form, giving a mixture of ketone products.

The first HBr addition follows Markovnikov's rule, putting Br on the more substituted carbon to form a bromoalkene; the second HBr addition again follows Markovnikov's rule on that bromoalkene, placing the second Br on the very same carbon, yielding a geminal dihalide.

Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: the mercurinium bridge is opened by water at the more substituted carbon, so the oxygen lands on C2 and the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone. The bulky borane would have delivered the oxygen to the terminal carbon instead, giving hexanal, and neither reduction installs an oxygen at all.

Only a terminal alkyne has a CH-bearing end carbon available for boron's steric preference to place OH there after oxidation, generating a terminal enol that tautomerizes to an aldehyde; internal alkynes lack a terminal position and instead give ketones.

More shared electron pairs (three bonding pairs in a triple bond) pull the bonded atoms closer together and require more energy to break, and the increased s-character of sp orbitals further shortens the sigma bond, making triple bonds the shortest and strongest, followed by double, then single bonds.

sp hybridization uses only one s and one p orbital, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and oriented perpendicular to each other; each of these forms its own independent pi bond with the matching p orbital on the other sp carbon, giving two distinct, perpendicular pi bonds plus the one sigma bond.

Because both triple-bond carbons of 2-butyne carry identical methyl substituents, it doesn't matter which carbon water's oxygen ends up on — both regiochemical outcomes converge on the same single ketone product (2-butanone), avoiding the mixture problem seen with unsymmetrical internal alkynes.
conjugated-systems: Read the chain for a run of sp2 carbons with the bonds alternating. Hexa-1,3-diene has double, single, double across C1 to C4, so its p orbitals overlap continuously. The 1,5- and 1,4-dienes each have sp3 carbons breaking the run, and the 1,2-diene is cumulated: its central sp carbon holds the two pi systems at right angles.

C1=C2 and C3=C4 form one unbroken run of sp2 carbons, so those two pi bonds — four electrons — are conjugated with each other. C5 is sp3 and stops the chain there, leaving C6=C7 on its own as an ordinary terminal alkene. The molecule contains a conjugated diene and an isolated alkene, and only the first four electrons count.

s-cis and s-trans interconvert by rotation about the central single bond, which is free in any open chain — so both butadiene and isoprene reach s-cis whenever they need to. Cyclopentadiene is already locked there by its ring. A diene whose two double bonds are in different rings of a fused system has its ends held on opposite sides of that bond, and no rotation is available to bring them round.

Conjugated beats isolated beats cumulated. Buta-1,3-diene collects about 15 kJ/mol of delocalization energy for having its p orbitals in one continuous run. Penta-1,4-diene collects none, because an sp3 carbon separates its double bonds. Propa-1,2-diene collects none either and pays besides, since its sp center holds the two pi systems perpendicular to each other.

An allene is not strained: its sp central carbon wants 180 degrees and gets it, and the two sp2 ends want 120 degrees and get that. What it cannot do is delocalize. The two pi systems meet at the same carbon but lie at right angles, so neither one stabilizes the other, and the molecule pays for two pi bonds while collecting nothing back.

Build a reference with the same number of pi bonds as the compound you are testing: two independent C=C should release 2 × 120 = 240 kJ/mol. The diene releases only 232 reaching the same saturated ring, so it began 240 − 232 = 8 kJ/mol lower down. Subtracting one cyclohexene instead measures the second double bond rather than the conjugation.

Both runs finish at the same kind of product, a saturated alkane, and both break the same number of pi bonds. If one gives out less energy on the way to an equally stable destination, the only place that difference can have come from is a lower starting point. That is exactly what delocalization energy means.
Shorter than an ordinary C-C single bond at 1.54 A, because the pi system is delocalized and the bond has partial double-bond character.
It describes the conformation about the SINGLE bond joining the two double bonds, not a double-bond geometry.
They are conformations about a single bond, so rotation is free. cis and trans across a double bond cannot interconvert without breaking the pi bond.

s-trans wins because s-cis brings the inward-pointing hydrogen on C1 and the one on C4 close enough to crowd each other. The penalty is around 12 kJ/mol — nearly the size of the whole delocalization energy, so it is not a rounding error. It is still small enough that rotation keeps refilling the s-cis population at room temperature.
The two ends of the diene must reach the two ends of the dienophile at once, which only s-cis allows.

The requirement is geometric. Both new bonds form at once, so C1 and C4 of the diene have to point the same way to meet the two ends of the dienophile together. A ring that holds them on opposite sides of the central bond makes that impossible, and no amount of electron-donating substitution changes it.
Draw both resonance forms: the charge appears at the termini and never in the middle.
An empty p orbital next to a pi system conjugates with it, which is the same delocalization you draw as resonance.
Conjugation needs a p orbital that can align, and all of these provide one.

Conjugation needs a row of parallel p orbitals, not a row of double bonds. One of oxygen's two lone pairs occupies a p orbital lined up with the alkene's, so it overlaps and the electron density spreads onto the alkene carbons. The same picture explains enamines and amides, and it is why an enol ether's terminal carbon is unusually nucleophilic.

Alignment decides it, not proximity. In CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ the empty p orbital on the CH₂ is parallel to the pi system next to it, so the two overlap and the charge spreads over both end carbons. In CH₂=CH⁺ the empty orbital is an sp2 orbital lying in the molecular plane, perpendicular to the pi bond, so there is no overlap to be had — which is why vinylic cations are among the worst intermediates in organic chemistry.
Conjugation needs p orbitals aligned closely enough to overlap. At right angles they cannot.

An sp3 carbon has no p orbital to contribute, so the row of parallel p orbitals simply stops there. Penta-1,4-diene has exactly one such carbon, C3, and that is already fatal: each alkene behaves as though the other were not in the molecule. Reading the rule as 'two or more' is the commonest way to mis-classify this compound.
Every carbon in the conjugated run is sp2, which is what lets the p orbitals line up.

Overlapping n parallel p orbitals produces n molecular orbitals, so four p orbitals give ψ₁ to ψ₄. Each carbon contributes one electron, so the four pi electrons fill the lowest two. ψ₂ is therefore the highest occupied orbital and ψ₃ the lowest empty one — the pair that decides how the molecule reacts and what wavelength it absorbs.

In ψ₂ the coefficients are biggest at C1 and C4 and smallest at C2 and C3, with the phase flipping once in the middle. That is the orbital statement of the same thing the resonance forms say, and it is why a conjugated system reacts at its termini — bromide capture in the next section, and both new bonds of a Diels-Alder.
It never has to pay the rotation penalty, and it dimerizes on standing as a result.
It is the orbital picture of the same delocalization you draw with resonance structures.
Its half-filled p orbital conjugates with the adjacent pi bond, spreading the unpaired electron.
The formula is the same as for an isolated diene. The other three all report on the electrons.
The termini carry the charge, the odd electron, or the largest orbital coefficients.
Abstracting an allylic hydrogen leaves a resonance-delocalized radical, which makes that abstraction much easier.

s-cis is a minor conformer, not an absent one. Rotation about the central single bond happens far faster than the cycloaddition, so every molecule consumed from the s-cis pool is replaced at once and the reaction drains the whole sample through that conformation. A diene held s-trans by a ring has no rotation available, which is why that case is fatal and this one is only slow.
diene-addition: The intermediate is an allylic cation with two reactive ends, so bromide has two places to attack.
Protonating C1 puts the charge next to the remaining double bond, so it delocalizes.
3-bromobut-1-ene keeps a terminal CH2= group.

Br₂ opens on the diene the same way HBr does: a bromonium ion forms at one end and collapses to an allylic cation, leaving bromide with two carbons to choose between. Warm conditions let the first-formed product ionize again, so the mixture drains into the one with the more substituted alkene — 1,4-dibromobut-2-ene. Cold, you would isolate 3,4-dibromobut-1-ene instead.
Bromide captures C2, the carbon carrying most of the positive charge.
Bromide captures C4, at the far end of the delocalized system.
Roughly 80:20 in favor of 1,2. Cold and irreversible means the rates decide.

Choose the end to protonate first. Adding H to C1 puts the charge on C2, which is tertiary; adding it to C5's end puts the charge on C3, which is only secondary. So protonate C1. Cold means kinetic control, so bromide takes the carbon carrying most of the charge — the tertiary C2 — and the alkene stays between C3 and C4. Warm the same flask and you get 4-bromo-2-methylpent-2-ene, whose alkene is trisubstituted.
The resonance form with charge on C2 is secondary and the other is primary, so the better form puts more charge on C2.
Alkene stability rises with substitution, and the 1,4-product's double bond is internal and disubstituted.
You will meet the same name in enolate chemistry, for the same reason.
They describe where the two new groups landed relative to the starting diene, not the product's own numbering.
Bromide can leave again and regenerate the allylic cation, so the system re-equilibrates.

The π system is the nucleophile in the room, so it reaches for the proton first; that is what generates the allylic cation. Only then does bromide, which has been a spectator, arrive at one of the two charged ends. Nothing about this is concerted, and the radical route needs peroxides deliberately added.
A secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary one, so it describes more of the real intermediate.
The charge lands on C2, which bears two methyls and the chain.
Bromide captures the tertiary carbon, leaving the terminal alkene intact.
Bromide captures the far end, and the alkene moves inward to become trisubstituted.
With a methyl at each end of the allylic cation, capturing at either end gives the same compound.
Neither resonance form places charge on the middle carbon of the three-carbon system.
Nothing shifts. The intermediate was already delocalized, and capture at the far end simply fixes the other form.
The pi system is nucleophilic and takes the proton, which generates the allylic cation.
Protonating an inner carbon would give a cation that cannot delocalize into the remaining double bond.
Cold conditions prevent the products from reverting, so the first-formed ratio is frozen in.

Thermodynamic control is bought with reversibility, not with temperature. Heat is only useful because it lets a product ionize back to the intermediate and try again; if that path is closed, nothing that has formed can be unformed and the ratio stays wherever the two rates put it.

Ionizing that C–Br bond regenerates exactly the allylic cation the HBr addition went through, and ethanol can return to either end of it. Capture at the far end gives 1-ethoxybut-2-ene alongside 3-ethoxybut-1-ene. Chemists call it allylic rearrangement; it is the substitution-side view of the same delocalized intermediate.
One HBr adds across the system, so both are isomers of the same formula.
They are constitutional isomers, differing in where the Br and the double bond sit.
A localized cation has one electrophilic carbon; a delocalized one has two.
A nucleophile adding to the far end of a conjugated enone is the same idea with a different intermediate.
kinetic-thermodynamic: Lower transition state, smaller activation energy. It need not be the most stable product available.
Lower in energy once formed. It need not be the one that forms fastest.
The system can only settle into the most stable product if it is able to leave the others.
Low temperature stops anything climbing back out, so the first-formed ratio is frozen in.

Rate depends exponentially on the barrier, so small-looking gaps are not small. At room temperature about 6 kJ/mol is already a factor of ten, and 10 kJ/mol is around fifty. Because nothing can revert, that rate ratio is frozen in as the product ratio — which is what kinetic control means.
How high the hill is on the way out. Thermodynamics is how deep the valley is when you land.

Thermodynamics is about where you land, not how hard the climb was. The depth of a well is the stability of the product that sits in it, so the deeper well holds the thermodynamic product. The lower hilltop answers a different question — which product forms faster — and on an interesting diagram the two answers point at different routes.

They coincide often enough, and when they do there is nothing to discuss. The vocabulary exists for the cases where the lower hill and the deeper valley point in opposite directions — HBr plus a diene being the standard example — because then the conditions, not the substrate, choose the product.
Stability and rates are properties of the system. Temperature decides whether the system is allowed to find out.
An unusually low temperature is there to stop the reaction reversing, which freezes in the faster-formed product.

A bulky base reaches the least hindered proton fastest, so that product forms first; at −78 °C nothing has the energy to shuffle the proton around afterwards, so the first-formed ratio is the final one. In Enolate Chemistry this product has a name — the kinetic enolate — but the reasoning is the one from this section.

Equilibrating conditions mean the proton can come off and go back on repeatedly, so the mixture is free to re-sort itself and drains into whichever product is lower in energy — here the more substituted one. Nothing about which formed faster survives that process.

Hot dilute acid drives the sulfonation backwards and the group leaves, which is a rare privilege among substitutions on a ring. That reversibility is exactly the condition for thermodynamic control, and it is what makes –SO₃H usable as a temporary blocking group in synthesis.

Thermodynamic control requires a way back, and an E2 has none: once an alkene has formed it stays. Under ordinary conditions the Zaitsev alkene happens to be both the faster-formed and the more stable one, so there is no contest to referee. Calling it the thermodynamic product invites the idea that it needs equilibration, and it does not.

The bulky base cannot reach the interior proton comfortably, so the transition state leading to the more substituted alkene is pushed up and the other route becomes the faster one. Nothing about the alkenes themselves has changed — the Zaitsev product is still the more stable, it is simply no longer the quicker.
Rates decide, and B's extra stability is irrelevant because nothing will ever visit it.

A ratio that changes with temperature from the same starting materials means the mixture is being re-sorted, which needs a route back to the common intermediate. Cold, the rates decided and P won, so P is the kinetic product. Warm, the stabilities decided and Q won, so Q sits in the deeper well.

Heat is useful only because it lets a product climb back out and try again. Close that route and B's extra stability never gets a chance to matter, because nothing that has formed can be unformed. All the extra heat buys you is more of the faster product, sooner.
Bromide attacks C2, which carries more positive charge, so that route is faster.

Equilibrium ratios depend exponentially on the free-energy difference, so a factor of a hundred needs surprisingly little: around 12 kJ/mol at room temperature, which is about the size of one weak hydrogen bond. It is the same steepness that makes a 10 kJ/mol barrier difference worth a factor of fifty in rate.
Nothing about the mechanism or the intermediate changes. What changes is what the products can do afterwards.

Kinetic is a statement about a barrier and only about a barrier. Sterics are usually what makes one barrier lower, which is why 'kinetic' and 'less hindered' so often travel together — but here a favorable orbital interaction outweighs the crowding, and the more congested arrangement is still the quicker one.

An unchanging mixture is consistent with two opposite situations, and the observation alone cannot separate them: the system may have finished equilibrating and be sitting in the deepest well, or it may be frozen because no product can get back to the intermediate. To tell them apart, start from pure one product and see whether the mixture reappears.
Reversibility, not temperature, is the actual requirement. Heat without a way back changes nothing.
That question determines which of the two comparisons you should even be making.

ΔG is the free-energy change between two real species, and it tells you where an equilibrium sits. ΔG‡ is the climb from the starting point to the transition state at the top of the hill, and it tells you how fast. The dagger is the notation's way of saying that the thing at the other end is not something you could isolate.
A branch point is what lets conditions select between outcomes.

Each of the others is a genuine branch point where one route is faster and another gives the more stable product, and where conditions pick between them. SN2 stereochemistry is not a competition at all: backside attack is the only geometry the reaction has, so inversion is forced by the mechanism rather than selected by the conditions.
Reversibility is what lets the warm run reach a different answer from the same intermediate.
Once formed it stays, so the product ratio simply records which route was faster.
diels-alder: Four pi electrons from the diene and two from the dienophile.

Both new bonds form on one face of the dienophile in a single step, so nothing is ever free to rotate and the starting geometry survives intact. Trans across the alkene becomes trans on the ring — on neighboring carbons, one up and one down. Run it with dimethyl maleate, the cis isomer, and you get the cis product just as cleanly.
Three pi bonds go in; two sigma bonds and one pi bond come out, which is why the reaction is downhill.
Every bond breaks and forms in one step through a single cyclic transition state.
With no intermediate there is nothing to shift, nothing to lose stereochemistry and nothing whose stability to compare.
Both ends of the diene must reach both ends of the dienophile at once.
It is a geometric requirement, and no amount of electronic tuning fixes it.
It pays no rotation penalty, and dimerizes on standing as a result.
It dimerizes at room temperature via a Diels-Alder, and the retro reaction on heating gives it back.
They lower its LUMO, bringing it closer to the diene's HOMO.
They raise its HOMO, narrowing the gap to the dienophile's LUMO.

Count the groups pulling the LUMO down. Maleic anhydride has two carbonyls flanking its C=C; methyl acrylate has one ester; ethene has nothing at all and needs forcing conditions. The narrower the gap to the diene's HOMO, the faster the pair reacts, so the order follows the electron-withdrawing power directly.

Polarize each partner. Isoprene's methyl sits on C2, which puts the nucleophilic end of the diene at C1; the ester on the dienophile puts the electrophilic end on the CH₂ that does not carry it. Bond those two, and the methyl and the ester finish 1,4 apart. A 2-substituted diene always gives this 'para' relationship; the 1,3 arrangement is not on the menu at all.
Nothing lowers its LUMO, so the orbital gap to the diene stays wide.
