Both bonds form on the same face in one step, so nothing can rotate and the relationship is preserved.

Cut the target at its retro-Diels-Alder disconnection: step one carbon out from each end of the ring double bond and break the two bonds leading away, which leaves buta-1,3-diene and a two-carbon piece carrying both esters. Since the reaction preserves the dienophile's geometry, cis esters in the product demand cis esters in the dienophile — dimethyl maleate. Fumarate would give the trans ring product, and cyclopentadiene would give a bicyclic one.

Stereospecific means the answer is read off the starting material rather than guessed: change the geometry going in and you get a predictably different geometry coming out. Both new bonds form on one face of each partner — suprafacial, in the formal vocabulary — so nothing gets a chance to scramble.
The endo transition state benefits from a secondary orbital interaction, making it faster.

That arrangement is the endo one, and it comes from the stack in which the anhydride is tucked under the diene as the bond forms. It is the more crowded of the two approaches and still the faster, because the anhydride's pi system touches the diene's in the transition state. Note that endo is the kinetic answer here: the exo adduct is usually the more stable of the two.
It forms faster, which is a useful corrective to reading kinetic as less hindered.
Heating a suitable cyclohexene sends it back to a diene and a dienophile.
Mentally cutting a six-membered ring at that disconnection is one of the most productive moves in retrosynthesis.

The defining feature is the single step with no intermediate and the electrons travelling in a closed circuit, not the shape of the product. Cycloadditions such as the Diels-Alder are one family; electrocyclic ring closures and sigmatropic shifts like the Cope and Claisen rearrangements are the others. Plenty of ring-forming reactions are not pericyclic at all.

The methyl sits on a terminal carbon of the diene, which makes this a 1-substituted diene, and those give the 'ortho' relationship. Check it by polarizing: the donor end puts the diene's nucleophilic carbon at the far terminus, that carbon bonds to the dienophile's CH₂, and the methyl-bearing end is therefore left bonded to the carbon carrying the CHO — next-door neighbors on the new ring.

An alkyne brings two pi electrons to the ring just as an alkene does, and its second pi bond is untouched by the reaction. So the product keeps that bond alongside the new one between the diene's old C2 and C3, and what you isolate is a cyclohexa-1,4-diene rather than a cyclohexene.
The two terminal carbons form the new sigma bonds, and the central bond becomes the alkene.
Sigma bonds are stronger, so trading two pi bonds for two sigma bonds releases energy.
One transition state, no intermediate, and every consequence of that follows.

Coordinating to the carbonyl oxygen drains electron density out of the C=C next to it, dropping the dienophile's LUMO closer to the diene's HOMO. Rates can rise by orders of magnitude and the endo preference usually sharpens. It is a genuine catalyst and not a requirement — the reaction is downhill on bond energies alone.
It can never reach the conformation where both ends point the same way.
uv-vis: A pi to pi-star transition, promoting an electron across the frontier orbital gap.
A bigger gap needs a higher energy photon, and higher energy means shorter wavelength.
Less energy is needed, and lower energy light has a longer wavelength.
More p orbitals give more molecular orbitals over a similar range, so the highest occupied rises and the lowest empty falls.

Count what is actually conjugated, not what is present. Hexa-1,3,5-triene has three double bonds in one unbroken run, so it has the most molecular orbitals packed into the same energy range and the narrowest HOMO-LUMO gap — 258 nm. Hexa-1,4-diene has an sp3 carbon between its two double bonds, so it behaves as two lone alkenes and absorbs below 200 nm, out of reach.

The wavelength tells you the gap; the ε tells you how allowed the jump is. A π to π* transition in a conjugated system runs to ε in the tens of thousands. A lone pair on a carbonyl oxygen points sideways relative to the π* it has to reach, so the n to π* band is nearly forbidden — ε of ten to a hundred — even though it sits at a long wavelength. A long λ with a tiny ε is the signature of a lone pair.

Derive it rather than memorizing it. A is a bare number, c is in mol per litre and l is in centimetres, so ε has to supply exactly what cancels those two: litres per mole per centimetre. Writing 'ε = 21,000' without units is shorthand for 21,000 L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹.

Rearrange first: c = A / εl = 0.63 / (21,000 × 1.00) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. Check the units as you go — L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹ times cm leaves L·mol⁻¹, and dividing a unitless absorbance by that gives mol·L⁻¹. Thirty micromolar is a few milligrams in a litre, which is what a large ε buys you.

Isolated double bonds do not pool their orbitals, so each behaves as a lone alkene absorbing below 200 nm where a routine instrument cannot look. A band at 258 nm needs a single run of three conjugated C=C. This is the one structural question UV-Vis answers sharply: how long the conjugation is, though not where in the molecule it sits.

In organic UV-Vis it is nearly always the conjugated π system, and sometimes a lone pair beside one. A group that is not itself a chromophore but shifts the band of a neighboring one — an OR or an NR₂ — is called an auxochrome, and that is how a dye's color is tuned without lengthening the chain.
It removes blue light around 450 nm, and what reaches your eye is the complementary color.
Without a long conjugated system the gap is too wide, so absorption stays in the ultraviolet.
Absorbance equals molar absorptivity times concentration times path length.
A constant for that compound at that wavelength, measuring how strongly it absorbs.
Conventionally 1 cm for a standard cuvette.
The Beer-Lambert relationship makes it the standard way to follow a concentration while a reaction runs.
Conjugated systems absorb strongly, which is part of why the technique is sensitive.
Conjugation narrows the gap, so the conjugated isomer absorbs at the longer wavelength.
It reports on conjugation, and on amount once ε is known — but nothing about position or connectivity. Pair it with NMR for that.
Below about 400 nm is ultraviolet, so a compound absorbing past that point can appear colored.
A single C=C absorbs below about 200 nm, which ordinary instruments do not reach comfortably.

The Woodward-Fieser increments make this arithmetic: each alkyl group or ring residue is worth about +5 nm and each extra conjugated C=C about +30, so 5 + 5 + 30 is roughly +40. Notice the size of the two terms — lengthening the conjugation dominates, and substituents only nudge, which is why UV-Vis counts double bonds well and identifies substituents badly.
Each technique answers a different question, and this is the one UV-Vis answers sharply.
IR reports on bond vibrations, which are characteristic of particular groups.
It turns the chapter's central claim into a number you can read off an instrument.
Read off the instrument, and proportional to concentration by Beer-Lambert.
Each additional conjugated double bond narrows the gap further and pushes absorption to longer wavelength.

Combining the p orbitals of a conjugated system gives a set of π orbitals; the bottom half are bonding and filled, the top half antibonding and empty. The lowest empty one is the π* that an absorbed photon promotes an electron into. Naming it matters because the other common band in organic UV-Vis ends in the same π* but starts from a lone pair instead, and that one is weak.
Extended conjugation brings its absorption into the visible, which is what makes vision possible.
It answers one question sharply and says little about connectivity, so NMR does the placing.
alcohol-reactions: Hydroxide is a strong base (poor leaving group); alcohols are typically first protonated (or converted to a better leaving group like a tosylate) before substitution/elimination.
Protonation turns the leaving group into neutral H₂O, which is a much weaker base (and thus a far better leaving group) than OH⁻.

TsCl converts the OH into OTs, a weak-base, excellent leaving group, via a mechanism that doesn’t touch the stereocenter’s configuration (unlike acid-catalyzed substitution, which can invert or racemize it).
Tertiary carbocations are stable enough to form, so the reaction proceeds through ionization (loss of water) followed by chloride capture, a classic SN1 pathway.

Primary carbocations are far too unstable to form, so a primary alcohol reacts with HX by SN2 instead: the acid protonates the oxygen, and bromide attacks the carbon from the back while neutral water - the actual leaving group - departs.
SOCl2 reacts through a chlorosulfite intermediate without generating a free carbocation, avoiding the hydride or alkyl shifts that can occur in purely acid-catalyzed routes.

PBr3 converts the OH into an ester of phosphorus that bromide then displaces in one backside step, so no carbocation is ever formed and nothing can shift. The HBr and H2SO4/NaBr routes both work by protonating the OH, which at a secondary carbon means ionization to a cation - and a cation is free to rearrange. NaBr alone does nothing at all, because hydroxide cannot leave.

Protonation and loss of water give a secondary cation at C2. Its neighbor C3 is quaternary, so it has no hydrogen to send across - but it can send a whole methyl group with its bonding pair, and that 1,2-methyl shift converts the secondary cation into a tertiary one. Bromide captures that rearranged cation, so the bromine sits on a carbon that never carried the hydroxyl.

POCl3 converts the OH into a dichlorophosphate ester under basic conditions, and pyridine then removes an anti-periplanar beta hydrogen in a single concerted E2 step. No acid is used and no carbocation is formed, so nothing else in the molecule is exposed and the skeleton cannot shift. Hot H2SO4 does the same dehydration but through a cation, and hydroxide is far too poor a leaving group for base alone to eliminate it.

Tosylation happens at sulfur: the alcohol oxygen attacks the S of TsCl and chloride leaves, so the C-O bond is never broken. Nothing at carbon moves, and the stereocenter is handed on intact. Any inversion you see later belongs to the substitution step that displaces the tosylate, not to the tosylation.

Zaitsev's rule favors the more stable, more substituted alkene; in the E1 mechanism the carbocation loses a proton preferentially toward the more substituted side, forming the more stable double bond.
The OH must first be protonated to become a good leaving group (water), which then departs to generate a carbocation; a base finally removes a beta-proton to form the alkene.

The rate-limiting step is carbocation formation; hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from additional alkyl groups stabilize more substituted carbocations, lowering the activation energy for their formation.

Because the mechanism passes through a carbocation intermediate, a hydride or alkyl shift can occur before the proton is lost, shifting the position of the resulting double bond or even the carbon skeleton.
Alcohols are weak acids; the reactive Na metal reduces the O-H proton, releasing H2 gas and leaving behind the sodium alkoxide salt.
The alkoxide, not the neutral alcohol, is the nucleophile needed to perform SN2 displacement on the alkyl halide partner, so a strong, non-nucleophilic base like NaH is used first to form it.

Count the steps that break the C-O bond at C2: exactly one. Tosylation happens at sulfur and leaves the stereocenter alone, then cyanide displaces the tosylate by backside attack. One inversion means the product is inverted, not racemic - a tosylate is a good enough leaving group that a secondary carbon has no reason to ionize with a strong nucleophile present.

Work in the order the mechanism runs: protonate, lose water to a secondary cation, then check for a shift before applying Zaitsev. A methyl migrates from the quaternary neighbor to give a tertiary cation, and losing a beta hydrogen from that rearranged skeleton gives the tetrasubstituted alkene. Applying Zaitsev to the original skeleton instead gives a confident wrong answer.

Once the OH is a tosylate, that carbon behaves like a secondary alkyl halide, so the SN2-versus-E2 competition from Substitution and Elimination applies unchanged. Ethoxide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile, and at a secondary carbon a strong base takes a beta hydrogen faster than it attacks the crowded carbon, so elimination dominates.

Alkyl groups donate electron density to the alkoxide oxygen and crowd it out of good solvation, so ethanol (pKa 16) and tert-butanol (pKa 18) are both weaker acids than water (15.7). Methanol is the exception that makes the wording matter: at pKa 15.5 it is slightly more acidic than water, because it carries the least alkyl bulk of all.
The added alkyl groups push electron density onto the already-negative alkoxide oxygen, destabilizing the anion (and hindering its solvation), which raises the pKa relative to methanol.
The O-H of an alcohol is acidic enough to protonate the strongly basic, carbanion-like Grignard reagent, quenching it as an alkane before it can perform any useful addition chemistry.

The alcohol oxygen attacks sulfur, which parks a leaving group on the oxygen rather than on carbon. That group departs as sulfur dioxide and chloride, two stable and weakly basic pieces, so chloride can finish the job with an ordinary backside displacement. Nothing is oxidized and no positive charge is ever built on carbon, which is why the product is cleanly inverted and never rearranged.

Hydroxide is the conjugate base of water, pKa 15.7, which makes it a strong base and one of the worst leaving groups in the course. Cyanide cannot displace it however hot the flask gets. The OH has to be activated first - as a tosylate, or by protonation - and then cyanide will do the SN2.

Acidity falls as alkyl groups are added around the oxygen: methanol 15.5, water 15.7, ethanol 16, tert-butanol 18. Those alkyl groups donate electron density into an already negative alkoxide and, more importantly in solution, wrap it in bulk that keeps solvent molecules from stabilizing the charge. Methanol carries the least bulk, so its alkoxide is the best solvated and methanol is the strongest acid of the four.

E1 requires the leaving group to depart before anything else happens, which means paying the full price of the carbocation. A primary cation is stabilized by almost nothing, so that route is closed. The elimination instead happens in one concerted step, with the base removing the beta hydrogen as water leaves, which never puts a full positive charge on carbon - and it is why primary alcohols need higher temperatures than secondary or tertiary ones.

PBr3 first converts the OH into a good leaving group, and bromide then displaces it in a single concerted backside attack, giving clean inversion rather than the racemization seen with carbocation intermediates.
Because PBr3 operates through a concerted SN2-type displacement without a free carbocation, bromide must attack from the side opposite the leaving group, inverting the configuration.

Protonation of the OH followed by loss of water generates a planar carbocation that can be attacked by bromide from either face, scrambling the stereochemistry relative to the clean inversion seen with PBr3.

Acid-catalyzed dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate; tert-butanol forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation most readily, so it reacts fastest, while methanol has no adjacent carbon to form a double bond with at all.
ether-chemistry: Like alcohols, ethers need protonation (acidic conditions) to turn the alkoxide oxygen into a viable leaving group (neutral alcohol) before cleavage.

A tertiary carbon ionizes readily once the oxygen is protonated, so the alcohol leaves on its own and iodide captures the resulting carbocation - SN1. A primary or methyl carbon cannot support a cation, so there iodide attacks directly, SN2. A secondary carbon sits between the two and does some of each.

Ethers lack an acidic proton and don’t have a good leaving group under neutral/basic conditions, so they tolerate strongly basic/nucleophilic reagents while still solvating them through the oxygen’s lone pairs.

Alcohols can hydrogen-bond to one another through their O-H groups, which raises their boiling points substantially; ethers lack an O-H bond, so they only experience weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces between molecules.
An ether oxygen has lone pairs that can accept a hydrogen bond from an O-H or N-H elsewhere, but since ethers have no O-H or N-H of their own, they cannot donate a hydrogen bond.

Protonation makes the oxygen a viable leaving group, but neither carbon here can carry a positive charge, so the cleavage has to be an SN2 - and an SN2 goes where the approach is clearest, the methyl. That gives methyl iodide and propan-1-ol. Only with excess HI and more heating does the propanol go on to become propyl iodide.

The tertiary carbon ionizes to a stable carbocation once the oxygen is protonated, so cleavage happens there and iodide captures the cation: tert-butyl iodide and methanol. Note that the most hindered carbon is attacked precisely because no backside attack is involved. With excess HI the methanol would go on to give methyl iodide as well.

The tertiary carbon can ionize to a stable carbocation far more easily than the primary carbon can undergo a slow SN2 displacement, so cleavage occurs preferentially at the tertiary center, releasing the primary alcohol intact.

Ask which mechanism is running before asking which carbon reacts. A secondary cation is not stable enough to form readily under these conditions, so the cleavage is an SN2, and an SN2 is decided by sterics: iodide attacks the primary ethyl carbon. Had one carbon been tertiary, the answer would have flipped, because that carbon would ionize without help.

A bulky, basic alkoxide approaching a hindered tertiary carbon strongly favors removing a beta-hydrogen (E2) over performing a backside SN2 attack, so elimination products dominate instead of the desired ether.

Because the alkyl halide is the electrophile undergoing SN2 attack, choosing one that is primary (or otherwise unhindered) avoids competing elimination, regardless of how bulky the alkoxide nucleophile itself is.
The ring of oxygen atoms in a crown ether can wrap around a metal cation of the right size, effectively dissolving otherwise poorly soluble ionic salts in nonpolar solvents.

Crown ethers show size selectivity, and the numbers to compare are diameters: 18-crown-6 has a cavity about 2.7 Angstroms across and K+ is 2.66 Angstroms, so the ion fills the hole and contacts all six oxygen lone pairs at once. Na+ is only 1.9 Angstroms across, so it sits in a cavity too large for it, touches fewer oxygens at a time and binds far more weakly.

Normally F- is tightly ion-paired with its counter-cation and poorly solvated in nonpolar media, dampening its reactivity; encapsulating K+ inside the crown ether frees the anion to act as a much more potent, less hindered nucleophile.

The halide is the electrophile in an SN2, so it has to be the unhindered partner - here, iodomethane. Pairing methoxide with a tertiary halide instead gives elimination: the alkoxide is a strong base, and at a tertiary carbon it removes a beta hydrogen rather than attacking. Put the bulk on the alkoxide and the simplicity on the halide.

THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metal cations (helping stabilize organometallic reagents in solution) while its ring is chemically unreactive toward most nucleophiles and bases, making it a versatile, widely used solvent.

Autoxidation at the carbon next to the ether oxygen slowly generates peroxide and hydroperoxide species that can concentrate and detonate, especially when the ether is evaporated or distilled, which is why old ether stocks are handled with caution.

Removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to the ether oxygen gives a radical that is stabilized by overlap with a lone pair on oxygen, making that particular C-H bond especially susceptible to slow radical autoxidation by atmospheric O2.

Every route through an SN2 fails at a tertiary carbon, because the alkoxide is a strong base and eliminates instead. Alkoxymercuration avoids SN2 entirely: mercury bridges the alkene, the alcohol opens that bridge at the carbon better able to carry positive charge (Markovnikov), and NaBH4 then replaces the mercury with hydrogen. No free cation is involved, so nothing rearranges either.

With excess strong acid and heat, both C-O bonds of the symmetrical ether are eventually cleaved by iodide via SN2, first releasing ethanol (which itself then reacts further with HI) and ultimately converting both ethyl groups into ethyl iodide.
Adding a proton to the ether oxygen gives it three bonds plus a formal positive charge, a species called an oxonium ion, which makes the adjacent C-O bonds much easier to break.

Chromium oxidation of an alcohol works by forming a chromate ester at the O-H and then removing a hydrogen from the carbinol carbon; with no O-H, an ether offers no way in, so these reagents leave it alone. That is a statement about deliberate oxidation at carbon, not about the slow radical autoxidation at the alpha C-H that forms peroxides in a bottle left open to air.

Ether solvents donate electron density from their oxygen lone pairs to the electrophilic magnesium center, which helps stabilize and solubilize the highly reactive organomagnesium species; nonpolar hydrocarbons cannot offer this coordination.

An alkoxide is a strong base as well as a good nucleophile, and a tertiary carbon offers it no backside to attack. So it takes a beta hydrogen instead and eliminates, giving 2-methylpropene plus methanol. This is the standard exam trap in Williamson planning: the two disconnections of an unsymmetrical ether are not interchangeable.
THF is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbons, making it a saturated cyclic ether rather than an open-chain one.

Rather than using a standalone 'ether' suffix, the preferred IUPAC approach treats the shorter alkyl-oxygen unit as an alkoxy substituent on the longer parent chain, giving names like methoxyethane for ethyl methyl ether.

The ether oxygen's lone pair can donate into the empty orbital of a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a stable donor-acceptor (Lewis acid-base) adduct, such as the BF3 etherate commonly used as a mild Lewis acid catalyst.

Although ethers cannot donate hydrogen bonds, their oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules, giving small ethers noticeably greater water solubility than alkanes of similar size.

After the ether oxygen is protonated, the halide ion must still act as the nucleophile (or cation-trapping species) that displaces the alcohol; iodide and bromide are considerably more nucleophilic than chloride, making the overall cleavage much faster and more practical.

Alkoxymercuration-demercuration adds methanol across the double bond with Markovnikov selectivity and no rearrangement, giving the ether directly. Alkoxide does not add to an isolated alkene; mCPBA then methanol gives a methoxy alcohol rather than a simple ether, because the epoxide leaves an OH behind; and HBr then methoxide is a Williamson on a secondary halide, which loses mostly to E2.
epoxides: The ~60° bond angles in the three-membered ring are far from ideal, so opening the ring relieves substantial strain, driving reactivity.
Basic/neutral conditions favor an SN2-like mechanism — backside attack at the less hindered carbon.

Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring-opening more SN1-like, so the nucleophile attacks the carbon that better stabilizes positive charge — the more substituted one — unlike the SN2-like base-catalyzed case.
Peroxyacids like mCPBA deliver an oxygen atom directly across the carbon-carbon double bond in a single concerted step, converting the alkene into an epoxide.

The peroxyacid transfers its oxygen to both alkene carbons simultaneously from one face in a single concerted step (often pictured as a 'butterfly' transition state), so the new C-O bonds form on the same side of the original double bond.

Syn addition preserves the original cis relationship of the two methyl groups, and the resulting epoxide has an internal mirror plane, making it a single achiral meso compound rather than a mixture of enantiomers.

Syn addition to the trans alkene produces a chiral epoxide (no internal mirror plane); because the peroxyacid can approach either face of the planar alkene with equal likelihood, both enantiomers form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

In both the basic and acidic mechanisms, the nucleophile approaches from the side opposite the breaking C-O bond, so the carbon under attack is inverted even though the overall regiochemistry (which carbon is attacked) differs between the two conditions.
Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the ring oxygen (backside attack), so the two new OH groups end up anti to each other, giving the trans diol rather than the cis one.

Hydride is a strong nucleophile that reacts via an SN2-like pathway, so like other strong nucleophiles it attacks the less sterically hindered carbon, which ends up bonded to the delivered hydrogen while the OH remains on the more substituted carbon.
Grignard reagents are strong, basic carbon nucleophiles that react with epoxides under essentially basic-type conditions, favoring backside SN2 attack at the more accessible, less hindered carbon.

Under acidic conditions the protonated epoxide is opened by bromide acting as the nucleophile at one carbon, while the oxygen (now an OH after losing its proton) remains on the adjacent carbon, giving a halohydrin.

Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the C-O bonds partial cationic character, concentrated at the carbon that would form the more stable carbocation; even a weak nucleophile like methanol is then directed to that more substituted carbon.

Under basic or neutral conditions the epoxide is not protonated, so the strong methoxide nucleophile simply performs a straightforward SN2 attack at the more sterically accessible, less hindered carbon.
An epoxide, or oxirane, is defined by this specific three-membered ring of two carbons and one oxygen, which is what gives it its characteristic angle strain and heightened reactivity.

Only one C-O bond breaks, and it is the one at the carbon under attack. Under basic conditions ethoxide attacks the less hindered carbon, so that carbon gets the new OEt group and the oxygen stays where it already was - on the more substituted carbon, picking up a proton at workup. Tracking which carbon keeps the oxygen is half of getting these products right.

Under acid, protonation weakens the C-O bonds and shifts positive character toward whichever carbon can better stabilize it (the more substituted one), directing even weak nucleophiles there; under base, the unprotonated, still-strained ring is simply attacked wherever the strong nucleophile can approach most easily, favoring the less hindered carbon.

Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring vastly more electrophilic, so weak nucleophiles that would otherwise be unreactive can now attack; without that activation, only strong, good nucleophiles can open the strained but un-activated ring at a useful rate.

Amines are good, strongly basic nucleophiles, so like other strong nucleophiles they attack the less sterically hindered carbon of the epoxide via an SN2-like pathway, generating a beta-amino alcohol.

A meso epoxide has two carbons that are enantiotopic to each other; an achiral nucleophile has no way to distinguish between them, so it attacks each one with equal probability, producing equal amounts of both resulting enantiomers.

Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the more substituted carbon significant carbocation-like character in the transition state, so water (even though it is a weak nucleophile) is directed there preferentially, just as with other acid-catalyzed epoxide openings.

The highly strained bond angles of the oxirane ring store considerable potential energy; opening the ring to form a less strained, acyclic product is thermodynamically favorable and is the underlying reason epoxides react so readily compared to ordinary ethers.

An unstrained ether's C-O bond is simply too strong and the oxygen too poor a leaving group for hydroxide to displace at room temperature, but the epoxide's ring strain dramatically lowers the barrier for the same kind of backside nucleophilic attack.

The reaction is usually described as borderline or concerted, with the nucleophile beginning to attack as the C-O bond breaks rather than waiting for a fully independent, freely rotating carbocation to form first; this is why some stereochemical and regiochemical control is retained even under acidic conditions.

A neutral ether oxygen is a poor leaving group, but once protonated it becomes a much better one (similar to protonating an alcohol); this protonation also pulls electron density away from the ring carbons, making them more attractive targets for even weak nucleophiles.

mCPBA delivers an oxygen to one face to give cyclohexene oxide, and hydrolysis then opens that ring by backside attack, so water arrives on the face opposite the oxygen and the two OH groups end up anti - the trans diol. Anything that delivers both oxygens to the same face, as cold dilute permanganate does, gives the cis diol instead.

Thiolate is a strong, highly polarizable nucleophile, so it follows the same basic-conditions pattern as other strong nucleophiles, attacking the less sterically hindered carbon via an SN2-like pathway to give a beta-hydroxy sulfide.

Because both new C-O bonds form in a single step without any intermediate that could allow rotation about the former double bond, the spatial relationship of the substituents on the alkene is carried over faithfully into the epoxide product.

If a nucleophilic group like an alcohol is positioned correctly within the same molecule, it can attack the strained epoxide ring intramolecularly, closing a new ring and forming a cyclic ether, a key step used to build many natural polyether frameworks.

The acetylide is a strong carbon nucleophile, so it opens the ring by SN2 at one of the two equivalent CH2 carbons; the alkoxide left behind picks up a proton at workup. The chain therefore grows by exactly two carbons and the OH lands two carbons from the new C-C bond: CH3-C(triple bond)C-CH2CH2-OH, pent-3-yn-1-ol. This two-carbon extension is the main synthetic reason to reach for an epoxide.
aldehydes-ketones: The carbonyl carbon has 3 regions of electron density (trigonal planar) — sp², just like an alkene carbon.
Extra alkyl groups add steric bulk (hindering attack) and donate electron density (reducing the carbonyl’s electrophilicity) compared to aldehydes.
An aldehyde has only one electron-donating alkyl group (vs. two for a ketone) and less steric bulk, leaving its carbonyl carbon more electron-poor and more reactive toward nucleophiles.

Ketones take the suffix -one (e.g., propan-2-one, acetone), while aldehydes use -al. The position of the carbonyl is indicated by a locant for ketones but not needed for aldehydes since the carbonyl must be terminal.
Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde, with two hydrogens bonded to the carbonyl carbon instead of one H and one R group. This makes it especially small and electrophilic.

Oxidizing an alcohol is the standard route into this chapter’s substrates, and the class of alcohol sets the product: a secondary alcohol has exactly one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so it goes up one rung and stops at the ketone. Reduction runs the ladder the wrong way, an unactivated alkane C-H is not a practical handle, and hydrating cyclohexene gives cyclohexanol rather than the ketone.
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls electron density from the C=O bond toward itself, leaving the carbonyl carbon electron-poor and susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

Aldehydes have a C-H bond on the carbonyl carbon that allows them to be oxidized to a carboxylic acid, reducing the diamine silver complex to metallic Ag(0). Ketones lack that hydrogen and resist oxidation.

Three levels of intermolecular attraction, in order. Butan-1-ol both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds, which is the strongest of the three and puts it on top. Butanal has a polarized C=O, so it has dipole-dipole attraction and can accept a hydrogen bond, but with no O-H it cannot donate one to another molecule of itself. Pentane has only dispersion forces. The carbonyl compound sits in the middle precisely because it is polar but not a hydrogen-bond donor.

Benzophenone has two bulky, electron-donating aryl groups that sterically block approach of a nucleophile and electronically stabilize the carbonyl carbon through resonance, making it one of the least electrophilic common carbonyls.

The aromatic ring can donate electron density into the carbonyl through resonance, partially stabilizing the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and making aromatic aldehydes somewhat less electrophilic than simple aliphatic aldehydes.

Only benzaldehyde has its carbonyl conjugated with anything. The ring’s pi system overlaps with the C=O, which spreads the pi electrons over more atoms and gives the C=O a little single-bond character; a weaker, longer bond vibrates at a lower frequency. The other three are isolated carbonyls and sit in the ordinary 1700-1750 window.

The second oxidation does not attack the aldehyde itself: it attacks the aldehyde’s hydrate, which is the only form carrying an O-H and a C-H on the same carbon. Take the water out of the flask and no hydrate forms, so the sequence has nothing left to grip and halts at the aldehyde. Adding water does the opposite, and neither base nor more reagent changes which species is available to be attacked.

Electrophilicity decreases as more alkyl groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon, since alkyl groups are electron-donating (inductively) and bulkier. Formaldehyde (two H's) is most electrophilic, acetone (two methyls) is least.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid requires removing the hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon. Ketones have two carbon substituents on that carbon instead of a hydrogen, so this oxidation pathway is unavailable to them.

Water adds reversibly across the carbonyl to give a geminal diol (two OH groups on one carbon). How far the equilibrium goes varies enormously - a trace for acetone, about half for acetaldehyde, essentially complete for formaldehyde and chloral - but the equilibrium itself is always there.

Formaldehyde's minimal steric hindrance and strongly electrophilic carbonyl carbon allow water to add efficiently, shifting the hydration equilibrium far toward the diol, unlike bulkier or less electrophilic carbonyls where the free carbonyl dominates.

Ask what is being stabilized. Stabilizing a transition state or an intermediate lowers the barrier and speeds a reaction up, which is the habit built in earlier chapters. Stabilizing the reactant does the reverse: it drops the starting material into a deeper well, so more energy is needed to climb out of it. Benzaldehyde’s ring donates into the C=O and stabilizes the compound you began with, which is why the aldehyde with the bigger resonance system is the less reactive one.

The nucleophile has to deliver its electron pair into the empty C=O pi antibonding orbital, whose larger lobe sits on carbon and points away from oxygen. Coming in along that lobe gives the best overlap while keeping the incoming pair as far as it can get from the oxygen’s lone pairs and the pi electrons. It is also the economical route to the product: as the bond forms the other three groups fold back, and the trajectory lands on tetrahedral geometry. This is the Burgi-Dunitz angle.
sp2 hybridization gives a trigonal planar geometry around the carbonyl carbon, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees between the three attached groups.

Both routes make an enol that tautomerizes, so the question is which carbon the OH lands on. Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and puts the oxygen on the more substituted carbon, giving a methyl ketone. Hydroboration puts boron, and therefore the oxygen, on the terminal carbon instead, so the enol tautomerizes to an aldehyde. Hydrogenation over a poisoned catalyst stops at an alkene, and ozonolysis cleaves rather than hydrates.

Sort on the aldehyde/ketone split first: acetone is the only ketone, with two donating and crowding methyls, so it goes last. Then compare what the single substituent does on the three aldehydes. Chloral’s three chlorines pull density away inductively and leave the carbon hungrier than a methyl does. Benzaldehyde’s ring donates into the carbonyl by resonance, which is a larger stabilization of the starting material than acetaldehyde’s methyl provides, so benzaldehyde sits below acetaldehyde.
When another group outranks the ketone in IUPAC priority (such as a carboxylic acid), the ketone oxygen is named as a substituent using 'oxo-' with a locant, rather than using the -one suffix.

The polarized C=O bond creates a substantial molecular dipole in aldehydes and ketones, leading to stronger dipole-dipole intermolecular forces and higher boiling points than nonpolar alkanes of similar size.

The electronegative oxygen pulls the pi electrons toward itself, so it ends up delta-minus and the carbon delta-plus. A nucleophile is electron-rich and goes to the electron-POOR atom, which is the carbon; the oxygen, with two lone pairs and the partial negative charge, is what an acid or a Lewis acid coordinates to. Both sites matter in carbonyl chemistry, and swapping them is the fastest way to write a mechanism backwards.

The test has to exploit the one structural difference: an aldehyde carries a hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon and a ketone does not. Tollens’ oxidizes exactly that C-H, and the silver(I) it consumes plates out as a mirror, so the readout is visible. Borohydride reduces both carbonyls with nothing to see, dilute acid does nothing to either, and bromine tests for unsaturation rather than for a carbonyl.

As the incoming nucleophile approaches the planar sp2 carbonyl carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate, larger substituents (two alkyl/aryl groups in ketones vs. one in aldehydes) crowd that approach and raise the energy of the transition state, slowing the reaction.

The aromatic pi system can conjugate with the carbonyl, delocalizing electron density toward the carbonyl carbon through resonance and reducing (though not eliminating) its electrophilicity relative to a simple alkyl aldehyde.

In the standard IUPAC seniority order of functional groups, aldehydes rank higher than ketones, so when both are present the molecule is named as an '-al' with the ketone indicated by an 'oxo-' substituent prefix and locant.

Glyceraldehyde is an aldotriose (aldehyde at C1) while dihydroxyacetone is a ketotriose (ketone at C2); both share the same molecular formula but differ in the position and type of the carbonyl group.
nucleophilic-addition: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ due to oxygen’s electronegativity, making it the site of nucleophilic attack.
The nucleophile forms a new bond to carbon while the C=O pi electrons shift entirely onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
The carbonyl carbon becomes sp³ and tetrahedral, bearing the new nucleophile bond and a negatively charged oxygen (alkoxide), which is then typically protonated.

For simple nucleophilic addition (not substitution), the nucleophile's attack on the electrophilic, sp2 carbonyl carbon to form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is typically the slow, rate-determining step; the final proton transfer is usually fast.

Protonating the carbonyl oxygen makes the molecule an oxocarbenium-like species, pulling even more electron density away from the carbonyl carbon and making it a much stronger electrophile, which speeds up nucleophile attack, especially useful for weak nucleophiles like alcohols.

A Grignard reagent is the conjugate base of an alkane, around pKa 50, so it is a far stronger base than it is a selective nucleophile. Anything with an O-H, N-H or terminal alkyne C-H hands it a proton faster than a carbonyl hands it a carbon, and the reagent leaves as methane. The fix is to protect the alcohol first, and this is the single most common reason a proposed Grignard route fails on paper.
Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon, and after protonation of the resulting alkoxide, the product is a cyanohydrin, which has both a hydroxyl group and a nitrile group on the same carbon.
A primary amine first adds to give a hemiaminal (carbinolamine), which then loses water to form a C=N double bond, known as an imine or Schiff base.

Count the hydrogens on nitrogen as the mechanism runs. A secondary amine R2NH brings exactly one N-H, and that proton is used up forming the neutral carbinolamine. Once water leaves, the iminium R2N+=C has no N-H left at all, so the usual route of losing a proton from nitrogen to give a neutral C=N is closed. The only acidic proton within reach is on the alpha carbon, and removing it gives a C=C conjugated with the nitrogen lone pair: an enamine.

Grignard reagents are strongly basic/nucleophilic and react irreversibly with carbonyls to form a magnesium alkoxide salt. This intermediate is stable until an aqueous acid workup protonates it, releasing the neutral alcohol product.

Reversibility in carbonyl addition depends on whether the newly added group can leave again. An alkoxide (from an organometallic addition) is a strong base and terrible leaving group, so once the strongly nucleophilic carbanion adds, it essentially never leaves, making the reaction irreversible under normal conditions.

An ester has a leaving group, so its tetrahedral intermediate collapses and expels the alkoxide, leaving a ketone in a flask that still holds Grignard reagent. That ketone is hungrier than the ester it came from, because the OR group that had been donating electron density into the carbonyl has just left. So it is attacked faster than the starting material was, and the reaction runs past the ketone every time. An ordinary ketone with no leaving group takes only one addition.

A negatively charged nucleophile like hydroxide has more electron density available to donate than a neutral nucleophile like water, making it significantly more reactive in attacking an electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
An electron-withdrawing group nearby pulls electron density away from the carbonyl carbon inductively, intensifying its partial positive charge and making it a better target for a nucleophile.

The three strongly electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms on the adjacent carbon pull electron density away inductively, greatly increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and favoring nucleophilic addition (chloral hydrate forms readily as a stable solid, unlike most simple hydrates).
The carbonyl carbon starts as sp2 and planar (bonded to three groups). After the nucleophile adds and the pi bond breaks, that carbon becomes sp3 with four substituents arranged tetrahedrally.
As the nucleophile forms a new sigma bond to carbon, the C=O pi bond breaks and its electron pair moves entirely onto the oxygen, generating a negatively charged alkoxide intermediate.

One equivalent of alcohol adds to the carbonyl carbon and the oxygen that was the C=O becomes an OH, so the product carbon holds one OH and one OR: a hemiacetal. Older texts call the ketone-derived case a hemiketal, but current usage says hemiacetal either way. Hydride and a Grignard give an alcohol with no second oxygen, and an amine leads toward an imine or enamine.

A planar sp2 carbonyl carbon is equally accessible to the nucleophile from either face (top or bottom) in the absence of a chiral catalyst or existing stereocenter nearby, so both possible stereochemical outcomes form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

Having two carbon substituents instead of one both physically blocks nucleophile approach (sterics) and donates more electron density into the carbonyl carbon (electronics), both factors working together to slow nucleophilic addition in ketones relative to aldehydes.

Esters, acid chlorides, and amides have an additional electronegative group (OR, Cl, NR2) on the carbonyl carbon that can leave after the tetrahedral intermediate forms, regenerating the C=O and substituting the nucleophile for the leaving group. Aldehydes and ketones have only H or alkyl/aryl groups (poor leaving groups), so the tetrahedral intermediate persists as the final addition product.

Hydride (H-) attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon just like other nucleophiles, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate that is then protonated (often during an aqueous workup) to give the alcohol product.

Hydride delivered from a reactive metal hydride is an extremely strong, essentially irreversible nucleophile toward carbonyls, a neutral amine is a good but more moderate nucleophile that forms reversible addition products first, and neutral water is comparatively weak, needing acid or base assistance to react efficiently.

Answer it as a thermodynamic question rather than a kinetic one. Iodide does attack the carbon, but the C-I bond it forms is weak and iodide is a superb leaving group, so the alkoxide simply expels it again: K for the addition is far below 1 and no product accumulates. Contrast a Grignard, where the carbanion is a hopeless leaving group and the same addition is effectively irreversible.

Because alcohols are weak, neutral nucleophiles, catalysis helps either by activating the electrophile (acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen) or by activating the nucleophile (base removes the alcohol's proton to generate a more reactive alkoxide).

Find the carbinol carbon and count its carbon substituents: phenyl, methyl and ethyl, so three, which means a tertiary alcohol and therefore a ketone plus one organometallic. Break any one of those three bonds and read off the fragments. Breaking C-phenyl leaves butan-2-one and needs PhMgBr, which is the pair offered here. The two aldehyde options would only ever give a secondary alcohol, and acetophenone plus CH3MgBr gives 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, one carbon short.

The alkoxide intermediate carries a negative charge on oxygen and is a strong base; an aqueous or mildly acidic workup simply transfers a proton onto that oxygen to give the stable, neutral alcohol final product.

As any nucleophile approaches the carbonyl carbon to form the crowded tetrahedral intermediate, a bulkier nucleophile experiences greater steric strain with the existing substituents on that carbon, slowing the reaction relative to a smaller nucleophile.

Protonation places a full positive charge on oxygen, which is stabilized by resonance delocalization onto the adjacent carbon, greatly enhancing that carbon's electrophilicity and priming it for nucleophilic attack by the alcohol.

Unhindered aldehydes combine low steric bulk with high electrophilicity, both of which favor fast nucleophilic addition, whereas bulky diaryl ketones are both sterically hindered and electronically stabilized by resonance, making them poor substrates for addition.
acetals: The first alcohol gives a hemiacetal; a second equivalent (after loss of water) gives the full acetal with two OR groups on the former carbonyl carbon.
Acetal formation/hydrolysis is acid-catalyzed and reversible — acetals are stable to base, making them useful as protecting groups, but hydrolyze back to the carbonyl in aqueous acid.

Converting a reactive carbonyl into a stable acetal lets other parts of a molecule be modified under basic/non-acidic conditions without the carbonyl interfering, then mild aqueous acid hydrolyzes the acetal back.

The oxocarbenium is the halfway point, and the second half of the mechanism repeats the first. The flat, positively charged carbon is attacked by a second equivalent of the alcohol, and losing the proton from that newly added oxygen gives the acetal. Water attacking is the same step run in the hydrolysis direction, which is what excess water is for; and nothing here rearranges, because the oxygen lone pair has already stabilized the charge.

A hemiacetal is the product of adding just one equivalent of alcohol to an aldehyde or ketone; that carbon now carries one OH (from the original carbonyl oxygen, now protonated) and one OR (from the added alcohol).

Count the atoms in the ring you want before choosing. The ring contains the old carbonyl carbon, both oxygens and the carbons between them, so a 1,2-diol closes a five-membered dioxolane and a 1,3-diol closes a six-membered dioxane. A 1,4-diol would have to close a seven-membered ring, which forms far more slowly. Methanol is not a diol, so it gives an acyclic acetal with no ring at all.

A protecting group has to come off under conditions the rest of the molecule tolerates, and that is the test this molecule fails. Acetal removal requires aqueous acid; a tert-butyl ether is cleaved by acid and a tertiary alcohol will ionize and dehydrate under it. The install and the survival criteria are fine here, so the judgement turns entirely on the third one. Acetals are stable to base, not removed by it.

Although modern IUPAC usage often groups both under 'acetal,' the traditional and still widely used term 'ketal' specifically refers to the double-alkoxy product derived from a ketone rather than an aldehyde.

Protonation of the hemiacetal's hydroxyl allows water to leave, generating a cation on the carbon that is stabilized by resonance donation from the remaining oxygen's lone pair, forming the key oxocarbenium intermediate that the second alcohol then attacks.

Ethylene glycol's two OH groups are positioned to both add intramolecularly to the same carbonyl carbon, closing a five-membered ring containing two oxygens (a 1,3-dioxolane), a very common cyclic acetal protecting group.

Because acetal formation is reversible, Le Chatelier's principle applies: increasing alcohol concentration or physically removing the water byproduct shifts the equilibrium in favor of acetal formation rather than staying as the hemiacetal or reverting to the carbonyl.

Only one hydroxyl group from within the glucose chain adds to the aldehyde carbon, giving a ring carbon with one OH and one OR (the ring oxygen) attached, the classic structure of a cyclic hemiacetal, not a full acetal.

When the open-chain aldose or ketose cyclizes, the original carbonyl carbon becomes a new stereocenter bearing both an OH and a ring oxygen; this carbon is specifically called the anomeric carbon, and its two possible configurations are the alpha and beta anomers.

The equilibrium constant is what changes, and the reason is entropic as much as anything. Making an open-chain hemiacetal means bringing two separate molecules together, which costs entropy; when the alcohol and the carbonyl are in the same molecule and can reach each other across a five- or six-membered ring, no second molecule has to be caught and the ring closes readily. The carbon still carries an OH and an OR, so it is genuinely a hemiacetal, and the ring can still open, which is why sugars reduce Tollens’ reagent.

The same structural features that make aldehydes generally more reactive toward nucleophilic addition overall (less steric hindrance, greater electrophilicity) also apply to acetal formation, so aldehydes convert to acetals more readily and under milder conditions than most ketones.

Because Grignard reagents react readily with ketones but an acetal is essentially inert to strongly basic/nucleophilic organometallic reagents, temporarily converting the ketone into an acetal shields it during the Grignard step; mild aqueous acid afterward cleanly unmasks the ketone again.

Acetal formation is nucleophilic addition, so it follows the reactivity order the chapter has already built: an aldehyde has one substituent instead of two, which leaves its carbonyl carbon both less crowded and more electron-poor. With one equivalent of diol, it is the aldehyde that gets masked. The exam trap is protecting the group you wanted to keep: decide which carbonyl you intend to react first, and check that the protection covers the other one.

Acetal formation (and its reverse, hydrolysis) proceeds through cationic intermediates that require acid catalysis; a strong base like NaOH does not activate the carbonyl for this pathway and acetals are, in fact, stable to basic conditions rather than promoted by them.

In acetal hydrolysis, one OR group leaves (after protonation) to form an oxocarbenium ion, and it is water (present in the aqueous acid medium) that then adds to that cation; losing a proton and losing the second equivalent of alcohol regenerates the free carbonyl.

In most open-chain cases, hemiacetals are typically in a facile equilibrium with the open carbonyl plus alcohol and are often not isolable (except in special cases like intramolecular cyclic sugar hemiacetals), whereas once a full acetal forms it is quite stable under neutral/basic conditions and can be isolated and purified.

Cyclic acetals undergo the same acid-catalyzed hydrolysis mechanism as acyclic ones: protonation, ring-opening to an oxocarbenium/hydroxy species, and addition of water, ultimately releasing the original carbonyl compound along with the diol that had formed the ring.

The defining structural feature of an acetal is that a single carbon bears two C-O bonds (both as -OR groups), which allows acid-catalyzed hydrolysis through a stabilized oxocarbenium intermediate; ordinary ethers have only one oxygen per carbon and lack this pathway, making them far more resistant to aqueous acid.

Work out what each reagent would do unprotected. LiAlH4 reduces the ester and the ketone alike, so it has to be run with the ketone already masked, which means the protection comes first and the deprotection last. NaBH4 is the wrong selectivity: it reduces the ketone and spares the ester, which is the opposite of what is wanted. An ester is not a carbonyl an acetal can protect, and reducing before protecting has already destroyed the thing the protection was for.

Counting atoms: carbonyl (C=O) plus two R-OH gives the acetal (C with two OR groups) plus H2O; the oxygen originally present as the carbonyl ends up, together with two hydrogens from the alcohols, as the water byproduct.

Acetal formation is not a redox process: no electrons are transferred to or from an external oxidizing/reducing agent. The carbon still has two oxygen-based substituents before and after (one C=O becomes two C-O), so its formal oxidation level is unchanged even though its hybridization shifts from sp2 to sp3.

Converting the anomeric hemiacetal hydroxyl into an -OR group by reaction with a second alcohol produces a glycoside, which is structurally a full acetal; glycosides are locked in one anomeric configuration and, unlike free sugars, no longer show mutarotation or act as reducing sugars.

Acetal formation/hydrolysis is a reversible, acid-catalyzed equilibrium. By Le Chatelier's principle, a large excess of water (one of the products of hydrolysis, consumed during formation) will push the equilibrium back toward hydrolysis, regenerating the carbonyl and alcohol.

Many carbohydrates exist predominantly as cyclic structures because an internal hydroxyl group on the same molecule is well positioned to add to the carbonyl carbon, forming a ring; with one more external alcohol this can further extend to a full (intramolecular/intermolecular combined) acetal, as in a glycoside.

The ring size of a cyclic acetal depends on the spacing between the diol's two hydroxyl groups: a 1,2-diol like ethylene glycol gives a five-membered dioxolane, while a 1,3-diol like 1,3-propanediol gives a six-membered dioxane when both oxygens bond to the same carbonyl carbon.

Esters have a carbonyl carbon that remains electrophilic and can undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution even under basic or strongly nucleophilic conditions. Acetals have no carbonyl at all (the carbon is fully sp3 and surrounded by two ether-like oxygens), so they are essentially unreactive toward bases and nucleophiles, which is precisely why they make good protecting groups used alongside such reagents.
oxidation-states: The electron-transfer definition is correct but unusable here, because organic reactions change what a carbon is bonded to rather than moving whole electrons.
The reverse of oxidation, on the same two counts.
Two new C-H bonds and nothing gained to oxygen. Worth saying explicitly, because the word does not contain it.
One new C-H (down) and one new C-Br (up), which cancel exactly.
Bonds to more electronegative atoms count +1, bonds to hydrogen -1, and bonds to carbon 0.
Which is why you can usually ignore the rest of the molecule when working out one carbon's oxidation state.
Four bonds to hydrogen at -1 each. Methane is the bottom of the ladder.
Three bonds to H at -1 and one to O at +1 gives -2, one rung above methane.
Two bonds to H at -1 and two to O at +1 cancel to zero.
Three bonds to oxygen at +1 each is +3, and the bond to the methyl carbon counts 0. Formic acid is the odd one at +2: there the fourth bond is to hydrogen and scores -1.
Four bonds to oxygen. Fully oxidized, and the top of the ladder.
Each rung is a two-electron oxidation.
One bond to an electronegative atom is traded for another, and the hydrogen count does not move.
All four sit on the same rung, which is why interconverting them is substitution rather than redox.
Oxidation removes that hydrogen and puts a second bond to oxygen in its place. With none there, nothing can happen.
Two hydrogens on the carbinol carbon means two rungs: aldehyde, then carboxylic acid.
One hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so it gives a ketone and stops.
Useful when the point is the transformation rather than the reagent, though most questions are about which reagent.
The reducing counterpart of [O].

One new C-H and one new C-O, which cancel. Any addition that delivers one hydrogen and one electronegative atom lands here; halogenation and halohydrin formation do not, because they deliver no hydrogen at all.
Both have one bond to an electronegative atom in place of one C-H.
Sitting on one rung means swapping a leaving group changes no oxidation level.
One two-electron step, which is why a single oxidation gets you there.
Alcohol to aldehyde is one, aldehyde to acid is the second.

Br and OH are both bonds to an electronegative atom, so trading one for the other leaves the count untouched - same rung, so a nucleophile does it. The other three each move one full rung: up, down and up.
Primary alcohol to aldehyde is one rung, aldehyde to acid is a second. Two rungs means an aqueous Cr(VI) oxidation, which does not stop, or two separate steps.

The carbonyl carbon goes from two bonds to oxygen (+2) to one bond to oxygen and three to carbon (+1). The Grignard carbon moves the other way, from a bond to magnesium (-1) to a bond to carbon (0). The two cancel, so nothing is oxidized overall.

Run the two counts. Bonds to hydrogen: unchanged. Bonds to an electronegative atom: up by one at each carbon. The tallies disagree, so this addition is a real two-electron oxidation. Any electronegative atom counts.
Four bonds to hydrogen puts it at -4, the bottom of the ladder.
Moving off the +3 rung is a change in oxidation level, which substitution cannot do.
alcohol-oxidation: Cr(VI) with no water present, so the aldehyde cannot hydrate and the oxidation stops.
Aqueous Cr(VI): the aldehyde hydrates to a gem-diol, which is oxidized a second time.
A ketone has no hydrogen left on the carbonyl carbon, so every oxidant stops there.
There is no C-H on the carbinol carbon to remove.
The gem-diol is structurally an alcohol, so the reagent oxidizes it a second time.
Both are Cr(VI). Anhydrous stops at the aldehyde; aqueous goes through to the acid.
Keeping water out is the entire point of the reagent.
Run at -78 C. No metal at all, and it stops at the aldehyde.
Mild and metal-free, and it stops cleanly at the aldehyde.
Metal-free, room temperature, and it stops at the aldehyde.
Group them by outcome and the list is short.
Water is what allows the second oxidation to happen.
Stoichiometry cannot fix an intermediate that is more reactive than the starting material.

No common oxidant distinguishes a primary alcohol from a secondary one, so the answer is a protecting group: mask the secondary alcohol as a silyl ether (TBSCl/imidazole), oxidize, then remove it with TBAF.

Two of these overshoot to butanoic acid, because both are aqueous and the aldehyde hydrates and is oxidized again. Of the two that stop at the aldehyde, the Swern has to be run at -78 C. DMP is metal-free and runs at room temperature.
It then loses the carbinol C-H to give the carbonyl.
It is what an aldehyde becomes in water, and it is structurally an alcohol again.
One hydrogen on the carbinol carbon means one oxidation, ending at the ketone.
It stops at the aldehyde, runs at room temperature and is neither metallic nor strongly acidic.
It is aqueous Cr(VI), so a primary alcohol goes through to the carboxylic acid.
And puts a second bond to oxygen in its place, which is why the hydrogen has to be there.
Aldehyde, then carboxylic acid, matching its two carbinol hydrogens.
The aqueous/anhydrous distinction only changes the answer for primary alcohols.
An alkyl halide and an alcohol are on the same rung, so the first step is substitution and needs no oxidant. Only then is there a carbinol C-H to take, and two rungs up means the aqueous oxidant.
PCC oxidizes the carbinol carbon and nothing else: it is not a hydrogenation catalyst and has no electrophile for a C=C. Anhydrous, so it stops at the aldehyde.
That equilibrium is the whole reason aqueous oxidations overshoot.
The aqueous reagent is precisely the one that goes on to the acid.
The same rule that stops tertiary alcohols reacting at all.
No carbinol C-H means nothing for the oxidation to take.
There is nothing site-selective about these oxidants. Both ends are primary alcohols with two carbinol hydrogens, and the reagent is aqueous, so both climb two rungs to the acid.
carbonyl-reduction: It is a nucleophile attacking the electrophilic carbon, which is the same general carbonyl addition you already know.
Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated on workup.
NaBH4 is far too mild, which is exactly what makes it useful for reducing a ketone in a molecule containing an ester.
Two hydrides are delivered: the first gives an aldehyde, which is more electrophilic and is reduced immediately.
The nitrogen stays attached and the oxygen leaves entirely. This is the standard amide-to-amine route and the row most often missed.
Reduction of the C-N triple bond leaves a primary amine.
Both reduce aldehydes and ketones, which is the row where the choice does not matter.
A hydride is a nucleophile and needs a polarized pi bond; C=C has no electrophilic end.
That single fact produces all the practical differences between them.
It reacts with protic solvents only slowly, which is a real convenience.
It reacts violently with water, including atmospheric moisture, and needs a separate aqueous workup afterwards.
Deliberately choosing the weaker reagent is the commonest way this material appears in a synthesis question.
You cannot stop a reaction at an intermediate that is more reactive than the starting material.
A deliberately weakened reagent, used cold. Worth knowing it exists even if the details come later.
Which is why an aqueous workup is part of the procedure.
Zn(Hg) and concentrated HCl. Use it when the molecule survives acid but not base.
Strongly basic, and the partner to the Clemmensen for acid-sensitive molecules.
Whichever your substrate tolerates, the other is available.
Both reactions attack a C=O directly, so they are aldehyde-and-ketone reactions. An ester's carbonyl is deactivated by its own oxygen and has a leaving group to expel instead.
It is not strong enough. LiAlH4 does reduce acids, all the way to the primary alcohol.
Giving a primary amine. Catalytic hydrogenation also reduces nitriles, but with a different catalyst and more forcing conditions than the 1 atm Pd/C case in the next section.
The alkoxide formed has nothing to expel, so the reaction stops after one delivery.
If you can draw one, you can already draw the other, with H- standing in for the carbon nucleophile.
Amides need LiAlH4, and the product is an amine rather than an alcohol.
The carbonyl carbon already bore two carbon substituents, and gains an H and an OH.
The carbonyl carbon bore one carbon substituent and one hydrogen.
An ester needs two hydrides and only LiAlH4 delivers them. NaBH4 is too mild for an ester, hydrogenation leaves esters alone, and PCC is an oxidant - the wrong direction.

Hydride reagents are the complement of hydrogenation: they take carbonyls and leave C=C. At one atmosphere over Pd/C only the alkene reacts; the ketone needs higher pressure and a catalyst such as PtO2.
NaBH4 does not react with a carboxylic acid at all.
The carbonyl carbon is flat and has two faces. Hydride arrives at each equally, so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts. An achiral substrate plus an achiral reagent cannot give one enantiomer.
hydrogenation: Hydrogen gas and an alkene together do nothing at room temperature; breaking the H-H bond needs a surface.
All work by adsorbing both hydrogen and the alkene onto a metal surface.
Both hydrogens come from the surface the alkene is lying against, so they arrive on the same face.
Syn addition to a ring shows up directly as the cis product.
Alkenes, alkynes, imines, nitro groups and azides are on the readily-reduced list.
Aromatic rings need high pressure and temperature, which is what makes the reaction useful on aromatic substrates.
The standard route to an aromatic amine from a nitroarene, and a row often forgotten.
Under ordinary conditions over Pd/C a ketone survives.
It is reduced past the alkene straight through to the alkane.
Deliberately poisoned palladium that stops at the alkene, and it is still a syn surface addition.
The poisoning is what makes it stop at the alkene rather than continuing.
Sodium adds an electron, ammonia protonates, a second electron gives a vinyl anion, and that anion is configurationally stable with its two R groups apart.

The sequence is electron, proton, electron, proton. The vinyl radical in the middle flips between its two bent shapes far too fast for its preference to matter; the vinyl anion after the second electron does not, and it sits trans. No surface is involved here.
Lindlar gives the cis alkene; plain Pd/C gives the alkane.
A molecule with an alkene and a ketone can be reduced at either position by choosing the reagent.

Every bar ends at the same molecule, so a smaller heat out can only mean a starting material already lower in energy. That gives trans-disubstituted > cis-disubstituted > monosubstituted - measured, not asserted.

Both carbons become stereocenters carrying different substituents. Syn addition fixes the relative configuration - one diastereomer - but not the absolute one, because the alkene can lie on the catalyst either face down. So it forms as a racemate.
The reaction is thermodynamically downhill already; the barrier is what stops it.
Which is why a catalyst is enough to make it go.
Esters, acids and amides are essentially untouched by catalytic hydrogenation.
Imines are on the readily-reduced list, which makes this the basis of reductive amination (which you will meet in Amines).
Exactly the complement of NaBH4, which does the reverse.
Hydride reduction needs a polarized pi bond, which C=C does not provide.
Quinoline and lead reduce its activity on purpose.
Which is why they can only arrive on one face.
Carboxylic acids, esters and amides are essentially untouched.
And it is reduced all the way to the alkane unless a poisoned catalyst is used.
Lindlar for cis, dissolving metal for trans, from the same starting material.
It is a direct consequence of both hydrogens being delivered by one surface.
One of the standard hydrogenation catalysts alongside Pd/C and Pt.
alkene-oxidation: A single oxygen delivered across the double bond in one concerted step.
It is concerted, so a cis alkene gives the cis-substituted epoxide and trans gives trans.
Both oxygens are delivered to the same face through a cyclic osmate ester.
OsO4 is expensive and toxic, so it is regenerated in situ.
Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the C-O bond being broken.
Backside attack puts the second oxygen on the opposite face from the first.
One delivers both oxygens to one face, the other goes via an epoxide and opens it from the other side.
The reductive workup stops at the aldehydes and ketones.
The oxidative workup takes the aldehyde fragment one rung further.
A ketone has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon to lose.
Two substituents means no hydrogen on that carbon, so it can only be a ketone.
With oxidative workup that aldehyde would go on to a carboxylic acid.
The same outcome as OsO4, more cheaply and less cleanly.
The conditions, not the reagent, decide which of the two rows applies.
A question specifying KMnO4 without conditions is incomplete.

Syn delivery onto a cis alkene puts the two OH groups on the same face of a molecule with an internal mirror plane, so the two stereocenters cancel: meso and achiral. The same reagent on trans-but-2-ene gives the racemic pair instead.
Rejoin at the carbonyl carbons: CH3CH2-CH=C(CH3)2, which is C6H12.
One carbon bore a hydrogen and the other did not.
The two fragments are identical, so you observe one compound at twice the molar amount.
The two ends stay connected through the rest of the ring.
Going via the epoxide changes the stereochemical outcome; no conditions convert a syn diol into an anti one.
The cyclic osmate ester forces both new C-O bonds onto the same side.
A peroxyacid, which is what delivers the single oxygen atom.
Which is what makes the ring-opening step of the anti-diol route possible.
In one concerted step through a cyclic transition state.
Dihydroxylation adds across the double bond; ozonolysis cuts through it.

Ozone adds to give a molozonide, which rearranges to an ozonide in which the two former alkene carbons are still bridged by oxygens. Nothing is a carbonyl compound until that ozonide is broken open, and the reagent that breaks it sets the level.
Both deliver both oxygens to the same face, giving the syn diol.
Cold and dilute gives a diol; hot and concentrated cleaves.

Cleavage gives a seven-carbon fragment with a hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, taken on to heptanoic acid, and a one-carbon =CH2 fragment, which ends up as CO2 and bubbles away. With Me2S you would isolate heptanal and formaldehyde.
carboxylic-acids: The carboxylate anion spreads its negative charge equally over two equivalent oxygens via resonance, which is far more stabilizing than an alkoxide’s localized charge.
Most simple carboxylic acids have pKa values around 4–5, far more acidic than alcohols (pKa ~16–18).

The two resonance structures of a carboxylate are equivalent, so the true structure is a symmetric hybrid with the charge (and bond order) shared equally between both oxygens, confirmed by equal C–O bond lengths.

Step 1: SOCl2 replaces the OH with Cl, giving 3-phenylpropanoyl chloride plus SO2 and HCl, both of which leave as gases. Step 2: methanol attacks that acyl chloride, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling chloride, and a proton is lost, giving the methyl ester. Because chloride leaves and never comes back, this route is irreversible - unlike Fischer esterification of the acid itself, which would leave the acid and its ester in equilibrium instead.

Count carbons first: 1-bromobutane has four and pentanoic acid has five, so the route has to ADD one. Cyanide is the one-carbon nucleophile: SN2 on the primary bromide gives pentanenitrile, five carbons. Hot aqueous acid then hydrolyzes that nitrile through the amide to pentanoic acid, with no oxidant needed because a nitrile carbon and an acid carbon sit on the same oxidation rung. The other three routes all keep four carbons.
The O-H proton donates a hydrogen bond while the carbonyl oxygen (and the hydroxyl oxygen) can accept one, which is why carboxylic acids dimerize strongly.
Formic acid, HCOOH, is the one-carbon carboxylic acid found in ant stings and formic acid solutions.
Most carboxylic acids have pKa around 4-5, meaning they are only partially ionized in water, unlike strong mineral acids which ionize essentially completely.
Each added electronegative chlorine withdraws electron density inductively, further stabilizing the negative charge on the conjugate base, so acidity increases with each additional chlorine.

Inductive electron withdrawal is transmitted through sigma bonds and falls off quickly with distance, so a halogen closer to the carboxyl group stabilizes the conjugate base more than one farther away.

The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing group that stabilizes the negative charge on the carboxylate through both induction and resonance, increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted benzoic acid.

Two carboxylic acid molecules can hydrogen bond to each other reciprocally (each O-H donating to the other's carbonyl oxygen), forming a stable cyclic dimer, especially pronounced without a polar solvent to compete for hydrogen bonding.

Water solubility depends on the balance between the polar, hydrogen-bonding carboxyl group and the nonpolar alkyl chain; as the chain grows, the hydrophobic character increasingly dominates and solubility drops.
Each carboxylic acid molecule can both donate and accept two hydrogen bonds in a dimer, giving a stronger net intermolecular attraction than a single alcohol O-H can provide.

Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4-5) are acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate (pKa of carbonic acid about 6.4), releasing CO2 gas; this bubbling test is used to distinguish carboxylic acids from weaker acids like phenols.

Phenol (pKa about 10) is not acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate significantly, so it does not produce a noticeable bubbling reaction, unlike carboxylic acids; this difference is a classic diagnostic test.

The carboxyl O-H can reach the ketone oxygen through a six-membered cyclic transition state. As that proton transfers, the C-C bond to the carboxyl breaks and CO2 leaves, giving an enol that tautomerizes to the ketone. Nothing else in the molecule has to move, which is why gentle warming is enough - and why the carbonyl has to be exactly at the beta position for the ring to be the right size.

The Grignard carbanion adds to the electrophilic carbon of CO2 to give a magnesium carboxylate, which is protonated on acidic workup to give the carboxylic acid; this is a classic way to build a carboxylic acid while adding one carbon.
Strong oxidants like hot KMnO4 or Jones reagent fully oxidize a primary alcohol through the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid, whereas PCC is a mild oxidant that stops cleanly at the aldehyde.
SOCl2 (or PCl3/PCl5) reacts with the carboxylic acid's OH group, converting it into a much better leaving group and producing the reactive acyl chloride along with SO2 and HCl gas.
LiAlH4 is a strong enough hydride donor to reduce carboxylic acids completely past the aldehyde stage to the primary alcohol; it does not stop partway.
NaBH4 is too mild a hydride source to reduce the relatively unreactive carboxylic acid carbonyl efficiently; LiAlH4 (a stronger hydride donor) is needed for that reduction.

Induction travels through sigma bonds and dies off fast with distance. The chlorine on C2 is next door to the carboxyl and stabilizes the carboxylate strongly: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is pKa 2.86. Move the same chlorine to C4 and it is two bonds further away and barely helps: 4-chlorobutanoic acid is 4.52, against butanoic acid's 4.82. So acidity falls, and pKa rises, in the order given.

The carboxyl carbon is doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to the other oxygen and to the R group, giving three sigma bonds plus one pi bond -- the sp2, trigonal planar geometry typical of carbonyl carbons.

The three highly electronegative fluorines withdraw electron density inductively, strongly stabilizing the conjugate base and dropping the pKa to 0.23, far more acidic than acetic acid's pKa of about 4.76.

Once the first carboxyl group loses its proton to become negatively charged, pulling a second positive proton away from the nearby second carboxyl group is both electrostatically harder and the inductive withdrawal helping acidity is reduced, so Ka2 is substantially smaller than Ka1.

Dilution changes nothing inside the molecule; it changes what the molecule is touching. Neat or concentrated, carboxylic acids sit as hydrogen-bonded dimers, and the hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen pulls density out of the C=O, weakening it and dropping the stretch to about 1710. Dilute far enough in a nonpolar solvent and the dimers break up, and the free monomer absorbs near 1760 - above an ester's 1735, not below it. That matters whenever you use IR to rank acyl derivatives: the familiar 1710 is a dimerization artifact, not a measure of how hard the OH donates into the carbonyl.
Removing the first proton changes the electronic environment (the molecule becomes anionic), so the second -COOH ionizes with a different, typically higher, pKa than the first.

This is a geometry question wearing a functional-group disguise. Losing CO2 here is not a general property of keto acids: the carboxyl O-H has to reach across to the ketone oxygen through a cyclic transition state, and only as that proton transfers does the C-C bond to the carboxyl break and CO2 leave. Count the ring for the beta-keto acid CH3COCH2COOH - ketone O, ketone C, alpha carbon, carboxyl C, carboxyl O, and the moving H. Six atoms, the size that closes with no strain, which is why gentle warming is enough. Put one more carbon between the two groups, as in the gamma-keto acid, and the same proton transfer would have to close a seven-membered ring; it does not happen at 80 °C. Note also what comes out first: the enol, which then tautomerizes to acetone.
Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to be fully deprotonated by a strong base like NaOH, giving the sodium carboxylate salt and water in a straightforward neutralization.
esters-amides: Amide resonance delocalizes nitrogen’s lone pair strongly into the carbonyl, making amides far less electrophilic and far more hydrolytically stable than esters.
Nitrogen’s lone pair donates into the carbonyl more than an ester oxygen does, giving the amide C=O more single-bond character and a lower, weaker stretching frequency.
Amides with N–H bonds can hydrogen-bond extensively (donor and acceptor), giving them notably higher melting/boiling points than comparable esters, which lack an O–H/N–H donor.
Fischer esterification is the acid-catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, releasing water and forming an ester; it is an equilibrium reaction.
