Because the amine is a base and the carboxylic acid is an acid, a simple acid-base proton transfer forming the carboxylate salt happens faster than nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl; forming the amide usually requires heating to drive off water or first converting the acid to a more reactive derivative (such as an acyl chloride).

This is transesterification. Ethanol attacks the ester carbonyl under acid catalysis, giving a tetrahedral intermediate carrying both OMe and OEt. Methoxide and ethoxide are almost equally good leaving groups, so nothing electronic decides the outcome - the large excess of ethanol does, by mass action. Methanol is expelled and ethyl propanoate is left. Note what does not happen: the acyl group never leaves the molecule, so the answer is still a propanoate.
Ester names follow the pattern 'alkyl acid-oate,' where the alkyl group names the alcohol-derived R group and the '-oate' part names the acid-derived acyl portion.

Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl pi system gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making it shorter and stronger than a typical single bond, and restricting rotation around it much like a true double bond.

In transesterification, a new alcohol attacks the ester's carbonyl carbon and displaces the original alkoxide leaving group, swapping one ester for another (commonly used, for example, in making biodiesel from vegetable oil).

Saponification is the hydroxide-mediated hydrolysis of esters, classically triglycerides, yielding glycerol and fatty acid carboxylate salts, which are soaps; this reaction is effectively irreversible.

Because Fischer esterification is acid-catalyzed and both the forward (esterification) and reverse (acid-catalyzed hydrolysis) reactions are accessible, the reaction reaches equilibrium and excess alcohol or removal of water is often used to push the equilibrium toward the ester.
LiAlH4 reduces the ester carbonyl all the way to a primary alcohol while releasing the original alkoxy group as its own (separate) alcohol, so two different alcohols are produced overall.

Reduction of an amide's C=O by LiAlH4 proceeds with loss of the oxygen (rather than the nitrogen), converting the carbonyl carbon into a CH2 group attached to nitrogen and giving an amine, unlike ester reduction which gives alcohols.

An ordinary amide is unreactive because the nitrogen lone pair lies in the carbonyl's plane and donates into the pi system, feeding electron density to the carbonyl carbon and tying the nitrogen in place. A four-membered ring cannot hold that arrangement: roughly 90 degree bond angles pyramidalize the nitrogen and twist its lone pair out of alignment with the C=O, so most of that donation is switched off. What is left is a carbonyl carrying an amide's leaving group without an amide's protection - electrophilic enough that a serine hydroxyl in a bacterial enzyme attacks it and is acylated, which is how penicillin works. Note what has not changed: nitrogen's electronegativity is the same and the carbonyl carbon is still sp2. What was lost is the orbital overlap.

Resonance donation of the nitrogen lone pair toward the carbonyl oxygen gives the amide significant C=N double bond character and delocalizes the electron density, so the nitrogen is a much weaker base than an ordinary amine nitrogen.
Because the amide nitrogen's lone pair is tied up in resonance with the carbonyl, it is a much poorer proton acceptor (weaker base) than the lone pair on a simple, non-delocalized amine nitrogen.
Without any N-H or O-H bond, a tertiary amide has no hydrogen to donate, but its carbonyl oxygen (made more electron-rich by nitrogen resonance donation) remains an excellent hydrogen bond acceptor.

Even without an N-H donor, the amide carbonyl is highly polarized by nitrogen lone pair donation, giving tertiary amides large dipole-dipole attractions and correspondingly high boiling points relative to their size.
Polyesters are condensation polymers in which a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) repeatedly reacts with a diol, forming many ester linkages along the polymer backbone.
Nylon is made by repeatedly forming amide bonds between a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) and a diamine, making it a polyamide.
A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of another, producing the same C(=O)-N bond found in any amide.

Mixing the acid with the amine directly does only one thing: an acid-base reaction, giving a dimethylammonium butanoate salt with a protonated nucleophile and a negatively charged electrophile. So the acid has to be activated first. SOCl2 replaces the OH with Cl, putting the acyl group at the top of the ladder, and dimethylamine then acylates it easily. Excess amine (or added pyridine) is needed because each acylation releases one HCl, which protonates a second equivalent of amine.

The first equivalent of Grignard reagent displaces the alkoxide to give a ketone, which is even more reactive than the ester and is immediately attacked by a second equivalent of Grignard reagent, giving (after workup) a tertiary alcohol.
Esters have no O-H or N-H bond, so they cannot donate a hydrogen bond; they can only accept hydrogen bonds through their carbonyl (and ether-like) oxygens.
A lactone forms when a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group within the same molecule condense intramolecularly, producing a ring containing an ester linkage.
A lactam is the nitrogen analog of a lactone: an intramolecular condensation between an amine and a carboxyl group within the same molecule forms a ring containing an amide linkage.
Saponification specifically refers to the hydroxide-driven hydrolysis of esters (classically fats and oils) into glycerol and carboxylate salts (soap).

Without an O-H to donate, ester molecules can only engage in weaker dipole-dipole interactions with each other, while carboxylic acids form doubly hydrogen-bonded dimers, giving acids a notably higher boiling point for comparable size.

The second contributor is O(-)-C=N(+): the nitrogen lone pair has moved toward oxygen, so nitrogen carries partial positive charge and oxygen partial negative. Carbon gains, not loses, electron density relative to a ketone - which is exactly why an amide is the least electrophilic derivative, and why its C=O stretch drops to about 1650 cm-1.
The ester functional group, -C(=O)-O-R, has a carbonyl oxygen double bonded to carbon and a separate ether-like oxygen singly bonded to carbon and to the R group.
acyl-substitution: Acyl substitution goes through a tetrahedral intermediate (addition step) that then expels a leaving group, regenerating the carbonyl — net substitution rather than simple addition.
Chloride is a much weaker base than an amine/amide nitrogen, making acyl chlorides far more reactive electrophiles than amides in acyl substitution.

Ethanol attacks one of the two carbonyls. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling the other half of the molecule as acetate, which then picks up a proton. So one acyl group becomes the ester and the other leaves as the acid: ethyl acetate plus acetic acid. Half the anhydride is spent as a leaving group, which is the atom-economy cost of acylating this way.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution proceeds by the nucleophile first adding to the carbonyl carbon, then a leaving group being eliminated to restore the carbonyl, an addition-elimination sequence distinct from simple substitution at sp3 carbon.
Nucleophilic acyl substitution begins with nucleophilic addition to the sp2 carbonyl carbon, producing a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, before any leaving group departs.

Trace the oxygen atom by atom. Methanol attacks the protonated acid using its own oxygen, so that oxygen forms the new C–O bond and is never asked to leave again; what departs as water is one of the two OH oxygens that came from the carboxylic acid, after acid protonates it. The label therefore stays in the ester, on the single-bonded oxygen still carrying its methyl group — the C–¹⁸O–CH₃ bond was never broken at any point. That is the experiment that settles where the ester bond is made and broken: at the acyl carbon, not at the alkyl carbon. Had the label come out in the water, esterification would have to be an SN2 at methyl, and it is not. Run the reverse reaction in H₂¹⁸O and the same bookkeeping puts the label in the carboxylic acid.

Reactivity tracks how good each group's substituent is as a leaving group and how poorly it donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance; chloride is the best leaving group and poorest resonance donor, while nitrogen in an amide is the worst leaving group and best resonance donor, giving this overall order.

Weaker bases are more stable as free anions (or neutral species) and are less prone to holding onto a bonding pair of electrons, which is exactly why chloride (a very weak base) leaves far more readily than an amide nitrogen (effectively a strong base, as NH2-/RNH-) leaves.

An anhydride needs a carboxylate as the nucleophile, not the neutral acid. Propanoic acid has its lone pairs tied up in the O-H and in resonance and is a poor nucleophile; deprotonating it gives propanoate, which attacks the acyl chloride readily, expels chloride and gives the anhydride. Propan-1-ol would give an ester instead, and water would give the acid.

Chlorine's lone pairs are in a larger, poorly overlapping orbital, so they donate little electron density into the carbonyl by resonance, leaving the carbon highly electrophilic; additionally chloride ion, being a very weak base, departs easily once the tetrahedral intermediate forms.

Carboxylate is a moderately basic, resonance-stabilized anion, but chloride is an even weaker base and therefore a better leaving group, which is part of why acyl chlorides outrank anhydrides in reactivity.

Water acts as the nucleophile, attacking the highly electrophilic acyl chloride carbonyl; after the tetrahedral intermediate collapses and chloride leaves, loss of a proton gives the carboxylic acid and HCl.
The alcohol's oxygen attacks the acyl chloride carbonyl; after chloride departs and a proton is lost (often assisted by a base or excess alcohol), the product is an ester plus HCl.

One equivalent of amine attacks a carbonyl and expels carboxylate, giving the amide. That carboxylate picks up a proton, and the carboxylic acid it becomes is a far stronger acid (pKa about 5) than the ammonium ion of the amine (pKa about 10) - so the second equivalent of amine is simply protonated. Net: one amide plus one ammonium carboxylate salt.

The alcohol attacks one of the anhydride's two carbonyl carbons; the other acyl-oxygen half departs as a carboxylate (which is then protonated), so the overall products are an ester and a carboxylic acid.

Addition always comes first: hydroxide attacks and the pi electrons go up onto oxygen (ii). The alkoxide then pushes back down and expels the better leaving group, ethoxide (iii). Only now does a carboxylic acid exist, and the ethoxide just released - a much stronger base than carboxylate - takes its proton (i). That final step is irreversible and is what drives the whole reaction; it cannot come earlier because there is nothing acidic to deprotonate until step iii is done.

This would require nitrogen (a strongly basic, poor leaving group) to depart, which is extremely unfavorable; amides are the least reactive acyl derivative and are not readily converted into more reactive derivatives like esters by simple nucleophilic substitution.

Protonating the carbonyl oxygen pulls electron density away from the carbon through the resulting resonance-stabilized cation, making the carbon much more attractive to a comparatively weak nucleophile such as water, which otherwise would react too slowly.

In Fischer esterification, the leaving group would have to be hydroxide (a poor leaving group), so acid catalysis is needed to make departure possible and the reaction is a slow equilibrium; with an acyl chloride, chloride is already an excellent leaving group, so the reaction proceeds quickly without a catalyst and is essentially irreversible.

Nitrogen is less electronegative and holds its lone pair less tightly than oxygen, making amines generally better nucleophiles than comparably substituted alcohols, which in turn are typically better nucleophiles than water.

The first Grignard equivalent adds to the ester carbonyl and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses, expelling the alkoxide leaving group to give a ketone; because the ketone is even more electrophilic than the starting ester, a second equivalent of Grignard reagent immediately adds to it.

The ketone intermediate generated from the first addition is actually more reactive toward the Grignard reagent than the original ester was, so under normal conditions with excess Grignard reagent the reaction proceeds on to give a tertiary alcohol rather than stopping at the ketone.

When the nucleophile's electron pair adds to the carbon, the carbon-oxygen pi bond breaks and its electrons move fully onto the oxygen, giving a negatively charged alkoxide oxygen in the tetrahedral intermediate.

A pi bond to oxygen is strong and energetically favorable to reform; the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is generally higher in energy than either the starting carbonyl compound or the product, so it collapses to restore the stable carbonyl as soon as a leaving group can depart.

Classic SN2 substitution occurs at an sp3 carbon with backside attack displacing a leaving group in one step; the carbonyl carbon in acyl substitution is sp2 and planar, so the nucleophile must add to one face to form a new sp3 tetrahedral intermediate before a leaving group can depart in a separate step.

Unlike nucleophilic addition (which destroys the carbonyl pi bond permanently), acyl substitution regenerates the carbonyl in the final product; only the group attached via the leaving position has been swapped out.

Thionyl chloride or phosphorus chlorides convert the poor -OH leaving group of a carboxylic acid into the excellent -Cl leaving group, producing the highly reactive acyl chloride used in many subsequent nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions.

Once hydroxide attacks and the carboxylate anion is formed, its negative charge (stabilized by resonance) makes it far too unreactive an electrophile to be attacked again by the departed alkoxide, effectively trapping the reaction as products; acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, by contrast, gives a neutral carboxylic acid that remains in equilibrium with the ester under the same conditions.

A carboxylate leaving group (departing from an anhydride) is a better leaving group than an alkoxide (departing from an ester), and the second carbonyl group in an anhydride also inductively withdraws electron density, both of which make anhydrides more reactive than esters.

Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so direct substitution at a carboxylic acid's carbonyl is slow; additionally, with basic nucleophiles such as amines, simple acid-base proton transfer (forming a salt) usually outcompetes attack on the carbonyl, which is why carboxylic acids are often first converted to a more reactive derivative (like an acyl chloride) before substitution.
alpha-hydrogens: Removing an alpha H gives a carbanion that resonance-delocalizes onto the carbonyl oxygen, forming a stabilized enolate — this is why alpha H’s (pKa ~20) are far more acidic than typical C–H bonds (pKa ~50).

The enolate is the whole anion, not one of its drawings. Its two resonance contributors put the negative charge either on the alpha carbon, the carbanion form, or on the carbonyl oxygen, which is the major contributor because oxygen holds a charge far better. So the charge is shared between the alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen - and it is the alpha carbon, the minor contributor, that does the attacking.
Deprotonating the central CH₂ gives an anion that can delocalize into either flanking carbonyl, doubling the resonance stabilization compared to a mono-ketone’s enolate.

The carbon directly attached to the carbonyl carbon is called the alpha carbon, so hydrogens on it are alpha hydrogens. The carbonyl carbon itself has no H in ketones and usually one in aldehydes, but that H is not called 'alpha.'

Alpha hydrogens are unusually acidic compared to ordinary C-H bonds because the resulting carbanion can be stabilized by resonance delocalization into the adjacent carbonyl, something an alkyl carbanion cannot do.

LDA is a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base that removes alpha protons quickly and cleanly without attacking the carbonyl carbon itself, driving deprotonation essentially to completion at low temperature.

Keto-enol tautomers differ only in the position of a proton and a double bond: the keto form has C=O and a C-H at the alpha carbon, while the enol form has C=C-OH. They are neutral isomers, not charged species.

An enolate is formed by removing an alpha C-H, not an O-H; a simple ketone or ester typically has no O-H to remove in the first place. The resulting negative charge is then delocalized onto oxygen by resonance.

The 'alpha carbon' on the aryl side of PhCHO is part of the aromatic ring; removing a ring C-H there would destroy aromaticity and is not the kind of alpha-deprotonation relevant to enolate chemistry, so PhCHO's only true alpha hydrogens would have to come from an alkyl substituent, which it lacks.

Even though both deprotonations are stabilized somewhat by electronegative oxygen, the alcohol O-H is still considerably more acidic, so only a weak-to-moderate base is needed there, while alpha C-H deprotonation needs a much stronger base such as an amide base.

Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it stabilizes negative charge better, making the oxygen-centered resonance form the greater contributor even though many enolate reactions proceed through the carbon end as the nucleophile.

Ethyl acetoacetate's central CH2 sits between a ketone and an ester carbonyl, giving it two stabilizing resonance pathways and a much lower pKa than acetone's single-carbonyl-stabilized alpha H, while a vinylic C-H has essentially no special stabilization and is among the least acidic C-H bonds listed.

In an ester, resonance donation from the alkoxy oxygen competes with the carbonyl's ability to stabilize an adjacent negative charge, making ester groups somewhat less effective than ketone carbonyls at lowering alpha C-H pKa, which is why malonates (two esters) are less acidic than 1,3-diketones (two ketones).

Nitriles, like carbonyls, have a pi system into which a negative charge on the adjacent carbon can be delocalized, so alpha hydrogens next to a nitrile are likewise more acidic than ordinary alkane C-H bonds, though typically less so than those next to a ketone.

The same resonance donation from the ester's -OR oxygen that makes ester carbonyls less electrophilic toward nucleophiles also makes them somewhat less effective at stabilizing an adjacent carbanion than a ketone carbonyl is.

Carboxylic acids have two acidic sites, but the O-H is dramatically more acidic because its conjugate base (carboxylate) is stabilized by two equivalent resonance structures with the negative charge shared between both oxygens; a much stronger base is needed to reach the alpha carbon, and the carboxylate must usually be protected or already formed first.

The carbonyl of cyclohexanone is flanked by two different alpha carbons, C2 and C6. Putting a methyl on C2 still leaves one alpha hydrogen there, and C6 still has two, so enolization can happen on either side. Watch what that does to C2: it is a stereocenter in the ketone, and forming the enolate on that side flattens the carbon and destroys the stereocenter, which is why alpha stereocenters racemize under base.

Like a carbonyl, the nitro group has resonance forms that can accept and stabilize a developing negative charge on the adjacent carbon, making nitroalkane alpha hydrogens strongly acidic despite nitro not being a classic carbonyl-type carbon.

A nitrile does provide meaningful resonance stabilization of an adjacent carbanion (just generally less than a carbonyl), so a beta-ketonitrile's alpha C-H is typically considerably more acidic than a simple ketone's (often in the pKa 9-13 range), not merely equal to it.

Acid-base equilibria favor the side with the weaker acid and weaker base; since a 1,3-diketone is more acidic than triethylammonium, its deprotonation is favorable, but a simple ketone is less acidic than triethylammonium, so that deprotonation is unfavorable and only a small equilibrium concentration of enolate forms.

Because a 1,3-diketone's pKa (~9-11) is well below water's pKa (~15.7), hydroxide readily and nearly completely deprotonates it; a monoketone's pKa (~20) is well above water's pKa, so hydroxide deprotonates it to only a tiny, unfavorable extent, illustrating why base strength must be matched to the acidity of the specific alpha hydrogens involved.

Number the enone out from the carbonyl: C1 is the carbonyl carbon, C2 is alpha, C3 is beta and C4 is gamma. Taking the gamma hydrogen gives the extended dienolate, an anion delocalized along O-C1-C2-C3-C4 with its charge density on the oxygen, on C2 and on C4 - including the carbon that was just deprotonated. Deprotonating the alpha-prime carbon on the other side of the carbonyl gives the cross-conjugated dienolate instead, and the two names are not interchangeable.

Enolate formation requires removing an actual hydrogen from the alpha carbon; if that specific carbon has been substituted until it bears no hydrogens (as in a ketone with a fully branched alpha carbon), there is no alpha C-H to remove at that position, regardless of what is going on elsewhere in the molecule.

Only the sp3 CH3 carbon attached to the carbonyl is the true alpha carbon capable of forming a resonance-stabilized enolate; the ring carbon on the other side of the carbonyl is aromatic and its hydrogens are not involved in this kind of carbonyl-stabilized deprotonation.

Cyclic 1,3-diketones such as 1,3-cyclohexanedione are known to be notably more acidic than their open-chain counterparts, partly because the enol tautomer is particularly stable and well-conjugated in the ring, pulling the equilibrium and making the corresponding proton unusually easy to remove.

Nitrogen is a better pi-donor than oxygen, so amide resonance (donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl) is even stronger than the ester case, making amide carbonyls notably less effective at stabilizing an adjacent alpha carbanion, which is why amide alpha C-H bonds are less acidic (pKa often above 30) than ketone alpha C-H bonds.

The one alpha carbon of 2,2-dimethylpropanal is the quaternary carbon, and it carries no hydrogen. The CHO hydrogen sits on the carbonyl carbon itself rather than next to it, so it is not an alpha hydrogen and it is not acidic. Each of the other three has a CH3 or a CH2 bonded straight to the carbonyl carbon.

Exchange happens through the enolate, so only alpha hydrogens exchange. The two alpha carbons are the CH3 on one side, with three hydrogens, and the CH on the other, with one: four in total. The two methyls of the isopropyl group are beta, one bond too far from the carbonyl, and they stay as they are.

The stereocenter is the alpha carbon. Forming the enolate makes that carbon sp2 and flat, and reprotonation happens on either face with equal probability, so the product is a 50:50 mixture. Note what does not happen: a clean inversion. A planar intermediate gives racemization, not inversion.

The central CH2 is alpha to both carbonyls, so its anion delocalizes into two of them at once: pKa about 11, against about 20 for the terminal methyl. The OCH2 hydrogens are on a carbon bonded to oxygen rather than to a carbonyl carbon, so they are not alpha and not acidic. Ethoxide, whose conjugate acid is pKa 16, takes the pKa 11 proton essentially completely and leaves everything else alone.
aldol: The aldol reaction is an enolate (nucleophile, from one carbonyl’s alpha carbon) attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, forming a new C–C bond and a beta-hydroxy carbonyl.

Work the condensation backwards. Put water back across the C2=C3 double bond, OH onto C3 and H onto C2, which gives 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal. Now cut the C2-C3 bond, the only bond an aldol makes: the alpha fragment keeps the CHO and its methyl and takes a hydrogen back, giving CH3CH2CHO, and on the beta fragment the OH becomes a C=O, giving CH3CH2CHO again. Two propanals, three carbons each, account for the five-carbon chain and its methyl branch.

With two different carbonyls that can each form enolates and each act as electrophiles, an uncontrolled mixed aldol gives up to four possible products — selectivity requires strategies like using one component in excess or pre-forming one enolate completely before adding the other carbonyl.

Base removes an alpha hydrogen to generate a resonance-stabilized enolate, and it is the nucleophilic alpha carbon of that enolate that attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule of aldehyde or ketone.

The new C-C bond forms between the alpha carbon of one molecule and the carbonyl carbon of the other; after protonation, that carbonyl carbon now bears an -OH group that is beta (two carbons away) to the remaining carbonyl group, giving a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound.

Both the enolate (or enol) formation step and the C-C bond-forming addition step are equilibria; the aldol product can revert to starting materials (a retro-aldol), which is part of why the overall process is often driven toward completion by subsequent dehydration.

The beta hydroxyl sits one carbon away from an acidic alpha C-H, so water is lost across the alpha-beta bond. Under base that is an E1cb: the alpha proton comes off first and the enolate left behind expels hydroxide. Under acid it runs through the enol instead, whose C=C pushes the protonated hydroxyl out as water. Either route ends at a conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, and that conjugation is the payoff that makes an otherwise unpromising elimination worth doing.

Conjugation between the new alkene and the carbonyl group extends pi overlap and lowers the overall energy of the product, providing a thermodynamic driving force for elimination of water even though the beta-hydroxy ketone itself is a stable, isolable compound.

In acid-catalyzed mechanisms, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, which both activates the carbonyl carbon toward nucleophilic attack and increases the acidity of the adjacent alpha hydrogens, facilitating enol formation in the next step.

Number the chain C1 to C7 with the two CHO carbons as C1 and C7. The alpha carbons are C2 and C6, equivalent by symmetry, so take the C2 enolate. C2 attacks C7 and the ring that closes is C2-C3-C4-C5-C6-C7, six atoms, which is one of the two sizes that close readily. Protonation gives 2-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde, and warming eliminates water across the alpha-beta bond, putting the new C=C inside the ring and in conjugation with the CHO.

Because the alpha-hydrogen-free partner cannot form its own enolate, it can only act as the electrophile, while the other carbonyl compound's enolate is the only nucleophile available, greatly simplifying the reaction to essentially one major crossed product.

As with most ring-forming reactions, five- and six-membered rings form fastest and most favorably due to good orbital alignment and minimal strain, so intramolecular aldol (and aldol condensation) reactions are typically designed to close five- or six-membered rings.

Acetone's enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second acetone molecule; after protonation, the product is a beta-hydroxy ketone known as diacetone alcohol, which can later be dehydrated (with acid and heat) to the conjugated enone mesityl oxide.

The same steric and electronic factors that make aldehydes more reactive toward nucleophiles in general (less crowding, less alkyl-group electron donation stabilizing the carbonyl) also make them better electrophilic partners in aldol addition.

By using excess strong base to exclusively deprotonate the first compound before the second carbonyl compound is even present, the chemist avoids having two competing enolates form simultaneously, which otherwise leads to an uncontrolled mixture of self- and cross-aldol products.

A dicarbonyl compound can undergo intramolecular aldol addition when one end's enolate attacks the other end's carbonyl, closing a ring; subsequent dehydration under the reaction conditions gives a cyclic, conjugated unsaturated carbonyl compound, a classic ring-annulation strategy.

Because aldol addition is an equilibrium, heating a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound with base (especially when the forward dehydration pathway is blocked, such as when there is no alpha-H available for elimination) can drive the reverse C-C bond cleavage, regenerating the two original carbonyl compounds.

The standard base-mediated elimination removes an alpha hydrogen (beta to the leaving hydroxyl, which is activated by the adjacent carbonyl) while the hydroxyl group departs; if that specific alpha hydrogen is absent, the usual E1cb route to the enone is blocked.

Under acid there is no strong base in the flask, so the molecule tautomerizes to its enol first. Protonating the beta hydroxyl turns it into water, a real leaving group, and the enol C=C pushes in as the water departs, so the departure is assisted and no cation is ever free. Losing the enol OH proton at the end restores the C=O and leaves the conjugated enone. A cation on the beta carbon would in fact be destabilized, not stabilized: it sits two atoms from a strongly electron-withdrawing carbonyl that has no pi density to lend it.

Under acid catalysis, only a small, neutral equilibrium concentration of the enol tautomer (not a charged enolate) acts as the nucleophile toward a protonated, activated carbonyl electrophile; under base catalysis, a genuine enolate anion is generated and attacks a neutral carbonyl electrophile.

4-Methylbenzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogens, so it can only be the electrophile, and cyclohexanone supplies the enolate. The new bond forms at cyclohexanone's alpha carbon, and heat then dehydrates the addition product to put the new C=C in conjugation with both the ketone and the ring, which is why a condensation like this one is hard to stop at the addition stage.

Both reactions begin the same way, with an enolate attacking a carbonyl to give a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, but what happens next differs: an aldehyde or ketone electrophile has no good leaving group so the intermediate is simply protonated (giving a hydroxyl), while an ester electrophile has an alkoxide leaving group that is expelled to regenerate a carbonyl, which is the defining difference between aldol addition and Claisen condensation.

Because 2-butanone is unsymmetrical, it has two distinct alpha carbons (the methyl and the ethyl side), each capable of forming its own enolate; each of those enolates can then add to the single type of carbonyl carbon present, generating several regiochemically distinct beta-hydroxy ketone products rather than one clean outcome.

When a dicarbonyl substrate offers more than one combination of enolizable alpha carbon and electrophilic carbonyl, the pathway that leads to the favorable five- or six-membered ring is strongly preferred over one that would form a strained or entropically unfavorable ring, so the reaction effectively self-selects the better regiochemical outcome.

Dehydrating an aldol always puts the new C=C between the alpha and the beta carbon, so it is conjugated with the carbonyl by construction - that is never what goes wrong. What can stop it is geometry: at the bridgehead of a small bicycle the two p orbitals are held perpendicular and no pi bond can form. When an aldol condensation fails, look for a geometric obstruction rather than an electronic one.

Acetone is the only partner able to form an enolate (benzaldehyde has none), so its enolate selectively attacks the aldehyde carbonyl; subsequent base- or heat-promoted dehydration gives a conjugated aryl enone, a classic and reliable crossed aldol condensation outcome.

Dehydration of the aldol product generally requires more vigorous conditions (heat, stronger acid or base, or longer times) than the initial addition step, so keeping conditions mild and the reaction time short allows the kinetically formed beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound to be isolated before the thermodynamically favored elimination occurs.

The retro-aldol mechanism specifically relies on the beta-hydroxy group and the adjacent carbonyl to drive C-C bond cleavage back to two carbonyl fragments; once dehydration has occurred and that hydroxyl is gone, replaced by a C=C double bond, the structural feature required for straightforward retro-aldol cleavage is no longer present.

Acetaldehyde's enolate attacks the carbonyl of a second acetaldehyde molecule to give 3-hydroxybutanal, which readily dehydrates under the reaction conditions (conjugation with the aldehyde provides the driving force) to give the alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde crotonaldehyde.

Put the water back across the C=C - OH on the beta carbon, H on the alpha - and then cut the alpha-beta bond, which is the only bond the aldol made. Both halves come out as CH3CH2CHO, so propanal acted once as the nucleophile and once as the electrophile. Counting carbons is the quick check: two three-carbon molecules give the six carbons of the product, because a condensation loses only water.
claisen: Claisen condensation is the ester analog of the aldol: an ester enolate attacks a second ester’s carbonyl carbon, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels an alkoxide (acyl substitution) rather than just forming an alcohol.
Because the electrophile is an ester (with an OR leaving group attached), the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling alkoxide, giving a β-ketoester rather than a β-hydroxy product.

The β-ketoester product has a doubly-stabilized, very acidic alpha proton; its deprotonation by excess alkoxide base is essentially complete, continuously removing product and driving the overall equilibrium toward completion.

Two molecules of ethyl acetate combine: one is deprotonated at its alpha carbon by ethoxide to form an enolate, which attacks the carbonyl of a second ethyl acetate molecule; loss of ethoxide from the tetrahedral intermediate gives ethyl acetoacetate, a classic beta-ketoester.

If the alkoxide base differs from the ester's own alkoxy group, it can also act as a nucleophile toward the ester carbonyl (transesterification) or get incorporated into the leaving group step, complicating the product mixture; matching the base to the ester's OR group avoids this issue.

False. The final deprotonation - the step that drives the whole reaction - takes a full equivalent of alkoxide and does not give it back until the acidic workup, because the product is held as its enolate until then. A catalytic amount of base would therefore drive only a catalytic amount of product. This is the most common misconception about the reaction, and it is why calling a Claisen base-catalyzed is imprecise.

The reaction mixture at the end of a Claisen condensation contains the sodium salt of the acidic beta-ketoester (since it was deprotonated in the final, driving step); an acidic aqueous workup is required to protonate this enolate and recover the neutral beta-ketoester product.

An ester with no alpha hydrogens cannot be deprotonated to form an enolate, so it cannot serve as the nucleophile in a Claisen condensation; it can, however, still act as the electrophile if combined with a different ester or ketone that does have alpha hydrogens, a strategy used in crossed Claisen condensations.

Both reactions begin identically: an enolate nucleophile attacks an electrophilic carbonyl carbon, generating a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. What happens to that intermediate next (simple protonation versus expulsion of a leaving group) is what differentiates the aldol reaction from the Claisen condensation.

Just as in a crossed aldol reaction, removing the possibility that one partner forms its own competing enolate (because it has no alpha hydrogens to deprotonate) simplifies the reaction to one dominant enolate attacking one dominant electrophile, favoring a single crossed product.

Because diethyl carbonate has no alpha hydrogens, it cannot compete as a nucleophile; its carbonyl carbon, flanked by two good ethoxide leaving groups, is an excellent electrophile for a ketone enolate, and after loss of one ethoxide the product is a beta-ketoester with a new -CO2Et group on the original ketone's alpha carbon.

The dramatic pKa drop from starting ester to beta-ketoester product means the ethoxide base can essentially completely deprotonate the product (but only poorly deprotonates the starting ester), and it is exactly this favorable, essentially complete final deprotonation that pulls the whole multistep equilibrium toward product formation.

The Dieckmann condensation is the intramolecular version of the Claisen condensation: a diester's enolate at one end attacks the ester carbonyl at the other end of the same molecule, expelling an alkoxide and closing a ring to give a cyclic beta-ketoester, typically favoring five- or six-membered rings.

By Le Chatelier's principle, continuously removing product from an equilibrium (whether by the final deprotonation step under normal conditions or by any other means of product removal) pulls the preceding unfavorable equilibrium (enolate formation and addition) toward producing more product, even if the concentration of the key intermediate at any instant is small.

In a mixed Claisen-type reaction between an ester and a ketone, it is advantageous to use conditions where the more easily and more completely formed ketone enolate serves as nucleophile and attacks the ester (which offers an alkoxide leaving group for a clean addition-elimination), giving a good route to a beta-ketoester while avoiding excessive self-condensation of the ketone.

As with other intramolecular ring-closing reactions, the Dieckmann condensation is strongly biased toward forming the kinetically and thermodynamically favorable five- and six-membered rings; substrates geometrically constrained to form much smaller (strained) or much larger (entropically costly) rings react far less efficiently or not at all under standard conditions.

The tetrahedral intermediate can revert to starting esters or go forward to expel the ethoxide leaving group; because this addition-elimination sequence (like the earlier enolate formation) is reversible, it is ultimately the final, thermodynamically favorable deprotonation of the acidic beta-ketoester that locks in the product and drives the overall multistep process forward.

Simply having a fully formed starting enolate does not prevent the subsequent addition and elimination equilibria from running in reverse; what actually commits the reaction to product is that the beta-ketoester, once formed, is acidic enough to be essentially completely deprotonated by the alkoxide present, continuously siphoning material out of the reversible steps and toward the stable enolate salt of the product.

A Claisen condensation fundamentally requires an enolate nucleophile generated by removing an alpha hydrogen; an ester like ethyl trimethylacetate, whose alpha carbon is fully substituted with three methyl groups and has no hydrogen to remove, simply cannot form that nucleophile and so cannot undergo self-condensation (though it could still act only as an electrophile if paired with a different ester that does have alpha hydrogens).

The Dieckmann condensation uses the same fundamental mechanism as the Claisen condensation (ester enolate attacking an ester carbonyl, expelling alkoxide), but because both ester groups are part of one molecule (a diester), the reaction closes a ring instead of joining two separate molecules.

Diethyl adipate is EtO2C-(CH2)4-CO2Et. Number the chain C1 to C6 taking the two ester carbonyl carbons as C1 and C6, so there are four methylenes between the ester groups. Ethoxide makes the enolate at C2, C2 attacks C6, and the ring that closes contains C2, C3, C4, C5 and C6: five atoms. Five- and six-membered rings are the ones a Dieckmann closure reaches, so this one goes; a diester one carbon shorter would have to close a four-membered ring and does not react this way.

Because the final, product-determining step of a Claisen condensation is deprotonation of the acidic beta-ketoester to its stable, resonance-delocalized enolate salt, the reaction mixture right before workup consists mainly of that salt; a mild acidic workup simply reprotonates it to recover the neutral beta-ketoester, rather than undoing the earlier carbon-carbon bond formation.

Although in principle many esters can undergo Claisen-type chemistry, using a small, matched alkoxide (methoxide with methyl esters, ethoxide with ethyl esters) keeps the mechanism clean, since the base and the leaving group are then identical and steric hindrance in the addition-elimination step is minimized.

Using a base whose alkoxide does not match the ester's own -OR group introduces the possibility of that alkoxide itself attacking the ester carbonyl (a transesterification-like pathway) or becoming incorporated into the leaving group step, which is why chemists typically match the base's alkoxide to the ester being used.

Just like the intermolecular Claisen condensation, the Dieckmann condensation relies on the final deprotonation of its acidic cyclic beta-ketoester product by the alkoxide base to lock the equilibrium in favor of the cyclized product, since the earlier intramolecular addition-elimination step alone is reversible.

Even though the overall sequence is ultimately pulled forward by the favorable final deprotonation of the product, the reaction must first generate enough starting ester enolate to initiate the addition step; a base too weak to meaningfully deprotonate the much less acidic starting ester (pKa about 25) will fail to get the sequence going in practical amounts of time.

The enolate forms at the CH2 alpha carbon and attacks a second molecule's carbonyl carbon, and EtO- leaves. The new bond joins that alpha carbon to the other molecule's acyl carbon, so the skeleton is CH3CH2-CO-CH(CH3)-CO2Et: a five-carbon chain with the ketone at C3 and a methyl at C2. That leftover methyl on the alpha carbon is the giveaway that the nucleophile was propanoate rather than acetate. Ethyl 3-oxopentanoate is the answer you get if you forget it, and ethyl 3-oxobutanoate is what ethyl acetate would have given.

Diethyl carbonate has no alpha hydrogens, so it can only be the electrophile, and the ketone at pKa 20 is deprotonated in preference to it. The crossed Claisen gives ethyl 2-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate. Ethyl acetate would compete as a nucleophile and give a mixture, while ethers and alcohols have no acyl carbon to attack in the first place.

Number the chain C1 to C5. The enolate at C2 attacking C5 would close C2-C3-C4-C5, a four-membered ring, which is far too strained to form. The intramolecular route is shut, so the substrate does intermolecular chemistry or nothing. Count the ring before predicting any Dieckmann: five and six work, four does not.

Cut the bond between the central CH2 and the acyl carbon on its left. The acyl half, PhCO-, has to come from the electrophile: ethyl benzoate, which has no alpha hydrogens and so can play no other role. The other half, -CH2CO2Et, is the enolate of ethyl acetate. Acetophenone with ethyl benzoate would give a 1,3-diketone instead, and benzaldehyde has no leaving group, so it would give an aldol.
amine-structure: Neutral amine nitrogen has one lone pair not involved in bonding, which it can donate to a proton (Brønsted base) or any electrophile (Lewis base).
Amide resonance pulls the nitrogen lone pair into conjugation with the carbonyl, making it far less available to accept a proton than a typical amine’s lone pair.
Aniline’s nitrogen lone pair partially conjugates into the benzene ring (similar to amide resonance), making it far less available to accept a proton than an alkylamine’s localized lone pair.
Classification counts how many carbon substituents are bonded directly to nitrogen, regardless of how many N-H bonds remain.
With three bonds and one lone pair, nitrogen adopts a pyramidal shape, similar to ammonia.
The same nonbonding electron pair can be donated to a proton (acting as a base) or to an electrophilic carbon (acting as a nucleophile).
Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so N-H bonds are less polarized and hydrogen bonds between amines are weaker than those between alcohols.
With four bonds to carbon, nitrogen has used its lone pair, so it carries a permanent positive charge and cannot act as a base or donate electrons further.

The amine (pKaH about 10.6) is fully protonated by 1 M HCl, and the ammonium chloride that results is an ionic salt, so it dissolves in the water layer. A ketone is nowhere near basic enough to be protonated by dilute HCl and stays in the ether. Adding NaOH to the aqueous layer regenerates the free amine, which is extracted back into fresh ether - this is how amines are separated and purified in practice.
Amines feature sp3 (or aryl-attached) nitrogen connected via single bonds to carbon and/or hydrogen, retaining a lone pair.
Amine basicity is conventionally tabulated as the pKa of the protonated ammonium ion; a higher pKa for the conjugate acid means a more basic amine.
Alkyl groups are weak electron donors through induction, which helps stabilize the resulting ammonium cation and raises basicity relative to ammonia.

The side-chain nitrogen is an ordinary alkylamine with nothing nearby, pKaH about 10.5. The alpha nitrogen sits one carbon from an electron-withdrawing carboxyl group, whose inductive pull destabilizes the ammonium ion formed on protonation and drops its pKaH to about 9. Induction falls off steeply with distance, which is why four CH2 groups are enough to remove the effect entirely.

More alkyl groups raise inductive electron density, favoring basicity, but also hinder solvation of the resulting ammonium cation in water, which disfavors basicity; these effects roughly balance out to favor the disubstituted amine.
Despite having three electron-donating groups, trimethylamine's bulky, poorly solvated ammonium ion makes it comparable to or less basic than dimethylamine in aqueous solution.
Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is required for the ring's aromaticity, so using it to bond a proton would disrupt aromatic stabilization, making it far less basic than pyridine or an alkylamine.
Because the nitrogen lone pair is tied up stabilizing the carbonyl, it is far less available to bond an incoming proton, making amides only weakly basic.
O-protonation produces a resonance-stabilized cation where positive charge is shared between O and N, which is more stable than the localized charge from N-protonation.
An alkyl group raises basicity relative to ammonia through induction, while conjugation with an aromatic ring in aniline drastically lowers it by delocalizing the lone pair.

Electron-donating substituents reduce how much the ring pulls on the nitrogen lone pair, leaving more electron density available on nitrogen for protonation; electron-withdrawing groups do the opposite and lower basicity.
A nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing by both induction and resonance, further depleting the nitrogen lone pair and decreasing basicity rather than increasing it.

One nitrogen in imidazole donates its lone pair to the aromatic system (like pyrrole, non-basic), while the other nitrogen's lone pair is not part of the aromatic system and is readily available to accept a proton, similar to pyridine.

What matters is which side of the acid-base equilibrium the resonance stabilizes. In an amide, resonance stabilizes the neutral form, so protonation costs that stabilization and basicity collapses. In guanidine, protonating the imine nitrogen gives a cation whose positive charge is shared equally over three nitrogens, so the resonance pays for the protonation instead of opposing it. Same phenomenon, opposite direction.

A localized sp3 lone pair (alkylamine, pKaH about 10.7) is most basic; pyridine's localized sp2 lone pair is next at 5.2; an amide comes next at about -1, its lone pair delocalized into the carbonyl; pyrrole is last at about -4, because its lone pair IS the aromatic sextet and protonating nitrogen would destroy the aromaticity outright.

Greater s-character lowers the orbital's energy and pulls the lone pair closer to the nucleus, making it less willing to be donated to a proton compared to the higher-energy sp3 lone pair of an amine.
Higher s-character means electrons are held closer to and more tightly by the nucleus, making them less available to bond an incoming proton, so basicity decreases.

Distorted bond angles in strained rings change the hybridization of the nitrogen lone pair orbital, typically increasing its s-character and somewhat reducing basicity relative to an unstrained analog.

A simple trialkylamine is most basic; pyridine's localized sp2 lone pair is less basic than an alkylamine but more basic than a ring-conjugated arylamine; aniline's delocalized lone pair is weak; the amide is essentially non-basic since its lone pair feeds the carbonyl.
Lower electronegativity on nitrogen means its lone pair is held less tightly than an oxygen lone pair, making it more willing to accept a proton.

A small, unhindered proton can still approach the lone pair easily (supporting basicity), while bulky alkyl groups block approach of larger electrophiles in a substitution reaction, lowering nucleophilicity without lowering basicity.
amine-reactions: A primary amine adds to a carbonyl, and after proton transfers and loss of water, the resulting C=N double bond is an imine.
This is nucleophilic acyl substitution — the amine nitrogen ends up bonded to the carbonyl carbon, and the leaving group departs, giving an amide.

With no second N–H to lose, the iminium-like intermediate instead loses a proton from the adjacent alpha carbon, shifting the double bond there and giving an enamine (C=C–N) instead of an imine (C=N).
Exhaustive SN2 alkylation keeps adding methyl groups to nitrogen until all four positions are filled, giving a permanently charged quaternary ammonium salt.
The nitrogen lone pair is protonated by the strong acid, giving a positively charged ammonium salt with the chloride as counterion.

Excess CH3I exhaustively methylates the nitrogen to cyclohexyltrimethylammonium iodide. That nitrogen has four bonds, a full positive charge and no lone pair, so it cannot attack the anhydride - and it has no N-H to lose even if it could. Order matters: run the acylation first and the amide forms cleanly.
The amine nitrogen attacks the acyl chloride carbonyl carbon, chloride leaves, and loss of a proton from nitrogen gives a neutral amide.
Nitrosation of the primary amine followed by loss of water forms the diazonium ion, R-N2+.
Aryl diazonium salts are typically only stable at low temperature (around 0 to 5 degrees C) and must be used immediately in further reactions rather than stored.
Each alkylation product still bears a nucleophilic nitrogen that can react further with remaining alkyl halide, so a statistical mixture of alkylation levels usually results.
Each amide-forming step releases HCl, which would otherwise protonate and deactivate remaining amine; an added base consumes the HCl, keeping the reaction moving.
The C=N product formed from a primary amine and a carbonyl compound after loss of water is classically known as an imine or Schiff base.

After the secondary amine adds to the carbonyl and loses the OH as water, nitrogen still bears one substituent and no remaining N-H to lose, so the molecule instead loses an alpha C-H to form the carbon-carbon double bond of an enamine.

The initial addition product, bearing both an OH and an NR2 group on the same carbon, is the hemiaminal, which can then dehydrate to the imine or enamine - though it is rarely isolable, since it usually dehydrates about as fast as it forms.
Although tertiary amines can add to a carbonyl using their lone pair, they have no N-H to lose in the dehydration step, so a stable neutral imine or enamine cannot form at that nitrogen.

This is a reductive amination. The ketone and the amine condense to the iminium ion and NaBH3CN reduces it. The mildly acidic pH is what makes it work: acidic enough to dehydrate the hemiaminal, not so acidic that the amine is all protonated, and NaBH3CN is attenuated enough to survive those conditions and to ignore the ketone. LiAlH4 added first would simply reduce the ketone to the alcohol.

Attack comes first (iii), because the amine is the nucleophile and the carbonyl carbon the electrophile. A proton transfer then converts the zwitterion into the neutral hemiaminal (v). The OH is a terrible leaving group, so it is protonated to water (ii), which leaves with a push from the nitrogen lone pair to give the iminium ion (i). Finally the iminium loses its N-H proton to give the neutral imine (iv).
Alkyl diazonium ions lose N2 almost immediately because there is no resonance stabilization of the cation, generating a carbocation that goes on to form substitution or elimination products.
Diazonium salts undergo a range of substitution reactions (with water, copper halides, or cyanide, for example) that install many different functional groups onto the aromatic ring.
The amine and ketone first condense to an iminium/imine intermediate, which the mild reducing agent then reduces in the same reaction vessel, avoiding isolation of the reactive intermediate.
Phthalimide blocks two of nitrogen's bonding positions during alkylation, and subsequent hydrolysis or hydrazine treatment releases only the desired primary amine, avoiding over-alkylation.
LiAlH4 is a strong enough hydride reducing agent to convert the amide carbonyl carbon into a CH2 group, converting the amide directly into an amine.

Amide formation requires the nitrogen to lose a proton after acyl transfer to become neutral; a tertiary amine has no N-H to lose, so it cannot form a stable neutral amide at that nitrogen, even though it may transiently act as a nucleophile or catalyst.
Hydrazine (or acidic/basic hydrolysis) breaks both amide linkages of the phthalimide ring, liberating the primary amine cleanly from the alkylated nitrogen.

Conjugation between the diazonium nitrogen and the aromatic ring delocalizes positive charge in the aryl case, slowing decomposition, whereas the alkyl diazonium ion has no such stabilization and loses N2 almost instantly, generating a reactive carbocation.
After nitrosation, a secondary amine's nitrogen has no remaining N-H to lose on the way to a diazonium-type species, so the reaction stops at the stable N-nitrosamine.

At the mildly acidic pH typically used, NaBH3CN reduces the more reactive, protonated iminium ion much faster than it reduces the neutral carbonyl starting material, improving yield of the desired amine over simple alcohol byproducts.

Because the secondary (and even tertiary) amine products are still nucleophilic, and proton transfer equilibria can regenerate free amine from its ammonium salt, the reaction tends to give a mixture of alkylation levels rather than one clean product.
The Balz-Schiemann reaction converts an aryl diazonium salt (commonly as its tetrafluoroborate) into the corresponding aryl fluoride upon heating, with loss of nitrogen gas.

Pyridine's job is to take the HCl each acylation releases, so the amine is not consumed as a base — and it can do that job without getting in the way, because it carries no N–H and so cannot be acylated into the product. It is not that pyridine fails to attack the acid chloride: it does, giving an N-acylpyridinium ion, and that ion is a better acylating agent than the acid chloride was, so the acyl group simply passes on to the amine. That relay is why pyridine and DMAP catalyze acylations rather than obstructing them. NaOH is the wrong choice for a different reason: hydroxide would attack the acid chloride and hydrolyze it to the carboxylate before the amine got its turn.
aromaticity: Hückel’s rule requires 4n+2 pi electrons (n = 0, 1, 2...) in a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system — benzene’s 6 pi electrons fits n=1.
4 pi electrons fits the 4n pattern (n=1), which Hückel’s rule predicts is destabilizing (anti-aromatic) rather than stabilizing.
With 4 pi electrons in a planar, fully conjugated ring, it fits the 4n pattern (n=1) that Hückel’s rule predicts is destabilizing — anti-aromatic, and indeed very unstable/reactive.

Work the requirements in order rather than counting first. The dianion is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated, so the count is allowed to decide: 10 fits 4n+2 with n = 2, so it is aromatic. The triene fails the conjugation requirement before the count is ever reached — two sp³ carbons break the loop of p orbitals — so it is non-aromatic, and its 6 pi electrons are beside the point. The trap is answering antiaromatic for the triene: antiaromatic means passing all three structural tests and then landing on 4n, which a ring with an sp³ carbon in it never does.

4n+2 with n = 2 gives 10, not 6. Benzene's six pi electrons correspond to n = 1: 4(1) + 2 = 6. The n = 2 count of 10 belongs to species such as the cyclooctatetraene dianion and the naphthalene ring system.
Naphthalene has five formal double bonds worth of pi electrons delocalized over the fused bicyclic system, totaling 10 pi electrons, which fits 4n+2 with n = 2.
sp2 hybridization leaves one unhybridized p orbital per atom perpendicular to the ring plane, allowing continuous pi overlap all the way around.

Addition across a ring double bond would convert an sp2 carbon to sp3, breaking conjugation and losing the large resonance stabilization energy, so substitution (which preserves the ring) is favored instead.

Real cyclooctatetraene twists out of planarity into a tub shape, which avoids the destabilization of antiaromaticity (8 pi electrons would be 4n) by sacrificing full conjugation rather than staying planar.
n = 0 gives 2 pi electrons, n = 1 gives 6, n = 2 gives 10, and so on; n cannot be negative or fractional.
Even very small rings can be aromatic if they meet all the criteria; 2 pi electrons satisfies 4n+2 when n = 0, making the cyclopropenyl cation aromatic and unusually stable for a carbocation.
Because the lone pair is in-plane rather than in a p orbital perpendicular to the ring, it is not part of the 6 pi electron aromatic system, which is why pyridine's nitrogen remains basic.

Furan has two ring double bonds (4 pi electrons) plus one oxygen lone pair donated into a p orbital, giving 6 total pi electrons and satisfying Huckel's rule; the other lone pair stays in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane.

The cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 pi electrons and is aromatic (very stabilized), the neutral diene is simply conjugated, and the cation has 4 pi electrons and is antiaromatic (highly destabilized), making the anion by far the most stable of the three.
Protonating pyrrole's nitrogen would remove that lone pair from the aromatic system and destroy aromaticity, so the lone pair is much less available to accept a proton than in ordinary amines.
Cyclobutadiene is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with 4 pi electrons, which fits 4n (n = 1) rather than 4n+2, making it antiaromatic and highly unstable/reactive.

Tropylium's positive charge sits in an empty p orbital identical in symmetry to the other six carbons' p orbitals, giving a fully conjugated 6 pi electron aromatic system despite being a seven-membered ring.
8 pi electrons fits the 4n pattern (n = 2), so a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with this electron count is antiaromatic, typically destabilized relative to an open-chain analog.

Having the right pi electron count is necessary but not sufficient; an sp3 atom interrupts the continuous ring of p orbitals needed for full conjugation, so the molecule is non-aromatic regardless of electron count.

Non-aromatic means neither stabilized nor destabilized — an ordinary diene, which cyclobutadiene plainly is not. It is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated with 4 pi electrons, so it is antiaromatic: actively destabilized relative to an open-chain diene, which is why it dimerizes on sight and can be observed at all in a frozen matrix at 4 K.

If benzene were just three isolated double bonds, hydrogenation would release about three times the heat of one alkene's hydrogenation; the actual value is substantially lower, revealing the extra stability (resonance energy) from aromatic delocalization.

Non-aromatic means the compound fails at least one structural requirement and behaves like an ordinary conjugated or non-conjugated system; antiaromatic means all structural requirements are met but the electron count is 4n, producing a system that is destabilized relative to the open-chain analog.
Adding two electrons to the 8 pi electron tub-shaped neutral molecule gives 10 pi electrons (4n+2 with n=2); when the ring flattens to allow full conjugation, this dianion is indeed aromatic.

Because the pi electrons are delocalized over all six p orbitals rather than localized into three discrete double bonds, every C-C bond has equal, intermediate bond order and length (about 1.39 Angstroms).

One lone pair can occupy the ring p orbital; the other stays in an sp² orbital lying in the ring plane, where it is perpendicular to the pi system and contributes nothing to it. Two ring C=C (4 electrons) plus that one donated pair gives 6, which is why thiophene is aromatic — and the spare in-plane pair is what sulfur still has available for ordinary chemistry.

Huckel's rule assumes a continuous ring of overlapping p orbitals, which needs a planar ring. A large annulene can satisfy the electron count and still twist out of plane to relieve strain, and the overlap goes with it.

Removing a proton from cyclopentadiene creates a planar, fully conjugated five-membered ring anion with 6 pi electrons, satisfying Huckel's rule, so the resulting aromatic stabilization makes cyclopentadiene unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon.
This value, derived from comparing the actual heat of hydrogenation of benzene to that expected for three isolated double bonds, quantifies the extra stability aromaticity provides.

Count each nitrogen separately by asking whether it already has a ring double bond. N3 does (the C=N), so its lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the ring plane and contributes 0 — which is exactly why that nitrogen is the basic one. N1 does not, so its lone pair has to occupy the p orbital and contributes 2. Add the C=C (2), the C=N (2) and N1's pair (2): 6 pi electrons, aromatic. This is the histidine side chain, and the same split explains why histidine has one basic nitrogen and one weakly acidic N–H.

1,3-Cyclohexadiene is cyclic but not fully conjugated around the entire ring (it has sp3 carbons interrupting conjugation), so it is simply non-aromatic, unlike fully conjugated cyclobutadiene (antiaromatic) or benzene and pyridine (aromatic).
eas: The electron-rich aromatic pi system attacks an electrophile, forming a resonance-stabilized cationic intermediate (arenium ion/Wheland intermediate), then loses a proton to restore aromaticity.
The strong stabilization of the aromatic system makes substitution (proton loss, keeping the ring intact) thermodynamically favored over addition, which would destroy aromaticity.

Forming the arenium ion intermediate requires temporarily breaking aromaticity, which costs significant energy — this is the slow, rate-determining step; the final proton loss (restoring aromaticity) is fast.

Attack of the ring pi system on the electrophile generates a cyclohexadienyl cation (arenium ion) in which one ring carbon becomes sp3, temporarily destroying aromaticity; this cation is stabilized by resonance across three positions.

Two decisions, in order. First step: tert-butyl chloride ionizes to a tertiary cation, which is already the most stable arrangement of those carbons, so nothing rearranges and tert-butylbenzene forms cleanly. Second step: an alkyl group is a weak activator and an ortho/para director, so the acylium ion goes ortho or para. tert-Butyl is very bulky, so ortho attack is almost entirely suppressed and the product is essentially all para. The trap is answering meta by reflex because the incoming group is an acyl group — the incoming group never directs; the group already on the ring does.

Direct alkylation with 1-chlorobutane fails for a predictable reason: the primary cation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the secondary cation before benzene ever attacks, so the product is sec-butylbenzene. Acylation with butanoyl chloride cannot rearrange, because the acylium ion is resonance-stabilized by its oxygen, and it also cannot over-react, because the ketone it installs deactivates the ring. Clemmensen reduction, Zn(Hg) in HCl, then turns the C=O into CH₂ and leaves the straight chain intact. Wolff-Kishner (H₂NNH₂, KOH, heat) does the same job when the molecule cannot survive strong acid.
AlCl3 coordinates to the halide and helps ionize the C-X bond, generating (or activating toward) a carbocation electrophile that the aromatic ring can then attack.
A Lewis acid such as AlCl3 helps an acyl chloride lose chloride, forming a resonance-stabilized acylium cation that acts as the electrophile attacked by the aromatic ring.
Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to generate the nitronium ion (NO2+), the actual electrophile attacked by the benzene ring.
Sulfur trioxide (present in fuming sulfuric acid) is a strong electrophile at sulfur; the aromatic ring attacks sulfur to form a sulfonated arenium intermediate.

Both halves are wrong. Benzene is a far weaker nucleophile than an alkene precisely because its pi electrons are tied up in the aromatic sextet, and attacking costs about 36 kcal/mol of that stabilization. Br₂ alone adds to an alkene on contact and does nothing at all to benzene; FeBr₃ is needed to polarize the Br–Br bond into an electrophile strong enough to be worth attacking.

The byproduct generated when the electrophile formed (e.g., FeBr4-, AlCl4-, or HSO4-) is basic enough to pluck off the proton from the sp3 ring carbon, regenerating the aromatic ring and the original catalyst.

Since a free (or nearly free) carbocation is generated, it can rearrange via hydride or alkyl shifts to a more stable cation before the aromatic ring traps it, often giving unexpected substitution patterns.
The acylium ion's positive charge is delocalized onto oxygen through resonance, making it stable enough that it does not need to rearrange to a more stable carbocation, unlike many alkyl cations.

The carbonyl group is electron-withdrawing and deactivates the ring toward further EAS, so acylation self-limits to mono-substitution, unlike alkylation where the alkyl product activates the ring toward further alkylation.

Alkyl groups are weak activators (electron-donating by induction/hyperconjugation), so the mono-alkylated product is actually more reactive than the starting benzene, making it prone to react again and give polyalkylation.

The overall reaction is driven forward because regenerating the aromatic ring in the final step releases substantial stabilization energy, even though the first step requires climbing over a substantial barrier to form the arenium ion.

Unlike bromination and chlorination, direct iodination is thermodynamically unfavorable without help; an oxidant (such as nitric acid or hydrogen peroxide) is used to drive the reaction forward, often by removing HI as it forms.

Sulfonation is the one reaction of the five that runs in both directions. Concentrated or fuming acid drives it on; hot dilute aqueous acid drives it back off. That makes –SO₃H a placeholder: install it so that it occupies the para position, run the substitution you actually want at ortho, then boil the sulfonic acid away. Nothing else in the EAS toolkit can be put on and taken off on demand, which is what makes an otherwise unreachable ortho product reachable.
Sulfuric acid, a stronger acid than nitric acid, protonates nitric acid's hydroxyl oxygen; the resulting species readily loses water, leaving behind the linear, highly electrophilic nitronium ion.

Benzene's aromatic pi system is a relatively weak nucleophile compared to, say, a free carbanion, so it generally needs help activating the electrophile; a Lewis acid catalyst polarizes or ionizes the C-X bond to create a sufficiently reactive electrophilic species.

One carbon is sp³ and out of the pi system entirely, so five carbons are left holding a pentadienyl cation — and resonance puts the charge on just three of those five, the two ortho and the one para to the sp³ center. That partial delocalization is real stabilization and is why the reaction runs at all, but it is nowhere near the six-carbon aromatic delocalization that was given up, which is why the arenium ion sits at an energy maximum for the whole route.

One ring carbon is sp³ and out of the pi system. The other five hold a pentadienyl cation, and its three resonance structures place the positive charge on the two carbons ortho to the sp³ center and the one carbon para to it — three carbons. The two carbons meta to the sp³ center carry no charge in any structure, and that is exactly why some substituents send an incoming electrophile meta: meta is the attack whose arenium ion never puts charge on the substituent's own carbon.

The carbonyl oxygen of the product ketone strongly complexes with AlCl3, sequestering it; an aqueous workup is then needed to free the product and regenerate the catalyst, which is why acylation needs more than catalytic AlCl3 while some other EAS reactions need only a trace.

The Lewis acid coordinates to one halogen atom of X2, pulling electron density away and making the other halogen atom electrophilic enough to be attacked by the relatively weak nucleophile that is the aromatic ring.

The final deprotonation is actually fast because it restores aromaticity and is thermodynamically favorable; the slow, rate-determining step is instead the initial attack that forms the high-energy, non-aromatic arenium ion.

Strong deactivators like -NO2 pull electron density out of the ring so much that the ring is not nucleophilic enough to attack even a reactive alkyl cation electrophile, a key limitation of Friedel-Crafts chemistry.

Unlike most EAS reactions, sulfonation's equilibrium can be shifted either direction depending on conditions; excess SO3 favors sulfonation, while dilute hot aqueous acid favors desulfonation, a useful synthetic trick for temporarily blocking a ring position.

Because sulfonation is reversible, chemists can install a sulfonic acid group to occupy and direct substitution at a particular ring position, then later remove it, effectively using it as a temporary placeholder.

Nitronium ion forms directly from nitric and sulfuric acid without a separate Lewis acid catalyst on the ring, whereas molecular halogens and alkyl halides are generally not electrophilic enough on their own and need a Lewis acid (FeX3 or AlCl3) to generate a reactive electrophile.
directing-effects: Strong electron donors (via resonance) stabilize the arenium intermediate best when the positive charge lands ortho or para to the substituent, directing new substitution there.

Strong electron-withdrawing groups destabilize the arenium intermediate least when the positive charge is meta (avoiding direct resonance overlap with the withdrawing group), so meta substitution dominates.

Ask what is actually on the ring under the reaction conditions. Nitrating acid is overwhelmingly acidic and aniline is a base, so most of it exists as the anilinium ion. –NH₃⁺ has no lone pair left to donate and carries a full positive charge next to the ring, which makes it a deactivating meta director — the opposite of what –NH₂ does. Both species react, giving roughly 2 % ortho, 47 % meta and 51 % para: the para still comes from the trace of free amine, and the huge meta fraction is the anilinium's. Aniline also oxidizes badly in nitric acid. The fix is a nitrogen that cannot be protonated: acetic anhydride gives acetanilide, still an ortho/para director but a milder one, so nitration goes cleanly para; aqueous acid or base then hydrolyzes the amide back to the free amine.
The -OCH3 group is an electron donor through resonance, placing extra electron density (and stabilizing the resulting arenium cation) most effectively at the ortho and para positions.

Acylate first. Acetophenone's acetyl group is a deactivating meta director, so the nitro group lands meta to it and the product is 3-nitroacetophenone. The other order fails outright: nitrobenzene's ring is far too electron-poor for Friedel–Crafts, which does not run on strongly deactivated rings at all, so the second step would simply not happen. Two independent reasons to acylate first, and either one settles it. Note also what this route cannot reach — the para isomer is not available from these two reactions in either order.

The strong electronegativity of halogens withdraws electron density through the sigma bond (slowing the reaction overall), but a lone pair on the halogen can still donate into the ring by resonance, which best stabilizes the arenium cation when the positive charge lands ortho or para to the halogen.

Alkyl groups donate electron density into the ring through hyperconjugation/induction, which both speeds up EAS (activating) and best stabilizes the cationic intermediate at the ortho and para positions.

The carbonyl carbon is electron-poor and, through resonance, withdraws electron density most strongly from the ortho and para positions, destabilizing cationic intermediates there, so substitution is directed to meta and the ring reacts more slowly overall.

Halogens are unique among common deactivators: their lone pair resonance donation directs ortho/para even though their strong inductive electron withdrawal makes the ring less reactive overall (deactivating).

Groups like -NO2, -C(=O)R, and -CN pull electron density out of the ring (lowering reactivity everywhere) and, through resonance, destabilize positive charge most severely at ortho/para, leaving meta as the relatively least-bad (least destabilized) option.

The nitrogen lone pair is readily donated into the aromatic pi system, placing significant negative character at the ortho and para positions and strongly activating the ring, making aniline react in EAS even without a catalyst in some cases.

The methyl group is a weak activator and an ortho/para director, so nitration gives mostly ortho- and para-nitrotoluene with only a few percent meta — about 58% ortho, 37% para and 4% meta in practice. Ortho actually leads, because there are two ortho positions to one para and a methyl group is small enough not to get in the way. Bulk changes that: nitrating tert-butylbenzene gives almost entirely para, because ortho attack now runs into the substituent.

The carboxylic acid group is electron-withdrawing by resonance and induction, deactivating the ring and directing incoming electrophiles to the meta position, where the destabilizing resonance effect is least severe.

Resonance donation of the lone pair into the ring pi system outcompetes the modest inductive electron withdrawal from these electronegative atoms, so the net effect is strong activation and ortho/para direction.

Electronics first, then sterics. Positions 2, 4 and 6 are each ortho or para to at least one methyl, and position 2 is ortho to both — on electronics alone it should win. But position 2 sits directly between the two substituents, and the incoming electrophile has to fit between them while that carbon goes sp³; in practice the position is almost entirely shut down. Positions 4 and 6 are equivalent by symmetry and take essentially all the product. The general rule this illustrates: a position with a substituent on each side is rarely substituted, however good it looks electronically.

Even without resonance capability, the three highly electronegative fluorines withdraw electron density strongly through induction alone, destabilizing positive charge most at ortho/para and making meta the relatively favored position, while also slowing the reaction overall.

-NH2 is a powerful resonance electron donor (strong activator), -CH3 is only a weak inductive/hyperconjugative donor (mild activator), and -Cl is actually a net deactivator despite directing ortho/para, so -NH2 is by far the strongest activator of the three.
The statement is false: -SO3H is electron-withdrawing by induction and resonance, making it a deactivator and a meta director, similar in behavior to -COOH and -NO2.

When the electrophile attacks para to -NH2, one of the resonance structures of the arenium cation places the positive charge on the ring carbon directly attached to nitrogen, allowing the nitrogen lone pair to form a new pi bond and place the positive charge formally on nitrogen (stabilized by its lone pair), which is an especially low-energy resonance contributor.

Resonance donation from the oxygen lone pair can only stabilize the arenium cation when one resonance structure places positive charge on the ring carbon attached to the methoxy group; this happens for ortho and para attack but not meta attack, leaving meta relatively less stabilized and thus disfavored.

Deactivating and meta-directing are two separate claims, and the halogens are the one common case where they come apart. Bromine withdraws inductively, which slows the reaction — that half is right. But its lone pair still donates by resonance, and that donation is available in just the arenium ions that put positive charge on the carbon bearing the bromine, which is what ortho and para attack do. So the major products are o- and p-dibromobenzene, formed more slowly than benzene's own bromination.

The nitrile's carbon is electron-poor and can accept electron density by resonance from the ring, withdrawing density most strongly from ortho/para positions, so it behaves like other deactivating, meta-directing groups such as -NO2 and -CHO.

The statement is false; the carbonyl carbon directly attached to the ring is electron-poor and withdraws electron density by resonance, making -COOCH3 an overall deactivator and meta director, similar to other carbonyl-containing groups, despite having oxygen atoms present.

Since both methyl groups favor ortho/para positions relative to themselves, and the remaining open ring positions are ortho to one methyl and meta to the other, those positions receive reinforcing activation from one group and are not disfavored strongly by the other, making them the preferred sites.

True, though not for the reason the question hints at. Fluorine's resonance donation is genuinely the best of the halogens, because its 2p lone pairs match carbon's 2p in size, not because it is electronegative. Electronegativity works the other way: it drives strong inductive withdrawal through the sigma bond. The two effects nearly cancel, so fluorobenzene is only a little slower than benzene — much less deactivated than chlorobenzene or bromobenzene — while the strong resonance donation makes it the most para-selective of the halobenzenes.
