Nitrogen is modestly electronegative, causing a small inductive electron-withdrawing effect, but its lone pair's resonance donation into the aromatic pi system is much more significant, so the overall and net effect is strong activation directed to ortho/para.

While it is a useful generalization that most deactivators are meta directors, halogens are the key exception: their resonance donation (available due to a lone pair adjacent to the ring) still directs ortho/para even as their strong induction deactivates the ring, so deactivating and meta-directing are not always linked.

The carbonyl carbon is electron-poor and, by resonance, withdraws electron density most strongly from the ortho and para positions, destabilizing cationic intermediates there, so the meta position is favored for the incoming nitronium ion.

This is the core reasoning behind ortho/para direction: only attack at ortho or para positions generates a resonance structure with positive charge adjacent to the donor substituent, where it can be most effectively stabilized by an adjacent lone pair or electron-rich group.

In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is partially pulled away into conjugation with the carbonyl group, leaving less electron density available to donate into the aromatic ring than a free amine has, so acetanilide activates the ring less strongly than aniline while still directing ortho/para.
ir: Different bonds (O–H, C=O, C≡N, etc.) vibrate at characteristic frequencies, so IR is mainly used to identify functional groups.

An alcohol O–H is broadened by hydrogen bonding and falls in the 3200–3550 window, well clear of the sharp, strong C=O near 1700. A carboxylic acid O–H is broader still and sits lower, sprawling over 2500–3300, so it is not what a band confined to 3200–3550 is reporting.
The C=O stretch is a strong, sharp, and very diagnostic IR absorption typically found around 1700-1750 cm⁻¹ (exact position shifts slightly by functional group: ester, ketone, acid, amide, etc.).
Carboxylic acids form strong hydrogen-bonded dimers, producing an unusually broad O-H stretch that spans and overlaps the C-H stretching region.
Simple ketones show a strong, sharp carbonyl stretch near 1715 cm⁻¹; other carbonyl types shift higher or lower depending on the neighboring atoms.
A primary amine has two N-H bonds and shows two bands; a secondary amine has only one N-H bond and shows a single N-H stretch.
C-H bonds on sp2 or sp carbons are stronger and stretch above 3000 cm⁻¹, while ordinary sp3 alkane C-H stretches fall just below 3000 cm⁻¹.

The 2100–2260 window holds both C≡C and C≡N, and intensity alone will not separate them: the alkyne band is weak, and vanishes entirely when the alkyne is symmetric, while a nitrile is sharp and medium. The discriminator is the second band — a sharp, narrow 3300 is the ≡C–H of a terminal alkyne, where an O–H at the same wavenumber would be broad and a nitrile has nothing there at all. An aromatic ring or a ketone absorbs nowhere near this region.
IR reveals which functional groups are present from characteristic bond vibrations, but not the full connectivity or 3D arrangement of atoms; other tools like NMR and mass spec are needed for that.
Both nitriles and alkynes absorb near 2100-2260 cm⁻¹, but only a terminal alkyne also shows the sharp sp C-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹; a nitrile has no such C-H to produce that band.

Below about 1500 cm⁻¹, absorptions arise from complex combinations of bending and skeletal vibrations unique to each molecule, making this region a usable fingerprint even when individual bands are hard to assign.
Vibrational frequency increases as reduced mass decreases, so light-atom bonds like C-H vibrate much faster, and thus at higher wavenumber, than heavier-atom bonds like C-Cl.

The alkoxy oxygen withdraws electron density inductively and its resonance donation into the carbonyl is weaker than an amide nitrogen's, leaving the ester C=O stiffer and higher in frequency than a simple ketone.
The C-H bond directly on the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde gives a characteristic weak doublet near 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹ that ketones, lacking that C-H, do not show.
Nitrogen's lone pair delocalizes strongly into the carbonyl pi system, increasing single-bond character in C=O and lowering its stretching frequency relative to a ketone.
Conjugation delocalizes pi electron density between the alkene and the carbonyl, giving the C=O bond more single-bond character and a lower force constant, shifting the stretch lower.
Carboxylic acids hydrogen-bond strongly to form dimers even in dilute solution, producing a very broad O-H absorption from roughly 2500-3300 cm⁻¹, broader than a typical alcohol O-H band.
A primary amine's two N-H bonds give two stretching bands, and a tertiary amine has no N-H at all, so a single N-H band points to a secondary amine.
The sharp high-frequency band near 3300 cm⁻¹ comes from a C-H bonded directly to an sp carbon, which only a terminal alkyne has; an internal alkyne lacks that C-H band.
Stretching frequency scales with the square root of the force constant divided by reduced mass, so for similar atoms a stiffer, more double-bond-like bond vibrates at a higher wavenumber.

As ring size decreases and angle strain increases, the carbonyl carbon's bonding shifts in a way that stiffens the C=O bond, shifting the stretch to higher wavenumber; this trend continues for even smaller rings.
The ring donates electron density through conjugation, reducing the double-bond character of C=O, which softens the bond and lowers its stretching frequency compared to an unconjugated ketone.
At low concentration, alcohol molecules are mostly isolated with a free O-H; at higher concentration, extensive hydrogen bonding weakens the O-H bond and broadens and lowers its absorption.
The two nearby carbonyls in an anhydride couple vibrationally, splitting the absorption into two bands, often one near 1820 and one near 1760 cm⁻¹, both higher than a typical ester.
Although weak, the aldehydic C-H doublet falls below most alkane and alkene C-H stretches, so even a small, distinct pair of bands there is a reliable clue when paired with a carbonyl absorption.

Stronger resonance donation and weaker inductive withdrawal (as in an amide) lowers the frequency, while poor resonance donation with strong inductive withdrawal (as in an acid chloride) raises it the most, placing amide lowest and acid chloride highest.
A carbonyl stretch combined with a very broad, hydrogen-bonded O-H absorption smeared across the C-H region, rather than a sharp free O-H, is the classic signature of a carboxylic acid dimer.
Enantiomers have identical bond types and strengths, so their standard IR spectra are essentially indistinguishable; other techniques are needed to tell them apart.

Good pi donors, like an amide nitrogen, soften the C=O bond by adding single-bond character; chlorine's lone pairs overlap poorly with carbon, so its strong inductive pull dominates and stiffens the bond.

The flat baseline from 2400 to 3600 is the decisive observation: it rules out every structure containing an O-H, which kills the acid and both alcohols. The survivor has to put both oxygens elsewhere, and 1735 is the ester carbonyl - a ketone would be 1715, an acid 1710, an aldehyde 1725 with a weak C-H doublet near 2720 and 2820 that is absent here. The strong 1240 band is the ester C-O.
h-nmr: Electron-withdrawing groups nearby deshield a proton, shifting its signal downfield (higher ppm); shielded protons appear upfield.
Spin-spin coupling with n equivalent neighbors splits a signal into n+1 peaks (e.g., 3 neighboring H’s give a quartet).

The delocalized aromatic pi electrons circulate in the applied magnetic field, generating a local magnetic field that reinforces the external field right at the ring’s edge, deshielding those protons and pushing their signal downfield.
Integration is proportional to the number of protons contributing to a signal, so comparing integrated areas gives the ratio of protons in each chemically distinct environment.

TMS's methyl protons are more shielded than almost any organic proton, so they appear as a single peak at the upfield end of the spectrum (defined as 0 ppm), and TMS is unreactive and easily evaporated from the sample afterward.

Reporting shift as a ratio (ppm) relative to the operating frequency cancels out the field-strength dependence, which is exactly why ppm, rather than raw Hz, is used for comparing spectra from different instruments.
Replacing ordinary hydrogens with deuterium removes the solvent's own strong ¹H signal, leaving a largely clean baseline so the sample's proton signals can be seen clearly.

The carbonyl's electron-withdrawing oxygen and its magnetic anisotropy both pull electron density away from the adjacent aldehyde proton, pushing its signal further downfield than an ordinary vinyl proton.

Fast proton exchange (often catalyzed by trace acid, base, or water) averages the local environment and can broaden or shift the O-H/N-H signal, making it variable from sample to sample and solvent to solvent.
Coupling is transmitted through the bonding electrons connecting the nuclei, which is why it typically falls off sharply beyond three bonds, not through direct spatial proximity.
Vicinal coupling is coupling between protons on adjacent (neighboring) carbons, which are three bonds apart (H-C-C-H), and is the basis of the simple n+1 splitting rule.

All four options are C₉H₁₀O₂, so the formula eliminates none of them and the spectrum has to. Two 2H doublets sharing one J is the para-disubstituted pattern, so the ring carries two different groups at the 1 and 4 positions — which rules out ethyl benzoate, whose monosubstituted ring gives a 5H multiplet and whose ethyl group would give a quartet and a triplet, not two 3H singlets. The flat baseline above 3100 rules out the acid O–H. The 3H singlets separate the two esters: 3.9 ppm is a methyl on oxygen (the 3.3–4.5 window), 2.4 ppm a methyl on the ring. In 4-methylphenyl acetate nothing would appear near 3.9.

Each electronegative chlorine pulls electron density away inductively; stacking more of them on the same carbon compounds this effect, progressively deshielding the remaining protons and pushing the shift downfield.

Geminal protons share one carbon (two bonds apart), while vicinal protons sit on neighboring carbons (three bonds apart); both can show coupling, but the structural relationship and typical coupling constants differ.
The CH3 protons have two neighboring CH2 protons, giving n+1 = 3 peaks (a triplet); the CH2 protons have three neighboring CH3 protons, giving n+1 = 4 peaks (a quartet).

When a molecule contains another stereocenter or similar feature, the two protons on a CH2 are no longer related by a simple symmetry operation, so they occupy genuinely different environments and can show different shifts and even couple to each other.

Unlike the carbonyl or aromatic pi systems, the circulating electrons around a linear triple bond generate an induced field that shields, rather than deshields, a proton sitting along the bond's axis, pulling its shift upfield despite the carbon's high s-character.

The pi electrons of the C=C double bond circulate under the applied field and generate a local induced field that adds to the external field in the plane of the alkene, deshielding the attached protons and shifting them downfield.
The nine equivalent methyl protons give one signal, and the single O-H proton gives a separate signal, for two total distinct environments despite there being ten hydrogens overall.
Vicinal (three-bond) proton-proton coupling constants in freely rotating alkyl chains commonly fall around 6-8 Hz, a useful benchmark when analyzing splitting patterns.

Although equivalent protons can technically couple, the splitting is not observed because identical nuclei in identical environments produce overlapping, indistinguishable transitions, so equivalent protons appear to ignore each other.

O-H and N-H protons exchange rapidly with any other exchangeable protons present, including the large excess of deuterium in added D2O, converting O-H/N-H into O-D/N-D, which is invisible in a standard ¹H NMR spectrum.
The central CH proton is flanked by six equivalent methyl protons, giving n+1 = 7 peaks (a septet), while each methyl group's protons see only the one CH neighbor, giving n+1 = 2 peaks (a doublet).

When the two CH2 protons are diastereotopic due to a nearby stereocenter, they are no longer chemically equivalent, so each can have its own shift and couple to the other proton on the same carbon as well as to outside neighbors, producing a more complex multiplet.

The n+1 rule is a simplification that works cleanly only when all relevant coupling constants are similar; unequal coupling constants to different sets of neighbors produce more complex patterns that must be analyzed as separate couplings rather than a single n+1 multiplet.

Plain alkyl CH3 is least deshielded (around 0.9 ppm); a carbonyl-adjacent CH3 is pulled somewhat downfield (around 2.1 ppm) by the electron-withdrawing carbonyl; an aromatic-ring CH3 is shifted further by ring anisotropy (around 2.3 ppm); and an O-CH3 is most deshielded (around 3.3-3.8 ppm) by the directly attached electronegative oxygen.

Coupling is transmitted through bonding electrons, and its magnitude typically shrinks quickly as the number of intervening bonds grows, so beyond three bonds the coupling constant in a flexible, saturated system is usually too small to resolve as visible splitting.

Because O-H protons exchange rapidly with any available exchangeable protons (like trace water), the effective population and position of this signal is sensitive to moisture and sample purity, making its integration and shift less reproducible than for non-exchangeable C-H protons.

One proton is shielded and the other deshielded by the same ring, so the ring's effect cannot be a single number attached to the group: it has a direction. The circulating pi electrons reinforce the applied field outside the ring and oppose it above the face - magnetic anisotropy. Geometry, not just which atoms are nearby, sets the shift.

Protons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule, such as reflection through an internal mirror plane, occupy equivalent environments on a time-averaged basis and therefore resonate at the same chemical shift.
c-nmr: ¹³C is only ~1.1% natural abundance, so two ¹³C atoms are rarely adjacent — carbon-carbon coupling is negligible, giving simple, usually unsplit peaks (with standard decoupling).
Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the adjacent electronegative, pi-bonded oxygen, pushing their signal far downfield (160–220 ppm).
Both the rarity of the ¹³C isotope and its inherently weaker NMR signal (lower gyromagnetic ratio) compared to ¹H make ¹³C NMR much less sensitive, requiring longer acquisition times.
Each unique carbon environment gives rise to its own peak, regardless of how many hydrogens are attached to that carbon, which is different from how ¹H NMR integration works.
Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the attached oxygen and the carbon's bonding, placing their signals well downfield of essentially all other common carbon environments.

A peak at 212 that is absent from DEPT is a ketone carbonyl with no attached hydrogen. That rules out the aldehyde, whose carbonyl carbon carries an H and would appear in DEPT, and the alcohol, which has no carbonyl and would put its C-O carbon near 70. Three peaks for five carbons means the molecule is symmetric, and the down peak at 35 (a CH2) with the up peak at 8 (a CH3) puts an equivalent CH2 and CH3 on each side of the carbonyl. Pentan-2-one is unsymmetrical and gives five peaks.

Because carbon sits at the center of bonding with more direct exposure to hybridization and substituent effects, its chemical shift is more sensitive to structural differences, spreading ¹³C signals over a much wider ppm range than ¹H signals.

Differences in relaxation times and the nuclear Overhauser effect between different carbons (especially quaternary versus protonated carbons) make simple peak height or area an unreliable guide to the number of carbons in ¹³C NMR, unlike in ¹H NMR.
The delocalized pi system and partial double-bond character of aromatic carbons deshield them into the roughly 100-150 ppm region, distinct from both simple alkyl carbons and carbonyl carbons.

Because ¹³C is rare (about 1.1 percent natural abundance), the odds that two bonded carbons are both the ¹³C isotope in the same molecule are very low, so carbon-carbon coupling is statistically almost never observed in a routine spectrum.

A decoupling pulse sequence continuously flips the attached protons' spins during the ¹³C experiment, averaging out C-H coupling so each unique carbon gives one clean singlet instead of a complex multiplet.

The ester oxygen's lone pair donates into the carbonyl pi system by resonance, increasing electron density at the carbonyl carbon and shielding it relative to a ketone, which lacks that extra donating oxygen.

The linear, cylindrically symmetric pi system of a triple bond interacts with the applied field differently than a planar double bond's pi system, producing an anisotropic effect that shields sp alkyne carbons relative to sp2 alkene or aromatic carbons.

Toluene has a mirror plane that makes the two carbons ortho to the methyl group equivalent to each other, and the two meta carbons equivalent to each other, giving five unique carbons total: the methyl carbon, the ipso carbon, the equivalent ortho pair, the equivalent meta pair, and the para carbon.

DEPT transfers polarization from attached protons to the carbon nucleus, so a carbon with no attached hydrogens has nothing to receive that transfer from and simply does not show up in the DEPT spectrum.

Quaternary carbons lack the nuclear Overhauser enhancement from directly attached protons and often relax more slowly, both of which tend to make their signals weaker relative to protonated carbons, even at equal molar amounts.

Ketone carbonyl carbons typically fall around 205-220 ppm, while aldehyde carbonyl carbons are usually a bit more shielded, around 190-205 ppm, due to differences in the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon.
Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density away from the carbon it is bonded to, deshielding that carbon and shifting its signal downfield relative to an ordinary alkane carbon.
Just as with ¹H NMR, carbons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule occupy chemically equivalent environments and therefore resonate at the same shift.

The shift ranges for these two carbonyl types overlap somewhat, so chemists often combine the ¹³C shift with other evidence, such as the presence of a broad O-H absorption in IR or an O-H proton in ¹H NMR, to tell them apart confidently.

115-120 ppm sits inside the 110-160 aromatic range and at the bottom of the alkene range, so the shift on its own cannot prove a nitrile. What settles it is a second technique: a sharp, medium IR band near 2250 cm⁻¹ in a region where almost nothing else absorbs.

The mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons makes the two carbons next to one substituent equivalent to each other, and the two carbons next to the other substituent equivalent to each other, giving four unique aromatic carbons: the two substituted carbons plus the two equivalent pairs.

Since roughly 99 percent of carbon atoms are the spin-inactive ¹²C isotope, the probability that a given ¹³C nucleus happens to be bonded to another ¹³C nucleus is small, so carbon-carbon coupling is rarely visible above the noise in a normal spectrum.

Because chemical shift differences and coincidental overlaps differ between ¹H and ¹³C environments, and because symmetry can relate protons without necessarily relating the carbons carrying them (or vice versa), the number of resolved signals does not have to match between the two spectra.

Because DEPT signal phase and intensity depend on the number of attached protons, comparing a DEPT-135 spectrum to the standard ¹³C spectrum lets chemists sort carbons into CH3/CH, CH2, and quaternary categories, something ordinary ¹³C peak height cannot reliably do.

Both techniques respond to the same underlying electron-withdrawing inductive and resonance effects, so electronegative substituents deshield nearby carbons in ¹³C NMR in a way that parallels ¹H NMR trends, even though the absolute ppm shifts differ in scale.

The four methyl groups are related by the molecule's high symmetry (effectively a tetrahedral arrangement around the central carbon), making them all chemically equivalent and giving just one methyl signal plus one signal for the unique central quaternary carbon.

Slow relaxation, particularly for quaternary carbons lacking nearby protons to help them relax, limits how quickly a ¹³C signal can be repeatedly sampled, so extending the number of scans (not just raising concentration) is often needed to achieve a usable spectrum.

Two windows do the work. A ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon comes at 190–220; an ester, acid or amide carbonyl is pulled upfield to roughly 165–185, because the attached O or N donates a lone pair into the C=O and puts electron density back on that carbon. A signal at 171 with a clean 190–220 region therefore says acid derivative and rules out ketone and aldehyde. What it does NOT do is say which acid derivative: those three overlap almost completely — acetamide 172.7, ethyl acetate 171.1, acetic acid 178 — so separating them needs the IR carbonyl position or an O–H / N–H signal, not the ¹³C shift.

Inductive electron withdrawal from an electronegative atom propagates through several bonds in both ¹H and ¹³C NMR, deshielding nearby nuclei, with the effect weakening as the number of intervening bonds increases.
mass-spec: The molecular ion forms when the neutral molecule loses an electron in the ionization source, giving a radical cation at the molecule’s full mass.
A mass loss of 15 corresponds to CH₃ (methyl, 12+3=15), a very common fragmentation for molecules with a methyl group attached to a stabilizing center.
The base peak is defined as the most intense peak in the spectrum (100% relative abundance) — it is often, but not always, the same as the molecular ion peak.
Mass spectrometers separate and detect ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, which for most singly charged ions in an intro course is essentially equal to the ion's mass.
A high-energy electron beam knocks one electron out of the neutral molecule, leaving behind an odd-electron, positively charged species called the molecular ion or radical cation.

The most intense peak is called the base peak, and it is very often a fragment ion rather than the molecular ion, especially for molecules that fragment easily; M+ itself can be weak or even absent for some compounds.
Since about 1.1 percent of carbon atoms are naturally ¹³C, the M+1 peak's relative intensity grows roughly in proportion to the number of carbons present, giving a rough estimate of carbon count.

Chlorine's two natural isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, occur in roughly a 3:1 ratio, so a single-chlorine compound's M+2 peak (containing 37Cl) appears at roughly one-third the height of the M+ peak (containing 35Cl).

Bromine's two natural isotopes, 79Br and 81Br, occur in nearly equal abundance, so a single-bromine compound shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly similar height, a distinctive pattern compared to chlorine.
Cleaving off a methyl group is a frequent and often favorable fragmentation pathway, especially when it generates a more stable remaining cation, which is common in branched structures.
Loss of 18 mass units corresponds to H2O, a very common fragmentation pathway for alcohols (and some other oxygen-containing compounds) under electron ionization conditions.

Because nitrogen has an odd valence (typically three bonds) while carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen follow patterns that keep the overall mass even in their absence, each nitrogen atom added in a stable structure shifts the molecular weight's parity, making an odd number of nitrogens correspond to an odd molecular weight.

Both CO (common from ketones, aldehydes, and aromatic ethers) and C2H4 (common from retro-type eliminations) have a mass of 28, so this loss alone does not uniquely identify the fragmentation pathway without additional supporting evidence.

When the bond next to an oxygen or nitrogen breaks, the heteroatom's lone pair can donate into the resulting cation through resonance, stabilizing it and making that fragmentation pathway especially favorable.

The McLafferty rearrangement requires a gamma-hydrogen relative to the carbonyl so that a six-membered transition state can form, transferring that hydrogen and cleaving a bond to release a neutral alkene while leaving behind a stable, even-electron cation.

Benzylic cleavage of an alkylbenzene's side chain generates a benzylic cation that readily rearranges into the highly stable, resonance-delocalized seven-membered tropylium cation, observed at m/z 91.

Branch points allow formation of more stable secondary or tertiary carbocations upon fragmentation, making it energetically easier for the branched molecular ion to fall apart rather than survive intact, weakening the M+ peak relative to a straight-chain isomer.

Both the isopropyl radical (C3H7, mass 43) and the acetyl cation-forming group (CH3CO, also mass 43) are common fragments lost from molecular ions, so a loss of 43 alone is often ambiguous without further context.
Alpha cleavage adjacent to the aldehyde carbonyl commonly ejects the formyl radical, CHO, which has a mass of 29, leaving behind a stabilized carbon-centered cation.

The aromatic ring can delocalize the positive charge and radical character of the molecular ion over the ring system, stabilizing it and making the intact M+ more likely to survive and be detected as a prominent peak.

M+1 at 8.8% of M means about 8.8/1.1 = 8 carbons. The missing M+2 rules out chlorine, whose M+2 would stand at roughly a third of M, and the flat baseline above 3100 rules out benzoic acid's very broad O-H. The base peak at 105 is M - 15, a methyl lost by alpha cleavage to leave the benzoyl cation, which then loses CO to give the phenyl cation at 77. Benzaldehyde has no methyl to lose and weighs 106.

Fragmentation in the gas phase favors pathways that produce the most stable cation, following the same substitution-based stability trend (tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary) used to rationalize carbocation stability throughout organic chemistry.

Alpha cleavage on either side of an asymmetric ketone's carbonyl generates two different acylium-type cations, explaining why both a methyl loss (15) and a loss consistent with the other alkyl substituent pattern can appear together in the spectrum of a compound like methyl ethyl ketone.

Because forming larger, more stable radicals (or undergoing favorable rearrangements like McLafferty) is usually more thermodynamically favorable than simply ejecting a lone hydrogen atom, simple H-loss is typically a minor pathway rather than the dominant one.

Individual isotopes have exact masses that are not perfectly whole numbers (for example, carbon-12 is defined as exactly 12, but hydrogen and oxygen have slightly different fractional exact masses), so formulas with the same nominal mass usually have distinguishably different exact masses when measured with sufficient precision.

Mass spectral peak intensities depend on how readily a given ion forms and survives under gas-phase ionization and fragmentation conditions, a distinct context from solution-phase stability, solubility, or reactivity, which are not what mass spectrometry intensities measure.

Molecular ions are not limited to a single fragmentation route; different bonds can break under the conditions of electron ionization, so a cyclic alcohol can plausibly show both a straightforward water loss and a separate ring-related elimination pathway in the same spectrum.
Alpha cleavage adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing carbon of a carboxylic acid commonly ejects the COOH group, which has a combined mass of 45, leaving behind the remaining alkyl cation.

Since a neutral organic molecule normally has all its electrons paired, knocking out just one electron during EI necessarily leaves an odd, unpaired electron along with the resulting positive charge, producing a radical cation.

According to the nitrogen rule, an odd molecular weight for a typical CHNO compound implies an odd number of nitrogen atoms, since each nitrogen (with its odd valence pattern) shifts the overall parity of the molecular mass.
retrosynthesis: It points the other way in time from an ordinary reaction arrow, which is why it is drawn differently.
Nothing physically breaks. You are asking which two pieces, joined by a reaction you know, would give that bond.
If you cannot say what reagents would rejoin the pieces, you have drawn a picture rather than planned a synthesis.

A C-C bond joining a ring to a carbonyl carbon is the acylation retron, and the forward step is benzene plus CH3(CH2)3COCl with AlCl3. Naming that forward reaction is what makes the cut legal. The alkylation cut builds the wrong skeleton - an alkylbenzene with no carbonyl at all - and its cation would rearrange on the way. An aldol needs two carbonyl partners and there is one here, and a Wittig makes an alkene rather than a ketone.
A carbanion is not a bottle on a shelf; RMgBr behaves like one.

Every polar disconnection hands you one nucleophile and one electrophile, because that is what a polar bond-forming reaction is. Ph- has an equivalent you can buy into - PhMgBr - and the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde is already the electrophile. The reversed assignment would need an anion at acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon, which is not a reagent at this level, and two nucleophiles or two electrophiles cannot bond to each other at all.

A tree is read back from its leaves, so the last disconnection you drew is the first reaction you run. The Grignard has to exist before it has anything to attack, so bromobenzene meets magnesium in dry ether first and the aldehyde goes in second. Putting the aldehyde in early, or everything in at once, leaves magnesium and a carbonyl in one flask with no control over what forms.
Learning to see retrons is most of what makes an experienced chemist fast at this.
Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the carbinol carbon: the fragments are an enolate and a carbonyl.
Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the second carbonyl, giving an ester enolate and an ester.
One disconnection undoing two bonds, which is why it is the highest-value move in the list.
Any C-C bond to the carbinol carbon can be disconnected into a carbanion and a ketone.
Functional groups are where reactivity lives, so those bonds are the ones you have reactions for.
Cutting a branch usually splits the target into two comparably simple pieces.
A question usually names the permitted starting materials, and that constraint is the real definition of done.
Yields multiply, which is why each extra step is genuinely expensive.
The synthons are the carbanion and the ketone; their equivalents are the Grignard and acetophenone.
Several valid answers is the normal state of a synthesis problem.
Which is what a polar bond-forming reaction is.
Deprotonating the alpha carbon generates the nucleophile in situ.

Count first: propan-1-ol has three carbons and butanoic acid four, so exactly one C-C bond is formed and the new carbon is the carboxyl carbon itself. That is a one-carbon extension, and two of them land at acid level: PBr3, NaCN, then H3O+ with heat; or PBr3, Mg, then CO2 and workup. Oxidizing propan-1-ol gives propanoic acid, because no oxidation has ever added a carbon.
The forward list is a claim: every step has reagents, a product, and a check that it survives the next step.
The forward route is the claim; the backward analysis is the search.
Cutting across a six-membered ring containing an alkene gives a diene and a dienophile.
Which halves the problem immediately.

The permitted pieces are two carbons each, so the six-carbon skeleton has to be assembled by acetylide alkylations - and those build alkynes, not ketones. Rewriting the ketone as hex-3-yne cuts nothing, but it turns the target into one whose C-C bonds you have a reaction for, which is what an FGI is for. Cutting next to the carbonyl first gives aldol fragments with alpha hydrogens on both sides, so the forward reaction would be a mixture, and a Grignard on CO2 makes carboxylic acids.
Though the arithmetic is worth doing: a longer route of good steps can beat a shorter one of poor steps.
The difference tells you how many C-C bonds must form and what size pieces you need.

Cut the bond between the carbinol carbon and the alpha carbon: the fragments are the enolate of acetone and benzaldehyde. It is a good disconnection precisely because benzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogen, so only one partner can enolize and no mixture results.

Either partner can enolize and either can be attacked, so a simple base gives all four aldol products. The disconnection is clean only if one partner has no alpha hydrogen, or if one enolate is formed quantitatively first with a strong hindered base.
carbon-carbon-bonds: Which is what makes synthesis learnable: the skeleton can only be built in a few places.
The carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon, and workup protonates the alkoxide.
One of the three standard one-carbon extensions.
Formaldehyde has no other substituent, so the product is primary.
An SN2 reaction, so it works best with primary halides.
Which can then be hydrolyzed to an acid or reduced to a primary amine.
The cyanide adds the carbon and the reduction converts the nitrile to CH2NH2.
Nitrile hydrolysis. RMgBr + CO2 is the other standard answer.
An enolate attacking a carbonyl.

Cyanide does an SN2 on the primary halide to give butanenitrile, four carbons, and hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile to the acid. LiAlH4 on that same nitrile would have given butan-1-amine instead, which is the pair worth keeping straight.
Conjugate addition of an enolate to an enone.
An ylide plus a carbonyl, giving a C=C where the C=O was.

A C-C bond to a carbinol carbon means a carbanion attacked the carbonyl carbon, and the carbanion here carries two carbons. Ethanol is not nucleophilic at carbon at all, cyanide would give a cyanohydrin, and bromoethane is an electrophile rather than a nucleophile.
Alkylation or acylation, though acylation is usually preferred.
Which is how you build a bond NEXT to a carbonyl rather than at it.
Two positions away from the carbonyl, which is the third attachment point a carbonyl offers.
Direct attack on the electrophilic carbon of the C=O.
The whole problem is functional group interconversion, which is much easier.
Counting tells you the ring came in whole rather than being built.
Ring formation is otherwise hard, which is why both are worth spotting early.
Which closes a five- or six-membered ring respectively.
The same Claisen chemistry with both esters in one molecule.
And roughly what size pieces you need, which narrows ten reactions to two or three.
An ylide replaces the carbonyl oxygen with a carbon fragment.
An enolate attacking something electrophilic, differing in what the electrophile is.
A tertiary halide would eliminate instead.
Hydroboration adds B and H across a C=C; no carbon-carbon bond is formed.
The carbonyl carbon, the alpha carbon via an enolate, and the beta carbon via conjugate addition.
Three attachment points from one functional group is unusual.
Two bonds undone in one step, with the stereochemistry already defined.
functional-group-interconversion: Sideways moves within one level are substitutions and need no redox reagent at all.
One bond to an electronegative atom traded for another, with the hydrogen count unchanged.
A C-H on the carbinol carbon is replaced by a second bond to oxygen.
A bond to oxygen becomes a bond to hydrogen.
Both carbons sit at +3, so it is nucleophilic acyl substitution.
SOCl2 does the chloride equivalent, and HX also works.
Hydroboration is the anti-Markovnikov partner of this pair.
Boron adds to the less hindered carbon, and the OH replaces it with retention.
A poisoned catalyst stops at the alkene, and the surface delivery is syn.
A dissolving-metal reduction through radical anions, which adopt the less hindered arrangement.
Reducing the same nitrile with LiAlH4 gives a primary amine instead.
The other half of the nitrile pair.
From which esters and amides follow directly.
Two hydrides are delivered, and you cannot normally stop at the aldehyde.
Down two rungs and back up one, because the reduction cannot be stopped halfway.
Eliminate to the alkene, then add back with the opposite regiochemistry.
You end up with the OH back where it started.

The peroxide effect belongs to HBr alone: the radical chain works because H-Br has the right bond strengths, and HCl and HI add Markovnikov whatever is in the flask. So there is no one-step anti-Markovnikov chloride. Hydroboration-oxidation puts the OH on the less substituted carbon, giving 2-methylpropan-1-ol, and SOCl2 then swaps OH for Cl without touching the skeleton. Had the target been the bromide, HBr with peroxides would have done it in one step.
The aqueous conditions let the aldehyde hydrate and be oxidized again.
Along with the Swern and DMP, all of which are anhydrous.
Both oxygens are delivered to the same face through a cyclic osmate ester.
The epoxide is opened by backside attack, putting the oxygens on opposite faces.
The carbonyl oxygen is replaced by a carbon fragment.
Down two rungs, and the pair exists because they tolerate opposite conditions.
An equilibrium, usually driven by removing water or using excess alcohol.

Dehydrate to propene, then hydrate under acid: Markovnikov puts the OH on the more substituted carbon, which is C2. Every other route here returns the oxygen to C1, because PBr3 and NaOH both act at the same carbon and each redox pair comes back down to the carbinol carbon it started from.
Syn addition of two hydrogens across the double bond.

Markovnikov hydration puts the oxygen on the more substituted alkyne carbon, giving an enol that tautomerizes to the methyl ketone. Hydroboration-oxidation of the same alkyne with a bulky borane is the anti-Markovnikov partner and gives hexanal instead.
It goes through a carbocation, so rearrangement is also possible.
Acid-catalyzed dehydration gives Zaitsev and can rearrange; E2 on a halide lets you choose.
protecting-groups: The Grignard becomes an alkane before it can reach any carbonyl.
More than acidic enough to destroy a carbanion instantly.
Any acidic proton, which is also why the reaction is run in scrupulously dry ether.
TBSCl with imidazole replaces the O-H with an O-Si bond, leaving no acidic proton.

The Si-F bond is exceptionally strong, so fluoride pulls the silicon off under conditions that disturb nothing else. Mild aqueous acid is exactly what a silyl ether is chosen to survive, which is what makes it orthogonal to an acetal.
The acetal has no C=O and no electrophilic carbon, so there is nothing to attack.
Ethylene glycol is standard, and the equilibrium is driven by removing water.
The same equilibrium run backwards, which is why it is so reliable.
Which lets a molecule carry both and have them unmasked in a chosen order.
Choosing a protecting group means checking it against every remaining step.
Using a protecting group here would be three steps where one works.
Not every functional group present is a threat.
There is no reagent trick that makes a Grignard tolerate a free alcohol.
The aldehyde is the MORE reactive of the two, so there is no way to reach the ester selectively.
Protection and deprotection, which is why it is a last resort.
Installing the interfering group later is always cheaper than protecting it.

The acid-base reaction is instant and consumes a full equivalent. What is left is a heterogeneous magnesium alkoxide that ties up reagent and makes the addition unreliable, so it is a bench expedient at best and protection is the answer a synthesis question wants.
The base mops up the HCl produced.

The driving force is the Si-F bond, one of the strongest single bonds in chemistry, so TBAF strips the silicon under conditions that are neither strongly acidic nor basic nor oxidizing - which is exactly what lets it act on a molecule carrying almost anything else.
No C=O means nothing for a hydride or Grignard to attack.
It gives a five-membered cyclic acetal.

Without protection, the first Grignard that forms attacks the ketone of the next molecule and the reagent destroys its own starting material. The acetal removes the electrophile, the Grignard then forms cleanly, and the aqueous acid workup after the addition takes the acetal off again.
Because no reagent choice can solve it.
Water does exactly what an alcohol O-H does, which is why dry ether is essential.
One needs fluoride and one needs aqueous acid, and neither touches the other.
The O-H becomes an O-Si bond with no acidic proton left.

LiAlH4 cannot tell a ketone from an ester and would reduce both, so the ketone is masked as an acetal first, reduced past, and unmasked in the workup. The acetal is inert to hydride, which is precisely why it is the standard carbonyl mask.
A common trap: protect the interfering group, not the target.
Formation is driven by removing water; removal is driven by adding it back.
Which is one of the cases where no protection is needed at all.
multistep-synthesis: Errors of order are invisible in a retrosynthetic tree and obvious in a forward list.
Look at every functional group present, not just the one you are aiming at.
Reordering is always cheaper than protecting.
The acylium ion is resonance-stabilized and does not shift.
Which leaves the unrearranged straight chain on the ring.
Friedel-Crafts does not work on a strongly deactivated ring.
An amine is a strong activator and its nitrogen complexes the Lewis acid.
Which is why the order of substitution is often the whole question.
Getting one enantiomer needs a chiral reagent, catalyst, starting material, or a resolution.
Any acidic proton destroys the reagent before it reaches the carbonyl.
Cyanide, CO2 and formaldehyde routes all add exactly one carbon, so mixing them up is easy.
Which is also why hydroboration and the Diels-Alder are trusted.
Making an aldehyde and then running a reaction in aqueous base will not leave you with an aldehyde.
The primary cation rearranges to the secondary one before it reaches the ring.
Acylating the more reactive ring first is the better order on rate grounds.
Which is why an alkyl group and a bromine end up para to each other.
Sterics, rather than electronics, breaks the tie between the two.
Reordering removes the problem entirely.
If the target has defined stereochemistry, some step has to set it, and you should be able to name it.
Water lets the aldehyde hydrate and be oxidized a second time.

Acylation puts an unrearranged propanoyl group on, Clemmensen strips it to propyl, and propyl is an ortho/para director, so nitration lands mainly para. Had step 1 been an alkylation with 1-bromopropane, the answer would have been the isopropyl compound instead.

The acyl group is a meta director, so nitrating acetophenone puts the NO2 meta and gives the target. The reverse order fails outright, because Friedel-Crafts does not work on a ring already carrying a nitro group.
Which is the second reason Friedel-Crafts fails on an aniline.

An aldehyde with alpha hydrogens enolizes in aqueous base and undergoes an aldol condensation with itself. This is the second of the four questions - does the product of one step survive the next - and an aldehyde followed by base is the commonest way to fail it.
Almost always the intended answer to that shape of question.
Strongly acidic, and the Wolff-Kishner is its basic partner.
For molecules that cannot survive acid.
Whichever your substrate tolerates, the other is available.
It is the cheapest final check available.

Bromine adds anti across a double bond, so the geometry of the alkene decides which diastereomer appears. Lindlar gives the cis alkene, and anti addition to it gives the pair of enantiomers named. Na in ammonia would give the trans alkene and hence the meso (3R,4S) dibromide, and Pd/C would over-reduce to hexane.
carbohydrates: Every property of a sugar follows from a carbonyl surrounded by alcohols on the same chain.

The ring is a hemiacetal in equilibrium with a trace of open-chain aldehyde, and hydride reduces that aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Consuming the open chain pulls the equilibrium across, so the whole sample converts to the alditol.
Six carbons and an internal carbonyl: keto- for the position, -hexose for the count.
C2 through C5 each carry an H and an OH; C1 is the carbonyl and C6 is a CH2OH.
Two to the power of four stereocenters.
One carbon carries the whole label, and it is the one at the bottom of the drawing.
Right means D. The label is read off the drawing, not off a polarimeter.
D fixes one stereocenter's drawn position; the observed rotation is a measured property of the whole molecule.
One alcohol plus one carbonyl gives a hemiacetal; it takes a second alcohol to reach an acetal.

A glycoside is a full acetal, so on its own it gives nothing: the ring cannot open. Aqueous acid reverses acetal formation, releasing methanol and free glucose, and the restored hemiacetal then opens to the aldehyde Tollens' oxidizes.
It was the carbonyl carbon, so after cyclization it holds the ring oxygen and an OH.
They differ at the anomeric carbon only, which is the one stereocenter the ring can open and reset.
Alpha is down and beta is up for the D series.
Mutarotation. Only the anomeric center can change, because only it opens.

Bromine water takes the open-chain aldehyde to a carboxylic acid and stops. Chromium(VI) would oxidize the secondary alcohols too, borohydride reduces, and methanol with acid caps the anomeric carbon as a glycoside.
Beta puts the anomeric OH equatorial, and glucose is the sugar that can get every substituent equatorial.
The test oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde, so the ring has to be able to open to supply it.
Two OR groups on the anomeric carbon is a full acetal, and the sugar-specific name for it is glycoside.
An acetal is stable to base, so no open-chain aldehyde is ever available.
The bond runs anomeric carbon to anomeric carbon, so neither ring can open.
A 1,4 link commits one anomeric carbon, leaving the other end free to open.

Bromine water stops at the aldehyde and gives the aldonic acid. Reaching the terminal CH2OH as well needs a stronger oxidant, and warm dilute nitric acid takes both ends at once to give the aldaric acid.
Alpha names the anomeric configuration; 1,4 names which carbon bonds to which.
One stereocenter on one carbon, and the two materials could hardly behave less alike.
The enzyme reads the configuration at the anomeric carbon, and it only fits alpha.
Alpha-1,4 chains coil into helices instead, which is why starch is soft.
The test medium is basic, and an alpha deprotonation gives an enediol that can collapse to the aldose.
Tollens' oxidizes the free aldehyde a hemiacetal supplies, and an acetal supplies none.
No 1,3-diaxial strain anywhere in the chair, which is a conformational argument, not a new one.
Left in Fischer becomes up in Haworth and right becomes down. The rule holds at every carbon but C5, whose OH has become the ring oxygen, and the anomeric configuration is set separately at C1.
amino-acids: The carboxyl (pKa near 2) is a far stronger acid than the ammonium (pKa near 9), so at any pH between them the proton has already moved across. Both ends are charged and the molecule is overall neutral, which is why amino acids behave like salts.
Its side chain is H, so the alpha carbon has two identical substituents.
Read from a Fischer projection with COOH at the top and NH2 on the left.
Sulfur outranks the carboxyl carbon in CIP priority, so the ranking around the alpha carbon reshuffles.
A pKa 2 acid and a pKa 9 base in one molecule transfer the proton to each other.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky puts a bromine on the alpha carbon, and excess ammonia displaces it by SN2. The aldehyde route is Strecker, reaching the same product class from a different start. Both form the stereocenter at a planar intermediate, so both give a racemate.
Typical for an alkylammonium ion, pulled down slightly by the adjacent carboxylate.
A zwitterion is ionic, and ionic solids behave like this.
Plus and minus cancel exactly, which is a property of the pH rather than of the molecule alone.

Build the charge ladder: +2 below 2.18, +1 from 2.18 to 8.95, zero from 8.95 to 10.53, -1 above. The uncharged form is bracketed by 8.95 and 10.53, so the pI is their average. Averaging the lowest two gives 5.57.
Half of the sum. Note it is below 7, so an isoelectric solution is mildly acidic.

Take the groups one at a time against pH 7. Both carboxyl pKa values are well below 7, so both are deprotonated. The ammonium pKa is 9.67, so it keeps its proton. Two minuses against one plus is a net -1.
More base than the isoelectric condition means more protons removed.
Below the pI it is a cation, and cations are drawn to the negative electrode.
Two acidic groups have to be neutralized before the molecule is uncharged, so the balance point drops.
A second amine has to stay protonated, so you must go to high pH before the charge cancels.
The side-chain ammonium has a pKa near 10.5, so at pH 7 it is overwhelmingly protonated.
The side-chain carboxyl has a pKa near 4.3, so at pH 7 it is deprotonated.
A benzyl group with no heteroatom, so water pushes it into the protein's interior.
A CH2OH hydrogen bonds well and carries no charge at any ordinary pH.
The ring stiffens the backbone, which is why proline interrupts helices.
Two SH groups oxidize to a disulfide, the only covalent link outside the backbone.
R-S-S-R, and reducing it undoes the cross-link.
The hydrophobic effect: burying them frees the water that would otherwise be ordered around them.
A pKa near the working pH means the residue can act as either an acid or a base in a mechanism.
A pH between the two pI values forces them to opposite signs, so they migrate in opposite directions.
Without a net charge there is no electrostatic repulsion keeping the molecules apart.
Two carboxyls and one ammonium, so three pKa values and a pI set by the lowest two.
An inductive effect stabilizing the carboxylate, on the neighboring carbon.
Thiols dimerize to disulfides under mild oxidation; alcohols do not.
peptides-proteins: A carboxyl joined to an amine with loss of water gives an amide, and nothing about proteins changes that.
Sequences run N to C, so the direction is part of the information.
That carboxyl was never consumed by an amide bond.
Same atoms and formula, opposite order, and the chain has a direction.
Twenty choices at each of three positions, and repeats are allowed.

Nothing tells either molecule which of its two groups to use, so every ordered pairing forms: Gly-Gly, Ala-Ala, Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly. Controlling it means protecting one amine and one carboxyl, activating what is left, coupling, then deprotecting.

An amine meeting a carboxylic acid takes its proton instead of attacking it, and the carboxylate left behind is a poor electrophile. DCC turns the acid's OH into a group that leaves readily, and the amine then does ordinary acyl substitution.
The two alpha carbons plus C, O, N and H, held flat by the partial pi bond.
Rotating would break the overlap that the second resonance structure depends on.
A lone pair already spent on the neighboring carbonyl cannot also grab a proton.
Protonating oxygen keeps the resonance stabilization; protonating nitrogen would destroy it.
The strongest lone-pair donation gives the greatest stabilization and the lowest reactivity.
An amide is the least reactive acyl derivative, so it takes force or an enzyme.
The only level whose structure is its covalent bonds, and the one from which the others follow.
Defined as involving the backbone only, which is why any sequence can form it.
Every residue supplies an N-H and a C=O regardless of its side chain.
Set mostly by side-chain interactions rather than by the backbone.

Phenyl isothiocyanate is attacked by the free N-terminal amino group, so the reagent reads from the N-terminus and removes one residue per cycle. The shortened peptide survives and goes round again; complete hydrolysis would destroy the order.
Burying nonpolar side chains releases the ordered water around them, which is the large term.
Everything else holding a fold together is noncovalent, which is why folding is reversible.
For example a lysine ammonium paired with a glutamate carboxylate.
Heat overwhelms weak noncovalent forces long before it touches an amide.
An amide is the least reactive acyl derivative, and 100 C water is nowhere near enough.
A disulfide is the oxidized form, so reduction takes it back to two thiols.
No N-H means no hydrogen bond donor at that position, and the ring restricts the geometry.
It changes one residue in the sequence, and the other levels change only as a consequence.
That restriction is what makes a finite, predictable set of folds possible.
Nineteen cleavage sites cut one chain into twenty pieces, because n cuts give n+1 fragments. A lysine already at the end of the chain would add no cut, which is why the question rules that out.
Secondary structure is a backbone property, so the side chains only tip the preference.
The fold puts the polar residues outside and the nonpolar ones in, which is the hydrophobic effect stated the other way round.
lipids: It collects the cell components that dissolve in nonpolar solvents, which is why it holds fats and steroids together.
The acid group is the only functional group on an otherwise plain hydrocarbon.
Biosynthesis adds acetate units, so the count comes out even.
Glycerol has three OH groups, and all three are esterified.
They are the same compound class in two physical states.
Catalytic hydrogenation reduces C=C and leaves esters alone, so the product is glyceryl tristearate. Taking the kinks out lets the chains pack, which is why an oil hardens into a fat.
Melting separates molecules, and a bent chain makes much less contact with the next one.
Chain length is held constant, so only the geometry can be responsible.
It is unsaturated and still nearly as high-melting as the saturated acid, because it is still straight.

Three ester groups means three hydrolyses, and the acyl groups on a natural fat differ, so the products are sodium stearate, oleate and palmitate plus glycerol. Excess hydroxide deprotonates each acid as it forms, so nothing runs back.
Hydrocarbon chains are nonpolar, so contact area is what matters.
Base-promoted ester hydrolysis three times over, and the excess base deprotonates each acid.
Literally soap-making, which is exactly what it produces.
A carboxylate is a poor electrophile, so nothing runs backwards.
A soap is the standard case: an ionic head on a long hydrocarbon tail.
It resolves the solubility conflict by hiding the tails from water.
The nonpolar core is a pocket of nonpolar solvent that water can carry away.
Two fatty acid tails and one charged phosphate group in place of the third.
A one-tailed molecule tapers into a sphere; a two-tailed one is a cylinder and tiles into a sheet.
Tails inward and heads facing the water on both sides, which is every cell membrane.
Four fused rings and nothing else, grouped as lipids purely by solubility.
Three six-membered and one five-membered, fused in a fixed arrangement.
A rigid ring system inserted among flexible chains changes how easily they move.
Aromatizing the A ring also converts the ketone there to a phenol.
Removing double bonds straightens chains, so the material packs better and melts higher.
An alkene that picks up one hydrogen and loses it again does not remember its original geometry.

One acid and one alcohol in a one-to-one ratio means a single ester joining two long chains, which is a wax. A triglyceride gives three acids and one glycerol, a phospholipid releases phosphate too, and a steroid has no ester.
One ester joining two long chains, which is why waxes are hard and very water-repellent.
A more reduced carbon has further to fall on oxidation, so more energy is released per gram.
Counting in fives is the quickest way to recognize one.
nucleic-acids: Assembling them in that order makes the vocabulary fall out on its own.
Sugar plus base is a nucleoside; adding the phosphate ester makes it a nucleotide.
Deoxy names the missing OH, and the missing OH is at C2 prime.

Pair each base first: G-C, G-C, A-T, T-A, C-G, reading CCTAG alongside the original. That runs 3' to 5', because the strands are antiparallel, so writing it conventionally reverses it to GATCC. The trap is right bases, wrong direction.
Both rings have numbered atoms, so the sugar's get primes.
Two fused rings. The single-ring bases are the pyrimidines.
Uracil is thymine without the methyl group.
A nitrogen displaces the anomeric OH, which is acetal formation with N in place of O.
The anomeric carbon is the electrophilic one, exactly as in ordinary glycoside formation.
Polymerases use 5 prime triphosphates, and the 3 prime OH of the chain is the nucleophile that attacks one. A 3 prime monophosphate is a perfectly good nucleotide too, but it is not what gets added.
One phosphorus esterified to two different sugars, 3 prime of one and 5 prime of the next.
The chain has distinguishable ends, so direction is part of the information.
A row of negative charges on the outside, which is also why they dissolve in water.
G-C uses three, which is why G-C rich DNA melts higher.
One more than A-T, and that difference shows up directly in melting temperature.
Weak bonds on purpose, because anything read must first be opened without being destroyed.
One large plus one small keeps every rung of the ladder the same width.
One runs 5 prime to 3 prime while its partner runs the other way.
Charges face the water and the flat nonpolar bases stack away from it.
Pairing forces A to equal T, so 30% adenine means 30% thymine and the two account for 60%. The other 40% is split evenly between G and C because they pair with each other, giving 20% guanine.
Melting separates the strands, so it measures what joins them.
Only the hydrogen bonds between bases are undone, which is why the strands can re-anneal.
An intramolecular attack through a five-membered ring is enormously faster than one from solution.
The five-membered ring the intramolecular attack closes.
Removing one hydroxyl removes the internal nucleophile, and with it the built-in self-destruct.
It is an N,O-acetal, and acetals are cut by aqueous acid and stable to base. The rate is very uneven: purines depurinate far more readily than pyrimidines.
The other end keeps the free 5 prime phosphate.

The 3' OH of the growing chain attacks the 5' phosphorus of the incoming triphosphate, and the leaving group is what makes that productive: the outer phosphates are anhydrides, and the departing diphosphate spreads its charge widely.
Sugar and phosphate repeat identically along the chain, so only the bases can vary.
That is what makes each strand a template for rebuilding the other.
organometallic-bonding: Carbon at 2.55 against magnesium at 1.31, so the bonding electrons sit on carbon.
An alkyl halide's carbon is an electrophile; the Grignard made from it is a nucleophile at the same carbon.

The O-H at pKa 16 is deprotonated long before anything adds, so the reagent leaves as methane and the magnesium alkoxide that remains is inert to its own ketone. Workup just protonates it back. Two equivalents fix it.

An N-H at pKa 36 is still far more acidic than an alkane at 50, so proton transfer happens first and the reagent leaves as methane. The magnesium amide left behind is not nucleophilic enough to add to its own ketone, and workup simply puts the N-H back.
Lithium at 0.98 is far below carbon, so the electrons stay on carbon.
A Grignard is not a free carbanion, though it behaves like one and the arrow starts at the C-metal bond.
The widest electronegativity gap gives the most carbanion character and the least selectivity.
Copper sits close to carbon, so the bond is barely polar and the reagent can be pointed at one site.
The two trade against each other more visibly here than anywhere else in the course.

Read it straight off electronegativity: the further the metal sits below carbon, the more the bonding pair belongs to carbon. Potassium is furthest, boron nearly matches carbon, and copper sits between - which is exactly the reactivity ladder the chapter is built on.
Water at pKa 15.7 against an alkane at 50 is not a close call.
Any O-H, N-H or S-H does it, and a terminal alkyne C-H as well.

Each molecule of reagent is quenched by the O-H of the next one, so the yield collapses. Silylating or otherwise protecting the alcohol first - or reordering the synthesis so the OH appears later - is the standard answer.
That coordination is what keeps the reagent in solution and usable.
The same destructive protonation, used deliberately to label one position.

Ethanol has an O-H at pKa 16 and the Grignard is the conjugate base of an alkane at 50, so the only thing that happens is proton transfer: methane leaves and magnesium ethoxide stays. The other three all join two carbons.
Whatever attacks is what gets attached, so attaching carbon means attacking with carbon.
Both are narrow: cyanide brings one carbon with a nitrile attached, and an acetylide must come from a terminal alkyne.
The metal inserts into the carbon-halogen bond; nothing is added and nothing leaves.

The same destructive protonation that ruins a wet Grignard, used on purpose. The carbanion takes a deuteron from D2O, so the label lands exactly on the carbon that bore the halide - a clean way to mark one position.
The reagent would destroy itself on its own acidic proton as fast as it formed.
Deprotonating an alcohol gives the same magnesium alkoxide that a Grignard addition does, but the reagent has been spent on a proton and no carbon was joined to anything.
The metal inserts into the C-X bond rather than displacing the halide from behind.
More charge on carbon means a more reactive and less discriminating reagent.
An ether has no acidic hydrogen, which is also why it can be the solvent.
The sp carbanion is stabilized, so that hydrogen is acidic enough to be taken.
Proton transfer is the fastest reaction available, so the reagent is spent before it can add.
Reordering costs nothing; protection costs two steps and therefore two yields.
Boron sits close to carbon, so the reagent is barely nucleophilic on its own.

Wet or undried glassware leaves an oxide-coated magnesium surface, so the insertion never initiates, the turnings sit there and the solution never goes cloudy gray. Any reagent that does form is protonated to R-H rather than going on to product.
grignard-reagents: Formaldehyde has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon, so after one R group is added that carbon still carries two.
One hydrogen and one R group were already there; the Grignard adds the second R.
The ketone brings two carbon groups and the Grignard adds a third.
One carbon longer, and it arrives already at the carboxylic acid oxidation level.
The attack is an SN2 at the less hindered carbon, and the alkoxide is protonated on workup.
There is no acid present, so no carbocation character develops and sterics decide.
The imine anion that forms is hydrolyzed on workup.
The ketone formed after the first addition is more electrophilic than the ester was.
Two identical R groups from the reagent end up on the carbinol carbon.
The OR group donates into the carbonyl and makes the ester the sluggish one of the pair.
Both additions come from the same reagent, so they cannot differ.
A cuprate is too mild to attack the ketone it just made; a Grignard is not.
Its chelated intermediate survives until workup, so no second addition can occur.
Formaldehyde adds one carbon and stops at a primary alcohol; CO2 adds one carbon already at the acid level. A nitrile R′CN brings R′ along with its carbon, and an epoxide brings two.
Which is why it is the standard two-carbon extension. A substituted epoxide adds more, and the attack still goes at the less hindered carbon.
A carboxylic acid at pKa 5 is the most acidic thing present by a wide margin.
The carbanion takes the proton and departs as the alkane.
The alkoxide or carboxylate intermediate has to be protonated.
Three carbons in, one carbon added, and it arrives as the carboxyl.
One carbon added, ending as a primary alcohol.
A ketone plus a Grignard gives a tertiary alcohol, here with methyl, methyl and propyl.
pKa 25 against an effective 50 for the reagent.
Two extra steps means two extra yields lost, so it is worth it only when the alternatives fail.

Two carbons in and four out, so the electrophile has to bring two and leave the OH on the end carbon: that is ethylene oxide, attacked at the less hindered carbon. Formaldehyde adds only one, and CO2 would give an acid.
A very strong base and an alpha hydrogen in the same flask is an acid-base reaction waiting to happen.
Having the electrophile present while the reagent forms invites enolization and self-condensation.
Esters, nitriles and ketones are all electrophiles the reagent attacks.
The metal insertion does not touch the double bond.

Two additions again, but not for the ester's reason: an acyl chloride is the most electrophilic acyl derivative, and the ketone it gives is simply still reactive enough to be attacked as fast as it forms.
Each cut gives a carbanion and a ketone, and there are three legitimate choices.
organolithium-reagents: Each lithium supplies one electron, and one departs as LiBr.
A wider gap puts more negative charge on carbon.
Smaller and more reactive, so addition outruns deprotonation.
Two equivalents: one takes the acidic proton and one adds to the carboxylate.
The ketone does not exist in the flask, so there is nothing for a second equivalent to attack.
One for the O-H and one for the addition.
An organolithium used as a base rather than as a nucleophile.
That pairing is what allows complete enolate formation without attack on the carbonyl.
An amine pKa near 36 against an alkane near 50, and it is still far more than enough.
Half its value is what it removes a proton from rather than what it attacks.

Bulk does slow its approach to a hindered carbonyl, but t-BuLi is still a fine nucleophile and the standard reagent for lithium-halogen exchange. LDA is the reagent for which basic-but-not-nucleophilic actually holds.
An alkene is 44 and an alkane 50, so the alkyne is by far the most acidic of the three.
Half s character holds the lone pair close to the nucleus.
You need a base whose conjugate acid has a pKa well above 25.
With anything more substituted the acetylide acts as a base and E2 wins.
A secondary halide plus a strong base means elimination, not substitution.
Ordinary nucleophilic addition, with the alkyne left intact.
Both hydrogens are delivered to one face on the catalyst surface.
A dissolving-metal reduction through a vinyl radical anion, which settles trans.
One substrate, two conditions, two geometries.

Lithium-halogen exchange is an equilibrium, and it settles where the carbanion is better stabilized. An sp2 aryl carbanion has more s character than an sp3 butyl one, so it holds its lone pair closer and is the weaker base.
The extra reactivity is mostly something to manage rather than something to use.
Alkylating a terminal alkyne makes it internal, and an internal alkyne has no acidic C-H.
Deprotonation, not addition, is what makes it nucleophilic.
Addition to the carbonyl, protonated on workup.

The first equivalent is spent on the O-H and the second adds to the carboxylate. The dianion cannot collapse, so it survives until workup and only then loses water to the ketone. A Grignard is not reactive enough to attack a carboxylate, and the acid chloride route adds twice.
The Grignard stalls and acts as a base; the smaller, hotter reagent gets in.
Two negative charges on one carbon's oxygens. It cannot collapse, because that would mean expelling O2- and adding a third charge, so it survives until workup.
Hydroxide gives an equilibrium, n-BuLi attacks the carbonyl, and pyridine is far too weak.
Which is why acidity rises sp3 to sp2 to sp.
gilman-reagents: R2CuLi, with one lithium iodide left over.
Soft nucleophile, orbital control, largest coefficient at beta.
Hard nucleophile, charge control, and the carbonyl carbon carries the most positive charge.
1,2 addition to the carbonyl, protonated on workup.
1,4 addition gives an enolate, which protonates and tautomerizes back to the ketone.
Same substrate and same R group; only the metal changes the answer.
A less polar C-metal bond means less carbanion character.
It picks up a proton on workup, which is how the carbonyl reappears.
The reagent runs at half efficiency, which nobody minds.
The vinyl and aryl cases are the point, since neither does SN2 at all.
A vinyl carbon is sp2 and its backside is shielded, so substitution is unavailable.
Cuprates couple with vinyl halides, which do no SN2 at all, and the alkene geometry survives the coupling. That retention is most of the reason the reaction is worth running.
The reagent is too mild to attack the ketone it just made.
The mildness is the property being used, not a limitation being worked around.
Which is what makes it usable on a real substrate rather than a model one.
Hard nucleophiles are charge-controlled, so they go where the charge is.
Soft nucleophiles are orbital-controlled, so they go where the coefficient is.
Which is exactly why the hard Grignard picks it.

A cuprate is too mild to be a general carbonyl nucleophile: it leaves esters, amides and nitriles alone, which is exactly why it tolerates them elsewhere in a molecule. What it does instead is conjugate (1,4) addition, coupling with halides — the Corey-House synthesis — and one clean addition to an acyl chloride.
Resonance puts positive character on the beta carbon as well as the carbonyl carbon.
Only the cuprate delivers the methyl to the beta carbon.
1,2 addition to the carbonyl gives a tertiary allylic alcohol.
An oxidation at that carbon needs a C-H to remove, and a tertiary alcohol has none.
That tolerance is why zinc reagents appear in palladium chemistry.
Choosing the reagent is how you choose the product here.
Low selectivity is the cost of high reactivity; a cuprate would leave the ester alone.
Cleverer conditions rarely solve a selectivity problem that the reagent causes.
The enolate tautomerizes once it is protonated.
The second R group stays on the copper.
Which points it at the largest LUMO coefficient rather than the largest partial charge.
cross-coupling: Copper appears as a cocatalyst in the Sonogashira, but palladium runs the cycle.
The first and last names describe what happens to the palladium's oxidation state.
Pd(0) becomes Pd(II), holding both pieces.

An sp3 group on palladium with a hydrogen on the neighboring carbon loses that hydrogen and leaves as an alkene, faster than the two organic groups can join. Aryl and vinyl groups have no such beta hydrogen, which is why they are the partners that work.
The palladium oxidation state does not change in this step.
Pd(II) becomes Pd(0) and the catalyst is back where it started.
Reductive elimination hands back the Pd(0) the cycle started with, so a few mole percent turns over thousands of times.
And it needs a base, which the Stille does not.
Chemically excellent, but organotin reagents are seriously toxic.
Zinc is mild enough that esters survive the cycle.
A copper cocatalyst forms the acetylide that transmetalates.
An alkene inserts into the Ar-Pd bond instead, so there is no transmetalation step.
A neutral boronic acid transfers its R group poorly; the four-coordinate borate does it well.
The chemistry of the Stille is at least as good; the toxicity of organotin is what settled it.
It replaces transmetalation, which the Heck has nothing to perform.
And the new bond forms at the less substituted carbon.
And SN1 is no better, since an aryl cation is badly unstable.
Nothing has to attack that carbon, which is the whole point.
Since yields multiply, joining two short branches beats one long chain.
Ten linear steps at 85% gives about 20%; two five-step branches joined gives about 37%.
The reactive carbon is bound to a metal throughout and never exists as a free carbanion.
Neither ring is nucleophilic or electrophilic enough for anything from earlier chapters.
Pd(0) inserts into the C-Br bond, the borate hands its phenyl across, and reductive elimination joins the two rings. Two aryl pieces, one new aryl-aryl bond.
A phenol pKa near 10 is easily acidic enough to consume the reagent.

Bromides and iodides go readily. Aryl chlorides are sluggish and need heat or activation, and aryl fluorides do not go at all. The trouble with the reagent is what it does afterward, not whether it forms.
Only the two elimination and addition steps move it.

Oxidative addition breaks the Ar-Br bond, which is why the halide sets the scope. Carbonate then adds to boron to give the four-coordinate borate, and only that anionic boron delivers its aryl group to palladium.
The organometallic partner arrives later, at transmetalation.
Fifty analogs cost fifty final steps rather than fifty syntheses.
The aryl halide is activated by the metal, not by attacking the ring.
wittig-reaction: The new double bond lands exactly at the old carbonyl carbon, in place of its C=O.
A negative carbon bonded directly to a positive phosphorus, neutral overall.

Join the aldehyde carbon to the ylide carbon: CH3CH2CH2-CH=CH-CH2CH3, which is hept-3-ene. The ylide carries alkyl groups alone, so it is unstabilized, and an unstabilized ylide gives mainly the Z isomer.
Triphenylphosphine is a large, polarizable, soft nucleophile.
The first step is an SN2, and that is the whole limitation on the reaction.
No phosphonium salt forms, so the route dies at step one - and even if one did form, a tertiary carbon on phosphorus has no hydrogen to remove, so there would be no ylide either.
Aryl groups reach a Wittig product from the carbonyl side instead.
The hydrogen next to P+ is acidic, but not that acidic.
Adjacent opposite charge is the stabilization, and it is why the ylide exists.
And forming it is the reaction's driving force.
Both of the first two are chemically real disconnections, so the halide decides between them: 1-bromopentane is primary and the SN2 is clean, while 2-bromopropane is secondary and sluggish.
It falls apart in the one way it can, giving the alkene and the phosphine oxide.
An elimination forms the C=C between two carbons already bonded, so Zaitsev chooses where.
Which is the problem a Wittig avoids entirely.
There is only one position available, so there is no competition to lose.
An exocyclic alkene, and the less stable of the two isomers, which is exactly the point.
It adds fast and irreversibly, so the geometry of the transition state is locked in.
It adds reversibly, so the equilibrium finds the more stable arrangement.
Delocalizing the carbanion makes it less reactive and the addition reversible.
That phosphonate anion is the Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons reagent: strongly E-selective, deprotonated by NaH rather than n-BuLi, and its phosphate by-product washes out in water.
The product that forms fastest, rather than the one that is most stable.
The aldehyde supplies the phenyl half, so the ester has to come from the ylide.
Both assignments are usually drawable, and you pick by which halide is easier.
The halide has to survive an SN2, and that is what eliminates one of the two.
Expensive, and the main practical objection to the reaction.
Ph3P=C(CH3)2 comes from the secondary halide 2-bromopropane. A tertiary halide is not an SN2 substrate, and it would in any case give a phosphonium with no alpha hydrogen to remove.
No carbocation is ever formed, so there is nothing to shift.
Zaitsev pushes an elimination toward the more substituted isomer.
SN2 on a secondary center is sluggish, so yields fall.
The ylide supplies the other half, and the two are joined at that bond.
imines-enamines: One hydrogen is left on nitrogen after the addition, so the C=N+ cation loses it.
No N-H is left, so the proton comes from the alpha carbon instead.
Losing water would demand a nitrogen with five bonds, so the addition simply reverses - which is why tertiary amines serve as bases here.
A tetrahedral carbon carrying both an OH and an NR2.

A Stork sequence: form the enamine, alkylate the alpha carbon with a reactive benzylic halide, then hydrolyze back to the ketone. One alkylation happens, because the first gives an iminium that cannot be turned back into a nucleophile.
An enamine needs its last proton to come from the alpha carbon. Benzophenone has no alpha hydrogen, so the sequence gets as far as the cation and stops.
C=C-NR2, because the proton had to come from the alpha carbon.
Enough acid to protonate the OH, not enough to protonate the amine.
A hydroxide is a terrible leaving group; water is a fine one.
An ammonium ion is not a nucleophile, so nothing attacks in the first place.
A Dean-Stark trap or molecular sieves; every step of the sequence is reversible.
Adding the water back runs the whole sequence in reverse.
NaBH3CN reduces the imine as it forms, avoiding the over-alkylation of direct SN2.
Direct SN2 on ammonia keeps going, giving a mixture of amine classes.
Mild enough to leave the ketone alone while reducing the more electrophilic iminium.
A crystalline derivative, which is how carbonyl compounds were once identified.
Pushing the lone pair into the C=C puts the negative charge at the far carbon.
Same job, reached without a strong base, and neutral rather than anionic.
Which is why it usually stops after one alkylation.
Net result is an alpha-substituted ketone, by a gentler route than an enolate.
Which is how the sequence releases its product at the end.
Not a matter of reactivity. The iminium has no nucleophilic carbon, and no base is present to turn it back into an enamine, so a second alkylation is impossible rather than slow.
A mild Michael donor, where a full enolate would compete with 1,2-addition.
A cyclic secondary amine, so two carbons on nitrogen and one hydrogen.

The cost of a neutral, controllable nucleophile is a short list of electrophiles: methyl, allylic, benzylic and alpha-halo carbonyls. Acid chlorides always work; ordinary primary halides often do not.
Which is why acid helps up to the point where it switches off the nucleophile.
Two carbons already on nitrogen means no N-H survives the addition.
It stops where you want it to, because the imine forms once.
A Wolff-Kishner reduction. The hydrazone loses N2 under strong base and heat, leaving a CH2 where the C=O was.
Acid helps one step and kills another, so the best rate is between the two.
michael-robinson: 1,4 rather than 1,2, with an enolate as the nucleophile.
Almost always a compound with an alpha hydrogen between two carbonyls.
An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, with the beta carbon as the electrophilic site.
Joining the donor alpha carbon to the acceptor beta carbon puts them five apart.
The nucleophile hit a carbonyl carbon and the oxygen stayed as an alcohol.
The nucleophile hit an ester and the alkoxide left.
