A Robinson annulation. The cyclohexanone enolate adds 1,4 to MVK to give a 1,5-diketone, an intramolecular aldol closes a second six-membered ring onto the first, and dehydration leaves the conjugated enone.
Low enough that a catalytic alkoxide deprotonates it completely.
Spreading the charge over two carbonyls is what makes the enolate soft rather than hard.

Hard, charge-dense and irreversible, so it takes the carbonyl carbon. Under reversible conditions - catalytic alkoxide, warm - the same enolate ends up adding 1,4 instead, which is why the classic Robinson works with an ordinary ketone.
So no strong base ever sits in the flask next to the acceptor.
An alpha hydrogen between two ester carbonyls, pKa near 13.
Cheap, and the ring its Robinson product gives is the one steroid chemistry needed.
And it builds a ring in the process.
A 1,5-dicarbonyl has its ends exactly far enough apart to meet without strain.
The final dehydration conjugates the new C=C with the carbonyl.
Conjugating the alkene with the carbonyl is the stabilization it cannot climb back out of.
The reaction is not choosing a ring size; the chain length already chose it.
Reverse order: put the water back, break the aldol bond, then cut beta to a carbonyl.
Which is exactly what puts the two carbonyls five apart.
A soft enolate adding 1,4, with the Michael fingerprint in the product.

An alpha,beta-unsaturated nitrile is a good acceptor: the CN withdraws, the beta carbon is electrophilic, and the donor's alpha carbon lands on it, leaving the ketone and the nitrile carbon 1,5 to each other in ethyl 2-acetyl-4-cyanobutanoate.
Orbital control rather than charge control, and the beta carbon has the larger coefficient.
Which is why a hard nucleophile picks it, and a soft one does not.
Five- and six-membered closures happen far faster than anything larger.
A Diels-Alder builds a ring too, but it gives a cyclohexene rather than a cyclohexenone.
If it does, a Robinson annulation made it and the two pieces fall out.
Two carbonyls flanking one carbon, so the carbanion is delocalized onto both.
An isolated alkene has no electron-withdrawing group conjugated to it, so its beta carbon is not electrophilic and a nucleophile has nothing to add to.
The electrons pushed out of the C=C end up on the carbonyl oxygen, so the first species formed is an enolate; protonation, or tautomerization from the enol, gives the 1,5-dicarbonyl.
ester-syntheses: Malonate has two esters: one carboxyl is lost as CO2 and the other stays as the acid.
One ester and one ketone: the ester's carboxyl goes, the ketone survives.

Two equivalents of base for two alkylations, both spent on the same dihalide, and the second closes the ring. The malonate alpha carbon plus the three carbons of the dihalide make a four-membered ring. Acetoacetate would give a ketone, and cyclobutyl bromide is secondary.
Delocalizing the carbanion onto two ester oxygens is worth twelve orders of magnitude.
Too high for a convenient base, and a strong base would attack the ester instead.
At pKa 13 the alkoxide that matches your solvent is enough.
Its alpha carbon carries two methyls and an ethyl - three substituents - and malonate's CH2 has two acidic hydrogens to give up. The other three need one primary halide each, or two.
This is the clearest example of one in the course.
Which is why the halide must be methyl, primary, allylic or benzylic.
The enolate is a base as well as a nucleophile, so E2 takes over.
The backside is crowded, so the enolate reaches for a beta hydrogen instead.
A six-membered cyclic transition state reaches from the carboxyl O-H to that second carbonyl. It is a ketone in the acetoacetic route and the other carboxyl in the malonic one, and either works.
And an enol forms, which tautomerizes to the product.
The geometry needs the second carbonyl exactly beta, whether that carbonyl is a ketone or another carboxyl.
Its CH2 has two acidic hydrogens, so both can be replaced in turn.
One CH2 between two ester carbonyls.
One ketone and one ester flanking the acidic CH2.
Only a carboxyl can decarboxylate, and the ketone is not one.
A methyl ketone carrying the benzyl group, after hydrolysis and decarboxylation.
The ethyl group ends up on the carbon alpha to the surviving carboxyl.
The alpha carbon of the target carries a methyl and a propyl, installed in two rounds.

All four are methyl ketones, so the product class does not decide it. 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one would need three methyls on the alpha carbon, and ethyl acetoacetate's CH2 has two acidic hydrogens to give - no choice of halide reaches it.
No O-H, no six-membered loop. That is why the ester has to be hydrolyzed first, and why the two operations are always written together.
One step does both, because the beta-keto acid does not survive the temperature.
pKa 25 against 13 is the whole reason the second carbonyl is installed.
Using ethoxide with an ethyl ester avoids scrambling the ester by transesterification.
The isobutyl group lands on the alpha carbon, and after hydrolysis and decarboxylation the chain is CH3CO-CH2-CH2-CH(CH3)2. Acetoacetate gives a methyl ketone, never an acid.
One of them is beta to the other, which is why exactly one is lost on heating.
Which is what makes every product of that route a methyl ketone.
The target never tells you whether the route works; the halide does.
baeyer-villiger: The product is an ester, and almost nothing else in the course touches that bond.
The same reagent that epoxidizes alkenes.
It collapses by migration, with a carboxylate leaving.
The same motion that rearranges a carbocation, running on a neutral intermediate.
Which is why it never exists as a free species and never loses its configuration.
The bond never fully breaks, so the other three bonds are undisturbed.
Carbocation stability arriving from another direction, with hydrogen at the head of it - which is why an aldehyde gives a carboxylic acid.
Whatever stabilizes a carbocation stabilizes this transition state.
Hydrogen is the best migrator of all, so in an aldehyde the H moves and the product is the carboxylic acid. Propyl formate would come from the propyl migrating, and it does not.
The oxygen goes between the carbonyl and the migrating group.
The migration is intramolecular, so the ring expands rather than opening.
Six carbons plus the inserted oxygen.
Ring expansion by exactly one atom, every time.
A cyclic amide would be a lactam.
Epoxidation is faster, so the alkene has to be dealt with before the ketone.
The phenyl migrates, so the oxygen ends up between it and the carbonyl.
The methyl-bearing carbon is secondary and the other is primary, and secondary migrates better, so the ring oxygen ends up attached to the carbon carrying the methyl. The ring still expands to seven.
And a carboxylate leaves as the migration happens.
The peroxyacid's other half, which is what makes the O-O bond a good place to break.
A peroxyacid's O-O bond with a good leaving group is what both exploit.
Which is how you read a product backwards to find what migrated.
Find the inserted oxygen and look at which side each group is on.
One of very few reactions at this level where a stereocenter survives a bond change intact.
Which you already know how to hydrolyze, so the reaction slots into longer routes.
Its two groups are identical primary ethyls, so whichever one moves gives the same product, ethyl propanoate. In each of the others the two groups sit at clearly different places in the series.
One of the few reliable ring expansions at this level, and the only one adding oxygen.
Which is what makes the 1,2-shift here unusual: it runs without a carbocation.
One of the two bonds from the carbonyl carbon to its substituents.
Esterifying a tertiary alcohol is hard; migrating a tertiary group is the easiest case.
The carbocation shortcut predicts the wrong thing here, and the reason it fails is that no free cation is ever made: the migrating carbon is bonded to both the old carbon and the new oxygen at once.
nucleophilic-aromatic: The carbon is sp2 and the trajectory a nucleophile needs does not exist.
The positive charge would sit in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, with no way to delocalize.

Addition first. The delocalization onto the nitro groups is what makes the Meisenheimer intermediate survivable long enough for the halide to leave, so it has to come before the loss of halide, and aromaticity is only restored at the very end.
Negatively charged and not aromatic, which is what the withdrawing groups pay for.
Only ortho and para can reach the negative charge by resonance.
The intermediate's charge lands ortho and para to the attack, never meta.
The reverse of every other substitution, because attack is the slow step.

The C-X bond is not breaking in the rate-determining step, so what matters is how electrophilic the halogen makes the carbon under attack - and that is electronegativity, which runs the opposite way from leaving-group ability.

One nitro group para to the halide is enough to run SNAr with a good nucleophile and some heat. SNAr never rearranges, so there is one product and it sits exactly where the fluorine was - and fluorine being the halide helps here rather than hurting.
The nucleophile arrives exactly where the leaving group was.
A very strong base is needed to remove a ring hydrogen.
The mirror image of SNAr.
They point away from each other rather than overlapping properly, which is why it is strained.
The triple bond is symmetric, so the nucleophile can attack either carbon.
That hydrogen is what the base removes in the first step.
No direct displacement could put the nucleophile on a carbon that never bore the leaving group.
There is no ortho hydrogen to eliminate.
Nitro groups ortho and para make this an SNAr, which gives one product.

NaNH2 plays both parts: it removes the ortho hydrogen in the elimination and then adds to the benzyne. That is why the reaction cannot be run with a strong base plus a separate weak nucleophile - anything basic enough to make a benzyne is already nucleophilic.
Delocalization onto the substituents is what makes losing aromaticity affordable.
Which is exactly why the leaving group order inverts for SNAr.
It lasts only long enough to be attacked.
No activation rules out SNAr, and no ortho hydrogen rules out benzyne.
Amide can attack either carbon of the benzyne, and the two are not equivalent.

No withdrawing group rules out SNAr, and both positions ortho to the bromine carry methyl groups, so there is no hydrogen for the base to remove and no benzyne either. Recognizing a substrate that runs NEITHER route is the skill being tested.
A third route, and the one that needs neither activation nor a brutal base.
Without them the intermediate is too high in energy to form.
Which is exactly why only ortho and para substituents help.

The benzyne forms between C2 and C3. Amide attacks the carbon that leaves the carbanion nearer the electron-withdrawing methoxy oxygen, which gives the meta product. Two products are possible from any benzyne, but a substituent decides how the two are weighted.
Iodine is the least electronegative of the four, so it activates the carbon least.
benzylic-reactivity: It is not part of the ring, and it behaves unlike any other sp3 carbon.
The charge spreads over the benzylic carbon plus both ortho and the para positions.
The benzylic carbon plus the two ortho and one para ring positions.

Same argument, counted the same way. An allyl system carries the charge on two positions, its two ends; a benzylic system carries it on four - the benzylic carbon plus both ortho positions and the para.
Rare, and it is why benzyl bromide is used as an alkylating agent everywhere.
It sits roughly where a tertiary alkyl halide does.
And a benzylic carbon is usually unhindered, which helps as well.
Light means radicals, and the benzylic radical is by far the most stable.
Low Br2 suppresses the ionic addition that would attack any alkene present.
Same reagent, same mechanism, and a selectivity problem if a molecule has both.
The side chain is cut back to one carbon and oxidized to the carboxyl.
Chain length makes no difference; everything past the benzylic carbon is cut away.
There is no benzylic hydrogen, so the reaction cannot start.
The one exception that shows what the mechanism requires.
Aromatic stabilization keeps the ring inert to conditions that destroy alkenes.
Stability of the radical formed is what selectivity tracks.
Oxidation converts any alkyl chain to a carboxyl, so the chain identity is free.

Bromination goes wherever the most stabilized radical forms. In this substrate the carbon next to the ring is also next to the double bond, so C1 is benzylic and allylic at the same time and there is no competition to resolve.
It appears in malonic ester and enamine chemistry for exactly this reason.
The same resonance that stabilizes the cation and the radical.
One alkene replaced by a whole ring, so the charge spreads further.
Cation, radical and anion are all delocalized by the same resonance.

Friedel-Crafts fails on a nitrated ring, so the alkyl group has to go on first. The methyl then sends the nitro group para. The oxidation must come last, because a carboxyl is a deactivating meta director that would have sent the nitro group to the wrong place.
Electrophilic substitution cannot deliver a carboxyl group directly.

Every side chain with a benzylic hydrogen is cut back and oxidized, not just one, so both ethyl groups become carboxyls. That compound is the monomer for PET, which is one industrial use of this reaction.
One benzylic hydrogen is enough, and both methyls go with the rest of the chain.

Benzylic means attached to the ring, and the definition says nothing about hybridization. But every reaction in this section - SN1, SN2, radical abstraction, permanganate - needs an sp3 carbon carrying a hydrogen. Reduce the ketone to CH2 and all of it switches on.
One reagent and one mechanism means it cannot tell them apart.
Bond strength tracks the stability of the fragments it gives.
Hydrogenolysis cleaves the benzylic C-O bond and gives toluene plus the free alcohol. It is the one deprotection that needs neither acid nor base, which is exactly why the group is worth using.
phenols: An OH on a carbon next to the ring is a benzylic alcohol, which behaves quite differently.
Six orders of magnitude more acidic than ethanol.

Count the resonance-capable withdrawing groups: two, then one, then none, then a donor pushing the wrong way. Methoxy from para donates its lone pair into the ring, which destabilizes the phenoxide, so 4-methoxyphenol is the weakest acid of the four.
Acidity is about the stability of the conjugate base, not the bond that breaks.
Which is also why only ortho and para substituents affect the acidity much.
Bicarbonate is not strong enough, which is what makes it useful as a discriminator.
Carbonic acid at pKa 6.4 sits between the two.
The acid leaves as its water-soluble salt and the phenol stays behind.

Bicarbonate, from carbonic acid at pKa 6.4, pulls out only the benzoic acid at 4.8. Hydroxide then pulls out the phenol at 10. Cyclohexanol at 16 is untouched by both and stays behind - a three-way separation run on nothing but a pKa table.
Nitro withdraws by resonance from para, taking the charge onto its own oxygens.

The Kolbe-Schmitt reaction. The phenoxide attacks CO2 with an ORTHO ring carbon rather than with its oxygen, because that is where the charge actually sits - and acetylating the resulting phenol gives aspirin.
From meta only induction is available, which is the smaller effect.
Anything that stabilizes the phenoxide strengthens the acid.
Only those can reach the negative charge by resonance.
The same lone pair that stabilizes the anion also donates into the ring.
Donation reaches the ortho and para positions, which is where the substitution goes.
No Lewis acid catalyst is needed, and all three activated positions react at once.
A Lewis acid is needed only for rings that are not already electron-rich.
The backside is behind the ring, which rules the trajectory out entirely.
The aryl carbon can never be the electrophile in a substitution.
Not aromatic any more, which is why quinones are colored.

A small HOMO-LUMO gap, from two carbonyls conjugated with the two remaining C=C bonds. Losing aromaticity is what makes that chromophore possible, but plenty of non-aromatic compounds are colorless - the conjugation is the cause.
Nothing that needs SN1 or SN2 at that carbon works.
Warm water on an aryl diazonium salt is the standard route.
Aspirin is one of these.

OH is one of the strongest activators there is, and one bromine barely dents it, so the second and third substitutions are about as fast as the first. Getting monobromination needs deliberately weaker conditions - Br2 in a nonpolar solvent, cold.
Donating electron density destabilizes the anion, which weakens the acid.
An ordinary alcohol has no way to spread the charge at all.
4.8 against 10, because a carboxylate spreads charge over two equivalent oxygens.

A carboxylate spreads its charge over two electronegative oxygens. A phenoxide spreads most of its charge onto ring carbons, which hold it far less well, and that is most of the five-unit pKa gap between them.
birch-reduction: The unconjugated isomer, which is the less stable of the two dienes.
A dissolving-metal reduction rather than a catalytic one.
The reducing agent is a free electron in solution.
Alternating, which is what makes the intermediates controllable.
One electron added to the ring.
The electrons come from the metal and the solvent is ammonia.
Protonation happens at the central carbon of the delocalized anion, which is not where the more stable product would come from.
And it is not what forms, which is how you know stability is not deciding.
A donor destabilizes charge on its own carbon, so the carbanion goes elsewhere.
A withdrawing group holds the charge on its own carbon, so that carbon is protonated.
Methoxy is donating, so its carbon stays on a double bond.
Carboxyl is withdrawing, so its carbon ends up sp3.
That carbon gets protonated and comes out saturated.
Both are dissolving-metal reductions running on solvated electrons, and both give the opposite outcome from catalytic hydrogenation on the same substrate.
It either leaves the ring alone or reduces it completely; there is no halfway.
An unconjugated diene is a handle nothing else in the course provides.

Hydrolyzing the enol ether unmasks the ketone at the carbon that carried the OCH3, and the OTHER double bond stays exactly where it was - two carbons away, not in conjugation. Reaching the Michael-accepting cyclohex-2-en-1-one takes a deliberate isomerization with stronger acid or base.
The methoxy stays on a double bond, and a C=C with an OR on it is an enol ether.
A conjugated diene reacts as one system, which makes single-site chemistry harder.
The product that forms fastest, rather than the one that is most stable.

An ester carbonyl is an acceptor, so the carbanion sits on the carbon bearing it, that carbon is the one protonated, and it comes out sp3. Same row of the table as benzoic acid, and the same single question answers both.

Three operations, and the third is the one people drop. The Birch gives the enol ether, mild hydrolysis gives the beta,gamma ketone cyclohex-3-en-1-one, and only a deliberate isomerization moves the double bond into conjugation. Without that step there is no Michael acceptor.

Opposite selectivities, and it is the cleanest chemoselectivity pair in the course. Adding an electron is easy for an aromatic ring and hard for an isolated alkene; adding hydrogens from a metal surface is the other way round.
Which is the opposite selectivity from catalytic hydrogenation.
The carbanion sits where the substituent lets it, and that carbon gets the proton.

Adding a single electron to a neutral molecule gives both at once: the electron is unpaired, and the molecule is now negatively charged. That is the first intermediate of every dissolving-metal reduction.
The pentadienyl anion is protonated at its middle carbon, and that is what puts the two remaining double bonds 1,4 rather than 1,3.
Methyl is a weak donor, and direction rather than strength decides the outcome.
Adding an electron to an isolated alkene is far harder than to an aromatic ring.
Which is why it can stop where a surface reaction cannot.
diazonium-chemistry: And it leaves as N2 gas, which is what makes it so useful.
Cold, because the salt decomposes above about 5 degrees.

The iodide row is the odd one out: no copper salt is required and plain KI does the job. That is worth noticing, because iodine is also the one halogen electrophilic substitution cannot install cleanly - direct iodination needs an added oxidant.
A gas that escapes the solution and cannot come back.
The first two are reactions the course already covered.
Or H2 with a catalyst, which does the same job.
A Sandmeyer reaction.
A group electrophilic substitution cannot install at all.
No copper salt is needed for the iodide.
The Schiemann reaction, and effectively the only route to an aryl fluoride.
The standard way phenols are made, since no substitution works at that C-O bond.
Which is the most useful row on the menu once you see what it is for.
Four groups no electrophilic substitution reaches.

A substituent installed to control one step and then deliberately deleted, which is a protecting group in aromatic clothes. The NH2 was never part of the target; it was there to steer the bromination, and H3PO2 removes it once it has.
Which is why it is worth installing purely to direct.
Same idea as the second carbonyl of a malonic ester synthesis.
Sulfonation is reversible, so the group can be removed afterwards.
The diazonium acts as a weak electrophile here rather than as a substrate.
The diazonium is too weak an electrophile for anything less activated.
Ortho/para directors send it there, and para is less hindered.
Two rings joined by a conjugated N=N bridge gives a small HOMO-LUMO gap.

The nitro group has to go on first and do the directing, because it is the only meta director available here, and bromine lands meta to it. Only then is the nitro group reduced, diazotized and hydrolyzed to OH. Reducing it first fails, because NH2 directs ortho/para.
Each bromine sends the next one ortho or para, so 1,3,5 is unreachable.
The amine directs all three bromines, then H3PO2 deletes it.
Strongly activated, so all three positions react without a catalyst.

Badly unstable, which is why it grabs whatever nucleophile is present at once. In warm aqueous acid that nucleophile is water and the product is the phenol. The copper-catalyzed Sandmeyer rows are the exception: those run through an aryl radical instead.
CuCl, CuBr and CuCN are the three standard cases.

Install a temporary director - usually an amine made from a nitro group - let it steer the substitution where you want it, then diazotize and delete it with H3PO2. You do not argue with directing effects; you change who is doing the directing.
An unactivated aryl halide does neither SN1 nor SN2.

Coupling needs the nitrogen lone pair donating into the ring. Protonate the nitrogen and that lone pair is gone, leaving a ring that is deactivated rather than activated - and a diazonium ion is far too weak an electrophile for a deactivated ring.
polymer-basics: The repeating piece inside the chain is the repeat unit, which may differ from the monomer.
For step-growth it is 1/(1-p), where p is the fraction of groups reacted.
One stops after a single bond; three or more gives a network.
Which is what makes a thermoset, and why it cannot be melted.
It makes one bond and is finished.
The pi bond simply opens, so the repeat unit matches the monomer.
Which is what the word condensation means.
A lighter repeat unit means something was expelled; matching formulas mean nothing was, so for an alkene monomer, addition.
The double bond supplies both reactive ends.
Esterification or amide formation, run repeatedly.
Heating lets the chains slide, so it can be melted and remolded.
Heating destroys it rather than softening it, because melting would mean breaking bonds.
A network has nothing to loosen.
Break the pi bond of ethylene and bracket what is left.
More surface in contact means more total intermolecular attraction.
Which is the whole difference between LDPE and HDPE.
A few make rubber elastic; many make a rigid thermoset.
Chains that match can lie against each other.

In a chain-growth polymerization a chain is either active or dead, and an active chain swallows thousands of monomers in seconds, so the flask holds long polymer beside untouched monomer with little between them. A step-growth mixture is the opposite picture: at 50% conversion the average piece is a dimer, so you would find a broad soup of oligomers and hardly any monomer left.
Which is why nothing is long until conversion is very high.
1/(1-0.99), and 99% sounds finished while giving a marginal material.

Rearrange DP = 1/(1-p) to p = 1 - 1/DP. With DP = 200 that is 1 - 0.005 = 0.995, so 99.5% of all the functional groups have to have reacted. Read the other way round, the figure that sounds impressive - 99% - buys you only DP = 100, half of what was asked for.
Two like groups cannot react with each other, so growth stops.
A small mole fraction of it wrecks the molecular weight.
From an alkene, with nothing lost.
A diacid and a diamine, losing water at each amide.
It equals the monomer only for addition polymers.

The one thing every chain polymer shares is two sites per monomer. Styrene's come from its C=C, terephthalic acid's from its two CO2H groups and the glycol's from its two OH groups. The other three statements are each true of one product and false of the other: only polystyrene keeps its monomer's formula, only the polyester loses water, and only polystyrene grows by a radical chain.

Count the reactive sites on one monomer and the answer is settled before any mechanism. The diacid has two, so on its own it would extend a line; glycerol has three, so every glycerol can tie itself to three different chains, and repeating that in all directions makes the whole sample one covalent molecule. The chemistry of each join is ordinary esterification, which is why it is still called a polyester - it is the count, not the reaction, that makes it a network.

Subtract the formulas: C6H12O6 minus C6H10O5 is H2O. The repeat unit is lighter than the monomer by exactly one water, so a small molecule was condensed out at every join and this was a step-growth. (These are glucose and cellulose.) Counting atoms answered the question without any knowledge of the compound.
addition-polymers: The same three as radical halogenation.
It breaks homolytically to give two radicals.
Generating a new radical at the end of a longer chain, thousands of times.

Two dead chains rather than one is the giveaway. Combination couples the two radicals into a single chain of the combined length; disproportionation has one radical take the hydrogen from the carbon next to the other radical center, which leaves that chain with a double bond and makes the abstracting chain saturated. Chain transfer and backbiting both keep the radical count the same, so neither of them can stop two chains at once.
So propagation runs a long way before two radicals find each other.
That leaves the radical on the substituted, more stable carbon.
It follows from taking the more stable radical every time.
Both come from asking which intermediate is more stable.
Foam cups and packaging.
Pipe, flooring and insulation.
Teflon, and there is no head-to-tail question because both carbons are identical.
Plexiglas, and it is transparent because it is amorphous.

A peroxide gives a free radical chain end, which is planar and has no facial preference, so the methyls land at random and the product is atactic - a goo, whatever its molecular weight. Only a catalyst that holds the chain at a defined metal site forces every monomer to arrive the same way round, and only the isotactic chains that result can pack into crystalline regions. Pressure and transfer agent change the chain length, which is not what is wrong here, and cross-linking would give a thermoset that cannot be molded at all.
Packs well, so the material is crystalline and strong.
Regular, so it packs well too.
Cannot pack, so the material is amorphous and soft.
A planar radical has no strong preference about which face the next monomer arrives on.
It holds the chain on a metal center so every addition happens the same way.
Nothing packs, so there is no strength.
The chain then continues from that point, leaving a branch.
High-pressure radical polymerization does this constantly.
A Ziegler-Natta catalyst suppresses the backbiting that makes branches.
Branched, badly packed and flexible.
Linear, well packed and rigid.
Same monomer, same repeat unit, different architecture.
Then write a bond leaving each side of the bracket.
Syndiotactic polystyrene has the same phenyl group and is crystalline, melting near 270 C, so bulk is not the cause. Atacticity is.
The growing cation has to be stabilized.
The mirror image of the cationic case.

Holding the growing chain at one defined, crowded metal site fixes how every monomer arrives, so the same feature sets the tacticity and suppresses branching. Rate and molecular weight depend on conditions as well.
condensation-polymers: Losing water at each ester bond.
Losing water at each amide bond.
The drinks bottle and the polyester shirt.
First number the diamine's carbons, second the diacid's: hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid.
Six in the diamine and six in the diacid, in that order, readable straight from the name.
Both aromatic and both para-substituted, which is what makes the chains straight.
Three factors compounding, none of them exotic.
Amides are the least reactive acyl derivative, which carries over to the material.
The property that makes it less durable is what makes it recoverable.
Same amide, same planarity, same interchain hydrogen bonding.
Backbone hydrogen bonds between neighboring chains.
The alcohol adds across the N=C=O group.
Which is why the class is properly called step-growth rather than condensation.
Polyurethane is the exception that forces the broader name.
Two oxygens on one carbonyl.
Transparent and extremely impact-resistant.
Which is why the last tenth of a percent is where the material appears.

The first number counts the carbons of the diamine, so 6 means hexamethylenediamine; the second counts the diacid's, so 10 means sebacic acid, HO2C(CH2)8CO2H - ten carbons including the two carboxyl carbons. Swapping the two slots gives decanediamine with adipic acid, which is a different polymer built from the same two numbers, and 6,6 would need adipic acid in the second slot.
Every step is an equilibrium, and the reaction has to be driven the whole way.
Two like groups cannot react with each other, so growth halts.
One monomer carrying both an OH and a COOH.
Two reactive sites is the only requirement, and they need not be the same kind.
Which is the handle that hydrolysis can select.
A straight chain lets neighbors touch along their whole length.

The alcohol adds across the N=C=O group rather than substituting at it, so every atom of both monomers ends up inside the carbamate link and nothing leaves. The polyester and the polyamide each lose water, and the polycarbonate loses HCl because phosgene is an acid chloride. Polyurethane is the reason the class is properly called step-growth rather than condensation.
Esterification or amide formation, and nothing else.
The acyl reactivity ladder applied to a material. It is not a blanket ranking: nylon is the one attacked by acid, chlorine and sunlight.

Caprolactam is already an amide, closed into a seven-membered ring. The ring opens onto the growing chain end and adds there, so the atoms are rearranged rather than removed and the repeat unit has exactly the monomer's formula. That makes nylon 6 a polyamide reached by a chain-growth ring-opening, which is why the two axes - addition against condensation, and chain-growth against step-growth - have to be asked separately.
No cross-links, so not a network. It has no melt either, decomposing near 500 C and spun from solution.
Cut the acyl C-O bond, leaving the oxygen on the alcohol side, and check each fragment has two reactive sites.
polymer-properties: Almost every real polymer has both crystalline and amorphous regions.
Packed chains occupy less space.
Their refractive indices differ, so light scatters at every boundary.
No crystalline regions means nothing to scatter light.
Essentially every polymer has one; only semicrystalline ones also have a Tm.
A fully amorphous polymer has no Tm at all.
Because every polymer has amorphous regions.
Below Tg the chains are frozen and cannot deform.
Its amorphous chains are mobile, and the cross-links pull them back.
Short S-S bridges form between the chains.
Chains can stretch apart and are pulled back, which is a tire.
Nothing can move at all.
Chains slide past each other permanently.
Releasing it lets entropy pull the chains back into a coil.
The entropic restoring force scales with temperature, unlike almost every other material.

Room temperature is roughly 20 C, so compare each Tg with that number. Rubber alone is above its transition, and with no crystallinity and only light cross-linking it is free to deform and spring back. The other three are all below their Tg, which is why they are rigid - and it is also why cooling rubber in liquid nitrogen turns it into a glass that shatters.
Which heat can overcome, so the chains slide and it can be remolded.
One network, so melting would mean breaking bonds.

The polymer is the same on both sides, which is what makes the case worth remembering. Unplasticized PVC has a Tg near 80 C, well above room temperature, so it is a glass. Mixing in 30 to 40% of a phthalate diester spaces the chains apart and weakens the forces between them, dropping Tg below room temperature - so the same polymer is now above its transition in ordinary use. Nothing chemical has happened, which is why the plasticizer can leach out again and leave old PVC brittle.
Bakelite and vulcanized rubber are others.
They raise Tg and slow crystallization. In polystyrene the random placement is what actually prevents packing.
Nylon and Kevlar both depend on them.
Straight chains stack and melt high; kinked or branched ones do not.

Passing Tg only frees the amorphous fraction; whether the sample then feels rubbery depends on what else is holding it together. In HDPE the crystallites tie the mobile chains to each other exactly as covalent cross-links would, and they keep doing so all the way to Tm at 135 C. The same is true of PET and nylon, which is the reason a polymer needs two transition temperatures rather than one.
Amorphous material softens over a range instead.
More mobility in the chain means less energy needed to unfreeze it.
The same repeat unit as LDPE, arranged differently.
Which is also how fibers are drawn to increase strength.

Vulcanization needs somewhere for the sulfur to attack. Polymerizing a diene 1,4 leaves a double bond in every repeat unit of polyisoprene, and the C-H bonds next to it are allylic and therefore weak - the same weakness that made allylic radicals easy to form in earlier chapters. A saturated hydrocarbon chain offers nothing comparable, so the double bond left over from the polymerization is not a leftover at all; it is the handle the whole process depends on.
Tg for the amorphous regions and Tm for the crystalline ones.
polymer-design: Put the double bond back into the repeat unit.
Cut the acyl C-O bond of each ester: OH to the acid side, H to the alcohol side.
Cut every amide C-N bond.
Every chain-forming monomer must have two, which is what let it join on both sides.
One water per ester bond, and a diacid-plus-diol repeat unit has two. PET: 166 + 62 - 192 = 36.
Rigid, straight chains that align along their whole length.
Amides are the least reactive acyl derivative.
Both lower Tg and prevent packing.
Crystalline regions scatter light at every boundary.
Three reactive sites gives a network.
They hydrolyze, and enzymes can reach them.
The honest version of the plastics problem rather than a failure of chemistry.
Thermoplastics only, and each cycle shortens the chains a little.
It needs a backbone bond that can be cleaved selectively.
Its ester bonds are a handle hydrolysis can select.
No bond hydrolysis can pick out from any other. Cracking it back to feedstock works, but that is pyrolysis, not selective cleavage.
The hardest case at end of life.
An ordinary metabolite, which is what makes it compostable.
Biodegradable is a claim about conditions as much as about structure.
One functional group is the whole difference.
Which is why mechanically recycled material degrades with reuse.
An amide is one too, though a more resistant one.
The backbone functional group is fixed by the monomer.
A polyester that hydrolyzes to a metabolite.
The properties that make it cheap and inert make it permanent.
That is the self-check that catches an error without knowing the compound.
The other three all improve with crystallinity.
PMMA through bulky side groups; polycarbonate through rigid bisphenol A units in the backbone.
A third reactive site lets chains tie to each other.

Two requirements have to be met at once. Clear means amorphous, which rules out HDPE whatever its melting point, because crystalline regions scatter light at every boundary. Rigid at 121 C means a Tg above 121 C, which rules out polystyrene - it would soften and distort at 100 C - and rules out plasticized PVC, whose plasticizer has already dropped its Tg below room temperature. Polycarbonate is amorphous because its bisphenol A backbone is too awkwardly shaped to crystallize, and that same rigid backbone puts its Tg near 150 C.
hydrates-cyanohydrins: Two OH groups end up on the one former carbonyl carbon.
The common name records where it came from, not its structure.
Only about 0.1%, since two methyls both crowd and feed the carbon.
One methyl instead of two puts it halfway between formaldehyde and acetone.
Its equilibrium sits essentially all the way over.
Three of them pulling makes the carbonyl carbon badly electron poor.
A flat carbon turns tetrahedral, and the substituents that sat 120 degrees apart are squeezed to about 109 — which is why crowding decides where the equilibrium sits.
Tetrahedral geometry, and groups that were comfortable at 120 no longer are.
Hydrogens have almost nothing to give up when the angle closes.
That donation stabilizes the starting material, so it has less reason to react.
Sterics and electronics point the same way, and the hydration table measures it.
The same pair sets every carbonyl reactivity order in the chapter.

Two species are doing two jobs. Cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon and leaves an alkoxide, and something has to hand that alkoxide a proton or it simply expels cyanide again and the equilibrium never closes. HCN is the proton source, and giving it up regenerates cyanide for the next turn, which is what makes the cyanide catalytic. HCN alone fails for the opposite reason: with its carbon holding a hydrogen instead of a lone pair, it is a poor nucleophile.

Three effects are in play and two of them are identical across the pair: both are ketones and both are conjugated with the same ring, so those cancel. What differs is the second substituent. A methyl donates weakly; a CF3 withdraws strongly through three C-F bonds, leaving the carbonyl carbon markedly more electron-poor and the hydrate correspondingly more favorable. CF3 is also the bulkier group, so this is a case where electronics beats sterics — the same reasoning that makes hexafluoroacetone essentially fully hydrated.
Attack at carbon, then protonation of the alkoxide.
One came from the old carbonyl oxygen, the other from cyanide.
Hydration and bisulfite addition build no new carbon skeleton.

Count the carbons in the target: one more than the ketone, and the new carbon is a carboxyl group sitting next to the old carbonyl carbon, which now holds an OH. That is a cyanohydrin whose nitrile has been hydrolyzed. Reduction would instead give a CH2NH2 and therefore an amino alcohol; a bisulfite adduct adds no carbon at all and just gives the ketone back; and hydration adds no carbon either.

CN- is the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl, and HCN is the acid that protonates the alkoxide that results. Too acidic and almost everything is HCN, with too little cyanide to start; too basic and there is no HCN left to finish the job, and the alkoxide simply expels cyanide again.
The nitrile becomes the acid and the OH is already in place.
The nitrile carbon becomes CH2NH2, one carbon away from the OH.
Losing the OH and an adjacent hydrogen conjugates the nitrile.
And that one carbon arrives with a functional group already on it.
Another one-carbon extension, chosen for what it leaves behind.
Same one-carbon logic, different functional group at the end.
Solid and water soluble, which is exactly what makes it handy.
Filter off the solid, then regenerate the carbonyl.
The same crowding that keeps hindered ketones from hydrating.
Reversibility is the point, since you want the carbonyl back.
Fluorine pulls like chlorine does in chloral.
aldehyde-oxidation: It is the one carbonyl in the chapter still able to climb a rung.

The tests in this section are diagnostics rather than preparations, so the practical answers are KMnO4, Jones reagent and Ag2O. Jones is the workhorse: it is aqueous, so the aldehyde hydrates and the oxidation runs on to the acid. PCC is deliberately anhydrous and stops at the aldehyde, borohydride reduces rather than oxidizes, and Tollens’ would technically work but nobody burns stoichiometric silver to make an ordinary acid.
The same hydrogen bookkeeping that ranked the alcohols.
A bare carbonyl carbon has no hydroxyl for an oxidant to grip.

Take the constraints one at a time. Hot permanganate cleaves the alkene, and Jones oxidizes the secondary alcohol to a ketone as well as taking the aldehyde up, so both are too indiscriminate. PCC is an alcohol oxidant that would also touch the secondary alcohol, and it is the wrong tool for the aldehyde in any case. Silver(I) is the mild option: it takes the aldehyde to the acid and ignores alkenes and alcohols, which is exactly why the expense is sometimes worth paying.
Anhydrous dichloromethane keeps the second oxidation from ever starting.
Water in the flask keeps regenerating the hydrate.
Held in solution by ammonia under basic conditions.
The diammine complex keeps silver soluble in base.
The solution is basic, so the acid is deprotonated as it forms.
Metallic silver plating out on clean glass.
The aldehyde is what gets oxidized, so silver has to go the other way.
A reagent that picks out one group and skips its neighbors.

A diagnostic reagent is built to be feeble and selective, so that a positive result means one specific thing — and feeble and selective is the opposite of what a preparation wants, where throughput and cost decide. Silver is consumed stoichiometrically, which settles the matter on its own. The basic conditions do give the carboxylate first, but that is undone by acidifying on workup, so it is not the real objection; and leaving alkenes alone is a virtue, not a fault.
Benedict's is the one built on citrate.
Through an enediol, which is why a free anomeric carbon rather than an aldehyde is the real test.
The red solid drops out of the blue solution that was there before.

A positive Tollens’ needs a carbon carrying both an oxygen and a hydrogen, so an aldehyde or something in equilibrium with one is present; a ketone and a non-reducing sugar are both ruled out by it. The negative Fehling’s then looks like a contradiction, and it is resolved by remembering that Fehling’s has a known blind spot: it is unreliable with aromatic aldehydes. Treating a negative result from a reagent with a known weakness as evidence of absence is the trap being set.
Citrate holds the copper better than tartrate does.
Aliphatic aldehydes are the case it handles well.
Opening exposes the aldehyde the ring drawing hides.
Delivered continuously, and consumed as fast as it appears.
The sugar is in fact the thing being oxidized.
The glycosidic bond ties up both anomeric carbons, and a free one is what a positive test needs.
One ring can still open and deliver an aldehyde.
No added reagent is needed at all.

Radical chains take whichever hydrogen leaves the most stable radical, and here that is the aldehyde C-H at roughly 88 kcal/mol — the weakest C-H in the molecule, because the acyl radical it leaves behind has its unpaired electron next to the carbonyl and delocalized onto it. Oxygen then adds to that acyl radical, and the resulting peroxy radical takes the same hydrogen from the next molecule, so the chain propagates. Acidity governs enolate chemistry, not radical abstraction, and a ketone has no such C-H at all.

The first step has to stop one rung short, which means anhydrous conditions: with no water there is no hydrate, and with no hydrate the second oxidation has nothing with an O-H to attack. PCC does that. The second step wants the opposite — aqueous Cr(VI), so the aldehyde hydrates and is oxidized again — which is Jones. Running them in the other order finishes the job before the aldehyde can be isolated, borohydride reduces rather than oxidizes, and Tollens’ is far too weak to touch an alcohol.
There is no hydrogen on that carbon to take.
An oxygen is inserted into one of the C-C bonds.
acyl-chlorides-anhydrides: Both leave as gases, so the equilibrium is pulled forward.
All three are gases, which is why workup is an evaporation.

Each acylation releases one HCl. The most basic species in the flask is the amine, so it takes that proton and becomes an anilinium ion with no lone pair left to attack. One equivalent of amine therefore supplies only half an equivalent of nucleophile. The fix is a second equivalent of aniline, or one equivalent plus pyridine - basic enough to mop up HCl, too weakly nucleophilic to compete for the carbonyl.

Acyl substitution swaps the leaving group and keeps the carbonyl: an alcohol gives the ester, an amine the amide, a carboxylate the anhydride. A secondary alcohol would need the carbonyl reduced AND one new carbon substituent added, which is not a substitution at all - it needs a hydride and an organometallic, and it is a different kind of step.
Gases escape as they form, driving the reaction to completion.
Acid-base transfer wins, leaving an ammonium carboxylate dead end.
Acidic enough that any good nucleophile takes the proton instead.
An alcohol, and unlike Fischer esterification the step is irreversible.
The carboxylate, not the neutral acid, is the nucleophile.

Trace the protons. The first equivalent of amine attacks the acyl chloride, chloride leaves, and the nitrogen still carries a proton it must lose - so one HCl is released per acylation. The most basic thing in the flask is the amine itself, so that HCl protonates a second molecule of amine and switches it off as a nucleophile. Two equivalents therefore give one equivalent of amide; one equivalent gives you half.
An ammonium ion has no lone pair left to attack with.
Basic enough to take up HCl without competing for the carbonyl.

Pyridine is a perfectly competent nucleophile toward an acid chloride: it attacks and gives an N-acylpyridinium ion. That is not a loss, because the acylpyridinium is itself a potent acylating agent — it hands the acyl group on to the amine, often faster than the direct route would. This is the whole basis of DMAP catalysis, where 4-dimethylaminopyridine speeds acylations up thousands of times by exactly this detour. And pyridine has no N–H, so unlike the amine it can never end up in the product. The sp² lone pair does explain pyridine's modest basicity (pKaH 5.2); it does not make pyridine a poor nucleophile.

Trace the tetrahedral intermediate: the nucleophile has added, and the oxygen now pushes back down and has to expel one of the two acyl-oxygen groups. What leaves is the other half of the anhydride, as a carboxylate. That anion is resonance-stabilized over two oxygens, so it departs willingly - but its conjugate acid is pKa about 5 against HCl's -7, which is exactly why an anhydride sits one rung below an acid chloride.
Tracks leaving-group ability: chloride beats carboxylate beats alkoxide.

Work down the ladder. Acetic acid needs activation before an amine or alcohol will acylate at all; ethyl acetate and acetonitrile are at or below the ester rung and far too sluggish. Acetic anhydride is the compromise: reactive enough to acylate an alcohol or an amine directly at room temperature, yet stable enough to weigh out in air, which an acetyl chloride is not.
That single acetylation converts salicylic acid into aspirin.
Half the anhydride leaves unused, which is the atom-economy cost.
One acyl group becomes product, the other becomes waste.
Water is expelled intramolecularly to close a five-membered ring.
Diacids that would need a larger ring do not cyclize this way.

The amine attacks one of the two carbonyls and the tetrahedral intermediate expels the other as a carboxylate - the ordinary anhydride reaction. The difference is that the carboxylate is tethered to the amide by the carbon chain, so it cannot wander off. What you isolate is an amic acid: an amide at one end, a carboxylic acid at the other, on one molecule. Heat that and it loses water and closes to the imide.
A second intramolecular condensation closes the ring again.
Two acyl groups share one nitrogen rather than one oxygen.
That cation is the electrophile the aromatic ring attacks.
The only reaction here that builds the skeleton rather than decorating it.
The ring cannot be acylated until the acid is activated; AlCl3 comes second.

Same reagent, same idea, different substrate. An alcohol's OH is a terrible leaving group; SOCl2 converts it into a chlorosulfite, which is an excellent one, and chloride then displaces it to give the alkyl chloride. On a carboxylic acid the sulfur does exactly the same thing to the carboxyl OH. In both cases the by-products are SO2 and HCl, both gases, so the reaction is pulled to completion.
A terrible leaving group is swapped for an excellent one.

Compare the leaving groups. Fischer esterification has to expel water and can re-form the acid just as easily, so it settles at an equilibrium near 65% and must be driven with excess alcohol or by removing water. Acylation of an alcohol by an acid chloride expels chloride, which is far too weak a base to come back and attack the ester, so the reaction runs to completion and needs no acid catalyst.
nitriles: Three bonds to heteroatom, all of them to the same nitrogen.
Also three carbon-heteroatom bonds, so interconversion needs no oxidant.

Count first: seven carbons in, nine out, so two have to be added and the product is a ketone. Cyanide adds one by SN2 on the primary benzylic bromide, giving PhCH2CN. A methyl Grignard then adds once to the nitrile carbon - it cannot add twice, because the intermediate is an imine anion rather than a carbonyl - and aqueous workup hydrolyzes that imine to the ketone, which is where the second carbon came from. Route 1 gives an amine, route 3 an acid, and route 4 adds only one carbon.

Count the bonds to heteroatoms on the carbon in question. A nitrile carbon has three, all to the same nitrogen; an amide carbon has three too - two to the carbonyl oxygen and one to nitrogen. Same count means same oxidation level, so adding water across the triple bond is a sideways move along the rung and needs no oxidant. Carry on under the same conditions and hydrolysis goes one step further to the acid, still on the same rung.
Cyanide displaces halide and the chain gains one carbon.
Backside attack, which is why primary substrates are required.

Two of these can be thrown out on the formula alone: butanamide is C4H9NO and but-1-yne is C4H6 with no nitrogen at all. That leaves two genuine C4H7N isomers, and only the spectrum separates them. C4H7N has two degrees of unsaturation, and both a C-N triple bond and a C=C plus a C=N account for exactly two, so counting does not settle it. The 2247 band does. The 2500-2000 window is almost empty in an ordinary spectrum, and a sharp medium band there means a triple bond - a nitrile, since the alkyne is already gone. The imine CH2=CHCH2CH=NH has nothing to put at 2247 and would instead show a C=N stretch near 1670, which the stem explicitly rules out by reporting nothing between 1650 and 1800. So the answer is butanenitrile, and notice that the negative evidence - an empty region - did as much work as the peak that is there.
Weakly basic conjugate base, so elimination is not promoted.

Start with what cannot happen: three alkyl groups shield the tertiary carbon, so there is no backside attack and no SN2, which takes the nitrile off the table however good a nucleophile cyanide is. DMSO then removes the other escape route — there is no water to solvolyze the halide, so no tertiary alcohol. That leaves elimination. Cyanide is a weak base (HCN pKa 9.2) and a poor one for E2, but with heat and nothing competing it is enough, and Zaitsev gives the more substituted alkene. Notice how much work the solvent is doing: run the same halide in hot aqueous ethanol and solvolysis takes over and you get mostly the alcohol — and still no nitrile. That is the standing limit on cyanide chain extension: primary substrates work, secondary are poor, tertiary give none of the nitrile at all.

Dehydration removes H2O from RCONH2, and the carbon ends up with three bonds to nitrogen instead of two to oxygen and one to nitrogen - the same count either way. So it is a move along the rung, not a reduction, which is why SOCl2 or P2O5 does it and no reducing agent is involved. Run it the other way with water and heat and the nitrile hydrates back to the amide.
Both strip water from the amide rather than changing oxidation level.
Addition to the carbonyl leaves an OH on the neighboring carbon.
CuCN replaces the nitrogen that leaves as N2.
So aryl nitriles come from a diazonium salt, or from dehydrating an aryl amide.
Through the amide, and no oxidant is needed because it is a move along the rung.

Water adds across the C-N triple bond to give first an imidic acid, which tautomerizes to the amide - and the amide is a real, isolable compound: stop at milder conditions and that is what you get. Push with more heat and more acid or base and the amide is hydrolyzed in turn to the carboxylic acid. Two acyl substitutions in series, both sideways moves on the same oxidation rung.
Stopping early exploits the amide being an intermediate, not a side product.
Two hydrides are delivered and the nitrogen stays attached.
The nitrile carbon becomes the CH2, so no carbon is gained or lost.
Workup hydrolyzes the intermediate rather than reducing it further.
It survives until water is added because nothing attacks it.

One hydride adds to the nitrile carbon and the product is a metalated imine anion. An anion is not an electrophile, so there is nothing left for a second hydride to attack, however long you wait or how much reagent you add - the aldehyde only appears when water hydrolyzes that anion on workup. Contrast LiAlH4, which is not stopped by anything: rationing it to one equivalent does not give an aldehyde, it gives a mixture. The reagent is crippled, not rationed.
The carbon-carbon bond forms before any carbonyl exists.
An imine salt is not an electrophile, so the reagent has nothing to attack.
That ketone is more electrophilic than the ester, so attack repeats.
Sharp and medium, in a region almost nothing else occupies.
Between 2500 and 2000 there is little else to confuse it with.

Follow the carbon. Cyanide does an SN2 on RX and the CN carbon is new, so RCN has one more carbon than RX. Hydrolysis then converts that same carbon into the COOH carbon without adding or losing any, since a nitrile and an acid sit on the same oxidation rung. Net result: one carbon longer, finishing as an acid. The Grignard-plus-CO2 route achieves the identical extension, and you pick between them on what else the substrate carries.
A Grignard would be destroyed by the acidic proton before reacting.
Any acidic proton quenches the organometallic reagent.
alpha-halogenation: Both the enol and the enolate are nucleophilic at that carbon.
Halogen is consumed only as fast as enol is made.
The halogen makes the carbonyl harder to protonate, so the second enol forms more slowly.
Enolization needs the oxygen protonated, and withdrawal makes that harder.
Halogen stabilizes the next enolate's charge, so each step speeds up the one after.
Acid generates the neutral tautomer, not the anion.
Base removes an alpha proton outright.
Three identical hydrogens on one carbon are required.
Every methyl hydrogen must be replaced before cleavage happens.
Three halogens stabilize the departing carbanion.
Hydroxide adds and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses.
Acidic workup then delivers the free acid.
Three carbons become two; the methyl leaves as CHI3.
The methyl group departs as the haloform itself.
Alkaline hypoiodite oxidizes it to a methyl ketone first.
It is the primary alcohol that oxidizes to acetaldehyde.
It is not a test for ketones as such.
The hydroxyl oxygen already donates into the carbonyl.
Red phosphorus serves as well, making PBr3 in situ.
That derivative enolizes where the acid will not.
Exchange with more starting acid releases it and carries the cycle on.
Ammonia displaces the alpha bromide by SN2.
Same SN2 displacement, different nucleophile.
Nothing in the sequence selects one face over the other.
Sitting next to the carbonyl lowers the barrier to displacement.
Loss of HX reaches the same enone the aldol condensation does.

The only alpha carbon carrying hydrogens is the methyl attached straight to the carbonyl, so base iodinates it three times and hydroxide then adds to the carbonyl and expels the CI3 group. What is left is the acyl fragment, (CH3)3C-CO2H. Count the carbons: six in, five out, because the haloform reaction always costs one.

Under acid the reaction runs through the enol, and the two enols are free to equilibrate, so the more stable of them - the more substituted one - is the one that reacts and it decides where the halogen lands. That is C2. It is the same more-substituted-is-more-stable logic used for thermodynamic enolates, arriving one section early.

A carboxylic acid has essentially no enol of its own, so direct halogenation fails in acid and in base alike. Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky makes the acyl bromide with PBr3 first; that enolizes, brominates at the alpha carbon, and exchanges back to give 2-bromobutanoic acid. Ammonia then displaces the bromide by SN2, in excess because the amino acid product is itself nucleophilic. The product is racemic.

The test reports a CH3CO fragment, or a CH3CH(OH) fragment that alkaline hypoiodite oxidizes into one. 3-Pentanol is CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3: its carbinol carbon carries two ethyl groups and no methyl, so oxidation gives 3-pentanone, which has no methyl on the carbonyl and can never form a CI3 to expel. The other three all carry the reported fragment.
enolate-regiochemistry: C2 is the crowded side; C6 has nothing on it.
The methyl group occupies what would be the second one.
The less substituted C=C, which is the kinetic choice.
The methyl already sits on a carbon of the new double bond.
Bulky, and strong enough to make deprotonation irreversible.
Reversible deprotonation lets the mixture settle on the stable enolate.
Against a ketone's 20, deprotonation goes to completion.
Two isopropyl groups do the discriminating; strength alone would not.
Statistics and access both point the same way.
Leftover ketone shuttles protons and equilibrates the two enolates.
Cold enough that nothing equilibrates once it has formed.

LDA's deprotonation does not reverse at any temperature, so warmth alone cannot undo it - that is the point of the question. A separate route is still open at room temperature, though: the diisopropylamine LDA generated can shuttle protons between the two enolates, which erodes the regiochemistry over time. An irreversible base, and a route still open.
Only a reversible first step lets the stable enolate accumulate.
It is the more stable one, and everything can revert to reach it.
The same ranking that makes Zaitsev products favored.
Leftover ketone or the amine the base generated will do it; NaH is irreversible and still thermodynamic.
Reversing it just moves a proton back onto the ketone.
A primary amine would stop at the imine instead.
The substituted alternative twists the nitrogen lone pair out of alignment.
The nitrogen lone pair pushes electron density out to that carbon.
No nucleophilic carbon is left and no base is present to restore one, so a second alkylation is impossible.
Alkylate the enamine first, then unmask the carbonyl.
That is exactly what limits which halides are usable.
Methyl and primary halides are the reliable ones.
The enolate acts as a base rather than as a nucleophile.
Enough SN2 to tempt you, enough E2 to hurt the yield.

LDA at -78 C with the ketone added to the base gives the kinetic enolate, formed at C6 - the open CH2 with two hydrogens. Nothing in the flask can equilibrate it, so C6 is still the nucleophilic carbon when CH3I arrives and the new methyl lands there. Under NaOEt in ethanol at room temperature the same two reagents give 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone instead.

Ethoxide's deprotonation reverses, so the two enolates interconvert and the population collects in the more stable one, the trisubstituted C1=C2 enolate. Alkylation therefore happens at C2, the carbon that already carries a methyl, giving the quaternary 2,2-dimethyl product. Ethoxide being too weak to deprotonate completely is not a problem here; it is the whole mechanism of thermodynamic control.

LDA's deprotonation never reverses, so that route really is shut. But forming the enolate also generated a full equivalent of diisopropylamine, which is a proton donor, and warming lets it carry a proton from one alpha carbon to the other. The cold in the recipe is there to stop the amine, not to stop the base.

The benzyl group has to land on C6, the unsubstituted carbon, which means the kinetic enolate: LDA, one equivalent, -78 C, with the ketone added to the base. NaOEt and NaH are both equilibrating conditions that leave a route open between the two enolates, so they alkylate at C2. Adding LDA dropwise to the ketone instead gets the base right and the technique wrong: dripping LDA into a flask of ketone leaves un-deprotonated ketone in solution, and free ketone shuttles protons between the two enolates until the more substituted one wins. The halide is fine either way, since benzylic halides are excellent SN2 partners for an enolate.
amine-synthesis: Each added alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen, so the product outruns the ammonia still in the flask.
Relative rates decide it, so adding less halide does not help; only a big excess of ammonia biases it.
There is nowhere further to alkylate, so one compound comes out.

Count first. 1-Bromobutane has four carbons and the target has five, so the route must ADD one. Azide and Gabriel both hand back exactly the skeleton you put in, so both would give butylamine, one carbon short, and excess ammonia has the same problem plus a mixture. Cyanide brings the extra carbon: 1-bromobutane plus NaCN gives pentanenitrile, and LiAlH4 turns the nitrile carbon into the CH2 bearing nitrogen.
The imide nitrogen's lone pair is also tied into both carbonyls.
Hot aqueous acid or base does the same job less gently.
The nitrogen leaves the imide carrying just one alkyl group.
The step is an SN2, so tertiary halides give only alkene, a secondary one gives poor yields with elimination alongside, and bromobenzene is an aryl halide, which does not do SN2 at all.
Nothing left after the displacement can attack more halide.
Both leave the nitrogen attached to the same carbon it displaced onto.
Only one alkyl group ever reaches that nitrogen.

LiAlH4 reduces the amide C=O all the way to CH2, so four carbons go in and four come out: butanamide gives butylamine. Br2/NaOH is the Hofmann rearrangement, which takes the same starting material to PROPYLamine by expelling the carbonyl carbon as CO2 - one substrate, one carbon's difference, decided entirely by the reagent.
Three carbons in, four out, because cyanide supplies one.
No leaving group is displaced, so the product amine has nothing to attack.
It survives the mildly acidic pH that imine formation wants.
The ketone is consumed before it has a chance to condense.
The attenuated hydride reagents were chosen to tolerate that range.
One carbonyl and one amine in decides the product.
Its lone pair is tied up in the carbonyl.
No carbon is lost, so the skeleton is unchanged.
Every SN2 route on a nitrogen surrogate stops at primary.
The carbonyl becomes CH2 and both alkyl groups stay on nitrogen.
The old carbonyl carbon leaves as CO2.
Four carbons in, three out.
That migration is what builds the isocyanate.
Its hydrolysis is where the carbon is lost in both.
It reaches the same isocyanate without bromine.

Azide displacement is an SN2: the nucleophile attacks the backside of the C-Br carbon and the configuration inverts. Reducing the azide to the amine never touches that carbon, so the inversion survives into the product. Note that the R/S letter may or may not flip with it - check the CIP priorities separately from the geometry. This control is a reason to pick azide over reductive amination, which builds the bond on a flat C=N and gives a racemic product.
That cuts most of the table before substitution level matters.
The nitrogen leaves the imide with a single substituent.
hofmann-elimination: Very strong bases make very poor leaving groups.
Nitrogen ends up quaternary and positively charged.
It carries no negative charge away, unlike R2N−.
The nitrogen was positive before it left and uncharged after.
Silver oxide and water together supply the hydroxide base.
That removes the competing nucleophile from solution.
One step and anti-periplanar, on an unusual substrate.
That is the opposite of the Zaitsev preference.
Bulk on the substrate shields the crowded beta carbon.

The nitrogen sits on C2, so the beta carbons are the two methyls on C2 and the CH2 of the ethyl group. Taking a hydrogen from a methyl gives 2-methylbut-1-ene, disubstituted; taking one from the CH2 gives 2-methylbut-2-ene, trisubstituted and more stable. Zaitsev would pick the trisubstituted one; Hofmann conditions do not, because the bulky trimethylammonium group shields the more substituted side.
Its bulk reaches only the least hindered beta hydrogen.
The C–H bond breaks well ahead of the C–N bond.
That is what shifts the transition state toward E1cb.
Alkyl groups destabilize a carbanion.

Each equivalent alkylates the lone pair in an SN2; the ammonium salt that results still has an N-H, which a base removes to hand back a neutral, more substituted amine that goes again. The count is the number of N-H hydrogens plus one, so a primary amine takes three.
The nitrogen stays on C2 and picks up three methyls.
The leaving group sits on C2.

This is a Cope elimination. The amine oxide's own oxygen removes the beta hydrogen through a flat five-membered transition state, so the C-H and the C-N that break must be on the SAME side - syn-periplanar, the opposite geometric requirement to E2. No hydroxide or other base is needed. The regiochemistry, though, comes out the same as Hofmann: the less substituted alkene, for the same steric reason.
Monosubstituted, and the less stable of the two choices.

Hofmann regiochemistry usually comes from two effects that agree: the bulky leaving group makes the hindered side hard to reach, and the positive nitrogen acidifies the beta hydrogens so the C-H breaks ahead of the C-N. Here one beta position is benzylic, its hydrogen is much more acidic, and removing it gives a conjugated alkene - so the acidity effect wins and the more substituted product forms. The real rule is the most acidic ACCESSIBLE beta hydrogen.
The neutral amine is the leaving group departing.

The nitrogen stays sp3 throughout - a quaternary ammonium nitrogen has four sigma bonds and is tetrahedral. The other three are genuine consequences of quaternization: what departs is now a neutral trialkylamine rather than R2N-, the positive charge acidifies the beta hydrogens and gives the transition state E1cb character, and the bulk of the N(CH3)3 group is what shields the more substituted beta carbon.
One methyl per N–H, plus one to quaternize.
It has no N–H, so only the quaternizing methyl is needed.
The first elimination only opens the ring.
One C–N bond survives the first elimination.
It answers the same question in minutes rather than weeks.
The class of the nitrogen came from the methyl count instead.

Two independent readings. One equivalent of CH3I means no N-H hydrogens at all, so the amine is tertiary. One round of elimination freeing the nitrogen means only one C-N bond held it to the fragment being degraded, so the nitrogen was not in a ring - a ring would take two rounds, because the first elimination only opens it.
Bulk on the leaving group alone can invert the regiochemistry.
